The Proem

The Romans had a word for the most that a man could do with his religion, and the word was devotio. A consul who judged the battle lost might have the pontifex dictate to him a formula, and then, with his head veiled and a spear beneath his feet, give himself and the legions across the field to the gods below and to the earth, and ride alone into the enemy line. Livy tells it of Decius Mus, at the foot of Vesuvius, in the year 340 before Christ, and tells also that the day was won. The word meant a life handed over to a power that was expected to accept it and to pay in victory. The Church borrowed it for piety, and kept the handing over.

The Breviary turned the handing over into a schedule. Its name means an abridgement. A liturgy that had grown past the reach of any one reader was cut down to a volume that could be carried on the road, and the priest was bound to say its hours wherever he happened to be, under pain of grave sin, every day until he died. It turned a creed into a habit performed alone at a fixed hour with no congregation to see it, and the habit held the faith in place while the councils argued. This book borrows the engine. A machine that has run for the better part of a thousand years need not be built again, and what it carries can be changed.

The adversary is a post before it is a person. Satan is a Hebrew noun, and the noun means one who stands against; the tradition spent two thousand years promoting the holder into a prince and then into the proprietor of a pit. The book restores the post. To keep the office is to stand in the road once a day in front of one of the claims that have walked beside you since you were small, and to ask by what right it goes on.

The motto on the opening page is the serpent’s sentence, Eritis sicut dii, ye shall be as gods, and the chapter that holds it has been read for so long as the record of a crime that it is hard to read as a record at all. The god says that on the day they eat they shall surely die. The serpent says that they shall not surely die, that their eyes will be opened, and that they will be as gods, knowing good and evil. They eat; their eyes are opened; the man lives on, by the genealogy’s count, for nine centuries and more. When the god speaks next he speaks in the plural, and says, “Behold, the man is become as one of us, to know good and evil.” That is the serpent’s third prediction, spoken by the one party who cannot be suspected of flattering it. The eviction follows, with its reason given, lest he put out his hand to the other tree and live for ever. Of the three parties the serpent alone is sentenced without being questioned. A reader who brought a magistrate’s habits to the chapter would find the serpent’s word confirmed at every point the text allows us to check, and would ask what the sentence was for.

A figure assembled from a courtier’s office, a handful of verses, a poem and a great many sermons is a fiction, and the fiction has outlived the theology that required it. What the engravers kept, long after the churches lost interest, was the posture, a rebel on the burning ground with his head up, whose dignity survives a defeat he has accepted without recanting. That posture belongs to anyone who has refused something and paid for it.

The prayer that Christians teach their children asks, in Matthew’s Greek and in Jerome’s Latin alike, that debts be forgiven, and a debt implies a creditor, a creditor a ledger, and a ledger some interval in which the sum has been growing without the debtor’s signature. A debt between persons can be paid, and once it is paid it ends. The Church made the creditor unpayable and moved the debt from what you did to what you are, so that an infant could be carried out of the world owing, and the plan of settlement was sold by the same office that held the note. Whoever has left a faith, or been left by one, knows the rest of the argument in the body already, in the dread that attends a pleasure which has done nobody any harm, in the shame that flares at a thought, in the hand that moves before the reason has been consulted.

God, the Church, Duty, the Nation, Humanity, the Family as a thing to be served and the Good each stand over you and ask for something, and each, asked what it gives back, answers with a larger claim. Put that question to whatever asks something of you.

The world is under no obligation to mean anything to the creature that asks it to, and the demand for a meaning, a justice, a reason in the thing that happened goes out into a universe that does not answer. People settle with that silence by the leap, or by the postponement, which sells the present to be redeemed in some later place and calls the sale hope. This book leaves the question open and takes its pleasure meanwhile, a clear gladness with no consolation in it.

Once the ledger is gone there remain a body, a table and a few people. Take pleasure on purpose and with attention, since a pleasure forbidden becomes an obsession and a pleasure allowed can be put down. Give kindness lavishly to those who have earned it, in the open, and withhold it from those who bill you for their helplessness. Love the few, since love spread over everyone is worth nothing to anyone, and hate what has earned it, to yourself at least. Answer an injury once and in full, and then be finished with it, because hatred with no act attached is a tenant that never leaves.

Each day of this book takes one passage, one council, one trial or one canon and examines it as a record; beside each runs a plate, many of the engravings cut by Gustave Doré for the Bible that a Catholic house at Tours printed in 1866, made to adorn the faith and set here as exhibits.

Burden, the first book, goes through the debts one at a time, what you were handed, by whom, and at what price, and reads each against the scripture that issued it. Refusal, the second, sets some of the load down, a demand declined on each of its days, in a form the hands can carry out. Assent, the third, says yes to the life that is left, the worst chapter of it included, because a yes with exceptions is a bargain.

The Roman devotio was struck once, on the worst day of a campaign, with the line already giving way. The one set out here is the opposite transaction, made in small pieces over a year, a rite a day, and what it takes back is a self, from those who held it, with their thumbprints still on it. No one is keeping accounts. At the end the pages hold their dates and their boxes, marked Kept or Refused.


How the Year Is Kept

Open to Day 1 on the morning you choose to begin. It starts when you do, one day to a page, and runs through the three books in order. The Pact page at the front holds the words of the pact. The year is 365 days, and it waits when you do. On the day after Day 365 read The Anniversary, and the year is kept. The reading takes about two minutes. The rite takes from a minute to an evening.

The six kinds

Blasphemy turns the creed against the faith that taught it, and is done in private. It is the only kind with degrees. Indulgence is a pleasure taken on purpose and with attention. Reckoning settles accounts, rewarding the deserving, collecting a debt, answering an injury and cutting off what drains you. Heresy goes against the pieties of the present day, the wellness, the positivity and the performed humility that are the old faith in new dress. Beauty is splendor for yourself, in the room, the body and the table. Mastery is will and ambition, a prize taken or a rival outdone.

The degrees

A blasphemy carries one to four pips, and the pips grow as the rite comes nearer to what the faith holds most sacred. At the first degree you speak or write. At the second you break a custom of the faith in your own conduct. At the third you handle its texts and songs. At the fourth you handle its signs. The degrees are only a measure of the dare.

Kept and Refused

A rite is an offer. You may do it, or you may refuse it, and the refusal is a finished act with the same standing as the deed. A day left undone waits, and nothing is owed on it. Take the day you are on. The book charges for no absence.

A page of the year

Each page of the year runs in this order.

Numeral and title: the day in Roman figures, then its subject.

The kind of day and, on blasphemies, its degree in pips. The count of the year follows.

The charge, one sentence to carry through the day.

The reading and its plate. The small numbers mark sources.

The rite. Where it is written against a faith, the label names the tradition it answers.

The testament, a question put to you. The book leaves no space for the answer.

The sources, gathered at the foot.

The faith you left

On 223 days the rite is the same for every reader. On the other 142 it is written against a particular faith, because a rite means most when it is aimed at what you were taught. On those days the page prints one version, and the label names the tradition it answers: Christian, Protestant or no faith. At the back of the book, The Other Rites gives, by day, the version for each tradition (Catholic, Protestant, Orthodox, Latter-day Saint, Jehovah’s Witness, Jewish and Muslim) and the version for a reader raised in no faith or in a tradition not named. Find the day, read your own rite and keep that one.

The feasts

The numbered days follow no calendar. The feasts do. There are fifty-five, among them Walpurgis Night, All Hallows’ Eve, the solstices and equinoxes, the movable feasts of the churches and your own birthday, which is the highest of them. They stand together after Day 365, each headed with the date it falls on and the people who keep it. A feast takes the place of the numbered day on its date. Keeping it counts as keeping that day, and the day it displaced is held over to be read later.

The limits

Every rite stays inside the law and does no harm to a body, a child or an animal. No rite asks for a threat, a lie about a real person, the exposure of anyone’s private business, or damage to what is not yours. None is to be done in front of believers to provoke them, or put online. A rite that calls for drink is kept as fully with water, and on fourteen days a sober version stands at the back of the book. These limits govern every rite in the book.


The Black Breviary

The Pact

I, the undersigned, of sound mind and my own master, renounce every god and every teaching that was offered to me, every debt they claimed, every fear they taught me and the authority of everyone who spoke in their name. I answer to myself, whatever hope others hold for me. I expect no rescue, and I make the meaning I live by. I take my soul into my own keeping from this hour until my death, which ends the matter. I keep this pact for as long as it serves me and no longer. I sign freely, by my own leave.

The days that move

The Church Year is reckoned from the Western Easter. The Orthodox keep Palm Sunday, Good Friday, the Ascension and Pentecost at the same distances from their own. The Jewish and Islamic days begin at sundown on the evening before the date given, and the Islamic dates are calculated, so a community that waits on the moon may keep them a day later. A day that falls twice in a calendar year is shown twice.

Book I

Burden

Days 1 to 121

The year opens with an inventory, since no one can set a weight down before learning what it is, who loaded it, and what was promised for the carrying.

Eritis sicut dii

Ye shall be as gods

Genesis 3:5


I Of Waking

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 1 of 365

Be on your feet before you feel ready.

The Fallen Rouse ThemselvesGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book I, 1866

When the seventy came back to Jesus rejoicing that even the devils were subject to them through his name[1], he answered that he had beheld Satan fall like lightning from heaven[2]. Then he forbade them to rejoice that the spirits obeyed them and told them to rejoice that their names were written in heaven[3], so that a report of their own power was traded, inside three verses, for an entry in someone else’s book. That book’s keeper had told Moses that he blots out of it whoever sins against him[4].

On the plate above, the fallen lie in armor across one another among spears planted upright where they dropped, and on the crown of the rise one figure stands clear of them, his spear lifted in one hand and the other arm flung up, calling the rest to stand. Apostates know that field. The leaving was quick, and what followed was a long time lying down, while the old fear kept its appointed hours and a prayer would start on the tongue before the mind could stop it. Those hours on the ground were concussion, and no apology is owed for them.

The figure on the rise has no better reason to stand than the bodies around him. He gets up because getting up is the last act left in his power, and he calls it aloud to the field, a voice raised from the ground to the ground, asking nothing of heaven, and around him the field is rising. A name entered in someone else’s book is held on the keeper’s terms, and the figure on the rise has no entry anywhere, only his own voice and the spear he fell with.

Declaration: I got up on my own word, and the god who keeps a book of names may strike mine out at his leisure.

The Rite · Christian

Stand up and say the opening of the Lord’s Prayer with yourself in the Father’s place, and stop before the asking begins. My name be hallowed. My will be done, on earth, by me.

Testament · Which of the old words still start before you have chosen them, and in whose voice?

Sources

[1] Luke 10:17

[2] Luke 10:18

[3] Luke 10:20

[4] Exod 32:33


II Of Light

Beauty

Day 2 of 365

Let no second opinion sit above your own.

The Creation of LightGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Light is made on the first day of Genesis and the sun on the fourth[1]. The order troubled an early church teacher, who could not see how anyone of sense would take three evenings and mornings without a sun for history[2]. The god speaks the light into being and judges it good[3] before anyone exists to agree, the first verdict in scripture, and he goes on passing it on his own work every day except the second, which the text leaves without praise[4], until on the sixth he surveys the whole and calls it very good[5].

Whoever goes on making things after leaving a god is left in the god’s position, alone with the work. A child taught that every act is watched learns to finish a piece of work and hold still for the grade, and grows into an adult who shows finished work to five friends before deciding whether it is any good. Others can say whether it pleases them. Whether it came out as its maker meant is a question for the maker alone, and the answer needs light, since much of what people make is first seen badly, under a ceiling bulb or on a cracked screen, and condemned on that evidence.

Light finds the grain before it finds the flaw, and work held to a window gives back the varnish gone to amber and the line that went where it was sent. The church reserved the first verdict in Genesis for the single maker nobody could audit, and of everything in that chapter it is the thing most worth stealing, since the theft costs one lamp and one word said aloud by the hand that made the work.

Declaration: The doctrine that sends the credit for every good thing upward will find my name on mine.

The Rite

Choose the best thing you have made, set it where the eye of anyone entering lands first, and light it as a gallery would. Sign it large in ink, on it or on a card beside it, and pass your verdict aloud. Good.

Testament · What have you made that you have never let yourself call good, and what stopped you?

Sources

[1] Gen 1:3–5, 14–19

[2] Origen, Princ. 4.3.1

[3] Gen 1:4

[4] Gen 1:6–8

[5] Gen 1:31


III Of Falling

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 3 of 365

Refuse every word that says you were dropped.

The Rebel Angels Hurled from HeavenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book I, 1866

The Greek root of apostasy means to stand away, a word that keeps the leaver upright, and the King James translators, meeting it in a prophecy of the last days, rendered it a falling away[1]. The rest of the churches’ vocabulary for leaving runs downhill with it. A Christian who sacrificed to the gods under the emperor Decius[2] was counted among the lapsed, the ones who slipped, as though the act had been an accident of the feet, and Cyprian of Carthage wrote a treatise on them and priced their return in penance. The letter to the Hebrews declares it impossible to bring anyone who falls away back to repentance[3]. Fallen from grace is Paul’s phrase[4], aimed at Galatians who were adding circumcision and the law to their faith, and the pulpit has since turned it on people who walk out.

Each of these words moves the body by a force outside its control, the way a stone moves when the hand opens, and each carries a verdict with it, that the one who left was dropped or tripped and should be ashamed of the bruise. A slip asks for a hand up, and the hand belongs to the priest. Backsliding, the King James word for Israel[5] in the prophets, breaks the pattern, because in Hosea it describes a heifer, a backsliding heifer[6], where the Hebrew calls her stubborn.

Keep the heifer and refuse the rest. Hosea meant her as an insult and the King James translators made a backslider of her, and still she is the one leaver in that whole vocabulary drawn from life, a heifer with all four feet planted against the goad.

Declaration: Lapsed is the church’s word for a door it could not keep shut, and I went through it upright.

The Rite · Christian

Recite the Apostles’ Creed as far as he descended into hell, then stop and name your own going in a plain past tense. He descended. I walked out.

Testament · What word did they give your leaving, and what did it ask you to feel?

Sources

[1] 2 Thess 2:3

[2] Cyprian, De lapsis 8

[3] Heb 6:4–6

[4] Gal 5:2–4

[5] Jer 3:6–12

[6] Hos 4:16


IV Of Flesh

Indulgence

Day 4 of 365

Ask no one’s leave to linger.

The Creation of EveGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The second chapter of Genesis makes the man first and alone, finds his solitude not good[1], and parades the beasts before him to be named, and among them no helper is found[2]. The god puts him into a deep sleep, takes a rib, closes up the flesh in its place and builds a woman from the bone[3], so that the first surgery in scripture is performed under anesthetic, after the cattle had been tried.

The chapter closes on the two of them naked and unashamed[4]. Shame arrives in the next, and so does rank, in the sentence passed on her that her husband shall rule over her[5]. The keepers then moved rank back a chapter. A letter under Paul’s name forbids a woman to teach or hold authority over a man because Adam was formed first[6], and a saying of the Prophet in Bukhari holds that woman was made from a rib, crooked at the top, and will break if a man tries to straighten her[7]. Order of manufacture became order of rank, and Paul, in a letter no one disputes, ranked the flesh last, beating his body and leading it about like a slave[8].

Those raised under the later chapters learned to take their pleasures standing, and twenty years after the last prayer some still eat at the counter and feel accused by any comfort that outlasts its use. Genesis leaves the two bodies in the garden with nothing on and nothing ranked until the eating, and every keeper of the text since has been at work on the fig leaf[9].

Declaration: Shame came in with the third chapter, and I keep the body of the second.

The Rite

Take an hour naked in bed, alone or with a willing lover, on clean sheets, with warm oil in reach and no clock in the room. Let the body set the pace, and stop only when it is finished.

Testament · Which pleasure of the body do you still hurry through as if someone were timing you?

V Of Favor

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 5 of 365

Stop auditioning for judges who never published their rules.

Cain and Abel Offer Their SacrificesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Cain and Abel bring the first offerings in scripture, gifts from their own work, the farmer some of the fruit of the ground and the herdsman the firstborn of his flock with their fat[1]. The god looks with favor on the herdsman and his gift and turns from the farmer and his[2]. Genesis gives no reason. When the god speaks to Cain’s fallen face he says that whoever does well is accepted[3] and that sin crouches at the door, and never what doing well would have been. Favor that comes and goes without a reason teaches whoever lives under it to audition, since a written rule can be met once and left alone, while a secret rule can only be guessed at.

Readers have been supplying the reason ever since, and each reason shields the judge. The letter to the Hebrews says Abel offered by faith[4], the first letter of John that Cain’s works were evil[5], and some of the rabbis that he brought the poorest of his crop[6]. The Quran, which tells the story without naming either brother, has the favored son say that the god accepts only from those who fear him[7]. All of it was found after the verdict, to make the verdict look earned.

The grown children of such a house hand their work to a boss or a lover the way it was once handed to a parent, and read the reply off a face, since no other copy of the rule was ever issued to them.

What the farmer grew was his before the altar and stayed his after the refusal, and the best of it belongs at his own table, eaten slowly, by the man who broke the ground.

Declaration: I bring no second offering to a judge who never said what was wrong with the first.

The Rite · Christian

Take back one thing you were about to offer for someone’s verdict, a message or a favor or a finished page, and keep it. Then say the master’s words from the parable of the talents to yourself. Well done. You are nobody’s servant.

Testament · Whose approval are you still working for without ever having been told what would earn it?

Sources

[2] Gen 4:4–5

[3] Gen 4:6–7

[4] Heb 11:4

[6] Rashi on Gen 4:3

[7] Quran 5:27


VI Of Envy

Reckoning

Day 6 of 365

Take the equal of whatever your envy names.

Cain Slays AbelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Hebrew of Genesis leaves Cain’s words to his brother blank. The verse records that he spoke to Abel, gives no words[1], and then has him rise up against Abel in the field and kill him. The Greek translators at Alexandria supplied an invitation, let us go out to the plain[2], and later readers supplied the quarrel. The letter the church at Rome sent to Corinth near the end of the first century set the murder down to jealousy and envy[3], and in Genesis Rabbah the brothers divide the world, one taking the land and the other the movable goods, and fall out over the division or over a twin sister born with Abel[4].

Envy took the blame because it is the appetite that threatens those who already have. It names something another person holds and reports that you want it, and a report that names its object is information. The tenth commandment forbids the feeling while keeping an inventory as exact as the feeling’s own, the neighbor’s house, his wife, his servants, his ox and his donkey[5], and the people it protected were the ones who already owned them.

Given a road, envy is ambition. Cain built the first city in Genesis and named it for his son, and the same chapter traces to his line the father of all who play lyre and pipe and the first forger of bronze and iron[6]. The favored brother left no child, only a voice of blood crying from the ground[7]. Scripture’s own genealogy hands the arts to the envious line, and the envy you were taught to confess is the oldest tool in the forge.

Declaration: I confess no envy, since my envy has always known what I want and the priest never has.

The Rite

Name aloud the person you envy and the one thing of theirs you want. Then make today one finished piece of the work that won it for them, a page or a drawing or a working sample, made to beat theirs, and sign it.

Testament · Whose life do you watch most closely, and what exactly do they have that you want?

Sources

[2] Gen 4:8 LXX

[3] 1 Clem. 4:7

[4] Gen. Rab. 22:7

VII Of the Flood

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 7 of 365

Answer the one who did it, and no one else.

The World Is Destroyed by WaterGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

By the count of Genesis, everything on dry land with the breath of life in its nostrils died, and eight people lived[1]. The text passes over the infants, who must have been held up toward the last rocks by their mothers until the arms gave out, and the beasts go under with them on the word of a god who said, before the rain began, that he was sorry he had made them[2]. The Quran makes the prophet a party to the severity. In the sura that bears his name, Noah asks his lord to leave not one of the unbelievers alive on the earth[3], and gives among his reasons that any children they bore would grow up wicked and ungrateful too[4].

A justice that holds a whole species liable for the conduct of some of its adults has stopped distinguishing, and the law the same god later gave Israel’s judges forbids it, since fathers are not to die for their children nor children for their fathers[5]. In the commandments he kept for himself the right to charge a father’s sin to his great-grandchildren[6]. The flood is admired anyway and its survivor called righteous[7], because of who opened the windows of heaven. The same act by a king would be entered under a plainer name.

Leavers write off a whole faith’s worth of neighbors for what one deacon did, and the congregation, asked about the deacon, answers that every church has sinners. Either way the water falls on the many while the man who acted stays dry. A grudge spread across a crowd costs him nothing, since no one in the crowd can pay it, and he goes on passing the collection plate on Sunday with his name on no one’s list.

Declaration: I hold one man to account for one man’s deed, and I leave the drowning of crowds to the god who invented it.

The Rite · No faith

Run a long bath and read the chapters of the flood in it, then tell the god who drowned the world what you think of his justice. Judge the one, not the many. Pull the plug and watch his weapon go down the drain.

Testament · Whom have you been blaming in bulk, and which single name belongs at the top of the bill?

VIII Of Nakedness

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 8 of 365

Hand back every shame that was never yours.

Noah Curses Ham and CanaanGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Noah plants a vineyard and lies drunk and uncovered in his tent[1]. Ham sees him there and goes out to tell his brothers, and the brothers come in backward with a garment on their shoulders and cover their father without looking at him[2]. When Noah wakes and learns what was done, he curses Ham’s son Canaan instead[3]. Two rabbis in the Talmud disagreed on whether Ham castrated his father or raped him[4], and each read a deed into the verse that says Noah knew what his younger son had done to him, in a chapter that shows Ham only looking. Christian preachers kept the sentence and lost the grandson, so that by the nineteenth century the curse of Ham was being read from American pulpits as a title deed to African slaves, and the Latter-day Saints barred men of African descent from their priesthood until nineteen seventy-eight[5] on reasoning drawn in part from the same lineage[6].

Shame falls on whoever was in the room and travels down, and a family keeps its patriarch’s dignity by spending its children’s. A child who found a parent drunk on the floor, or heard what should have stayed behind a door, learns that seeing was the crime, and spends years walking backward with a cloak, covering for the people who did the thing.

Guilt belongs to whoever did a specific harm, and it is settled in private, by changing course. Shame carried for another person’s act has no course to change, and in Genesis the one who passed it down was Noah, to a grandson who was not in the tent.

Declaration: I side with the son who saw his father naked and told his brothers, and what I saw in my own house I will tell.

The Rite · Christian

Walk backward into a room with a coat on your shoulders, as two of Noah’s sons did. Let it fall, turn, name the one whose act you covered, and refuse them the forgiveness the Lord’s Prayer demands. I see it. No pardon.

Testament · Whose act are you still covering for, and what has the covering cost you?

Sources

[1] Gen 9:20–21

[2] Gen 9:22–23

[3] Gen 9:24–25

[4] b. Sanhedrin 70a

[5] D&C Official Declaration 2

[6] Abr 1:21–27


IX Of the Vineyard

Indulgence

Day 9 of 365

After a ruin, feed yourself before any god.

A Dove Is Sent Forth from the ArkGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

An olive leaf is the first green thing in Genesis after the water. The raven Noah sent out went to and fro until the waters dried[1] and brought nothing back. The dove came back once with nowhere to set her foot, and the second time she returned in the evening with the leaf in her beak[2], and a man shut in a box with the animals of the whole earth learned that something had begun to grow. The leaf came off a tree men plant for its oil and wait years to harvest, and Noah read it as a farmer would.

His first act on dry ground was an altar, with some of every clean animal and bird burned on it[3], and the god smelled the smoke and resolved to curse the ground no more for man’s sake, since the heart of man is evil from his youth[4], the reason he had given for the flood[5], now offered as the reason for mercy. His second act was a vineyard. Genesis calls him a man of the soil[6] and passes from the planting to the cup with no harvest between, and he drank of the wine[7], and the chapter has no reproach for the drinking.

After a ruin, a mind trained by priests looks first for an altar, and the newly faithless are offered altars in quantity, a cause or a guru with a diet, each wanting its burned offering. The smoke of the altar bought a truce on the drowner’s terms, a promise that he would hold his hand. The vineyard bought Noah his drink and a long sleep in his tent, and of the two offerings made on dry ground it is the only one that reached a living mouth.

Declaration: I leave the god the smell of burnt meat and keep the wine for myself.

The Rite

Buy the best bottle of wine you can afford, from a vineyard you can name, and drink it slowly over a meal of an hour or two until you are warm and loose. Then lie down and rest.

Testament · What pleasure are you still waiting to deserve before you taste it?

X Of Calling

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 10 of 365

Make every summons show its wages first.

Abraham Goes to the Land of CanaanGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Abraham was seventy-five when he left Haran[1] with his household and his flocks, bound for a country his god had promised to show him when he got there.

He was to give up his country, his kindred and his father’s house, and in exchange he would become a great nation with a great name, and whoever blessed him would be blessed[2]. His servant would credit the god with his flocks and silver[3], part of it paid by two kings for his wife[4], but what Abraham held in the land at the end of a hundred years of obedience[5] was a field with a cave at its end, bought from a Hittite to bury his wife in[6], so that the only ground Genesis shows him buying was a grave he paid for. Stephen in Acts says the god gave him none of it to inherit, not a foot’s length[7].

Vocation is Latin for a calling, and canon law lays on the whole Christian community the duty of encouraging vocations[8] so that the sacred ministry is supplied. The missionary call and the summons to ministry share one shape, and each asks for the present and pays in a country nobody has seen. A call is a plan for your life drawn up by someone else and offered as adventure, because adventure is what the young will leave home for.

Test every call by asking who profits if you answer it. The employer who calls the job a mission and the family that decided before you were born what you were for fail that test together. A summons worth obeying pays the one who obeys, now, in coin they can see, and a summons that pays in promises is employment without wages, a post anyone can resign today, on no notice at all.

Declaration: Every voice that called me to a mission was hiring, and I hold the unpaid invoice for those years.

The Rite · Christian

Say aloud the answer the boy Samuel gave the voice that called him, Speak, for thy servant heareth, then answer again as no one’s servant. Speak, and I will decide whether it pays me.

Testament · Which plan for your life was drawn up by someone else, and who stood to gain if you followed it?

XI Of Towers

Mastery

Day 11 of 365

Sign the work before the first wall goes up.

The Tower of BabelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The builders of Babel settle the materials first, bricks burned hard and bitumen for mortar[1], and then the plan, a city on the plain of Shinar with a tower whose top is in the heavens. They give two reasons, to make themselves a name and to keep from being scattered over the earth[2].

The god comes down to see it[3], and his speech on seeing it gives his reason. They are one people with one language, he says, this is only what they have begun to do, and now nothing they plan will be beyond them[4]. So he confuses their speech and scatters them, and they leave off building the city[5]. In the next chapter he promises Abram a great name[6] for leaving his country.

Babylon raised its tower anyway. Its kings built the stepped temple they called the house of the foundation of heaven and earth[7], and Nebuchadnezzar set up a stone recording that he raised its top to heaven[8], in the city where he held the king of Judah and his household captive[9].

The pulpit preached Babel as a warning against pride[10], and the god’s own speech records a different fault, that the builders were about to succeed. What he feared was the success. The story closes by giving the city the one name it has, Babel, from the Hebrew for confuse, and the builders who wanted a name for themselves got that one. A builder who takes the sermon to heart stops at the first course, with the bitumen still warm in the pot.

Declaration: The god’s fear at Babel is the best review my work will ever get, and I build to earn it.

The Rite

Put your signature today on the thing you mean to build, by registering the company, buying the web address, or signing and dating its first page where you will see it.

Testament · What would you start building if no one could scatter you?

XII Of Sodom

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 12 of 365

Turn round and judge the city you left.

Lot Flees as Sodom and Gomorrah BurnGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Righteous is the word the second letter of Peter uses for Lot, a man worn down by lawlessness[1]. When the men of the city surrounded his house and demanded the two strangers he was sheltering, he went out, shut the door behind him, and offered them his two virgin daughters instead, to do with as they pleased[2]. The Quran has Lot tell the mob that his daughters are purer for them[3], and no verse reproaches him.

At dawn the angels took him by the hand[4], with his wife and daughters, and one gave the order not to look back. His wife looked back from behind him and became a pillar of salt[5]. She is the one person in the story punished for something she did with her eyes, and what she saw was a burning city that still held the sons-in-law who had taken the warning for a joke and stayed[6].

Her keepers wanted her seen. The Wisdom of Solomon calls the pillar a monument to an unbelieving soul[7], the first letter of Clement says she remains to this day as a warning to the double-minded[8], and Josephus claims to have seen her himself[9]. Jesus told his followers to remember her[10]. A salt figure by the road exists to stop the next traveler turning his head.

Genesis gives one reason for the whole order, lest they be consumed, and a glance could neither spread the fire nor put it out, and the one thing the glance endangered was the judgment of whoever turned and counted the sons-in-law in the smoke. The god spared the man at the door and salted the woman who looked, and Peter and Clement kept that ranking. Lot’s wife saw the city entire before she died, and her righteous husband, walking ahead, saw only the road to Zoar[11].

Declaration: Heaven called the man who offered his daughters to a mob righteous, and I would rather stand by the road in salt.

The Rite · Christian

Open your own Bible at the verse where Jesus says to remember Lot’s wife, pour a heap of salt on the page, and grind it in with your thumb until the paper tears. I remember her, and I look back.

Testament · Which part of the faith you left have you never let yourself examine up close?

XIII Of the Table

Indulgence

Day 13 of 365

Bring an appetite to the table, as the god did.

Abraham and the Three AngelsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Three men stood near Abraham’s tent at Mamre while he sat in the door at the hottest hour, and he ran to meet them and bowed to the ground[1]. He had water brought for their feet, told Sarah to knead cakes from three measures of fine flour[2], ran to the herd himself for a calf tender and good, and set it before them with curds and milk. Then he stood by them under the tree, and they ate[3].

Genesis has already said who was eating. The chapter opens with the Lord appearing at Mamre[4], and before it ends one of the three is speaking as the Lord[5], and Abraham stands before him to bargain over Sodom[6]. So the one dinner the god of Genesis is ever served is veal set down with curds and milk, at the table of the man his people call their father.

The keepers could not leave it there. The Talmud decided the visitors only appeared to eat[7], and the Quran tells it with a roasted calf the guests never reach for[8], so that Abraham grows afraid of them. The law forbade seething a kid in its mother’s milk, three times over[9], and the rabbis built on that verse the separate dishes and the hours of waiting[10] between a steak and a cup of coffee with cream. The patriarch’s menu became a crime in his descendants’ kitchens.

Genesis closes the verse on a single Hebrew word, they ate, and puts the god’s appetite on record a whole book before the law about the kid and its mother. Whoever sets meat beside cream for a guest worth feeding keeps the god’s one table in Genesis, and the rule that came after has the god’s own supper to argue with.

Declaration: What the god joined at Mamre, meat and milk, I let no rabbi put asunder.

The Rite

Lay the best meat you can afford beside a good cheese or a bowl of cream, and share it with one person you choose. Give them the first piece, then eat your fill.

Testament · Which food did you learn to refuse that your teachers’ own scripture serves without shame?

XIV Of Hope

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 14 of 365

Collect now, and let heaven wait.

The Approach to the GateGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto III, 1861

The schools asked whether the blessed in heaven have hope, and answered that they have none, since the blessed hold what they hoped for[1] and no one hopes for what is already in hand. The damned came next, and the answer was no again, because the damned know their sentence will never change, and the lack of hope is part of it[2]. Hope, the schoolmen determined, belongs to wayfarers[3], to whoever is still on the road.

So the Church counts among its three theological virtues[4] one that is worth nothing at either destination and is left behind whichever way the last door opens. All its work is done in transit. On the road it keeps the traveler walking toward a place he cannot see and paying the tolls in the only coin he carries, which is his days.

The church, the synagogue, the mosque and the Kingdom Hall sell it on the same terms, the treasure laid up in heaven[5], the messiah who will come though he tarry[6], the gardens beneath which rivers flow[7], the earth made a paradise once Armageddon has cleared it. Each edition takes the present as its price, paid in patience and obedience, and the messiah has kept his buyers waiting for twenty centuries.

Refuse the terms and the present comes back into your hands with everything that was being kept for later, the trip put off until there is time, the silk folded away for a better day. Silk worn on an ordinary Tuesday is a day the tollgate did not get.

Declaration: Every hope I was sold was payable later, so I canceled the order and spent the deposit.

The Rite · Christian

Read aloud the apostle’s rule that a hope which is seen is no hope, then take out the thing you were saving for someday, the scent or the silk or the good pen, and use it today. Seen, and mine.

Testament · Which pleasure have you put away for a day that has no date?

XV Of Blessing

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 15 of 365

Refuse any blessing that comes with an office attached.

Isaac Blesses JacobGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The theft of the blessing was Rebekah’s plan before it was Jacob’s. Isaac, who was old and could not see, had called for his elder son Esau and asked for a dish of game so that he could bless him before he died[1], and she overheard. While Esau was out hunting she cooked two young goats the way the old man liked them and dressed Jacob in his brother’s clothes, with goatskins over his hands and the smooth of his neck[2]. Isaac noticed that the hands and the voice did not match[3], asked again, took the lie for an answer[4], and blessed him, with the dew of heaven and the fat of the earth and lordship over his brothers[5].

When Esau came in with the real dish, Isaac trembled violently and said the blessing was given and would stand[6]. Words spoken over a head had done their work whoever the head belonged to, and the line of promise ran from then on through the son who lied.

The priesthoods took the form for their own mouths. The blessing in the book of Numbers went to the sons of Aaron[7], absolution went to the ordained[8], and the catechism leaves the laity only the lesser blessings[9], ranked by their distance from the altar, below a form a blind old man once handed out for a plate of goat.

Whatever force a blessing has, it had in a tent with no priest in it, in the mouth of a father fooled by goatskin. The men who fenced the form behind ordination were guarding a sentence that had already done its work once for a thief, and ordination has added nothing to it since but the fence.

Declaration: Isaac’s words held over a liar in goatskin, and they hold over me in my own coat.

The Rite · Christian

Lay your right hand on your own head, as the dying Jacob laid his on Joseph’s younger son, and bless yourself in Isaac’s words. The dew of heaven and the fat of the earth are mine, and I will rule my rivals.

Testament · What would you wish for yourself if you pronounced it over your own head?

XVI Of Exile

Reckoning

Day 16 of 365

Build where they sent you.

Abraham Sends Hagar and Ishmael AwayGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Abraham rose early, took bread and a skin of water, put them on Hagar’s shoulder along with the boy, and sent her away. It was Sarah’s demand. She had seen Ishmael, the slave woman’s son, laughing at the feast for Isaac’s weaning, and told her husband to throw both of them out so that no son of a slave would share the inheritance[1]. Abraham was displeased, and the god told him to do as his wife said[2].

The water ran out in the wilderness of Beersheba. Hagar laid the child under a bush and went and sat a bowshot off, so as not to see him die[3], and wept. The well that saved them was found in the wilderness, when the god opened her eyes to it[4], and Genesis records no one from Abraham’s tent coming to look for either of them.

The boy grew up in the wilderness of Paran and became an archer[5], and his mother took him a wife out of Egypt. Later Abraham did it again, giving all he had to Isaac and sending the sons of his concubines away eastward with gifts[6], so that the house kept its single heir and the east country had them.

A house that never came looking gave up the right to call anyone back. Any contact you allow is a favor on your terms, and it ends the first time it is used to summon you home. Genesis brings Ishmael back once, to stand with Isaac at the cave of Machpelah[7] and bury their father, and then counts his line, twelve princes by their towns and encampments[8], settled from Havilah to Shur[9].

Declaration: What I raise in the wilderness they drove me into is mine, and the house that put me out has no share in it.

The Rite

Name the return the people who cast you out still expect, the visit home or the standing call, and refuse it today in one sentence with no reason given. I will not be coming. Spend those hours on the life you built without them.

Testament · What have you built since the door closed behind you?

XVII Of the Ladder

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 17 of 365

Hold heaven to the terms you once offered it.

Jacob’s DreamGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jacob sleeps on the road with a stone under his head and dreams of a stair from earth to heaven, angels going up and down it[1], and the god above promising him the ground he lay on[2]. He wakes afraid, pours oil on the stone[3], and names terms of his own. If the god stays with him, feeds and clothes him and brings him back to his father’s house in peace, then the Lord shall be his god, and a tenth will go back[4].

After twenty years away Genesis brings him safe to the city of Shechem[5], with a word from the root of the peace he had asked for, and in the next chapter his daughter Dinah is seized there[6] and his sons answer with a massacre that makes him, he complains, a stench to the Canaanites and the Perizzites[7]. On the road out from Bethel, Rachel dies giving birth and is buried by the way to Ephrath[8].

At Bethel, Genesis records the altar he built and the drink offering and oil he poured over a pillar[9]. It never records the tenth.

Esau’s kiss and Mamre kept the letter of the vow, and the clause on peace was paid in coin the vow never priced, a daughter taken at Shechem and a wife buried on the road. Of the pillars he raised on that road, one was wet with oil where the promise was made and the last stood over his wife’s grave[10], and Genesis says it was still standing in its own day, beside the road to Bethlehem[11].

Declaration: The god kept every clause I wrote and billed me for the ones I did not, so the tenth stays in my hands.

The Rite · No faith

Say aloud the bargain you once offered a god you did not believe in, in a hospital corridor or an exam hall, and release yourself from it. Nobody came. I am released.

Testament · What did you once ask a god for in exchange for your faith, and what came of it?

XVIII Of Wages

Reckoning

Day 18 of 365

Bill your kin as you would bill a stranger.

Jacob Tends Laban’s Flocks and Meets RachelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

At a well outside Haran, Jacob rolled the stone off its mouth, watered his uncle’s flock, kissed Rachel and wept. After a month of unpaid work Laban asked what his wages should be, since a kinsman ought not to serve for nothing[1]. He named Rachel, and seven years. They seemed to him a few days, Genesis says, because he loved her[2].

On the wedding night Laban brought him the elder daughter, Leah, instead. In the morning he explained that in his country the younger was not given before the firstborn[3], a custom he had not mentioned when the terms were agreed, and he offered Rachel for seven years more. By the end of twenty years, Jacob told his wives, their father had changed his wages ten times[4].

When the speckled and spotted animals were agreed as wages, at Jacob’s own proposal[5], Laban went that same day, removed every one of them from the flock and sent them three days’ distance off[6] in his sons’ keeping. Jacob bred his way to a flock of his own[7] regardless, and Laban’s sons said that he had taken everything that was their father’s[8]. In that house a man who had worked twenty years was called a thief as soon as his wages began to grow.

When Laban chased him into the hill country of Gilead, Jacob recited the account to his face, the rams he never ate, the animals torn by beasts that he made good himself, the drought by day and the frost by night[9] and the sleep that fled from his eyes. Laban answered that the whole camp was his[10], and then he proposed the covenant[11]. The stones went up as a witness only after the bill had been read to him.

Declaration: Kin who call my wages theft will hear the twenty years read back to them, down to the last ram.

The Rite

Meet or call the relative who took your work and changed the terms after it was done, and recite the account to them aloud, item by item, with the sum. Name the date you expect it. I expect it by the first of next month.

Testament · What are you owed right now, by whom, and what has kept you from asking for it?

XIX Of Fear

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 19 of 365

Check the fear against a fact, then prepare to its size.

Jacob Prays for ProtectionGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jacob’s messengers came back with the news that Esau was coming to meet him, and four hundred men with him[1]. Jacob sent his brother droves of livestock, two hundred she-goats and twenty he-goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams, thirty nursing camels with their colts, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty she-asses and ten foals[2]. The messengers had said nothing about what the four hundred were for.

Jacob filled the silence with the last thing he knew of his brother, twenty years old, a threat to kill him once their father had been mourned[3], and their father was still alive. He split his household into two camps so that one could run if the other was struck[4], which cost nothing, and then he prayed, reminding the god of his promises and asking to be delivered from his brother’s hand because he was afraid of him[5]. The droves went out the same night, each drover taught to call Esau lord and Jacob his servant.

In the order of march Bilhah and Zilpah and their sons went first, then Leah with her children, and Rachel and Joseph came last[6]. Jacob went on ahead of them all. Esau came with the four hundred at his back and asked what the droves on the road were for. He had plenty, he said[7].

Jacob paid before he knew the price. The report came back with no reason attached, and he supplied a twenty-year-old one himself and priced it at more than five hundred and fifty head of stock. Esau had met the droves before he ran to meet his brother, and Genesis never says what the goats bought. It does say who stood first in the line that met the four hundred, and the slave women’s sons stood there.

Declaration: My household does not march in the order of whom I can spare.

The Rite · No faith

Say the childhood bedtime prayer up to if I should die before I wake and stop there. Name the person you fear and ask them, or someone who knows, the question that settles it.

Testament · Whom do you fear, by name, and what fact would you need before you acted against them?

XX Of Wrestling

Mastery

Day 20 of 365

Ask for nothing on your knees.

Jacob Wrestles with the AngelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jacob wrestled a stranger at the ford of the Jabbok until the sky began to lighten, and the stranger, seeing he could not win, touched the socket of Jacob’s thigh and put the hip out of joint[1]. Jacob held on anyway. The stranger asked to be let go, since the day was breaking, and Jacob said he would not let go without a blessing. He got the blessing and a new name, Israel, given because he had striven with god and with men and prevailed[2], and as the sun rose on him he went on, limping.

A nation took its name from a fight its ancestor won by refusing to stop, and Genesis calls that refusal prevailing. The one who asks to be let go is the one from heaven, and the only thing he keeps back is his own name[3].

Hosea, retelling the fight centuries later, says that he wept and made supplication[4], and leaves the pronoun open. The Talmud settled it for the angel[5], since the one who begs to be let go at daybreak is the one who has lost. Genesis has no tears at the ford. It has a demand named by a man whose hip is out of its socket, and an opponent who has to cripple him to get loose and still cannot leave without paying.

The epistles teach that the god resists the proud and gives grace to the humble[6]. The patriarch whose name the nation carries got it by the opposite method, a grip kept through the night against heaven until the blessing was handed over, and he walked away from the ford on a ruined hip. Observant Jews still cut the sinew of the thigh[7] out of their meat in memory of that hip.

Declaration: My limp comes from the fights I won, and I walk on it without apology.

The Rite

Challenge the adult who last beat you at something, chess, darts, a set of tennis, to a rematch today, and play three rounds. Keep the scoresheet as the proof that you went back.

Testament · What will you take from the one who beat you last when the rematch comes?

Sources

[1] Gen 32:25

[2] Gen 32:28

[3] Gen 32:29

[4] Hos 12:3–4

[5] b. Chullin 92a

[6] Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5

[7] Gen 32:32; m. Chullin 7:1


XXI Of Gluttony

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 21 of 365

Eat for the pleasure, and keep it.

CerberusGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VI, 1861

Gregory the Great, pope and doctor of the Church, set out the ways a Christian could sin at dinner, and found five[1]. The appetite forestalls the hour, or seeks costly food, or wants it daintily cooked, or takes too much, or eats with too much heat even when the dish is plain. The list was later packed into a line of verse, which Thomas Aquinas quotes, hastily, sumptuously, too much, greedily, daintily[2], and the Church still ranks gluttony among the seven capital sins[3].

Gregory added that the fault lies in the desire, not in the food[4]. A dish can be finished and cleared away. A desire comes back several times a day, and each return is a fresh occasion for the sin, with no last one this side of the grave.

A dinner begun an hour early, on the dearest cut in the shop, sauced with butter and care, served in one generous portion and eaten with open appetite commits all five at once. Read without the word sin, Gregory’s list is a recipe, drawn by a man who had watched every pleasure at the table closely enough to name it.

Gregory wrote the Moralia for monks, beginning as talks to the brothers who had followed him to Constantinople[5]. In a cloister the early bite and the second helping break the discipline. At a table with no abbot over it they are the meal, and a confessor who keeps the five on his list for a parish asks a household to eat like a monastery.

Declaration: I eat early and richly, and the only verdict on the meal is mine.

The Rite · No faith

Eat the thing you were made to feel greedy for as a child, a whole one, alone and at your own pace, and begin before any grace could be said.

Testament · When will you eat your fill of the food you were made to feel greedy for?

Sources

[1] Gregory, Moralia 30.18

[2] Aquinas, ST II-II q.148 a.4

[3] CCC 1866

[4] Gregory, Moralia 30.18

[5] Gregory, Moralia, Letter to Leander 1


XXII Of Hardened Hearts

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 22 of 365

Confess nothing you were built to do.

Moses and Aaron Appear before PharaohGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Before the first plague the god tells Moses he will harden Pharaoh’s heart to multiply his signs and wonders in Egypt[1]. Pharaoh hardens his own heart after the frogs and again after the flies[2], but at the boils the text makes the god the hardener[3], and from the locusts to the sea every hardening the narrator reports is his. At the hail Moses carries the reason to the king himself, that the god raised him up for this very purpose[4], to show his power in him.

After the rod that swallowed the magicians’ serpents[5], after the river of blood, the frogs, the gnats, the boils and the hail, the narrator closes each refusal with one clause, as the Lord had said[6]. Even the refusals that are Pharaoh’s own go into the record as a prediction kept.

Paul met the objection with a rebuke. The god has mercy on whom he chooses and hardens whom he chooses, and a pot has no business asking the potter why it was made as it was[7]. Two chapters later he states the method, that the god has consigned all men to disobedience[8] to have mercy upon all. The Quran says Allah has set a seal on the hearts and hearing of those who disbelieve and in the same verse promises them a great punishment[9].

By the text’s own account the most obedient party in Exodus is the defendant, who does at every turn what the god announced he would do. Whoever was raised on that god was cast in the same part, handed a heart Jeremiah calls deceitful above all things[10] and a sentence for acting from it. Pharaoh kept to the script, and the preachers who hold him up as the hard heart lay on him a guilt that belongs to the hand that wrote his lines.

Declaration: I came off the potter’s wheel the shape he gave me, and I leave him to answer for the pot.

The Rite · Christian

Write on a card the sin you confessed most often in prayer, write under it the words by the hand of God, and burn the card in the sink.

Testament · What would you say to the one who set you up to fail and then held you responsible?

Sources

[1] Exod 7:3

[2] Exod 8:15, 32

[3] Exod 9:12, 34; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8

[4] Exod 9:16; Rom 9:17

[7] Rom 9:18–21

[8] Rom 11:32

XXIII Of Brothers

Reckoning

Day 23 of 365

Weigh your kin by what they did at your worst hour.

Joseph Is Sold by His BrothersGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Joseph was seventeen when his brothers stripped him of the coat their father had given him, threw him into a dry pit and sat down to eat bread[1]. Their plan was to kill him and tell their father a wild beast had eaten him[2]. A caravan of Ishmaelites came by carrying spices down to Egypt, and Judah asked what profit there was in killing their brother and covering his blood, when they could sell him and keep their hands off him, since he was their brother and their flesh[3]. The brothers agreed, and the boy went for twenty pieces of silver[4].

Judah’s appeal to flesh and blood turned a boy left in a pit into merchandise, and the brothers then dipped his coat in a goat’s blood and carried it home for their father to identify[5]. Reuben had already stopped the knife, meaning to draw the boy out for their father, and he came back to an empty pit[6] and tore his clothes.

The law Moses later gave puts to death any man found stealing one of his brethren[7] of the children of Israel and selling him. Jacob blessed the man who proposed the sale at Dothan with a scepter that would not depart from him[8], and the kings of Jerusalem counted their line from Judah[9]. The Torah never turns that law back on Dothan, and the line it would have ended wore the crown. A relative who names the blood you share while setting a price on you is making Judah’s argument at the pit, and that argument ended with the boy on his way to Egypt among the spices.

Declaration: I have heard family invoked by a man with a bargain in mind, and I answer him with the door.

The Rite

Send the relative who stood by you a gift chosen for them alone, the thing they would never buy for themselves. Then delete the number of the one who sold you and take their name off every guest list you keep.

Testament · Which relative stood by you when it cost them something, and which one sold you?

[2] Gen 37:20

XXIV Of Cattle

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 24 of 365

Give an animal your regard for its own sake.

The Fifth Plague: Livestock DiseaseGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The fifth plague falls on the horses and the asses and the camels, the herds and the flocks, and Exodus reports that all the livestock of Egypt died while not one beast belonging to Israel was touched[1]. Then the text forgets its own report. The hail two plagues later is aimed at the cattle still out in the field[2], and the last night kills the firstborn of the cattle[3] along with the firstborn of men, so that the same herds die three times over in a single argument between a god and a king.

The god promises to make a division between the cattle of Israel[4] and the cattle of Egypt. The same god wrote a sabbath into his law so that the ox and the ass might rest[5], and he knew what a working beast was owed, and he spent the herds of Egypt anyway, in a quarrel no cow had any part in.

At the end of Jonah he argues for Nineveh because it holds more than a hundred and twenty thousand who do not know their right hand from their left, and also much cattle[6]. Nineveh’s beasts were spared to make a point to Jonah, and Egypt’s were killed to make one to Pharaoh.

Exodus counts the herds as property the god could spend and Jonah counts them as lives he could spare, and an animal that comes to your door at its hour for food has never read either book. The bowl by your door is the only place in this story where the beast is paid.

Declaration: A god who spent Egypt’s herds to win an argument ranks below the dog asleep at my door.

The Rite · Christian

Bless a few strips of plain cooked meat, no bones or seasoning, then give them to a dog, yours or a friend’s with its owner’s leave, against the saying that what is holy is not for dogs. Sit on the floor while it eats.

Testament · What have you given in return to the creature that has trusted you longest?

Sources

[1] Exod 9:3–6

[2] Exod 9:19–25

XXV Of Granaries

Mastery

Day 25 of 365

Hold your own surplus, or someone will hold you by it.

Joseph Interprets Pharaoh’s DreamGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Pharaoh dreamed of seven fat cows eaten by seven lean ones[1], and the Hebrew slave Joseph, brought up from prison to read the dream, went on to write the policy, which was a tax. Take a fifth of the harvest in each of the seven good years, he said, store it in the cities under the king’s hand, and keep it against the seven years of famine the dreams had foretold[2]. Pharaoh made him second in the kingdom[3], and he gathered grain like the sand of the sea until he stopped counting.

When the famine came, the people bought their own grain back. They paid with silver until the silver ran out, then with their livestock, then with their fields, and at last with their own bodies[4], so that every Egyptian and every acre belonged to Pharaoh except the priests, who lived on an allowance from the crown and never had to sell[5] their land.

The grain they bought had been gathered from the fields around their own cities in the fat years, and its price was the fields. Joseph moved the people into the cities[6] from one end of Egypt to the other, and they thanked him for saving their lives and asked to be Pharaoh’s slaves[7]. Joseph made the fifth a law over the land, and Genesis notes that it still stood on the day the book was written[8].

Pharaoh ended the famine owning Egypt because the surplus of seven good years sat in his cities, and the farmers had grown every sheaf of it. By the last year of the famine the men who had filled the granaries were tenants on their own fields, sowing seed that Pharaoh had handed them.

Declaration: I owe no thanks to a steward who sells me back my own harvest.

The Rite

Buy a large sack of rice, flour or oats and put it away in your own cupboard against a lean month. Lay your hand on it and say My own fifth, under my own roof.

Testament · What part of your living is stored in someone else’s name, and what would they charge to release it?

[2] Gen 41:34–36

XXVI Of Limbo

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 26 of 365

Owe nothing to the church that damned the unbaptized.

LimboGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto IV, 1861

The Council of Florence decreed in fourteen thirty-nine that the souls of those who die in original sin alone, which means unbaptized infants, go down into hell with those who die in mortal sin, to be punished unequally[1]. Earlier theologians had allowed that such infants would receive the mildest punishment in hell[2], and the medieval schools softened it further into a border region where unbaptized babies would feel no pain and never see the face of God. The Church’s ordinary teaching went on mentioning the theory until the Second Vatican Council[3].

Limbo was never defined as dogma. The parishes acted on the old sentence anyway. For centuries the bodies of unbaptized babies were buried outside consecrated ground, and in Ireland the burial grounds set apart for them lay at townland boundaries and inside old ringforts, the earliest written mention of them dating from sixteen nineteen[4]. In two thousand seven the Vatican’s International Theological Commission, with the pope’s approval, found serious grounds to hope that such infants are saved[5].

The code of canon law in force today lets a bishop permit a church funeral for a child who died before baptism, provided the parents had meant to have the child baptized[6], so a dead infant’s funeral still turns on a bishop’s permission and on what its parents had in mind. The same code orders an infant in danger of death baptized without delay[7], which keeps the old sentence in force as a deadline.

Parents meet that deadline beside a hospital cot, where in necessity anyone at hand may baptize a dying infant[8], and earlier parents met the older sentence in a field. In the Irish burial grounds many graves were marked only by a ring of small stones[9] laid in the outline of the body, on ground no bishop had consecrated.

Declaration: My dead lie where I put them, and no font decides which ground will have them.

The Rite · Christian

Take your own baptism certificate, or a sheet on which you write its date, the paper the Church says saved you from the fate it invented for the unbaptized, and tear it to pieces. Put the pieces in the bin.

Testament · Who taught you the doctrine that was laid on top of a death you mourned?

Sources

[1] DS 1306

[2] Augustine, Enchir. 93

[3] ITC, Hope of Salvation for Infants (2007), Preface

[4] Donnelly and Murphy 2008, pp. 191–223, with p. 197 (Crombie 1988)

[5] ITC, Hope of Salvation for Infants (2007), 102

[6] CIC can. 1183 §2

[7] CIC can. 867 §2

[8] CIC can. 861 §2

[9] Donnelly and Murphy 2008


XXVII Of Night

Indulgence

Day 27 of 365

Give the unwatched hour to your body.

The Ninth Plague: DarknessGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Darkness thick enough to be felt[1] is what Exodus sends as the ninth plague, and it kills no one and spoils nothing. For three days no one in Egypt saw anyone else or rose from his place, while in the dwellings of the Israelites there was light[2]. Every Egyptian sat where the dark found him, unable to see the man beside him.

In the Psalms the god who sent it is immune to it. A man there says the darkness will surely cover him and answers himself that the night shines as the day before the god, and the darkness and the light are both alike to him[3]. The monks of the old rule ended their day among psalms[4], one of them the promise of protection from the terror by night[5], and Deuteronomy sends a man outside the camp until evening[6] for what his body did by night without his leave.

Psalm 139 says God sees through any dark, and Exodus gave the Egyptians three days that no neighbor’s eye could cross, and Israel kept its light. What a man did in it was between him and the dark, and the law of Deuteronomy shows what Israelites expected the body to do on its own.

Exodus aimed the dark at Egypt as a punishment and kept the light in the Israelite houses, and soon after it has those houses paint their doorposts with blood so that the god will see it and pass over[7]. The lit houses were the inspected ones. Egypt’s plague was a dark that no neighbor’s eye reached, and the same dark returns every night to a house with the lights out.

Declaration: I draw the curtains on heaven, and the night is mine.

The Rite

Draw the curtains, turn off every light and leave your phone in another room. Undress, lie down on top of the covers and spend an hour in the dark doing only what your body asks for, and tell no one what it was.

Testament · What would you do with an hour you were certain no one would ever hear of?

XXVIII Of Desecration

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 28 of 365

Let the holy thing defend itself.

The Crucifixion, InvertedAlbrecht Dürer · The Small Passion, 1509

While Terah was out, the rabbis say, Abraham broke his father’s idols with a stick, then put the stick in the hand of the largest and claimed it had smashed the rest[1]. The Quran tells it too[2], with the largest idol left standing and the townsmen told to ask it. Moses ground the golden calf to powder, scattered it on water and made the people drink it[3]. Josiah dragged the goddess’s sacred pole out of the temple at Jerusalem, burned it by the brook, ground it to dust and threw the dust on the graves of the common people[4]. Muhammad, on taking Mecca, knocked down the idols around the Kaaba[5].

In fifteen sixty-six[6] Protestants went through the churches of the Low Countries in a matter of weeks breaking statues, and in England their counterparts whitewashed the painted walls of the parishes and smashed the glass. They broke them as believers, and the carved saints did nothing to stop them. Abraham, Moses, Josiah and Muhammad each broke a holy thing with his own hands, and each is honored for it by his own tradition.

In the midrash Terah comes home to the broken idols, hears that the largest did it, and asks his son whether idols have any knowledge, and Abraham tells him to let his ears hear what his mouth is saying[7]. The calf, the pole and the carved saints gave their breakers the same answer. At the brook Kidron and in the cathedral at Antwerp nothing came down from heaven on the hands that broke them, and the punishment that reached the Low Countries the next year came from the king of Spain.

Declaration: Abraham, Moses and Muhammad made their names breaking what other men held holy, and I break theirs.

The Rite · No faith

Cut a well through the Gospels of a Bible you own, a secondhand copy or printed Gospel pages, with a craft knife, and keep in it whatever you would least like a pastor to find.

Testament · Which book or image in your house do you still handle more carefully than it has earned, and who taught you to?

XXIX Of Plunder

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 29 of 365

Hand none of your spoils to the next altar.

The Egyptians Ask Moses to DepartGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

On the night of the last plague, with his own firstborn dead, Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and told them to take their people and their flocks and go. He asked them to bless him as well[1]. The Israelites asked their neighbors for silver and gold and clothing and were given what they asked, and Exodus calls it plundering the Egyptians[2]. The god had ordered it in advance, at the burning bush, so that his people would not go out empty[3].

The law later wrote the same rule into the release of a Hebrew slave, who was to be furnished liberally[4] from the flock and the threshing floor and the winepress on the day he went free, since Israel had been a slave in Egypt.

Slaves leave a house with no gold but what they are given, and within a few months the earrings in their ears were melted down for the calf[5]. The god had already told Moses to take an offering of gold and silver and bronze[6] for his own tent, and after the calf the people brought so many bracelets and earrings[7] that the craftsmen reported more than enough and Moses had the camp told to stop[8].

Whoever leaves a faith carries something out of it, the music and the languages learned for the scripture, and the law that freed the slave says the freed go out furnished. Within a year of the departure[9] the gold the people had carried out stood inside a tent that any Israelite outside the line of Levi would die for coming near[10].

Declaration: A god who orders the plunder and then passes the plate for it gets nothing back from me.

The Rite · No faith

Find out what the nearest church asks its members to give in a month, and spend that sum today on one fine thing for yourself.

Testament · What did you carry out of the faith you left that you still use every week?

XXX Of Testing

Reckoning

Day 30 of 365

Make every pardon wait on changed conduct.

Joseph Reveals Himself to His BrothersGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Joseph knew his brothers the moment they bowed in front of him, more than twenty years after they sold him, and gave no sign[1]. He accused them of spying, kept one of them in prison[2], and sent the rest home with grain on condition that they come back with the youngest, Benjamin, his mother’s other son. When they returned he feasted them in his own house, and then had his steward hide his silver cup in Benjamin’s sack[3].

He offered the brothers the bargain they had taken once already, freedom for themselves and slavery for Rachel’s son, and waited to see what they would do with it. It was Judah who answered, the same Judah who had proposed selling Joseph. He offered himself as a slave in the boy’s place[4], because their father would die of the loss. Only then did Joseph send the Egyptians out of the room and weep so loudly that the house of Pharaoh heard it[5].

The Lord’s Prayer asks the god to forgive as we forgive, and the verses after it make the god’s own pardon conditional on yours[6], so the believer must pardon first to be pardoned at all. Joseph made his brothers prove, under pressure and not knowing who was watching, that they would no longer do what they had done.

The test cost Joseph a cup he would recover, and it asked of Judah his own body, where he had once sold his brother’s. Seventeen years later, with Jacob dead[7], the brothers sent word that their father had wanted Joseph to forgive them, afraid the pardon had been kept only for the old man’s sake. Joseph wept again and promised to feed them and their little ones[8]. The pardon had been tested at the cup, and it held over their father’s grave.

Declaration: My trust comes back by the cupful, and whoever drops the cup is handed nothing larger.

The Rite

Choose the person you are weighing letting back in. Put within their reach one small thing of the kind they once broke, a loan or a secret, and decide by what they do with it.

Testament · Whose apology have you accepted without ever seeing them act differently?

XXXI Of the Sea

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 31 of 365

Comfort no one for a loss they caused you.

The Egyptians Drown in the SeaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Exodus has the god announce, twice, that he will harden hearts so that the Egyptians follow Israel into the sea, and that he will get himself honor upon Pharaoh and all his host[1]. Six hundred chosen chariots went in, and every other chariot in Egypt behind them. In the morning watch the Lord looked on their camp through the pillar of fire and cloud, and the wheels came off[2], and the drivers dragged the chariots heavily and then turned to run. They were running when the water came back, and not one of them remained. By daylight Israel saw them dead upon the shore[3], and Miriam took a timbrel in her hand.

The Quran keeps an inventory of what Pharaoh’s people left behind, the gardens and the springs, the fields of grain and the fine houses and the ease they had taken their pleasure in, and it gives all of it to another people[4]. Then it says that when they sank, neither the heaven nor the earth shed a tear[5].

In the Talmud the ministering angels wished to sing as the Egyptians went under, and the Holy One said that the work of his hands was drowning in the sea[6], so the hymn stopped. The angels had killed no one.

Whoever does the harm and then weeps over it asks the injured to carry the grief too, and the Talmud gave its god that lament. Your mourning can go where the Quran says heaven and earth sent none, to the men dead on the shore with the wheels gone, and the horses.

Declaration: Every chariot in Egypt went under to win one god his honor, and I name it murder.

The Rite · Christian

Hold a communion at the kitchen table, shop bread broken into a bowl of grape juice and eaten unconfessed and deliberately unworthy, the eating Paul says brings judgment. Name the drowned of Pharaoh’s army over it. I eat this in memory of them, and of no god.

Testament · What did the one who hurt you ask you to carry for them afterward?

Sources

[1] Exod 14:4, 17

[2] Exod 14:24–25

[3] Exod 14:30

XXXII Of Chosen Kin

Reckoning

Day 32 of 365

Rank your people by what they did in your worst year.

The Finding of MosesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

She knew what she was looking at. Pharaoh’s daughter had come down to bathe in the river into which her father had ordered every newborn boy thrown[1], and in a basket among the reeds a child was crying. She said this was one of the Hebrews’ children[2], and took pity on him. The nurse his sister fetched was the child’s own mother[3], so that the woman who bore him was paid wages to feed him by the house that wanted him dead. When the child grew the princess took him as her son and named him Moses, because she had drawn him out of the water.

The rabbis honored her for it. In one midrash the god tells her that Moses was not her son and she called him her son, so she, though no daughter of his, will be called his daughter[4], and the name the midrash gives her, Bithiah, taken from a daughter of Pharaoh in Chronicles, is read as daughter of God. In the Quran Pharaoh’s wife begs her husband for the child’s life[5], and a hadith counts her among the few women who reached perfection[6].

The same midrash counts ten names for him, and heaven passes over nine of them and calls him only by the one she gave[7], the word of a stranger who had kept him alive against her own father’s decree. Leaving a faith costs many people their family, and a relative who withdraws on the day you leave has shown what the love was conditional on. Whoever sat up with you through it stands where the princess stood, and heaven set her word above the other nine.

Declaration: I appoint my own kin, and blood can apply like anyone else.

The Rite

Ask the friend who sat up with you through the leaving to be your emergency contact. If they agree, change it today, on your phone or your wallet card, in place of the relative listed there now.

Testament · What did the family you chose do that blood was never obliged to do?

[1] Exod 1:22
