XXXIII Of Commandments

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 33 of 365

Write your own ten in the order you would defend them.

The Giving of the Law on Mount SinaiGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The first of the ten words gives the author’s name and then his bill. He is the god who brought you out of the land of Egypt and out of the house of bondage[1], so every law after it arrives as an account already due. It is a preface in the Catholic and Reformed counts and a command to believe in Maimonides’s. Murder and theft can wait. The opening clauses go to the speaker, his rivals forbidden and his likeness forbidden, his name kept out of careless mouths, and his own rest on the seventh day copied by everyone under him, down to the servants and the cattle[2].

The ban on images gives its own motive, which is jealousy, and its own penalty, which falls on the offender’s children to the third and fourth generation[3]. The tenth commandment, which reaches inside the skull to govern a wish, lists the neighbor’s wife among his house and his slaves and his ox and his ass[4]. Nowhere in the ten is a man forbidden to own another man, and the next chapter prices the matter exactly. A master who beats his slave to death is to be punished, unless the slave survives a day or two, since the slave is his money[5].

A child taught the ten recites the speaker’s claims before the neighbor’s life, and learns which rule outranks the rest before learning to weigh any of them. The god took that first seat with the first clause, a rescue performed on other people’s ancestors and charged ever since to every child taught to recite it. The child signed nothing. A debt run up by strangers for a stranger’s escape is enforced by the creditor and his clerks, and the adult who finally reads the terms can send the invoice back unpaid.

Declaration: A law that lists a wife between the house and the ox has no say in my house.

The Rite · No faith

Print the Ten Commandments, or copy them out by hand. Strike out the first, write your own name over it, pin the page inside a cupboard door. Then write your own ten beneath it.

Testament · Which of your ten real laws exists to protect someone else’s opinion of you?

[2] Exod 20:8–11

[5] Exod 21:20–21


XXXIV Of Cunning

Mastery

Day 34 of 365

Give the strong exactly what their words demand, and no more.

The Child Moses on the NileGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Shiphrah and Puah lied to Pharaoh’s face. Ordered to kill every Hebrew boy at the birthing stool, the two midwives let the boys live, and when the king summoned them they told him the Hebrew women were so vigorous that they gave birth before any midwife could arrive[1]. The order could be carried out only by the women told to carry it out, in rooms no king would enter, and their lie flattered his contempt for his slaves. Exodus records that the god dealt well with the midwives, and because they feared him he made them houses[2].

Pharaoh then gave the order to his whole people, that every son born should be thrown into the river[3]. A Levite woman hid her son for three months[4], and when she could hide him no longer she sealed a basket of rushes with bitumen and pitch[5] and laid it among the reeds at the river’s brink, so that the river the order named became his cradle. The engraving above adds a company of angels to watch over the basket. The text has none, only a sister standing off at a distance to see what would happen to him[6].

Power writes its orders loosely and trusts force to fill whatever the wording leaves out, and force cannot stand at every birthing stool or every bend of the river, so a lie or a literal reading will do for a hand to slip through. Courts have long read a drafter’s doubtful words against the drafter[7]. Every order of the strong reaches its object through someone’s hands, and the king who wrote river raised in his own house the child it carried.

Declaration: Where a command leaves a gap, I go through it, and let the king call that cheating.

The Rite

Take the contract between you and whoever leans on you hardest, a lease, an employment contract, the terms of an account. Find the clause that binds them, and invoke it against them in writing, over your own signature.

Testament · Who above you depends on your hands to do what they never put in writing?

XXXV Of the Calf

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 35 of 365

Phone someone the elders expelled, and keep the line open.

Moses Comes Down from Mount SinaiGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Aaron credited the fire. Asked by his brother what the people had done to him, he said they had given him their gold, he had thrown it into the fire, and out came this calf[1]. Twenty verses earlier he had taken their earrings, shaped the gold with a graving tool and proclaimed a feast to the god. The chapter closes on a plague sent because the people made the calf, which, the narrator adds, Aaron made[2]. The Quran clears him and hands the work to a man called the Samiri[3].

Moses ground the calf to powder, strewed it on water and made Israel drink it[4]. At his call the sons of Levi went through the camp, each man killing his brother and his companion and his neighbor, about three thousand[5], and Moses told them they had consecrated themselves by it. Deuteronomy adds that the god was angry enough with Aaron to destroy him, and that Moses prayed for him. The tribe that did the killing was set apart to carry the ark, and the man who made the calf was anointed high priest[6].

The priesthood of Israel descends from the man who cast the idol and the men who cut down their brothers to purge it, and the institution has kept the inheritance in a gentler form. The sword gave way to the door. In the Quran the Samiri’s sentence is a shunning, his lot for life to tell anyone near him, do not touch me[7], and Jehovah’s Witnesses hand a like sentence to a member who leaves and works against them[8]. Those who carry it out are told the cutting is loyalty to the god, as the Levites were told the sword consecrated them, and the elders who pass the sentence leave the work to the mother and the brother at the door.

Declaration: A god who wants my sister shunned can knock and tell her himself.

The Rite · No faith

Knead a slice of bread into a calf, stand it on a printed page of the Ten Commandments, grind it to crumbs, and strew them on a bowl of water as Moses did. Pour it down the drain.

Testament · Who were you told to cut off, or who cut you off, to prove a loyalty?

XXXVI Of Tablets

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 36 of 365

Treat every commandment you grew up under as a draft.

Moses Breaks the Tables of the LawGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The rabbis kept the pieces. In their reading the fragments of the first tablets, which Moses smashed below the mountain[1] when he saw the calf and the dancing, were gathered up and laid in the ark beside the whole tablets[2] that replaced them, so that Israel carried the broken law through the desert alongside the mended one. The book of Exodus says those first stones were the god’s own work, the writing on them written by his finger[3]. Moses threw them down anyway. The text records no rebuke.

One teacher in the Talmud read the god’s later mention of the tablets Moses broke as a compliment, as though the voice in the cloud had thanked him for breaking them[4]. The replacement was a cheaper production. Moses cut the stones himself[5], and the laws the god dictated on that second climb, just before the writing, run to feasts, firstborn sons and a kid boiled in its mother’s milk[6].

The dread you feel at breaking an inherited rule was put there to guard it, and the record gives it no ground. The first edition of the law, the god’s own handiwork, went to pieces under the hand of its own prophet, and heaven sent him back up the mountain with stone he had cut himself. Whoever breaks one of the copies for pleasure finds the dread sharpening the pleasure it was put there to prevent. The rules you keep after that are kept by your own choice, and the rest can travel as the first stones traveled, in a box on the shoulders of the devout.

Declaration: I owe the tablets the reverence Moses showed them at the foot of the mountain.

The Rite · Christian

Write six hundred sixty-six on your right palm in ink, the mark Revelation says no one may buy or sell without and the faithful must refuse, and buy yourself something you want with that hand.

Testament · Which inherited rule did you break for pleasure, and how did the old dread taste?

XXXVII Of Thrones

Beauty

Day 37 of 365

Wear your gold without asking anyone for leave.

Satan EnthronedGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book II, 1866

The lampstand of the tabernacle was hammered from a talent of pure gold[1], Solomon overlaid his temple with gold down to the floor[2], and his ivory throne stood on six steps with twelve lions[3] along them. In the book that splendor is the god’s own, or lent to the king who sat on the throne of the god[4].

The plate above gives the fallen a throne of their own, a hall of columns and a long stair with a seat at its summit lit like an altar. Isaiah gave that ambition to the king of Babylon, who said in his heart that he would set his throne above the stars of God, and was promised the pit[5]. Ezekiel dressed the king of Tyre in every precious stone and had the god cast him to the ground because his heart was lifted up by his own beauty[6]. When the daughters of Zion wanted splendor of their own, Isaiah went through their ornaments one by one, the anklets and the crescents, the perfume boxes and the rings, and promised them a stink where the perfume had been[7].

Each prophet brings the same charge. The offense is splendor worn on the wearer’s own account, and the ornament is never the crime. Gold on the lampstand was worship and a bangle on a woman’s ankle was pride. The letter to Timothy that sends women out without gold or pearls[8] has been read for centuries beneath a bishop’s carved chair, the cathedra that gives every cathedral its name, by clergy in vestments stiff with gold thread. The guilt you were taught to feel at a fine thing guards somebody else’s chair.

Declaration: The church gilds its altars and calls my rings vanity, and I keep the rings.

The Rite

Make a throne of the chair you sit in most. Drape it in the richest cloth you own or can buy today, set something gold or brass within reach, and sit in it dressed as if for an audience, receiving no one.

Testament · Where in your home have you accepted ugliness as though you deserved it?

XXXVIII Of Dissent

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 38 of 365

Demand the warrant of anyone who claims to forgive you.

The Death of Korah, Dathan, and AbiramGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Bronze plates covered the altar, beaten from the two hundred and fifty censers of men who had died holding them, as a memorial that no one outside the seed of Aaron should come near to burn incense[1]. The men had come with Korah, a Levite and first cousin to Moses[2], to tell Moses and Aaron that they took too much upon themselves, since the whole congregation was holy and the god was among them all.

The ground opened under the tents of Dathan and Abiram, who stood at their doors with their wives and their sons and their little children, and they went down alive into the pit. When the congregation complained that Moses and Aaron had killed the people of the god, a plague killed fourteen thousand seven hundred more[3]. The question of office was then settled with twelve rods laid up overnight by Moses before the testimony and brought out by him the next morning[4], when Aaron’s had budded and borne almonds.

The rod was the warrant for the priesthood. Numbers has it laid before the testimony[5] as a token against the rebels. After the fire and the pit, the claim rests on a stick kept overnight in a tent by the claimant’s brother.

The priest who absolves you, the bishop who interviews you and the elders in committee over you each claim an office, and every such claim reaches back to a founding authority no one can check. The words of absolution are printed in books anyone can buy, and what kept them out of your mouth was the story of the ground opening.

Declaration: I absolve myself, and the floor holds.

The Rite · No faith

Sit facing an empty chair, as a confessor sits, name a pleasure you were once made to apologize for, and pronounce your own release. I hold this office by my own claim. Then take that pleasure again.

Testament · Whose authority over you, traced back to its source, turns out to rest on nothing but a claim?

XXXIX Of Grasshoppers

Mastery

Day 39 of 365

Go up against the rival you have been avoiding.

The Spies Return from the Promised LandGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

One cluster of grapes needed two men and a pole. The spies cut it in the valley afterward named Eshcol for that cluster[1] and carried it home with pomegranates and figs after forty days in the land. Then ten of the twelve gave the rest of their report. The cities were walled and very great, the sons of Anak lived there, and so did the giants of the days before the flood[2], whom the flood was supposed to have drowned. Beside them, the ten said, they had been grasshoppers in their own sight, and so they were in the giants’ sight as well[3].

That last clause sank them. A spy can pace a wall and count a garrison, and the inside of another man’s head is beyond his survey. One rabbi in the Talmud called the ten liars for that clause alone[4], asking how they could know what they looked like in the giants’ eyes. Fear did the measuring and signed the giants’ names to the result. The sentence was forty years in the desert, a year for each day of spying, until every man of twenty and over had died there except the two who had argued for going up[5].

Caleb walked the same ground as the ten, saw the same walls and the same sons of Anak, and told the people they were well able to take the land[6], and the text says he had another spirit. He left the giants’ opinion out of his report. Whoever sizes a rival by what can be counted, and keeps out of the sum the contempt he imagines on the rival’s face, is filing Caleb’s report. Forty-five years later Caleb drove out of Hebron the three sons of Anak the spies had seen there[7], and took the city.

Declaration: Every giant I have measured came up shorter than the one fear described.

The Rite

Write down, side by side, your numbers and those of the rival who looks too big to beat, years in business, prices and clients. Then take the step the figures allow today, whether that is dropping the discount you give out of fear or buying the tool you lack.

Testament · Whose opinion of you have you been reporting to yourself without ever hearing it?

XL Of the Bronze Serpent

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 40 of 365

Use what healed you, and owe it no devotion.

The Bronze SerpentGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Hezekiah broke a bronze snake that Moses had made. The book of Kings lists the breaking among his reforms, because the children of Israel had been burning incense to it[1] down to his own day, and then says that none of Judah’s kings trusted the god as he did[2]. Kings says he called it Nehushtan, a lump of bronze.

In the book of Numbers the people complain of the manna, the god sends fiery serpents among them and many die, and when they repent he prescribes the remedy, a serpent cast in bronze and raised on a pole, so that whoever is bitten and looks at it will live[3]. Somewhere in the centuries between the desert and the hammer, the antidote acquired a congregation.

The Mishnah ruled that the serpent could neither kill nor heal, and that the bitten lived when they turned their hearts to their father in heaven[4]. The Gospel of John made the pole a prophecy, so that the son of man must be lifted up as Moses lifted the serpent in the wilderness[5]. Each reading moved the cure’s power somewhere else, into trust in the one and into a crucifixion in the other, and left the serpent standing as a prop.

The medicine that got you through, or the book that broke a spell, is a tool in your hand. Defend it with the heat once given to a creed and it has begun to own you. The incense in Hezekiah’s day was burned by people who had never been bitten, to a cure that had cured no one living.

Declaration: My cure works or goes in the drawer, and no one collects incense on it.

The Rite · Christian

Read the verse in John that makes Moses’ serpent a figure of the crucified. Take the cross from your wall, or tie two sticks into one, use it once as a straightedge or a wedge, and put it in the drawer with the tools.

Testament · What cure in your life has started asking you for loyalty?

[1] 2 Kgs 18:4

[2] 2 Kgs 18:5

XLI Of the Ass

Reckoning

Day 41 of 365

Ask what they saw before you punish the stop.

An Angel Appears to BalaamGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Scripture first gives the Hebrew word satan, adversary, to an angel of the god[1], posted in a road with a drawn sword to stop a man the god had just told to travel. Balaam, a seer hired by the king of Moab to curse Israel, had asked leave, received it and set out, and the divine anger was kindled because he went[2]. The ass saw the angel.

Three times she balked, once crushing his foot against a wall, and three times he beat her, the third time with his staff[3], and then she spoke. The rabbis counted the mouth of the ass among the ten things made at twilight on the eve of the first Sabbath[4], so that it waited from the week of creation for one conversation. She asked whether in all the years he had ridden her she had ever behaved this way before[5]. His eyes were opened, and the angel told him that if she had not turned aside he would now be dead and she alive[6].

She lays her years of carrying him against the one day she stopped and he has to admit she never balked before. Balaam was the seer who would soon call himself the man whose eyes are open[7], and the animal under him saw first.

A long record is evidence, owed a hearing before the stick. When a friend or a tradesman who has carried you for years suddenly balks, the years say something stands in the road, and whoever beats them for stopping beats the only one who saw it. A man who stalls every week with an excuse ready has built no such record, and the next job goes to a stranger who answers the telephone.

Declaration: I trust the ass that balked sooner than the prophet who beat her.

The Rite

Of two people who kept you waiting lately, a friend, repairer or colleague, call the one with years of good work behind them today, ask what held them up, and pay what you owe. Give the other’s next job or favor to someone else.

Testament · Whose record with you has earned a hearing, and whose has run out?

XLII Of Jericho

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 42 of 365

Stop singing what you would refuse to say.

The Walls of Jericho Fall DownGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jericho is a song children learn before they can read, with the marching acted out and a crash for the walls. The song stops where the walls fall. The book of Joshua keeps going, and its next verse records that the Israelites utterly destroyed everything in the city, man and woman, young and old, ox and sheep and donkey, with the edge of the sword[1]. The silver and the gold went into the treasury of the god[2], and the city was burned.

Excavators who dug the mound in the middle of the last century found no wall standing at Jericho in the age the conquest is usually given[3]. With the walls already gone, the trumpets brought down nothing, and the slaughter was composed by a writer who chose the killing of a town’s children and its animals as the picture of the god’s favor. Joshua laid a curse on any man who rebuilt the place, that he would lay its foundation at the cost of his firstborn and hang its gates at the cost of his youngest son[4], and the book of Kings records a man of Bethel losing both, according to the word of the god[5].

The song keeps the trumpets and drops the sword, so a child who brings the walls down every week learns to cheer the hand that knocked them flat and never hears what that hand did inside. Read to its end, the chapter turns the song into a confession, and a grown voice can sing it that way or set it down.

Declaration: I clapped along to a massacre at six, and I take the applause back.

The Rite · No faith

Sing the spiritual about Joshua and the battle of Jericho through once, then sing it again with the next verse of the book of Joshua put back in, to the same tune.

Testament · Which song from your childhood celebrates something you would call a crime if it were said plainly?

[1] Josh 6:21

[2] Josh 6:24

[3] Kenyon, Digging Up Jericho (1957)

[4] Josh 6:26

XLIII Of the Ferryman

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 43 of 365

Stop paying fares for a crossing you do not believe in.

CharonGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto III, 1861

Many of the Greek dead went into the ground with a coin in the mouth[1], the fare for the boatman who poled souls across the river of the underworld. Excavators still find the coins in the graves. That fare, at least, stayed with the dead.

The faiths that came after kept the ferry and moved the coin into the collection. In fourteen seventy-six Pope Sixtus the Fourth issued his first bull extending an indulgence[2] to the souls in purgatory, in favor of the church of Saintes, so that a living donor who paid toward the building bought the dead a relaxation of their pains, and the money stayed in the masonry. Forty-one years later the charge that preachers promised the soul would spring from purgatory as soon as the coin rang in the chest became the twenty-seventh of the Ninety-five Theses[3].

No traveler has sent word back from the far bank. Every coin that can be followed was spent on the near one, on the church at Saintes and, in the campaign of fifteen seventeen, on Saint Peter’s in Rome and an archbishop’s debt to the Fugger bank[4], by living men who knew where it went.

Insurance kept up after the belief is gone is the same fare paid without the faith that once justified the price, the grace mumbled over a meal, the abstinence held to just in case. It buys nothing on the far bank, and it is paid out of the one life that can be shown to exist, in hours and pleasures that will not come back.

Declaration: The ferryman can wait at his dock until the river dries.

The Rite · No faith

Hold a coin to your lips for a moment, as the Greeks set one in the mouths of their dead for the ferryman, then say I keep my fare and spend it today on something you enjoy.

Testament · Which practice do you still keep only as insurance against an afterlife you no longer believe in?

Sources

[1] Lucian, Luct. 10

[2] Sixtus IV, bull for the church of Saintes (1476)

[3] Ninety-five Theses, 27 (1517)

[4] Albrecht of Brandenburg, St. Peter’s indulgence (1517)


XLIV Of Treason

Reckoning

Day 44 of 365

Keep only the loyalties you would buy today.

Joshua Spares RahabGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Rahab hid Israel’s spies under stalks of flax on her roof, sent the king’s men off the wrong way, and let the spies down the wall on a cord[1] from her window. She set her price before the cord went out, an oath that her father and mother, her brothers and sisters and all they had would live[2], and when the city burned the spies brought them out. Matthew sets her in the line of Jesus, one of four women in it before Mary[3], the Epistle to the Hebrews praises her faith and the Epistle of James her works[4], and the rabbis married her to Joshua[5].

She had heard what the god did at the sea and to the kings beyond the Jordan, and the hearts of her people had melted[6], and she sold her own city to the army at the river for the lives of her house.

Scripture has no honor for the trade run the other way. Deuteronomy orders a man to stone his own brother, son or wife who secretly urges him toward other gods, and forbids his eye to pity them[7]. Classical Islamic law put the apostate to death[8]. A loyalty that is a virtue when broken toward the god and a capital crime when broken away from him was never a virtue. It is a claim, and it belongs to whichever side is collecting.

Every loyalty handed down at birth is a claim of that kind, a bargain struck in your name before you could speak, like the church that enrolled you as an infant and still counts you. Rahab weighed what she was born into against the best terms on offer and took the terms. Having canonized her, the book has no ground left to refuse the same terms to a child born into a faith.

Declaration: Rahab named her price before she lowered the cord, and any faith that wants me will hear mine first.

The Rite

Tie a red cord in your window, as Rahab marked the house her bargain saved. Then write to one body that counts you only by birth, a church, a party, a club, and ask to be taken off its roll.

Testament · Which membership do you still hold only because you were born into it?

Sources

[1] Josh 2:4–6, 15

[2] Josh 2:12–13; 6:23

XLV Of Achan

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 45 of 365

Keep your secrets from anyone who holds stones.

Achan Is Stoned to DeathGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A fine cloak from Shinar, two hundred shekels of silver and a bar of gold weighing fifty shekels were what Achan took from the spoil of Jericho and hid in the earth under his tent[1]. When Israel lost thirty-six men at Ai[2], the god told Joshua that someone had stolen from him, and lots were cast tribe by tribe and down to the household until the lot fell on Achan[3].

The lot had already found him. Joshua asked for a confession anyway, calling him my son and telling him to give glory to the god[4], and Achan told where the silver was. They dug it up[5], took him to the valley of Achor with his sons and daughters, his oxen and asses and sheep and his tent, and all Israel stoned them and burned them[6]. All the confession added to the lot’s verdict was the glory, and the glory went to the god.

Joshua’s words became a precedent. The Mishnah has every man its court condemned to stoning told, ten cubits from the place, to confess, since whoever confesses has his portion in the world to come[7], and it names Achan as the proof. The sentence stands either way. The Witnesses still bring a member’s serious sin before the congregation elders, and by their own account the unrepentant are removed and the congregation told[8].

A court that has already decided wants the confession for itself, to close its file with the guilty man’s agreement. The Mishnah pays him in the world to come and keeps the stones for this one. Whatever you tell a body that can sentence you becomes its evidence, and the truth about your life belongs where Achan kept his silver until he was talked out of it, under your own tent.

Declaration: What I did wrong I settle with the one I wronged, and no court of the faithful hears a word of it.

The Rite · Christian

Write on a card the thing a pastor or a parent once pressed you to confess, seal it in an envelope, and hide it under your mattress or a floorboard, as Achan hid the silver under his tent. This is mine and no one’s business.

Testament · What did the confession you once made buy you from the one who heard it?

XLVI Of the Sun

Mastery

Day 46 of 365

Give one order upward today.

Joshua Commands the Sun to Stand StillGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Joshua had marched all night from Gilgal and was chasing five Amorite kings[1] along the road to Beth-horon. In the sight of Israel he spoke to the god[2] and told the sun to stand still over Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Aijalon. The text says they stopped for about a whole day, until the people had avenged themselves on their enemies[3]. There was no day like it before or since, the narrator adds, when the god listened to the voice of a man[4].

The church that used this verse against Galileo read it as astronomy. In sixteen sixteen the consultants of the Holy Office found it formally heretical to hold that the sun stands motionless at the center of the world[5], and a preacher in Florence[6] had already taken Joshua’s order as his text against the new astronomers. The order presupposes a moving sun, and the sermon needed no more. The narrator’s interest is rank. The god who had given Joshua his orders since the first chapter took one from him, and his own book marks the day as unique for that alone.

The hours of most working days are set by whoever sits above, and the evening is whatever is left once the last demand is met. Joshua made the sky keep his schedule, and spent the hours on a slaughter. A deadline moved by your own word puts the sky’s lesson into a working week, and the hour it frees is the only one on the calendar that no superior has billed.

Declaration: The sun took an order from a man once, and my deadlines can take one from me.

The Rite

Take one task whose deadline someone else set. Tell them aloud, in person or by voice, a later hour at which you will deliver it, and spend the first hour you have won on something you want.

Testament · Whose timetable did you obey for years when you could have set your own?

Sources

[1] Josh 10:5, 10

[2] Josh 10:12

[3] Josh 10:12–13

[4] Josh 10:14

[5] Holy Office consultors, 24 Feb 1616

[6] Caccini, sermon at Santa Maria Novella (1614)


XLVII Of Ai

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 47 of 365

Fix the count before you look for a sinner.

Joshua Burns the Town of AiGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The scouts sent up to Ai told Joshua not to weary the whole people, since two or three thousand men would take a town with so few defenders[1]. About three thousand went up, thirty-six died on the slope[2], the rest ran, and the hearts of the people melted like water. Joshua tore his clothes and lay before the ark until evening[3], asking why the god had brought them over the Jordan at all.

The god answered with a sin. Something devoted to him had been stolen, and Israel could not stand before its enemies until the thing was found and burned with its thief[4]. The lot fell on Achan, and the chapter ends at a heap of stones in the valley of Achor[5]. The scouts never appear again.

The next chapter changes the plan. The god told Joshua to take all the people of war and to lay an ambush behind the town[6], and the second attack was a feigned retreat built on the defenders running out after Israel as they had the first time[7]. The thirty-six died because a small force went against a town that would come out and fight, and the god’s second order answers exactly that. The theft was punished in one chapter and the estimate corrected without comment in the next.

A failure charged to sin is a failure whose plan escapes review. A pastor who meets a lost job or a failed business by searching the camp for the hidden sin runs the same audit, and the plan that sent you up the slope walks away clean, ready to send you up the next one.

Declaration: Thirty-six men died for a scout’s estimate, and no pulpit will ever pin my losses on my soul.

The Rite · Christian

Write your last failure on one line, and on the next the sin a pastor would have blamed for it, and strike the second line through. Below, write the count you went in with and the true figure, and say aloud The count was wrong.

Testament · Which of your failures were you told to repent of that a better count would have prevented?

Sources

[1] Josh 7:3

[2] Josh 7:4–5

[3] Josh 7:6–7

[4] Josh 7:12–15

[5] Josh 7:24–26

[6] Josh 8:1–2

[7] Josh 8:5–6


XLVIII Of Tent Pegs

Reckoning

Day 48 of 365

Answer your real enemy once, in law.

Jael Kills SiseraGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A treaty stood between Sisera’s king and Jael’s husband, and for that reason the beaten general ran to her tent[1]. She gave him milk when he asked for water, covered him with a rug, and when he slept drove a tent peg through his temple[2] into the ground. The book names no wrong he had done her, and the song that follows calls her blessed above women and lingers where he fell at her feet.

Saul was sent to war on a grievance centuries old. Samuel sent him against Amalek for what that people had done to Israel on the road out of Egypt[3], with orders to spare no infant or suckling, and for sparing the king and the best of the sheep he was told the kingdom would be taken from him[4].

The heads of seventy sons of Ahab lay in two heaps at the gate of Jezreel[5], and afterward the god told Jehu he had done well in destroying the house of Ahab[6] and promised him sons on the throne to the fourth generation. In the days of Jehu’s great-grandson the god told Hosea that he would avenge the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu[7].

A grievance borrowed from a god stays the god’s to settle, and the god settled with Saul for sparing one king and, through Hosea, charged to Jehu’s house the blood Jehu had shed on the god’s word. Hatred for someone who did you real harm has no sponsor and no one to settle it for you. Kept in the head it is rehearsed for years, the peg driven a thousand times in imagination and never once in the world. The one who did the harm is owed one full answer in the world, by law, and after it not another hour of rehearsal.

Declaration: Jael was blessed above women for killing her husband’s ally, and I keep my hatred for the people who earned it.

The Rite

Write the enemy’s name and the exact injury on a sheet. Under it write the one lawful move that answers it, a complaint or a claim, then file or send it today and say I answer this once, and in full.

Testament · Which lawful move against the one who wronged you would cost them most?

[1] Judg 4:15–17

[2] Judg 4:21

[3] 1 Sam 15:2–3

[4] 1 Sam 15:9, 26

[5] 2 Kgs 10:7–8

[7] Hos 1:1, 4


XLIX Of Victory Songs

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 49 of 365

Savor your last win aloud.

Deborah Praises JaelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Sisera’s mother looks out through the lattice and asks why his chariot is so slow in coming[1]. Her wisest ladies answer her, and she answers herself, that the men must be dividing the spoil, a girl or two for every man, in a Hebrew word that means womb, and dyed embroidered cloth for Sisera[2], fit for the necks of those who take the spoil. The listeners know what she does not. Her son lies in a tent with a peg through his skull.

The chapter’s heading gives the song to Deborah and Barak, sung on the day of the victory[3]. The prophetess lingers at the window of an enemy’s mother so that the hearers can savor the wait with her, lets the ladies’ guesses run on line by line, and closes on a prayer that all the god’s enemies perish so[4].

The book of Proverbs forbids rejoicing when an enemy falls, and the reason it gives concerns the god’s wrath alone. He might see it, be displeased, and turn his wrath away from the man[5]. Read through, the ban on gloating is advice on keeping the punishment at full strength, a matter of the god’s accounts with the loser’s feelings nowhere in it.

The song breaks the proverb in every line it gives the mother, and Israel kept both in one canon. Gloating was forbidden to the private man and kept for the prophetess and her god. On the proverb’s own terms the winner’s silence kept the god’s blow at full weight on the loser, and it cost the winner the best hour of the win.

Declaration: A prophetess gloated in scripture over a dead man’s mother, so I will gloat over my rivals at dinner.

The Rite · Christian

Tell friends at your own table how your last rival lost and what it cost them, the rejoicing at an enemy’s fall that Proverbs forbids, and let the friends laugh.

Testament · Which enemy’s defeat have you never let yourself enjoy in full?

Sources

[1] Judg 5:28

[2] Judg 5:29–30

[3] Judg 5:1

[4] Judg 5:31

[5] Prov 24:17–18


L Of the Undecided

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 50 of 365

Close the question you have left open longest.

The Shore of AcheronGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto III, 1861

Of the seven churches addressed in the book of Revelation, Laodicea alone gets no word of praise. It was neither cold nor hot, and the risen Christ tells it he wishes it were one or the other, and that because it is lukewarm he will vomit it out of his mouth[1]. The god who speaks there would sooner be refused than half believed.

When Paul made his defense at Caesarea[2], King Agrippa answered him, in the old English Bible, that he was almost persuaded to be a Christian[3]. Then he rose with the governor, agreed that the prisoner had done nothing worth death or chains, and went on as he was. A gospel hymn of eighteen seventy-one took the phrase for its title and pleaded with the almost persuaded, warning them that the harvest was past and that almost was lost[4]. The letter to the Hebrews supplies the deadline, that it is appointed to everyone once to die and after that the judgment[5].

On the book’s own terms the question left open is closed at death by default, and the god of Laodicea has already said what he does with the lukewarm. A life spent almost persuaded buys the one standing that god ranks below open refusal, and pays for it in years of Sundays.

Revolt answers that letter in the one form it accepts besides zeal. Said once, aloud, a cold refusal closes the question on terms the god’s own words concede, and the hymn goes on pleading with the rest of the congregation.

Declaration: My answer to the god is no, cold and on the record.

The Rite · Christian

Answer the letter to Laodicea aloud, to the god who wrote it. I am cold toward you, and I am staying cold.

Testament · What has staying almost persuaded cost you so far?

Sources

[1] Rev 3:15–16

[2] Acts 25:13, 23

[3] Acts 26:28

[4] P. P. Bliss, Almost Persuaded, The Charm (1871)

[5] Heb 9:27


LI Of the Few

Mastery

Day 51 of 365

Keep the glory of your own work.

Gideon Chooses 300 SoldiersGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Gideon had thirty-two thousand men, and the voice said they were too many, in case Israel should boast that its own hand had saved it[1]. Whoever was afraid was sent home, and twenty-two thousand went[2]. The ten thousand left were taken down to the water, where Gideon was told to set apart those who lapped it like dogs, bringing their hands to their mouths, from those who knelt to drink. Three hundred lapped[3]. With three hundred, said the voice, Israel would be saved, and the rest went back to their tents.

The army was thinned for a reason the text states outright, so that nobody but the god could take the credit. Gideon heard the reason and overrode it. The cry he chose for his three hundred, when they broke their pitchers and blew their trumpets around the camp of Midian in the dark, was for the sword of the god and of Gideon[4], his own name shouted beside the name of the god who had cut his army to keep it out.

If you were raised to give all glory to heaven, you were raised on the same rule. The psalm prays that the glory go to the god’s name[5] and twice refuses it to the singers, and the letter to the Ephesians says salvation comes by grace and not of works, lest any man should boast[6]. Every success went upward and every failure stayed with you.

Judges credits the rout to the god, who set every man’s sword against his fellow[7], and lets the shout stand with no rebuke. Heaven’s name and Gideon’s went up in one breath, and the book charges neither to the other.

Declaration: The work is mine, and so is the glory the psalm wants sent upstairs.

The Rite

Take one piece of your own work that was credited to a boss, a team or heaven. Put your name on it where the people who judge such work will see it, or tell them in your own words that it was yours.

Testament · What did you build that you let heaven or the people above you take the credit for?

[1] Judg 7:2

[2] Judg 7:3

[3] Judg 7:5–7

LII Of Vows

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 52 of 365

Break one vow you keep only to avoid admitting you were young.

Jephthah’s Daughter Comes to Meet Her FatherGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jephthah’s daughter came out dancing with timbrels, the first thing through the doors of his house, and she was his only child[1]. Before his battle with Ammon he had sworn that whatever came first out of those doors to meet him, when he returned in peace, would belong to the god as a burned offering[2]. At the sight of her he tore his clothes and told her she had brought him very low[3], since he had opened his mouth to the god and could not go back.

He could have gone back, and the rabbis found the way in the law he swore under. Leviticus sets a price in silver on any person vowed to the sanctuary, ten shekels for a girl between five and twenty[4], and in the midrash one rabbi holds that Jephthah owed only her value in coin[5], while another holds that such a vow never touched her at all. Phinehas the high priest was at hand, with power to release him. Jephthah, ruler of Israel, would not go to Phinehas, and Phinehas would not wait on an ignoramus, and between the two dignities the girl was lost[6].

The book of Judges records without comment that he did with her according to his vow[7], and the Epistle to the Hebrews enrolls him among the heroes of faith[8]. Scripture filed the man among the faithful, and the rabbis found the pride in it. A pledge card signed at fourteen in a youth group, or a covenant sworn at eight over a font, is held long after its reasons have died for the same cause, since breaking it confesses that the one who swore was a child doing what the room expected. That confession costs less than ten shekels, and the release is in the gift of the mouth that swore.

Declaration: Let the god who never said a word at Jephthah’s door come and collect my vows himself.

The Rite · No faith

Say aloud the duty to God of a scout oath or the under God of a flag pledge, whichever was recited for you as a child, and release yourself from it. That was said for me, and I take it back.

Testament · Which vow sworn before you could weigh it still governs your days?

LIII Of Lament

Reckoning

Day 53 of 365

Pay the friends who kept you before anyone who claimed you.

Israelite Women Mourn with Jephthah’s DaughterGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The chapter that gives Jephthah’s daughter to her father’s vow closes on other girls. Four days in every year, the book of Judges says, the daughters of Israel went out to lament her[1], and with that custom the chapter ends. She has no name in the book. Her father receives six years as judge of Israel and a grave in Gilead[2], and she receives what the other girls gave her.

Her one request, once she knew what he had sworn, was for time, two months to go up and down on the mountains with her companions[3], and she spent it with the girls and away from his house. After her the daughters of Israel made it a custom to give four days a year to someone who could repay nothing, and for as long as the custom lasted the vow that took her body could not take her memory.

Her father swore her away before she came out of the door. The debts a faith teaches run upward, to the god who gave you life and to the parents who answer to him, and this chapter shows one of them collected. The one debt in the chapter that no father enforced ran sideways, from women to a girl who could repay nothing, and nobody owed it until it was given. Whoever gave you days when your upbringing refused you holds that debt now, the friend who drove six hours, the cousin who lied to the elders for you. That debt outranks every claim the household made on you, since the household laid its claims on her and the girls laid this one on themselves.

Declaration: My debts run to the people who came, and the ones who claimed me can wait in line.

The Rite

Call the one person who stood by you when your family would not, and give them a whole day of yours on a date they pick. You came when they would not, and this day is yours.

Testament · Who gave you their time when you had nowhere else to go, and what did it cost them?

Sources

[1] Judg 11:39–40

[2] Judg 12:7

[3] Judg 11:37–38


LIV Of the Virtuous Pagans

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 54 of 365

Honor one good unbeliever above every council that damned them.

The Poets in LimboGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto IV, 1861

In fourteen forty-two the Council of Florence copied a sixth-century bishop’s sentence[1] into its decrees nearly word for word. Fulgentius of Ruspe had told the faithful to hold most firmly and doubt in no way that pagans and Jews, heretics and schismatics, whoever ended this life outside the Catholic Church, would go into the everlasting fire prepared for the devil and his angels[2]. By the decree’s own logic the great dead of antiquity stood with the rest, the lawgivers and the astronomers, dead outside the Church and most of them before it existed.

By a report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet told a man who asked after his dead father that the father was in the Fire, and called him back to add that his own father was there too[3], and another report has him ask leave to pray for his mother’s forgiveness and be refused[4]. Against his colleague Rabbi Eliezer, Rabbi Joshua held that the righteous of the nations have a share in the world to come[5], so that the rabbis disputed the line within a single generation. A pope allowed hope to the invincibly ignorant in eighteen sixty-three, and a council in nineteen sixty-four opened salvation to those ignorant of the gospel through no fault of their own[6].

The line fell where birth and date put it. Every faith that drew it has quarreled over where it falls. A sentence its own judges keep revising was written by them and handed down as the god’s. Under it stood the grandmother who prayed in another tongue and the teacher who believed nothing and taught you to think, condemned by the same accident that spared you. Whatever they were owed, they collected in this life, from the people who knew them, and the only verdict on them that anyone living can still pass is yours.

Declaration: I would stand outside with the astronomers before I would stand inside with the men who sentenced them.

The Rite · Christian

Name a great pagan the Church consigned to the fire, a lawgiver or a physician of the old world, and say grace over your next meal to them by name in place of the god. Thanks to you, and none to the god who damned you.

Testament · Whom did your faith condemn that you would trust over any council?

Sources

[1] Council of Florence, Sess. 11 (1442); DS 1351

[2] Fulgentius, De fide ad Petrum 38.79

[3] Sahih Muslim 203

[4] Sahih Muslim 976a

[5] b. Sanhedrin 105a; t. Sanhedrin 13:2

[6] Lumen Gentium 16


LV Of Honey

Indulgence

Day 55 of 365

Let no law decide what tastes defiled to you.

Samson Slays a LionGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

British kitchens have kept a dead lion in the cupboard since eighteen eighty-three. Golden syrup comes in a green and gold tin that carries the carcass with bees swarming over it, and beneath it the riddle Samson set at his wedding feast, about sweetness coming out of the strong[1]. The picture records a contact the law counted as defiling.

Samson had torn the lion apart with his bare hands on the road to Timnah[2], and told neither his father nor his mother. Going down later to his wedding, he turned aside to look at the carcass and found a swarm of bees and honey in it[3]. He scooped the honey out with his hands and ate it as he walked, and gave some to his father and mother, who ate, and he did not tell them where it came from[4]. He was a Nazirite from the womb[5], and the law made anyone who touched the carcass of a beast that walks on paws unclean[6].

His silence on the road is the one place in the honey story where the law weighs anything. One word about the carcass would have made his parents unclean in their own eyes.

Judges never collects on the carcass. Before the chapter ends the spirit of the god rushes on Samson again at Ashkelon[7], and he goes on to judge Israel twenty years[8] with the same hands. The uncleanness never traveled to the tin, since it had never lived in the honey. It lived in the word and lasted only as long as someone kept saying it. Whatever sweetness you were taught to take in secret carries no more defilement than the syrup in that tin, and it tastes the same at a table where everyone knows where it came from.

Declaration: The law can keep the carcass, and I will have the honey.

The Rite

Buy honeycomb, or the sweet you were told was too much. Eat it slowly with your fingers at your own table, in front of anyone who shares it, and give the rest to someone who has earned it. This was unclean once.

Testament · Which sweetness do you still take only where no one can see you take it?

[1] Judg 14:14

[2] Judg 14:5–6

[8] Judg 15:20


LVI Of the Concubine

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 56 of 365

Pass sentence on the book you were given.

A Levite Finds a Woman’s CorpseGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Levite’s concubine was found in the morning at the door of an old man’s house in Gibeah of Benjamin. Her hands were on the threshold[1]. The narrator gives the detail as the Levite opens the door to go on his way. He tells her to get up so they can be going. Nobody answers, and the reader, given nothing yet but her hands, has already convicted somebody.

The night before, men of the town had surrounded the house and demanded the guest, so that they could know him. The host offered them his own virgin daughter and the concubine instead, telling them to humble the women and do with them as they pleased, so long as nothing so vile was done to the man[2]. The Levite brought his concubine out to them, and they abused her all night and let her go at dawn[3]. At home he took a knife and divided her, with her bones, into twelve pieces[4], and sent them through Israel. The Hebrew does not say she was dead when he picked up the knife.

The tribes assembled, the Levite told them a version in which he never said he had put her out[5], and the war that followed nearly erased the tribe of Benjamin. Three times during that war the tribes asked the god for counsel, and three times he told them to go up[6]. In none of his answers does the woman appear.

Your revulsion at the threshold came before a word of the story behind it, and it reached a verdict the god never reached in three answers. A book that holds this chapter and is still read as his word has lost its claim on you, and the copy on your shelf is paper.

Declaration: I read that book as the tribes should have heard the Levite, a man covering for himself.

The Rite · Christian

Read the chapter of the Levite’s concubine aloud from your own Bible, say over it This book is condemned, then cut that page into twelve pieces, one for each piece sent through Israel, and drop them in the bin.

Testament · Which chapter of the book you were raised on did you discover only after you stopped trusting the pulpit?

[1] Judg 19:26–27

[2] Judg 19:22–24

[3] Judg 19:25

LVII Of Brides

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 57 of 365

Strike from your life every sexual rule a father wrote.

The Benjaminites Take the Virgins of Jabesh-gileadGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The elders of Israel had sworn at Mizpah that none of them would give a daughter to a Benjaminite[1]. Once the tribe of Benjamin was nearly exterminated they sent twelve thousand men against Jabesh-gilead with orders to kill everyone but the girls who had never lain with a man, and came back with four hundred[2]. That was not enough. The surviving Benjaminites were told to hide in the vineyards at the god’s yearly feast in Shiloh and carry off the daughters who came out to dance, and the elders promised to answer the fathers and brothers when they came to complain, since nobody had given the girls and so nobody had broken the oath[3].

Every party to that settlement was a man, down to the complaint the elders expected. The founders’ marriages in two later faiths were struck the same way. In the collection of Bukhari the Prophet asks Abu Bakr for his daughter Aisha[4], and the same collection has her married at six and taken into his house at nine[5], when he was in his fifties. Helen Mar Kimball, sealed to Joseph Smith a few months before she turned fifteen[6], wrote that her father taught her the principle and offered her to him[7].

Defenders plead the customs of the age, which concedes everything, since a revelation that only repeats the customs of its age was written by the age. Each time the bargain ran between men, the one who wanted the girl and the one who held or answered for her, and every rule about marriage and a woman’s body that descends from those bargains descends from a man’s yes. Between adults the only yes that counts belongs to the body in question, and every rule built on his falls the moment hers is asked.

Declaration: My yes was never my father’s to give.

The Rite · No faith

Print the last chapter of Judges, rewrite it turned to consent so that every girl is asked and free to say no, and read your version aloud over a meal.

Testament · Which rule about your body was settled between other people before you were asked?

[7] Helen Mar Kimball Whitney, autobiography (1881)


LVIII Of Harlots

Indulgence

Day 58 of 365

Excuse nothing in your next pleasure.

Samson Carries away the Gates of GazaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Judges gives Samson’s night in Gaza three verses. He went to Gaza, saw a prostitute there and went in to her[1], and the book tells it in the level voice it uses for his lion. The townsmen heard he was in town and lay in wait at the city gate all night[2]. He lay with the woman until midnight, then got up, took hold of the doors of the city gate and both its posts, pulled them up bar and all, and carried them to the top of the hill that faces Hebron[3].

The text passes no judgment on the visit and offers no reason for it, and the readers who came after could not leave it so. A teaching of the rabbis holds that his first wrong was done at Gaza[4] and so at Gaza he was struck down, and their Mishnah says that because Samson followed his eyes[5] the Philistines put them out. Medieval picture Bibles set Samson with the gates of Gaza on his back beside Christ rising from the tomb, so that a night with a prostitute became a picture of the Resurrection.

One reading made the night a crime and the other a sermon, and both refused what the book allowed. A long bath now arrives excused as good for the back and a rich supper as time with the family, each pleasure let in at the door only as the servant of something worthier, and each excuse you pin to your own does the commentators’ work on a night they did not spend.

Declaration: Samson owed no one a reason for Gaza, and my pleasures owe none either.

The Rite

Take the long bath or the slow supper you usually excuse, today, for no purpose but itself. If anyone asks why, give them only this. Because I wanted it.

Testament · Which pleasure do you still allow yourself only once you have found a respectable excuse for it?

[1] Judg 16:1

[2] Judg 16:2

[3] Judg 16:3

[4] b. Sotah 9b

[5] m. Sotah 1:8


LIX Of the Temple

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 59 of 365

Keep your next wish in your own hands.

The Death of SamsonGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Samson was blind and grinding at a mill[1] in the Philistine prison. They brought him out to entertain the lords of the Philistines at a sacrifice to their god Dagon[2], in a house so full that three thousand men and women were watching from the roof alone[3]. He asked the boy who led him to let him feel the pillars, and took hold of the two on which the house stood, one with each hand.

Then he called on the god to remember him and strengthen him this once, to be avenged on the Philistines for his two eyes[4], and he said, let me die with the Philistines, and pushed. The house came down on the lords and on everyone inside it, and the dead Samson killed at his death outnumbered all he had killed in his life[5]. His request named the Philistines without exception, and the roof carried the crowd, come to see a blind man made into sport[6], down with the lords.

Before you could read you were taught to address the same listener, for the sick to recover and the test to go well, and the asking survives at the edge of sleep and in the minute before the results come back. A wish put in that ear is held to the letter of its asking. At Gaza the narrator records no reply from heaven, only that the house fell on the words Samson spoke, and the letter covered three thousand people who had come for a show. Kept in your own hands, a wish can reach only as far as those hands.

Declaration: I ask no god for anything, and no crowd pays for my wishes.

The Rite · Christian

Say aloud the thing you most often ask the god for, then write on a card who it would hurt if it were granted to the letter, and do the first step of it yourself today.

Testament · What do you still ask for by reflex, and whom would it hurt if it were granted to the letter?

Sources

[1] Judg 16:21

[2] Judg 16:23–25

[3] Judg 16:27

[4] Judg 16:28

[5] Judg 16:30

[6] Judg 16:25


LX Of Confidences

Reckoning

Day 60 of 365

Judge a listener by the last secret they held.

Samson and DelilahGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Samson gave up the secret of his strength at the fourth asking, with three proofs of her purpose behind him. A wife at Timnah had once wept his riddle out of him[1] the same way and told it to her people. The lords of the Philistines had promised Delilah eleven hundred pieces of silver each[2] for it. He said seven fresh bowstrings would hold him, and she bound him with seven fresh bowstrings[3] and called the Philistines, and he snapped them. He said new ropes, and she tied him with new ropes[4]. He said to weave his seven locks into the loom, and she wove them in[5]. Every lie he told was tried on his body before she asked again.

Then she said he could not love her if he kept mocking her, and she pressed him day after day until he was sick to death of it[6], and he told her everything. She lulled him to sleep on her knees and called a man to shave his head. He woke expecting to shake himself free as before, not knowing the god had left him, and the Philistines put out his eyes[7].

She called her asking love, and the word did the work the silver paid for. Delilah kept to the terms of her bargain, and the lords came up with the silver in their hands.

Among the people who have held a secret of yours, one passed it on and another kept it for years. The first has shown what a key to you is worth in their hands. The second kept it for nothing, in a market where the Philistine lords paid eleven hundred pieces of silver each for one secret, and has earned your next one.

Declaration: Whoever sells one of my secrets has bought the last.

The Rite

Tell the one person who has kept every secret you gave them one thing you have told no one else, face to face or by voice. Then block the number of whoever spent your last secret, and take them off every list you share.

Testament · Who has had your secrets, and what did each of them do with the last one?

Sources

LXI Of Judges

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 61 of 365

Dismiss the judge you never appointed.

MinosGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto V, 1861

Minos, a king of Crete in the Greek telling, sat as judge among the dead[1], a man trying men. The court the Christian is promised has a stranger bench. The Gospel of John says the Father judges no one and has committed all judgment to the Son[2], and the First Epistle of John names the same Son as the advocate who pleads for sinners with the Father[3], so that the judge and the counsel for the defense are one person.

The Quran admits no intercession with its god except by his leave[4], so that the only advocate allowed in the room is one the bench has licensed, and it hands each person the record spread open with the order to read it, since on that day he is sufficient as his own accountant[5]. The Mishnah keeps the ledger open and the hand writing[6], with the collectors going their rounds every day and taking payment with the debtor’s consent or without it. Another saying in Avot gives a man one advocate for each commandment he keeps[7], so that the voice raised in his defense is the court’s own law.

A religious childhood installs that court in the head, where it sits long after the catechism is shut, ruling in a parent’s voice or an elder’s, with the defense still appointed by the bench. Every acquittal it grants arrives as mercy, and the accused goes home thanking the judge for sparing him a sentence the judge wrote. The office it kept from him was counsel of his own choosing, and he can take it without anyone’s leave by refusing the bench’s books along with its mercy.

Declaration: I choose who speaks for me, and I have chosen myself.

The Rite · No faith

Take the chair at the head of your table, strike the tabletop three times with a spoon for a gavel, and rule This court has no judge, and the case against me is dismissed. Then stand and walk out as one acquitted.

Testament · Whose voice does the judge in your head actually use, and what was its last ruling against you?

Sources

[1] Homer, Od. 11.568–571

[2] John 5:22

[3] 1 John 2:1

[4] Quran 2:255

[5] Quran 17:13–14

[6] m. Avot 3:16

[7] m. Avot 4:11


LXII Of the Jawbone

Mastery

Day 62 of 365

Trust the bone in reach over the forge’s price.

Samson Destroys the Philistines with an Ass’ JawboneGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

No smith was allowed anywhere in Israel[1], the first book of Samuel reports, because the Philistines reckoned that the Hebrews would otherwise make themselves swords or spears. Every farmer who wanted a plowshare, a mattock or an ax put to an edge went down to the Philistines and paid for the sharpening, at a price the book records to the fraction of a shekel[2], a third of one for the sharpening of an ax, and when the armies met at Michmash only Saul and his son Jonathan had a sword or a spear[3].

A generation or more earlier, the men of Judah had told Samson that the Philistines were their rulers[4], and handed him over at Lehi bound with two new ropes. The ropes went like flax caught by fire[5], and he found the jawbone of a donkey within reach. Judges says the bone was fresh[6]. A thousand Philistines fell to the leavings of a dead animal. The record credits the spirit of the Lord, which rushed upon him[7].

The Philistines could price every sharpened ax and could not price a dead donkey’s jaw. Judges sets the jawbone in the years of Philistine rule before Saul. Long after Lehi, Saul’s army went to Michmash with two men armed, and the weapon that had killed a thousand Philistines was cast away at a place named for it[8], Ramath-lehi, the hill of the jawbone. Their forges sold edges to a people who walked past that hill. The monopoly had no hold on a man who bent down and took what lay there.

Declaration: I make my edge from what lies at hand, and the forge has lost a customer.

The Rite

Using only what is in the house, make one thing a better-equipped rival is paid to make, a photograph, a recording, a repair. Price it below his price and offer it to one person who would have gone to him.

Testament · What do you pay someone else to do that your own hands could do today?

Sources

[1] 1 Sam 13:19

[2] 1 Sam 13:20–21

[3] 1 Sam 13:22

[4] Judg 15:11–13

LXIII Of Looking

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 63 of 365

Open the box you were told would kill you.

The Ark Is Returned to Beth-shemeshGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Two milk cows that had never worn a yoke[1] brought the ark home, lowing for their shut-up calves and never turning aside. The Philistines had sent it back after seven months of plague[2], with five golden tumors and five golden mice in a coffer[3] beside it, and the reapers of Beth-shemesh looked up from the wheat and were glad. Where the cart stopped by a great stone, they broke up its planks and offered the cows on them as a burned offering[4].

Then some of them looked inside. The god struck them for it, and the Hebrew gives the dead as seventy men and fifty thousand men[5] run together, a figure so absurd for a country town that many modern translations keep the seventy and let the rest go. The survivors sent word to Kiriath-jearim[6] to come and take it away. The book of Kings later reports that there was nothing in it but two tablets of stone[7], and the letter to the Hebrews adds a jar of manna and a rod that had budded[8].

Men died for looking at objects any temple storeroom could have held. A lock would have kept the reapers out for an afternoon, and the corpses did a lock’s work on a whole country, since the survivors asked who could stand before so holy a god and never asked what the box held.

Whatever your faith kept from your eyes, the painting it would not hang or the film it warned the young against, was guarded on the same terms, by a penalty large enough that the contents never had to be produced. The price of the look was set by the one party who knew how little was inside, and whoever looks and lives carries home the report the reapers never lived to make.

Declaration: I have looked at everything the pulpit said would damn me, and the god who guarded it never came to collect.

The Rite · Christian

Choose a film your church or your parents forbade, the one you were told would stain the eyes, and watch an hour of it with the lights up and your eyes wide open.

Testament · What do you expect to see when you finally look at what you were forbidden to look at?

LXIV Of Amalek

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 64 of 365

Read the sentence your old book passes on you.

The Death of AgagGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Samuel hewed Agag in pieces before the Lord at Gilgal[1]. The god had told Saul to strike Amalek and spare none of it, down to the camels and the asses, in payment for an ambush laid on Israel’s stragglers[2] in the wilderness. Saul killed the people and kept their king alive with the best of the cattle, so the old prophet finished the work with his own hands, on a king who had come to him saying that surely the bitterness of death was past[3].

Well over sixteen centuries later another prophet closed a siege the same way. A Jewish tribe of Medina surrendered and accepted an arbiter, who ruled that the men be killed and the women and children taken captive, and the most trusted collection of the Prophet’s sayings has him approving the verdict as the judgment of the god[4]. The earliest biography puts the trenches in the market and the men beheaded into them in batches, six or seven hundred by its count[5], and a report in another collection says the boys were sorted by whether their pubic hair had grown[6].

Both records keep the killing as a credit to the god, and Deuteronomy turns the same sword inward. The brother, the wife or the friend who secretly urges the worship of other gods[7] is to be stoned, the hearer’s own hand first upon him, and the hearer is told not to spare him in the very word Samuel used against Amalek[8], the only other verse in the Bible where it stands in that form. Saul lost his kingdom for sparing Agag[9]. A leaver whom a brother hears urging him after other gods stands in that book under the same order, and the brother’s is the hand it names to throw the first stone.

Declaration: The word that doomed Amalek was written for me too, and I strike it out wherever I find it.

The Rite · No faith

Print the verse in which Samuel hews Agag in pieces before the Lord, black out every word of it with a thick marker, and throw the page away.

Testament · How would you read your old book if you read it as the court that sentenced you?

LXV Of Staying

Reckoning

Day 65 of 365

Explain nothing to the relatives who already wrote your part.

Naomi and Her Daughters-in-LawGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Orpah kissed her mother-in-law and went home[1], and the book of Ruth never names her again. Naomi, widowed in Moab and then bereaved of both sons, had set out for Judah with her two Moabite daughters-in-law, and on the road she told them, more than once, to go back to their mothers’ houses[2] and find husbands there, since she had no more sons to give them, and both wept. Orpah took the advice. Ruth refused it in the speech weddings still borrow, your people my people and your god my god[3], and the narrative follows her to Bethlehem, to a rich kinsman, and through her son to a great-grandson named David[4].

What Orpah went back to was her mother’s house, her own people and her own gods[5], and what she gave up was a dead husband’s mother who had released her and asked nothing back. The book gives her no speech of her own. Her one line is spoken in chorus with Ruth, that they would go on with Naomi to her people, before Naomi talked them out of it.

The rabbis could not leave a silent woman alone. The Talmud made her the mother of Goliath and his three giant brothers, paid out, it says, for the four tears she shed at parting[6], and another passage has David’s nephew Abishai kill her[7]. The book gave her no reason, and the four giants of her line fell to Ruth’s great-grandson David, while the one speech the Talmud gives her asks a young man to bring her spindle.

Declaration: I left with a kiss, and every line my family adds to the story is its own.

The Rite

Hug the relative who let you go with no terms, tell them in a dozen words what you left or changed, and leave the story there. Answer nothing the others send about it.

Testament · Which relative let you go without a sermon, and what do they deserve to hear from you?

LXVI Of Heresy

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 66 of 365

Spend here what you set aside for heaven.

The Tombs of the HereticsGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto X, 1861

A council sitting in Rome in fifteen thirteen condemned as heresy the proposition that the human soul dies with the body, and its bull says the error was being scattered in its own day. Every professor of philosophy who taught the old authorities was ordered to refute it from the lectern[1]. A doctrine given such a guard is one the opposite keeps occurring to, and in the lecture halls of Italy it was occurring often enough to bring the bishops out.

The opposite is old. The Sadducees, the priestly party of the Temple in Jerusalem, held that there was no resurrection[2], and the gospels show them baiting Jesus with a riddle about a widow married to seven brothers in turn[3]. The rabbis’ earliest code answered with a penalty, that whoever denies the resurrection of the dead loses his portion in the life to come[4], a threat that can only frighten the man who already believes it.

Everything promised for the hereafter was paid for here, in the tithe and the fast, the pleasure deferred until it could be had without sin. The sellers took payment in years and promised delivery in a country from which no account has ever come back to be audited. The self is a body and what the body does, and when it stops there is no remainder left to collect on.

A sentence spoken to a living ear outweighs any credit banked in heaven, and one dinner at a table where the people you love are still alive outweighs the whole wedding supper of the Lamb[5].

Declaration: I mean to use this body up before the worms get it, and no priest will bless the leftovers.

The Rite · Christian

Say aloud The soul dies with the body. Then eat well today with the money you once would have put in the plate, and say over the first mouthful This is my body, and this is its only life.

Testament · To whom could you say today what you have been saving for some hereafter?

Sources

[1] Lateran V, Sess. 8, Apostolici regiminis (19 Dec 1513)

[2] Acts 23:8

[3] Mark 12:18–23

[4] m. Sanhedrin 10:1

[5] Rev 19:9


LXVII Of the Threshing Floor

Indulgence

Day 67 of 365

Ask for it yourself instead of waiting to be told.

Ruth and BoazGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Wash yourself, Naomi told Ruth, anoint yourself and put on your best clothes, and go down to the threshing floor, and do not let the man see you until he has finished eating and drinking. When he lies down, note the place, go in, uncover his feet, and lie down there[1]. Boaz had already told his young men to drop handfuls among the sheaves on purpose[2] for the widow to find. At midnight he woke with a start to find a woman lying at his feet, a word some scholars read as a euphemism for the genitals[3]. He sent her home before dawn with six measures of barley and the instruction that nobody should know a woman had come to the floor[4].

To defend David’s descent from a Moabite woman, the Talmud ruled that the law shutting Moab out of the assembly binds only its men[5], since Moab’s women were never expected to come out with bread, and it proved the point with a psalm, the king’s daughter is all glorious within[6]. The king’s great-grandmother was saved by a doctrine that women stay indoors, and she had gone out at midnight to a man’s bed.

Naomi’s plan ended with the man in charge, he will tell you what to do[7]. Ruth threw that line away. She told him what to do, spread your garment over me[8], the book’s idiom for a proposal of marriage, and he promised in the dark to do all she asked[9]. A man who drops barley on purpose has the desire without the nerve, and a woman who waits on him hands her life to his nerve. Israel’s greatest king descends from that sentence, said at midnight to a man who had gone to sleep at the end of the heap of grain[10].

Declaration: I go down to the floor anointed and ask, and a refusal costs me one night’s sleep.

The Rite

Put on the scent you wear best and ask whoever has signaled interest in you, once and in so many words, for exactly what you want. Take the answer as given, and if it is yes, take your time.

Testament · What have you been waiting for someone to offer that you could ask for tonight?

LXVIII Of Evil Spirits

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 68 of 365

Feed what your faith called a demon.

Saul Attempts to Kill DavidGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

When the army came home, the women of every town sang that Saul had slain his thousands and David his ten thousands[1], and Saul was very angry and eyed David from that day on[2]. The next day an evil spirit from the god came upon Saul[3], and he raved in the house while David played the lyre as he did every day, and Saul, spear in hand, threw it to pin the young man to the wall. David slipped aside twice[4].

The chapter gives the cause and then the spirit, in that order and a day apart. The envy came out of a song and the spirit came the next day, so that one spear has two authors on the page, a jealous man and a visitor from heaven, and only one of them can be made to answer for it.

The gospels give a boy who falls into fire and water to a spirit and cure him by rebuking it[5], and deliverance ministries still cast out spirits of lust and rage by name, so that the lust and the rage belong to a lodger who can be evicted by command, and the person is cleared of both. The eviction cannot feed them.

His servants had once prescribed a lyre[6], and the lyre served until the player became the rival, after which the spear went at the music. Whatever you were taught to cast out answers to your name. Owned, it is a hunger that can be fed, and disowned it is a spirit that throws spears.

Declaration: Whoever calls my hunger a demon has an exorcism to sell, and I would rather pay for dinner.

The Rite · No faith

Play an album the churches once burned at record bonfires as the devil’s music, start to finish, as loud as your walls allow, and play the loudest track twice for the god who was said to hate it.

Testament · What does the appetite you were taught to call a spirit actually want?

[2] 1 Sam 18:8–9

LXIX Of Stones

Mastery

Day 69 of 365

Fight with the weapon you have already tested.

David Slays GoliathGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Saul put his own armor on David, the bronze helmet and the coat of mail. David belted the king’s sword over it and tried to walk, then said he could not go in these, since he had never tested them[1], and took them off again in front of the king. He went down to the brook and chose five smooth stones, put them in his shepherd’s bag, and walked out with his staff and his sling.

Goliath carried a coat of mail weighing five thousand shekels of bronze[2] and a spear with a shaft like a weaver’s beam, its iron point alone six hundred shekels, and all of it belonged to a man too loaded to get out of the way of a stone. David had no sword in his hand[3]. He cut off the giant’s head with Goliath’s own.

Goliath had presented himself morning and evening for forty days[4], and for forty days Israel’s army stood in its ranks and listened. Saul promised riches and a daughter to whoever would go, and when a shepherd went, he buckled his own bronze onto him. Whoever passes down the method he rose by passes down gear the next man has never tested, and this gear had gone forty days without once being tried against the giant.

The giant fell to a smooth stone out of a brook, sunk in his forehead, thrown by a shepherd in his own coat. The victory went into the record under a sling, with the king asking afterward whose son had thrown the stone[5].

Declaration: Untested bronze stays on the peg. I go out in what I have proved.

The Rite

Delete or shred your own copy of the template, script or plan someone above you handed you to work from, then do today’s piece of the work your own way and put your name on it where the one who handed it down will see.

Testament · What were you handed to fight in that you have never once tested?

[1] 1 Sam 17:38–39

[2] 1 Sam 17:5–7
