LXX Of Necromancy

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 70 of 365

Owe your loyalty to whoever fed you.

Saul and the Witch of EndorGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The mediums and the wizards had been put out of the land by Saul himself[1]. Then the Philistines gathered for war, and Saul was afraid, and his heart shook. He asked the Lord what to do, and the Lord answered him neither by dreams, nor by the sacred lots, nor by prophets[2], so the king disguised himself and went by night to a woman who could raise the dead. She suspected a trap. He swore to her by the Lord, the same Lord who would not speak to him, that no punishment would come of it, and she brought up Samuel, rising out of the earth like a god[3].

The prophet was annoyed to be disturbed. He told Saul that the kingdom was given to David and that by the next day Saul and his sons would be with him among the dead[4]. Saul fell full length on the ground, and the record adds that he had no strength in him, because he had eaten nothing all that day and all that night. Then the woman told the king he must eat, and she and his servants pressed him until he got up off the floor. She killed the fatted calf she had and kneaded flour and baked unleavened bread[5], and set it before him, and he ate, and went out to die in the hills.

Heaven answered Saul with silence and the dead prophet with a death sentence. Supper came from the woman the law had outlawed, cooked for the king who had outlawed her, and the Chronicler later counted the visit among the reasons Saul died[6]. The book that kept every word the dead prophet said never kept her name.

Declaration: My loyalty goes where the bread came from, and no law that banned the cook can call it back.

The Rite · No faith

Hold a seance at your kitchen table and call on the god of Saul. When he answers as he answered Saul, by no dream, no lot and no prophet, tell him the line is closed, then thank aloud the one who fed you instead.

Testament · Who fed you after your faith had warned you against them?

LXXI Of Popes

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 71 of 365

Strip off the title and judge the man.

The Tomb of Pope AnastasiusGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XI, 1861

A pope put a corpse on trial[1] in the year eight hundred ninety-seven. Stephen the Sixth had Formosus, pope before him but one, dug up, dressed in his vestments and propped on a throne in the cathedral of Rome, with a deacon beside it to answer the charges. The dead man was convicted. They cut off the three fingers of his right hand that he had used to bless, stripped him, and threw what was left into the Tiber. Stephen was deposed within months and strangled in prison, and Theodore the Second had the body, recovered from the river, reburied in Saint Peter’s in its vestments[2]. John the Ninth annulled the trial[3], and Sergius the Third upheld it again. The papal chronicle did as much for Anastasius the Second, whose sudden death it called a stroke from the god[4] for his dealings with the eastern church.

Canon law still holds that the first see is judged by no one[5], and its own holders judged it three times within a dozen years, convicting the dead man, clearing him and convicting him again. Office was supposed to carry a respect that did not depend on the man underneath, and in those years the popes paid it or withheld it by faction. In two thousand eighteen a grand jury in Pennsylvania reported more than three hundred predator priests[6] in six dioceses, and bishops who had moved them from parish to parish and called the removals sick leave, while the files sat in what the dioceses themselves called secret archives.

A respect the popes themselves dug up and reburied as it suited them is owed by nobody outside the palace. The man in the vestments is owed what any stranger is owed for the same conduct, and for the conduct the grand jury recorded, a stranger gets a prosecutor.

Declaration: No vestment on a man buys my silence about what he did in it.

The Rite · No faith

Print a photograph of a cardinal in full scarlet, cut away everything but his face and hands, and pin up what is left with his plain name written under it in your hand.

Testament · Which title still makes you lower your voice, and what has the person wearing it done to deserve that?

[1] Acts of John IX’s synods of Rome and Ravenna, 898 (on the synod held by Stephen VI)

[2] Liber Pontificalis, Life of Theodore II

[3] Synods of Rome and Ravenna, 898; Auxilius, In defensionem papae Formosi

[4] Liber Pontificalis, Life of Anastasius II

[5] CIC can. 1404

[6] Pa. 40th Statewide Investigating Grand Jury, Report I (14 Aug 2018)


LXXII Of Love

Indulgence

Day 72 of 365

Love openly, and let the spear-thrower keep his table.

David and JonathanGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jonathan stripped off his own robe and put it on David, with his armor, his sword, his bow and his belt[1]. It was the day his soul was knit to David’s, and the text says he loved him as his own soul. He was the king’s son and the heir. At a feast of the new moon his father turned on him, told him he had chosen the son of Jesse to his own shame and to the shame of his mother’s nakedness[2], and threw a spear at him[3].

Saul gave his reason in the same breath. As long as the son of Jesse lived on the earth, he said, neither Jonathan nor his kingdom would be established[4]. Jonathan rose from the table in fierce anger and ate nothing that day[5]. In the morning he walked out to the field where David was hiding, shot the arrows they had agreed on as a signal[6], sent the boy back to the city with his weapons, and went to the man his father wanted dead. They kissed and wept together, David the longer[7], and years afterward David’s lament for him called his love wonderful, passing the love of women[8].

The spear was thrown for an inheritance, and queer children of believing families know that meal, where the son’s love is the threat to every portion. In the wilderness of Ziph, Saul’s son went to David in the woods and told him that he would be king over Israel and Jonathan second to him[9], and that Saul his father knew it too. The heir gave the crown away with his own mouth and went home[10]. The book has him dead on Gilboa[11] beside the man who threw the spear, and the narrator never calls the love a mistake.

Declaration: Call it my mother’s shame. It is the best thing I ever chose.

The Rite

Give the person you love something of yours that you have worn, a jacket, a ring, a belt, as Jonathan gave David his robe, and watch them put it on. Keep it. I will not ask for it back.

Testament · Whom do you love that some father would throw a spear over?

LXXIII Of Messengers

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 73 of 365

Call this world good to its face.

The Messenger from HeavenGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto IX, 1861

Before he was pope, Innocent the Third wrote a treatise on the misery of the human condition. It walks the body from conception to corpse with a connoisseur’s disgust, through the seed it comes from, the filth it lives in and the worms that finish it. Copies survive in hundreds[1], under a second title, On the Contempt of the World. The Salve Regina, sung at the close of the monastic day for the better part of a thousand years, calls the place a valley of tears[2].

A letter ascribed to John tells its readers to love neither the world nor the things in it[3], and the letter of James calls friendship with the world enmity with the god[4]. Worldly became an insult and carnal a diagnosis, every pleasure of the body was entered from the pulpit as a debt to be worked off, and the monks who took vows to leave it all called their calling flight from the world[5].

Malachi calls the priest the messenger of the Lord of hosts[6], with the Hebrew word that elsewhere names an angel, and the Church’s priests, who took the title for themselves, carried the contempt down to the parishes and came back with a tenth of everything the contemptible earth grew. In England, when a man died, the parish priest led off his second-best beast as a mortuary, the earth he had preached against following him home on a halter. An institution that holds its nose at the only life a person will ever have, while its hand stays out for the harvest, has forfeited any claim on your manners, and its messengers can be walked to the gate without the beast.

Declaration: Worldly is the best thing anyone ever called me, and I had it from a pulpit.

The Rite · Christian

Say the song of the angels over the manger, glory to God in the highest and on earth peace, and then put it in the right order. Glory on earth, and none in the highest.

Testament · What do you love that the insult you were taught for this world was meant to shame?

Sources

[1] Lotario dei Segni, De miseria condicionis humane, ed. R. E. Lewis (1978)

[2] Salve Regina (Liturgia Horarum, Completorium)

[3] 1 John 2:15

[4] Jas 4:4

[5] fuga mundi

[6] Mal 2:7


LXXIV Of Windows

Mastery

Day 74 of 365

Keep the truth from anyone who watches your door.

David Escapes through a WindowGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A household god lay in David’s bed on the night he escaped, with a net of goat’s hair at its head[1] and a cloth pulled over it. Saul’s men were watching the door, with orders to kill him in the morning[2]. His wife Michal, Saul’s daughter, warned him that if he did not save his life that night he would be dead by the next day, and let him down through a window[3], and he fled. Then she dressed the idol as a sick husband. When the messengers came, she told them David was ill, and Saul sent back word to bring him in the bed so that he could kill him in it.

The household idol, which the text records without comment, did more for David that night than the god of Israel, who goes unmentioned in the whole account. The rest was a lie. Questioned afterward by her father about why she had deceived him and let his enemy go, Michal said that David had threatened to kill her[4], and the book records no punishment for her.

Michal knew her father, and a leaver from a house that punishes apostasy knows hers the same way. Pew counted twenty-two countries with laws against apostasy in two thousand nineteen[5], and a family needs no court to stop the allowance and take the phone. A family that keeps watch on the door has given up its claim to the truth about the bed, and it gets what Saul got, a believer at prayer in the evening and, by morning, the passport and the savings already gone out through the window.

Declaration: I got out by a lie and a dressed-up idol, and I would use both again.

The Rite

Put a little cash somewhere your family never looks, and spend some of it today on something they forbid, enjoyed where they will never see it.

Testament · If your family looked closer, what would they find behind the shape they expect?

Sources

[1] 1 Sam 19:13

[2] 1 Sam 19:11

[3] 1 Sam 19:12

[4] 1 Sam 19:17

[5] Pew Research Center, Four-in-ten countries had blasphemy laws, 25 Jan 2022


LXXV Of Sin

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 75 of 365

Let men look, and keep their looking off your account.

Satan Meets Sin and Death at the GateGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book II, 1866

A North African father of the Church, writing on how women ought to dress, told them they were the devil’s gateway[1]. They were, he went on, the first deserters of the divine law, and for their desert even the Son of God had to die. Sin was drawn female long before he wrote. A wisdom book of the Catholic Bible has sin begin with a woman and death come to all because of her[2], and the first letter to Timothy clears Adam of being deceived and lays the deception on the woman[3].

The remedy prescribed was cloth. Paul told the church at Corinth that a woman who prayed with her head uncovered dishonored her head[4] and might as well be shorn, since she is the glory of the man. A verse addressed to the Prophet’s wives, his daughters and the believing women tells them to draw their cloaks about them so that they will be known and left unmolested[5]. A rabbi of the Talmud went past the cloth to the voice and ruled a woman’s singing voice nakedness[6]. Paul covered her for the man’s glory and the later rules for what the man would see and hear, and each time the woman answered for him.

A grown woman who covers because she wants to has made a decision about her own head. The girls put into it before they could decide were handed something else, the conscience of every man they would ever pass, strapped on before they could read the verses that put it there. When the cloth comes off, on whatever day the wearer picks, an afternoon or a decade from now, the conscience goes back where it was born, behind the eyes of the men in the street.

Declaration: If a woman is the devil’s gateway, I hold the door open.

The Rite · Christian

Read aloud Paul’s rule to Corinth that a woman must cover her head to pray, then read it again with your head the way Paul forbade, a woman bareheaded and a man in a hat. My head is my own.

Testament · Which modesty rule do you keep only for someone else’s conscience?

Sources

[1] Tertullian, Cult. fem. 1.1.2

[2] Sir 25:24

[3] 1 Tim 2:14

[4] 1 Cor 11:5–7

[5] Quran 33:59

LXXVI Of Mercy

Reckoning

Day 76 of 365

Read a second confession as evidence.

David Shows Saul How He Spared His LifeGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

David brought one corner of cloth out of the cave at En-gedi. Saul, out hunting him with three thousand chosen men[1], had gone in to relieve himself, and David crept up from further back and cut it from the king’s robe[2], and his heart smote him afterward for doing even that much to the Lord’s anointed. He bowed to the ground and held the cloth up, and Saul wept and said David was more righteous than he[3].

Two chapters later Saul was hunting him again with three thousand men. David went by night into the camp at Hachilah, where the king lay asleep inside a ring of soldiers, and carried off the spear planted in the ground at his head[4] and the jug of water beside it. He showed them from a hilltop far off, and this time Saul said in plain words that he had sinned, called himself a fool[5], and promised to do David no more harm.

Saul had confessed twice, to repaying good with evil and then to sin, and the first had held only until the Ziphites told him[6] where David was hiding. After the second, David said in his heart that one day he would perish by the hand of Saul, and took his six hundred men to the Philistines at Gath. When Saul was told where David had gone, he sought him no more[7].

A second apology for the same injury, from the brother with the borrowed money or the parent with the old cruelty, is the sequel to the first and the notice of the third. Whoever makes it has learned that confessing costs less than changing, and the one who keeps listening pays the difference. David stopped listening, and the next verses find him in Ziklag, a town of his own[8], given him by a Philistine king.

Declaration: Tears are the cheapest coin a man carries, and I have stopped making change for them.

The Rite

Choose one thing the twice-sorry person still gets from you, a lift, a loan, a weekly call, and end it today without explanation. Write their apology on a slip and burn it. I heard you the first time.

Testament · Who has apologized to you twice for the same harm, and what did either apology cost them?

LXXVII Of Walls

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 77 of 365

Guard your door as the god guards his gate.

The Walls of DisGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VIII, 1861

As the gates of Jerusalem began to grow dark before the Sabbath, Nehemiah ordered them shut[1] and set his own servants on them so that no load could come in. The merchants lodged outside the wall once or twice. He warned them, asked why they were lodging against the wall, and said that if they did it again he would lay hands on them[2]. From that time, the book says, they came no more on the Sabbath.

In Ezekiel’s vision of the temple the god keeps his own gate shut too. Ezekiel is shown the east gate of the sanctuary[3] and told that it shall stay shut and no man shall enter by it, because the Lord has entered by it, and a few lines later every uncircumcised foreigner is barred[4] from the place, uncircumcised in heart or in flesh.

Luke has Jesus send seventy out two by two[5], to stay in whatever house would have them and not go from house to house, and to wipe the dust of an unwelcoming town off their feet against it. The Latter-day Saints send missionaries up your path and admit no one to a dedicated temple without a recommend. A faith that bars the stranger from its own sanctuary and sends its callers to your door has made clear which gates it counts as holy, and yours is not among them. The householder owes it the courtesy it demands for its own, the bolt drawn and the rule given once at the threshold, with the caller who stays after being told to go treated as the law already treats him, a trespasser.

Declaration: A holy city shut its gates at dusk, and my house is holier to me than the city was.

The Rite · Christian

Read aloud the verse in Revelation in which Jesus stands at the door and knocks, then bolt your front door from inside and answer him. This house is mine. Go away.

Testament · Who still holds a key to your house or your hours that you never handed them?

Sources

[2] Neh 13:20–21

LXXVIII Of the Rock

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 78 of 365

Refuse the verdict, and enter what it barred.

Moses Strikes the Rock at HorebGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

At Rephidim the god told Moses to strike a rock with his staff, and water came out. Nearly forty years later, at Kadesh, the people were thirsty and complaining again, and this time Moses was to take the staff and speak to the rock[1]. Moses and Aaron gathered them, Moses called them rebels, asked whether he and Aaron must fetch them water out of this rock, and struck it twice[2]. The water came all the same.

The punishment followed at once, and the ground the god gave for it was the eyes of the people. Because the brothers had not believed in him enough to sanctify him before the assembly, neither would bring it into the land[3]. Deuteronomy restates the charge as a trespass committed in the midst of Israel[4], a psalm blames the people for provoking Moses into rash words[5], and Moses himself says three times that the god was angry with him[6] on their account. The rabbis have argued ever since about the sin, the striking or the temper[7].

Numbers records no casualty, since the people drank. Where the god spells the injury out, at Kadesh, in Numbers 27 and in Deuteronomy 32[8], it is his standing before the assembly, the holiness Moses failed to show the crowd, and for that he took from an old man the land he had walked toward for forty years.

The old man begged to be let across and was told to speak no more of it[9]. He went up Nebo and died there[10] looking at the land. A raised conscience still bars its owner from his own country for faults of that kind, a doubt said aloud or a body enjoyed, and whatever it has kept you from, the career or the love you thought forfeited, lies across an unguarded Jordan.

Declaration: No god’s bruised pride stands between me and anything I want.

The Rite · No faith

Lay a hand on a Bible, or the heaviest book you own, name aloud the thing an old verdict barred you from, and swear to have it. I swear it on my own name.

Testament · Which fault that harmed no one still keeps you out of something you want?

LXXIX Of Monsters

Beauty

Day 79 of 365

Give your eyes back to the shapes you were taught to fear.

The Monsters of HellGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book II, 1866

The masons who built the cathedrals of Europe carved their rainspouts as horned and scaly beasts that grin with mouths stretched wide for the gutters. The Church that paid for them filled its pictures of hell with the same crowd, serpents with wings and fiends with too many mouths, and carved them over its west doors in the stone of the Last Judgment, where the congregation passed under them every Sunday on the way in.

At the close of Job the god, having refused to tell a ruined man why he was ruined, spends a long chapter on Leviathan, whose scales are shut up together as with a close seal[1] and whose eyes are like the eyelids of the morning[2], and declines to keep silent about its comely proportion[3]. Leviticus records his other taste. The law bars from the altar any descendant of Aaron with a blemish[4], the blind and the lame, the man with a flat nose or a limb too long, the hunchback and the dwarf[5]. Such a man may eat the holy bread, provided he keeps away from the veil[6].

The god admired the proportions of a sea monster and could not bear a dwarf at his altar, and he kept the first taste for himself and handed his worshipers the second. A long look takes the first taste back. The scales of the winged thing you were raised to flinch from lie in rows like chain mail, the horn curves from the brow with the polish of a fingernail, and the flinch, held long enough, turns into appetite, first for the shape and then for every body the old law kept back from the veil, until it reaches the one in your own mirror.

Declaration: Leviathan has the god’s admiration and mine, and the dwarf has mine alone.

The Rite

Buy, print or draw a picture of a creature you were raised to call monstrous, scaled, horned or winged, frame it, and hang it in the best-lit place in the room where you sleep.

Testament · What in your own body were you taught to count a blemish, and who taught you?

Sources

[1] Job 41:15

[2] Job 41:18

[3] Job 41:12

[4] Lev 21:17

[5] Lev 21:18–20

[6] Lev 21:22–23


LXXX Of Jealousy

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 80 of 365

Put the jealous one’s rivals where he can see them.

An Angel Appears to the IsraelitesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Lord, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous god[1], Exodus says, and gives it as the reason his people must break the altars and cut down the sacred poles[2] of the peoples whose land they enter. In Judges an angel of the Lord comes up from Gilgal to a place called Bochim[3] to collect on the order, and his complaint is that the altars are still standing.

A god secure in his uniqueness would have no reason to be jealous. The commandment that forbids rivals presupposes them. Storage jars from a desert waystation in the Sinai, from around eight hundred before the common era, ask blessing by the Lord and by his Asherah[4], and a list of temple dues from the Jewish garrison at Elephantine on the Nile, four centuries later, divides the silver among three gods[5], with nearly as much going to a goddess called Anat-Bethel as to the god of Israel.

Jealousy at that pitch is a confession that the offer would lose a comparison. When Josiah purged the temple, Kings has him carry out vessels made for Baal and for Asherah[6] from inside the house of the Lord, and pull down the rooms beside it where women wove hangings for the goddess[7]. The one god of Israel was imposed by a king’s purge on worshipers who, left to themselves, had kept a goddess at his elbow, and two centuries after Josiah the garrison on the Nile was still paying her.

The same note sounds in a church that calls your other loves idols and in a partner who reads your messages and resents your friends. Whoever needs to be the only love in a life has to clear out the others to get there, and every friend he resents and you keep is a loom still working beside the temple.

Declaration: I keep several loves, and the only one I have thrown out is the jealous one.

The Rite · Christian

Set a small figure of an old god, Pan or Dionysus, or a drawing of one, on the shelf where a cross once stood, and leave it there for good.

Testament · What have you given up to keep calm the one who demands to be your only loyalty?

LXXXI Of Contempt

Reckoning

Day 81 of 365

Spend your contempt on the office and its deed.

Filippo ArgentiGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VIII, 1861

Amos called the rich women of Samaria cows of Bashan[1]. They crush the needy, he said, and tell their husbands to bring them drink, and they will be hauled out through the breaches in the wall on hooks. Luke has Jesus, warned that Herod meant to kill him, send word back to that fox[2], and Paul told the Galatians he wished the men unsettling them would go the whole way with the knife and, on the usual reading, castrate themselves[3].

The psalm that marvels at being fearfully and wonderfully made[4] has its singer, near the end, hating the god’s enemies with a perfect hatred[5] and counting them his own. Every one of these insults has an address, and every one is answering a deed. Amos himself turned from the women of Samaria to Bethel with the words come to Bethel, and transgress[6], an address of its own.

The Church handed the pew the Sermon on the Mount’s love for enemies and prayer for persecutors[7]. The older law had put the two in order. Leviticus forbids hating your brother in your heart[8] and in the same verse commands you to rebuke your neighbor, and only in the next does it forbid the grudge and ask for love[9].

Contempt with a name and a deed attached is the scriptural kind, the kind the prophets spoke aloud and the law turned into rebuke. Hatred kept in the heart, the only kind the pew was left and the kind Leviticus forbids, has no one to be said to and no place to end.

Declaration: My contempt has an address and a deed, and I owe that office no respect.

The Rite

Write the name of an institution or office whose deed you despise and, beneath it, what it did. Read both aloud in an empty room, say Contempt is owed here, and pin the page to a wall for a day before you bin it.

Testament · Which office or institution has your contempt by right of what it did, and what act of yours would finish it?

LXXXII Of Relics

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 82 of 365

Throw out the object you are afraid to throw out.

The Paradise of FoolsGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book III, 1866

Two merchants of Venice carried Saint Mark[1] out of Alexandria in the ninth century in a basket under a layer of pork, trusting the Muslim officials of the port to recoil from searching it. Venice celebrated the theft and built a basilica over the corpse. The evangelist, packed in with the meat, did nothing to the men who took him, and the city that stole him put his lion on its flag.

Thomas Becket lay behind the high altar at Canterbury from twelve twenty, in a shrine plated with gold and set with jewels[2], and pilgrims carried home water tinged with his blood. A window beside the shrine still tells how a Yorkshire knight, Jordan son of Eisulf[3], revived his dead boy with that water and promised the martyr four pieces of silver, and the next panels show another son dying because the silver came late. Every kneeling pilgrim walked past a picture of what the saint did to slow payers. In fifteen thirty-eight the king’s commissioners broke up the shrine and carted off its jewels[4], and the saint did nothing to them either.

In these three stories the relic’s anger falls only on the man who believed he owed it. Thieves who stole one saint and a king who stripped another went unharmed, and the knight who believed lost a son for being slow. A rosary kept in a drawer long after belief has left, because throwing it away still feels dangerous, is held there by the debt the window was glazed to teach, and that feeling is the object’s only power. A household that throws its last blessed bead in the trash joins the merchants of Venice and the king’s men, among whom the record counts no dead sons.

Declaration: What stays in my house stays because I like it, and every blessed thing I owned failed that test long ago.

The Rite · No faith

Find the lucky object you keep and would be uneasy to lose, a charm, a coin, a ring, and throw it in the trash today.

Testament · What harm do you expect from parting with the sacred object you still own?

Sources

[1] Translatio Sancti Marci (Venice, 828 or 829)

[2] Canterbury, translation of Becket to the Trinity Chapel shrine (1220)

[3] William of Canterbury, Miracula S. Thomae; Canterbury Cathedral, Trinity Chapel window n.II

[4] Canterbury, 1538 (dissolution of the monasteries)


LXXXIII Of Lust

Indulgence

Day 83 of 365

Do what the confessor asked about, and enjoy it.

The Whirlwind of the LustfulGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto V, 1861

The confessors’ manuals of the late Middle Ages gave the priest page after page of questions on the sins of the flesh. They were prepared for every estate of life, the married along with the rest, and asked about positions and forbidden seasons and pleasure sought for its own sake[1]. The man putting the questions was bound by his orders never to marry, and the manuals that warned him not to teach a sin by naming it still walked him down the list with a wife kneeling before him, until her marriage bed had been described aloud to someone who would never have one.

The evangelical purity movement had no Latin and no celibate, and drew up its own list. It handed teenagers pledge cards to sign and rings to wear until a wedding, and taught that every touch stood on a slope toward intercourse, so that a generation learned the map of its own body from the warnings posted along it. Both systems trained a small alarm that sounds at the first touch, and both called it conscience.

The alarm has authors. The first wrote in Latin and would never marry, and the second ran the youth rally. The questions ran one way, and the answers went home with the man who asked them. In many people raised under either list, what rings in a grown body at a lover’s hand is a list someone else drew up, still running in flesh its authors never owned. A body that knows whose voice the alarm uses can treat it as it would a stranger found at the bedroom door, and put him out.

Declaration: I take my pleasures without a chaperone, living or six hundred years dead.

The Rite

Take one pleasure the purity talk or the confessor’s list warned you against, alone or with a consenting adult, and take it slowly to the end. If you hear the old voice, say You were never invited and carry on.

Testament · Which pleasure did the alarm first sound against, and who taught you to hear it?

Sources

[1] Tentler, Sin and Confession on the Eve of the Reformation (1977), ch. 4


LXXXIV Of Hail

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 84 of 365

Say the unforgivable sentence aloud, once, in your own voice.

The Army of the Amorites Is DestroyedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Five Amorite kings fled down the slope of Beth-horon toward Azekah, and the Lord threw great stones from heaven on them all the way. More of them died of the hail, the book of Joshua says, than the Israelites killed with the sword[1]. A child taught that one sentence is the sin never forgiven builds a sky like that over the sentence and keeps it loaded.

Mark names it. Every sin of the sons of men shall be forgiven, the gospel says, and every blasphemy but one, the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which has no forgiveness ever[2]. The occasion follows in the next breath, the scribes having said Jesus had an unclean spirit. Murder falls inside the pardon. The one sin kept past the reach of repentance is a sentence about the god, and it costs nobody a hair.

Gideon pulled down his father’s altar to Baal by night and cut the grove beside it, and when the town demanded his death his father Joash told them that if Baal was a god he could plead for himself[3]. Gideon lived, and the town called him Jerubbaal, let Baal plead against him. The book counts the living man as the verdict on Baal.

Joash’s rule convicts the tradition that taught you the unforgivable sentence. A god with power pleads for himself, and a god whose honor is guarded by a child’s terror has handed his case to the child. The hail at Beth-horon fell once, in a book, on men running for their lives, and by the measure of Judges everyone who has since said the sentence and lived to eat breakfast carries Gideon’s second name.

Declaration: Let the Holy Spirit plead for himself, since I have given him the occasion and my address.

The Rite · Christian

Go outside after dark, as Gideon went to his father’s altar, and say under the open sky The Holy Spirit is an unclean spirit, the one sentence Mark puts past forgiveness. Stand there a full minute, then go in and eat the richest dessert in the house.

Testament · How did your body answer when you came near the words you were taught could never be forgiven?

Sources

[1] Josh 10:11

[2] Mark 3:22, 28–30

[3] Judg 6:25–32


LXXXV Of the Desert

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 85 of 365

Quit any discipline that measures your virtue by your torment.

The Temptation of Saint AnthonyJacques Callot, 1635

Bread and salt, once a day after sunset and sometimes once in two days or four, was what Antony of Egypt allowed his body. He had given away his inheritance[1], and lived later among the tombs and then in the desert. He slept on a rush mat or on bare ground and would not oil his skin[2]. The devils came. Athanasius of Alexandria, who wrote his life, says they appeared as a woman at night[3], beat him so badly in his tomb that a friend carried him out for dead[4], and came back as lions and bears and as serpents and scorpions.

Matthew knew what a fast breeds, since the devil’s first offer to the starving Jesus is bread[5]. In nineteen forty-four, at the University of Minnesota, thirty-six young men who had refused to bear arms volunteered to live for six months on about half their usual food[6]. Within weeks they were dreaming of food, collecting recipes, reading cookbooks and licking their plates clean. The regimen produced the obsession on schedule, in ordinary men with no saint among them.

Athanasius offered the devils as proof of Antony’s holiness, and the artists who came after measured the saint by the crowd in his sky, until he shrinks into a corner of his own temptation. The sky in the etching is a portrait of bread and salt once a day. A discipline that presents the torment it causes as proof that it works cannot fail by its own reckoning, since every new devil is scored as progress and the starving man is told he is winning, and he goes on winning until a friend carries him out of his tomb for dead.

Declaration: Whatever I starve grows horns, so I keep a full table.

The Rite · Christian

Eat, in one sitting, a feast of everything Antony refused, meat and butter and sweet things and the richest cream or chocolate drink you love, slowly and until you are fully satisfied.

Testament · What need have you starved for so long that it now visits you as a temptation?

Sources

[1] Athanasius, Vit. Ant. 2–3

[2] Athanasius, Vit. Ant. 7

[3] Athanasius, Vit. Ant. 5

[4] Athanasius, Vit. Ant. 8

[5] Matt 4:3

[6] Keys et al., The Biology of Human Starvation (1950)


LXXXVI Of Disdain

Mastery

Day 86 of 365

Keep your eyes level before anyone who would shame you.

Farinata RisesGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto X, 1861

Acts lists the bench by name, Annas the high priest and Caiaphas and John and Alexander[1] and the rest of the high priest’s family, the house that had handed Jesus over to Pilate[2] not long before. In front of them stood Peter and John, held overnight[3] for preaching in the temple[4] after healing a lame man at its gate[5]. The question put to them was by what power, or by what name, they had done it.

Peter told the rulers and elders that the man stood whole by the name of the one they had crucified[6], so that the accused charged the court with a killing in its own chamber. The council saw their boldness, Acts says, perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, and marveled[7]. Ordered never again to speak in that name, the two told the council to judge for itself whether God wanted them to obey men in place of him[8], and after more threats they were let go. A court reduced to marveling at the accused has stopped doing the work of a court.

The engraving above shows a damned man risen to the waist from a burning tomb, holding hell in contempt. Every accusation carries the accuser’s standing inside it, and an answer given with lowered eyes grants that standing before it disputes a word. Peter gave them their titles and then named their deed. Whoever shames you for a body or a pleasure that harmed no one is asking by what right you live so, and the question presumes a bench with clean hands, the one thing Peter’s bench lacked.

Declaration: Whoever wants my head bowed can bow his own first.

The Rite

Write to the person who still tries to shame you one sentence naming a thing they did that you can prove and they would rather forget. Send it with no greeting and no apology. Skip it if that person could be dangerous to you.

Testament · Who still tries to shame you, and what have they done that they never mention?

[2] John 18:13, 24, 28

[4] Acts 4:1–2

LXXXVII Of Holy Water

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 87 of 365

Say the blessing yourself, and owe the bishop nothing.

Saint James and the Magician HermogenesPieter Bruegel the Elder, 1565

The Roman Ritual makes holy water in three movements[1]. The priest exorcises a pinch of salt, commanding every unclean spirit out of it, then exorcises the water and prays that it cast out demons and banish disease, and last pours the salt into the water in the form of a cross. Salt and water and a spoken command against fever were the stock in trade of the village cunning woman too, and the difference between her bowl and the priest’s lay in who had been licensed to stir it.

The Church told the story of that license itself, in the legend of the apostle James. A magician called Hermogenes sends demons to fetch the saint in chains, an angel binds them in chains of fire, and they are sent back to fetch the magician instead. Freed and afraid of their revenge, Hermogenes asks for something of the apostle’s to carry, is given his staff, throws his books into the sea[2], and ends the story a penitent working wonders. The legend that celebrates the end of magic leaves its magician holding a charm against demons, his license transferred to the apostle.

The same centuries tried cunning women for charms and spoken cures, and in fourteen eighty-four a pope authorized inquisitors[3] against witches in Germany. A healer and a parish priest could say the same command over the same salted water, and only one of them answered to a court for it. The Universal Life Church now ordains anyone online[4], of any belief and at no charge, and advertises the standing to perform legal weddings. A clergyman’s title can be had for nothing by anyone who asks, and the words over the water keep the only force they ever had, the breath of the mouth that says them.

Declaration: The font at the church door was filled from the same pipes as my kitchen sink, and blessed by a man no better than I am.

The Rite · Christian

Fill a jug with tap water, hold your hand over it and say I bless this water in my own name and need no one’s leave, then pour yourself a glass and drink it.

Testament · What would you bless first if your mouth needed no license?

Sources

[1] Rituale Romanum, Ordo ad faciendam aquam benedictam

[2] Jacobus de Voragine, Golden Legend 99

[3] Innocent VIII, Summis desiderantes affectibus (5 Dec 1484)

[4] Universal Life Church, ulchq.org; themonastery.org


LXXXVIII Of Being Seen

Beauty

Day 88 of 365

Stop performing for an audience no one has ever seen.

Everywhere Eyeballs Are AflameOdilon Redon · The Temptation of Saint Anthony, 1888

A child is told that the god watches even the bath. Hagar, alone in the desert after running from her mistress, named the god who found her there the God who sees me[1], and children’s classes in church set the idea to a tune that tells small eyes and hands to mind themselves[2] because a father above is looking down.

In two thousand six, psychologists at Newcastle University fixed a strip of paper above the honesty box where staff paid for their hot drinks, a photograph of a pair of eyes one week and of flowers the next. Over ten weeks the staff paid nearly three times as much[3] in the weeks of the eyes. The photograph could see nothing, and every one of them knew it. The reflex answered the shape of an eye and asked nothing about who stood behind it.

A child given an invisible audience receives that reflex with a name and a voice attached, and a reflex that answers paper does not stop to ask whether the god is still believed. If a photocopy can move a hand at a tea box, a god named to a child in the bath can follow the grown body into the water, and the habit is the only thing of his still in the room.

The researchers changed the picture each week, and for ten weeks the payments rose and fell with it. An adult who turns around to look straight back at the eyes over the bath finds paper, and paper comes off a wall in one pull.

Declaration: A god who needed to watch a child in the bath has lost his view of the grown one.

The Rite

Draw or print a pair of eyes and tape it above your bath or shower. Bathe there slowly, naked under its gaze and for as long as you like, and say to it Look all you like. When you are done, drop it in the draining water.

Testament · Whose eye are you still living under when nobody is watching?

Sources

[1] Gen 16:13

[2] Be Careful Little Eyes, children’s song (print copyright 1944)

[3] Bateson, Nettle and Roberts, Biology Letters 2 (2006), 412–414


LXXXIX Of the Abyss

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 89 of 365

Want more than you were raised to ask for.

Satan Locked in the AbyssAdriaen Collaert, 1585

For three days the evil inclination sat in a cage. The Talmud says the sages of Nehemiah’s day prayed that the urge behind sexual sin be delivered into their hands, and it was, and having been warned that killing it would end the world they held it prisoner[1], until someone went looking for a fresh egg for a sick man anywhere in the land of Israel and found none to be had. They put out its eyes, which by the Talmud’s account cured men only of desire for their own kin, and let it go. The last book of the Christian Bible chains the adversary in the abyss[2] for a thousand years and then, on its own schedule, lets him out.

A rabbinic commentary on Genesis reads the god’s verdict on the sixth day, very good, as including the evil inclination, because without it no man would build a house, take a wife, father children or engage in trade[3]. The sages wrote the confession into their own books.

By the sages’ own list, the appetite for a body and the appetite for a larger house are one urge, and an upbringing that cages the first has caged the second with it. The sages learned in three days what a barren land costs. The urge to idolatry they had sealed in a pot of lead for good, and this one they released with its sight for kin put out and nothing else taken. A life that keeps the creature caged is the land of Israel in those three days, a sick man waiting and no egg.

Declaration: I call my ambition pride to its face and feed it anyway.

The Rite · Christian

Name aloud the thing of a neighbor’s you covet most, which the tenth commandment forbids, say I will have one of my own, and spend the next hour beginning it.

Testament · Which ambition have you kept small because wanting it felt like sin?

Sources

[1] b. Yoma 69b

[2] Rev 20:1–3

[3] Gen. Rab. 9:7


XC Of Sleep

Indulgence

Day 90 of 365

Give your hours back to the body that owns them.

The Sleep of Reason Produces MonstersFrancisco Goya · Los Caprichos, 1799

Paul once preached a boy out of a window. Acts records that a young man named Eutychus, sitting in a window while the apostle talked past midnight, sank into a deep sleep and fell from the third story and was taken up dead[1]. Paul went down, fell on him and said his life was in him, then went back up, broke bread and talked until daybreak[2]. The rule of Benedict woke its monks in the small hours for the night office[3], and a revelation in the Doctrine and Covenants tells the Latter-day Saints to cease sleeping longer than is needful, to retire to bed early and rise early[4].

Sleep is the single portion of the day in which the body serves no master and produces nothing, and every order that wants its hours, from the abbey with its bell to the ward with its early rising, has eyed that portion greedily and called the eyeing virtue.

Sloth was entered among the deadly sins, and the desert monks named their listlessness after the noonday demon of the psalm[5], the one who made a hermit stare at the sun and count how far it stood from the ninth hour and his meal. In the monks’ own descriptions the demon arrives as a hungry stomach, a long afternoon and a wish to be anywhere but the cell, and the church built a mortal sin out of a tired body in a hot room.

Clean sheets are cool at the first touch and warm within a minute. An afternoon spent in them is taken back from every rule that claimed it, and the body that wakes at dusk has spent its hours on its own skin.

Declaration: The bell that woke the monks before dawn can ring until the rope wears through, and I will sleep through every stroke.

The Rite

At three in the afternoon, the monks’ ninth hour, draw the curtains, get into bed and stay there until you wake on your own. The ninth hour is mine.

Testament · What would you do with an afternoon in bed if nobody had taught you guilt for lying down?

Sources

[1] Acts 20:9

[2] Acts 20:10–11

[3] Rule of Benedict 8

[4] D&C 88:124

[5] Ps 90:6 LXX; Evagrius, Praktikos 12 (acedia)


XCI Of Divorce

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 91 of 365

Count your leaving as final, whoever calls you back.

The Great FloodGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

It repented the Lord that he had made man on the earth, Genesis says, and it grieved him at his heart[1], and the flood that followed took every living substance upon the face[2] of the ground. Sorry for what he had made, the maker drowned everything that breathed on dry land but one boatload. When his people disappointed him again, Jeremiah has him reach for paper.

He puts away his wife Israel for her adulteries and gives her a bill of divorce[3]. Earlier in the chapter he quotes his own law from Deuteronomy, that a man may not take back a wife[4] he has put away once she has been another man’s, and asks whether such a return would not greatly pollute the land. Four verses after the bill he calls after the divorced woman, Return, thou backsliding Israel[5], and two verses on he tells her children that he is married unto them[6].

The faiths people leave keep the habit on file. The Latter-day Saints keep a member’s record unless the member writes to have it removed. The elder at the door and the dread at a funeral speak the third chapter of Jeremiah, a husband with his own signed bill in the drawer saying I am married unto you.

His own chapter shows what his claims on a departed wife are worth. He signed the bill and then called her back against his own law, so the marriage he keeps announcing is one his paper ended and his statute forbids him to resume. A bill written in your own hand follows his precedent, and every call after it is the voice from Jeremiah crying Return at a door the bill has already shut.

Declaration: The god’s bill of divorce held for four verses, and mine holds for good.

The Rite · Christian

Write I put you away, and this is your bill of divorce on a sheet, sign it, and leave it in your own Bible at the third chapter of Jeremiah. Then sell a religious gift you were given and spend every coin of it on yourself.

Testament · What does a marriage or a faith you left still collect from you, and on what claim?

Sources

[1] Gen 6:6

[2] Gen 7:23

[3] Jer 3:8

[4] Deut 24:1–4

[5] Jer 3:12

[6] Jer 3:14 (KJV)


XCII Of the Dark Wood

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 92 of 365

Go where you were forbidden to go, and stay.

Lost in the Dark WoodGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto I, 1861

In Luke the shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness to go after one. When he finds it he lays it on his shoulders[1], calls in his friends and neighbors, and tells them to rejoice with him, because he has found his sheep[2]. The joy is a proprietor’s, and the word that carries it is his. Relatives who pray for an ex-believer by name, and the congregation that keeps the name on a visiting list, use the same grammar when they call the one who left lost.

Ezekiel’s god, rebuking the shepherds of Israel, lists what they took from the flock, the fat eaten, the wool worn and the fed ones killed[3]. His remedy is to deliver the sheep out of their mouths and feed them himself in a fat pasture[4]. The flock changes keepers. It stays a flock, and it stays his. Luke follows the lost sheep at once with a lost coin, swept for by lamplight[5], and the pairing is exact, since nobody asks a coin where it would rather lie.

From inside the fold, a month in the wood is an emergency to be ended by the next visit. From inside the wood it is the first ground you have stood on with no path laid down by anyone and no tree on it forbidden, and an animal left there long enough finds its own grazing and learns which shade it likes. The sheep carried home on the shepherd’s shoulders went back to the ninety-nine and the count, and a counted sheep is kept for its wool. The one that stays in the wood keeps it.

Declaration: The shepherd who searched the wilderness for me can strike my name off his count, because the wood has fed me ever since.

The Rite · No faith

Go alone for an hour to a place the god of your culture would have called the devil’s ground, a bar, a club or a dark wood, and sit with your back to the wall. This ground is mine for the hour.

Testament · Which of the places your fold forbade do you want to walk into first, and why that one?

Sources

[1] Luke 15:5

[2] Luke 15:6

[3] Ezek 34:2–3

[4] Ezek 34:10–15

[5] Luke 15:8–9


XCIII Of the Bodies

Reckoning

Day 93 of 365

Repay whoever stood by you, most of all once they fall.

Jabesh-Gileadites Recover the Bodies of Saul and His SonsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

All night the men of Jabesh-gilead walked toward Beth-shan. The Philistines had found Saul and three of his sons dead on Mount Gilboa[1], cut off the king’s head and fastened his body to the town wall[2]. When the fighting men of a small place across the Jordan heard of it they got up, crossed in the dark, took the king and his sons down, burned them at home, buried the bones under a tree at Jabesh and fasted seven days[3].

Twenty chapters back, Nahash the Ammonite had besieged Jabesh and offered terms, the town’s surrender on condition that he thrust out every man’s right eye as a disgrace upon Israel[4]. Saul, newly anointed and still coming in from the field behind his oxen, cut a yoke of them in pieces, sent the pieces through the tribes, raised an army and broke the siege in the last watch of the night[5].

By the time of the wall, heaven had finished with Saul. The spirit of the Lord had left him years before, and at the end he went to a medium at Endor because heaven no longer answered him[6]. The men of Jabesh left heaven’s verdict to heaven. They owed him that siege.

They paid at the highest price on offer, a march into enemy country for a king whose god had dropped him and whose army had broken on Gilboa. Saul had struck for them at the end of a night, and they answered with a night march of their own. By morning the wall at Beth-shan was bare.

Declaration: I pay my rescuers, and their disgrace buys no discount.

The Rite

Choose someone who helped you when it cost them, above all one others now run down. Today, where those others can hear, say This one stood by me, and tell exactly what they did for you.

Testament · Whom do you owe for a rescue, and how much of it have you paid?

Sources

[1] 1 Sam 31:8

[2] 1 Sam 31:9–10

[3] 1 Sam 31:11–13

[4] 1 Sam 11:2

[6] 1 Sam 28:6–7


XCIV Of Crowds

Heresy

Day 94 of 365

Find the few who refused what you refused.

The Fallen Hover over HellGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book I, 1866

One hundred and thirty-three million, three hundred and six thousand, six hundred and sixty-eight angels fell with the adversary, by a reckoning attributed to a Franciscan friar at Salamanca[1] in the fifteenth century. Revelation gives a proportion instead. The dragon’s tail draws down a third of the stars of heaven[2], and his angels are cast out with him[3].

Whatever else the fallen lost, they fell in company. People who leave a strict congregation usually fall alone, sometimes announced from the front of the room in a single sentence to people they have known since childhood, and within a season they can lose every friend they had and the dozen people who would have brought food after a death. Many spend years taking that loss for the fixed price of leaving, because the people who set it said so from the front of the same room.

The fallen paid a different price. Their company was made by one refusal, made once, and it sent them no bill afterward. A congregation keeps its members by billing them every week, in Sunday hours on a hard pew and in shame said aloud to an elder or a priest, while a bond formed by refusing the same thing is paid off on the day it forms. Whatever its members keep up after that, the long dinners and the private jokes, they keep because it pleases them, and they drop it the week it stops. Three people who left the same church and meet on their own terms keep a table no elder can announce them off.

Declaration: A third of heaven went down behind one refusal, and I would rather eat with my third than kneel with the rest.

The Rite

Invite one or two people who left what you left to the best dinner you can afford, and pay for the whole table. When the plates come, say We fell together.

Testament · Whose company did leaving cost you, and whose has it brought you since?

Sources

[1] Attributed to Alonso de Espina, Fortalitium Fidei

[2] Rev 12:4

[3] Rev 12:9


XCV Of Pride

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 95 of 365

Like the face in the mirror, and say so.

The LionGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto I, 1861

English still calls a family of lions a pride, and the animals earn the word, since the males eat first at a kill and ask leave of nobody. Sirach, a book Rome kept and later Protestant Bibles dropped, dates the beginning of pride to the moment a person departs from the Lord and the heart turns from its maker[1].

The Quran gives the case its clearest speech. Ordered with the angels to bow to a man made of clay, Iblis answers that he is better than Adam, being made of fire[2], and refuses. Gregory the Great called pride the queen of the vices[3], standing outside the seven and handing the heart she has conquered over to them as her captains. Lust and gluttony send a sinner to the confessional asking pardon, and the sin crowned over them is the one that keeps a person off their knees.

Pretension is a different animal, the borrowed grandeur of someone who needs to be seen as great and has done nothing in particular, and it bows constantly, to whoever hands out the titles. Pleasure in your own work, credited to yourself and to no giver, is the first of the four kinds of pride Gregory counts, and it bows to nobody.

Painters of vanity set a skull beside the woman at her mirror, a warning addressed to whoever looked into the glass and liked what looked back. Whoever likes it still, and says so in a full voice, keeps what the skull was painted to take, and takes the place Iblis took, refusing in a room where everyone else is on the floor.

Declaration: A heaven entered on the knees can keep its door, and I will keep my spine.

The Rite · Christian

At a meal take the head of the table and the best portion on purpose, against the gospel’s counsel to take the lowest seat, and say no grace. This is mine, and it is good.

Testament · To whom will you say aloud what you were taught never to boast of?

Sources

[1] Sir 10:12–13

[2] Quran 7:12

[3] Gregory the Great, Moralia 31.45.87


XCVI Of the Leopard

Indulgence

Day 96 of 365

Feed the appetite, then stop where you chose to.

The LeopardGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto I, 1861

A square of dark chocolate resists the teeth for an instant, snaps clean, and gives way against the roof of the mouth, bitter at the edge and sweet at the heart. Eaten slowly, it has given everything it has, and a second square repeats the first.

Jeremiah sends a leopard against a faithless city, one that watches the towns and tears whoever comes out[1], and eight chapters later asks whether the leopard can change its spots[2]. People long trained in evil, he meant, cannot learn good. Paul, writing to the Romans, confessed how the training works. He had not known coveting, he said, until the law said thou shalt not covet, and then sin, taking its occasion from the commandment[3], worked in him desire of every sort. The prohibition fed the hunger it named.

A letter to the Colossians written under Paul’s name says of the rules touch not, taste not, handle not that they have a show of wisdom and no value against the indulgence of the flesh[4]. The pulpits kept the rules anyway, and abstinence kept up for a lifetime leaves the leopard lean at the door.

A pleasure owned is taken when its owner chooses and in the measure its owner names, with the whole attention on it, and it is put away before it cloys. The abstainer has practiced only the refusal and has no skill in the stopping, so the first open box finds them with one skill, which is surrender. Fed to a measure, the leopard keeps every spot it was born with and sleeps on the rug.

Declaration: The commandment taught Paul to covet everything, so I keep commandments off my table and set my own measure there.

The Rite

Buy the finest chocolates you can find, name how many you will eat, and eat them in the best chair you own with nothing else in your hands. Then shut the box and leave it in plain view. I set it down.

Testament · Which pleasure have you only ever refused, and how much of it would you take?

Sources

[1] Jer 5:6

[2] Jer 13:23

[3] Rom 7:7–8

[4] Col 2:21–23


XCVII Of Sullenness

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 97 of 365

Give the black mood its hour.

Phlegyas Ferries the TravellersGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VIII, 1861

My tears have been my meat day and night[1], says the singer of the forty-second psalm, while they ask me all day long where my god is. In the same psalm the waves and billows have gone over him[2]. Three times, across this psalm and the next, he turns on himself with the same question, why art thou cast down, O my soul[3], and gives himself the same answer, hope thou in God.

Paul sorted sorrow into two kinds for the Corinthians. Sorrow after the god’s fashion works repentance, and the sorrow of the world works death[4], so grief was weighed by where it ended. John Cassian ranked dejection among the eight principal faults[5]. A low mood was a sin long before it was a diagnosis, and a remedy on offer was more devotion and more hope.

A low mood presses on every side, as water does, and the psalmist’s own report names its causes, the enemy’s oppression and the daily taunt, where is thy god[6]. The hope he prescribed himself answered neither, since the same question stands again at the end of the next psalm. Given an hour of its own, with the music as black as it likes and the self-pity let run, the mood gets to speak with no psalm in the room, and the hour ends by the clock, not by a verse.

What the mood reports, that the world has promised nothing, is so, and the quarrel it opens stays open. The psalm closes its own question with a refrain and no reply, and the hour closes by the clock.

Declaration: I give my sorrow its hour with the book shut, and I owe heaven no hope for it.

The Rite · No faith

Tie two sticks into a cross, sink it in a bucket of water, and leave it under for the hour you give the mood. This low is mine, and you have no claim on it.

Testament · What does your sullenness want to say when nobody is there to hear it?

Sources

[1] Ps 42:3

[2] Ps 42:7

[3] Ps 42:5, 11; 43:5

[4] 2 Cor 7:10

[5] John Cassian, Institutes 5.1; Book 9

[6] Ps 42:9–10


XCVIII Of the Long Way

Mastery

Day 98 of 365

Take up the trade heaven claimed for itself alone.

Satan Crosses ChaosGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book II, 1866

The earth was without form and void, the second verse of Genesis says, in Hebrew two words that rhyme like a nursery chant for nothing at all, tohu and bohu. Darkness lay on the face of the deep[1]. The waters parted on the second day and the dry land raised on the third are worked out of that material. In the seventeenth-century English retelling of the fall, Satan crosses the same blank alone, with his own wings for a road.

Isaiah has the god insist on the monopoly. He is the maker of all things, who stretched out the heavens alone[2] and spread out the earth by himself, and he will give his glory to no other[3]. In chapter forty-five he pronounces woe on whoever strives with his maker, the clay that asks the potter what he is making[4]. The creed opens on the trade, maker of heaven and earth[5], and leaves the clay a shape to take and thanks to give.

Whoever makes something from a blank, a business from a bare idea or a book from an empty file, works the trade Isaiah’s god said he worked alone, and works it without omnipotence, which makes the labor harder and the credit larger. The parable of the talents, which gave English its word for a gift, was preached as heaven’s capital lent out to be returned with interest[6], so the credit for every made thing was owed to the lender before the thing was finished. Isaiah’s god signed heaven and earth as his own and shared none of the glory, and by that rule the first page made from a blank carries one name at its foot, the maker’s.

Declaration: Let the potter pronounce his woe, because my name is already on the work.

The Rite

Sit before a blank page or an empty file and say Let there be something here. aloud. Within the hour make the first piece of something that did not exist this morning, and sign it in full.

Testament · What have you made that you were taught to credit to heaven?

Sources

[1] Gen 1:2

[2] Isa 44:24

[3] Isa 42:8

[4] Isa 45:9

[5] Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed (381)

[6] Matt 25:27


XCIX Of Wrath

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 99 of 365

Aim your anger at its author before sunset.

The Wrathful in the StyxGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VII, 1861

Nahum opens his book on a god who is jealous and avenging and furious, a lord who keeps his wrath in store for his enemies[1]. A psalm, in the King James Version, has him angry with the wicked every day[2]. The letter of James, meanwhile, tells believers that the wrath of man does not work the righteousness of God[3]. Nahum and James together make anger a privilege of rank, kept by the throne and refused to the subject.

The letter to the Ephesians holds both positions five verses apart. It allows its readers to be angry and sin not, provided the sun does not go down on their wrath[4], and then orders all bitterness and wrath and anger put away from them[5]. A long line of pulpit teaching took the later verse, and its cure was to swallow the anger and call the swallowing meekness.

Whoever has swallowed anger knows where it goes next, to a dish left in the sink or a partner’s late reply, and it lands on someone who did nothing, while the one who earned it goes about the day untouched and unaware. Anger carries an address. It records an injury and the hand that did it, and in Nahum the god at least names his enemies before he strikes.

Ephesians set the subject a deadline, the sunset, and a deadline assumes the anger will be used before it falls due. Nahum’s god is also slow to anger[6], and Ephesians grants the subject no such patience, only until sundown. Aimed at its author, named aloud with the deed beside the name before dark, anger keeps Nahum’s rule, wrath held for the enemy, and spends itself in a day.

Declaration: I guard my grievances as jealously as any god, and I spend them only on the guilty.

The Rite · Christian

Alone, name aloud the person who earned your anger and call them a fool three times at full voice, the word the Sermon on the Mount says puts you in danger of hell fire. You fool.

Testament · Who earned the anger you have been spending on someone else?

Sources

[1] Nah 1:2

[2] Ps 7:11 (KJV)

[3] Jas 1:20

[4] Eph 4:26

[5] Eph 4:31

[6] Nah 1:3


C Of the Furies

Reckoning

Day 100 of 365

Be your own avenger of blood, on paper.

The FuriesGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto IX, 1861

Numbers sets apart six cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan[1]. Someone who had killed without intent could flee to one ahead of the avenger of blood, and Deuteronomy orders the roads to them prepared in advance[2]. Inside the walls the killer was safe until the congregation judged the case[3]. A killer cleared of intent lived there until the death of the high priest[4], and then he could go home.

The law that built the cities never doubted that a murderer’s blood was owed. Numbers says the avenger of blood himself shall put the murderer to death when he meets him[5], and Deuteronomy has the elders fetch a deliberate killer out of the refuge and deliver him into the avenger’s own hand[6]. Heaven supplied the roads and the hearing and left the avenging to a kinsman. The Furies of Greek belief hunted kin-killers by the scent of blood, and in Aeschylus they chased Orestes from Delphi to Athens before a court of citizens sat to hear him.

For most readers neither the kinsman nor the Fury will ever knock. What survives of both arrangements is the hearing, a court and a clerk, which move when somebody carries in the papers.

Most injuries worth answering have a court somewhere that can be turned on the one who did them, a small claims judge or a licensing board or the grievance office of an employer. A complaint filed there sets what they took, the money or the year, in plain words beside their name, with the evidence attached. It costs them hours and the composure of anyone who assumed nobody would bother, and it sits in a file under the clerk’s date stamp.

Declaration: The blood owed me is collected in ink, and I sign for it myself.

The Rite

Find the court, regulator or board with power over one person or firm that wronged you, and file the complaint by the body’s own form or by letter, signed in your own name, stating only what your evidence shows. Pin the confirmation where you eat.

Testament · What did someone take from you that a court, board or regulator exists to judge?

CI Of Thrift

Heresy

Day 101 of 365

Do today what your future tense has been promising.

The Hoarders and the WastersGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VII, 1861

A man in the crowd asks the teacher to make his brother divide the inheritance[1] with him. The teacher answers that a life does not consist in the abundance of what a man possesses, and tells a parable. The ground of a certain rich man[2] brought forth plentifully. He thought within himself what he should do, because he had no room where to bestow his fruits. He said that he would pull down his barns, and build greater[3], and there bestow all his fruits and his goods. He would say to his soul, Soul, thou hast much goods laid up for many years, take thine ease, eat, drink, and be merry. But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night[4] thy soul shall be required of thee, and then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided. So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.

Later in the same chapter the same teacher tells his hearers to sell what they have and give alms[5] and lay up a treasure in heaven.

Whoever pays their own way and carries what they owe to the people who depend on them has earned the rest, the good coat or the long dinner, and owes nobody an apology for it. Luke’s god calls the saver a fool and collects his soul before one new barn stood. Every plan the man made for his goods was in the future tense, I will pull down my barns, I will say to my soul, and the reply he got named this night.

Declaration: I pay what I owe and then enjoy my evening, with no sermon attached to it.

The Rite

Write down one thing you keep saying you will do when the barns are full, a trip, a dinner, a purchase. Pick the version you can afford today. Do it before the day ends, and say This night. when you start.

Testament · Which of your I wills is waiting on a barn?

[1] Luke 12:13–15

[2] Luke 12:16

[3] Luke 12:18

[4] Luke 12:20

[5] Luke 12:33


CII Of Mammon

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 102 of 365

Say your wage aloud to the people you live with.

PlutusGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VII, 1861

Mammon is an Aramaic word for wealth, and Matthew sets it in a chapter that opens on keeping things out of sight. Give alms so secretly that one hand is kept ignorant of the other[1], pray in a closet with the door shut[2], fast with a washed face[3], and then, a few verses on, nobody can serve both God and mammon[4]. Medieval theologians later promoted the noun into a demon of greed[5]. The purse the twelve kept in common was carried, John says, by Judas, who helped himself to what was put in[6].

In twenty nineteen a former employee of the investment arm of the Latter-day Saint church alleged, as the Washington Post reported that December, that a fund of about a hundred billion dollars had been built up from members’ tithes[7]. In twenty twenty-three the Securities and Exchange Commission found that the church’s investment manager had failed to file its required holdings reports from nineteen ninety-seven to twenty nineteen, and the manager agreed to pay four million dollars, and the church one million, to settle the charge that its holdings had been filed behind thirteen shell companies[8].

A tithe is a tenth, and a bishop who sits down each year with a family to ask whether they are full tithe payers, over a donation record listing every payment, can work the income out. The institution could see the household’s number, and the household could not see the institution’s. A wage kept from the family at the table hides it from no one but the family.

Declaration: Mammon is only my wage, and I say the figure out loud.

The Rite · Christian

Open your own Bible, or a printout, at the verse that says nobody can serve God and mammon, write your yearly wage across it in ink, and say it aloud to someone you live with, or to the room, then say This wage is mine.

Testament · Which figure do you keep from the people you live with, and who gains by it?

[2] Matt 6:6

[3] Matt 6:17–18

[4] Matt 6:24; Luke 16:13

[5] Peter Lombard, Sentences 2, dist. 6

[6] John 12:6

[7] Washington Post, 17 Dec 2019

[8] SEC Press Release 2023-35, 21 Feb 2023


CIII Of Paying in Full

Reckoning

Day 103 of 365

Pay what it costs and own what you stand on.

The Burial of SarahGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Ephron the Hittite offered Abraham the field and the cave of Machpelah as a gift, in the hearing of everyone who went in at the city gate[1], so that he could bury Sarah. Abraham, a resident alien at Hebron, refused the gift and insisted on paying. Ephron named the price the way a man waves a matter aside, land worth four hundred shekels of silver, what is that between friends[2], and Abraham weighed out the whole sum on the spot at the merchants’ rate[3]. Genesis spends a chapter on the bargaining and a single verse on the burial[4].

The field and the cave were made sure to Abraham as a possession[5] before every witness at the gate. Ground accepted as a gift stays under the giver’s goodwill for as long as he cares to remember the giving, and a grave on borrowed ground is a grave the giver’s sons can order the next generation to leave. The silver bought title instead. Isaac and Rebekah were buried there in time[6], and Jacob was carried up out of Egypt[7] to lie beside Leah, on land nobody could say had been lent.

A gift that comes back later as a debt in another currency was a loan from the start. The parents’ deposit on a house that comes with a say in the marriage is one, and so is a congregation’s help through a bad year that falls due in attendance and silence. Paid off at its full price, such a gift stops collecting, and the next holiday at the parents’ house becomes a visit instead of an installment.

Declaration: Keep your gift. I would rather pay a merchant’s rate than owe a benefactor.

The Rite

Name one gift or favor you are still repaying in visits, silence or deference. Return it, or pay its fair price in money to the giver, saying aloud what the payment settles.

Testament · Which gift are you still repaying in obedience, and what would it cost to clear it outright?

Sources

[1] Gen 23:10–11

[2] Gen 23:15

[3] Gen 23:16

[4] Gen 23:19

[5] Gen 23:17–18

[6] Gen 49:31

[7] Gen 50:13


CIV Of the Bramble

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 104 of 365

Refuse the office that would cost you your own harvest.

The Death of Gideon’s SonsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Seventy pieces of silver from the temple of Baal-berith[1] paid for the killing. Abimelech, Gideon’s son by a concubine in Shechem, hired idle and reckless men with the money, went to his father’s house at Ophrah and killed his seventy half-brothers on one stone[2]. The youngest, Jotham, escaped by hiding, and the men of Shechem made the killer their king.

Jotham answered from the top of Mount Gerizim[3] with a fable. The trees went out to anoint a king over themselves. The olive refused, since it would have to leave the oil by which, it says, God and man are honored[4], and the fig would not leave its sweetness, and the vine would not leave the wine that cheers God and man[5]. Only the bramble accepted, and it offered the trees its shade[6], with fire to devour the cedars of Lebanon if they refused.

Every tree with a yield of its own turned the crown down and named what ruling would cost it. Gideon, whom the fable has in view, had told Israel I will not rule over you[7], and it was his seventy sons who were killed for the vacancy. The bramble had nothing to lose by accepting, and its first speech as king was a threat. The fable charges Shechem for crowning the bramble and prices the refusal, since when the fruitful decline, someone with nothing to lose takes the crown. Three years on, the fire came out of Abimelech as Jotham had said[8], about a thousand men and women of Shechem burned in the stronghold of their own god’s temple[9]. Offices still go looking among the fruitful first, the church calling or the promotion that lifts the best hand off the bench. An olive that accepts spends its season swaying over the other trees, and its oil stays in the fruit.

Declaration: Let the brambles have the crowns and the cedars their fire. I have oil to press.

The Rite · Christian

Write to whoever runs your church’s committees or rotas and resign one post, or refuse the next one offered, in a single sentence. Eat a fig slowly while it sends, then say I keep my fruit.

Testament · Which post you were offered would eat the work only you can do, and what will you grow in the hours you keep?

CV Of Evening

Indulgence

Day 105 of 365

Put the evening first, and make the day earn it.

The Day DepartingGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto II, 1861

And the evening and the morning were the first day, Genesis says, and it counts every day of the creation the same way, from its evening[1], which is why the Jewish day still begins at dusk. A psalm gives the night to the young lions roaring after their prey and the day to man, who goes out to his work and his labor until the evening[2].

The rabbis built the week on that order. The Sabbath begins at sundown with candles lit, a short evening service, a blessing over wine and a long meal, so that its first hours are spent at a table and its longest prayers wait for the morning. The Talmud names the eve of the Sabbath as the proper night for scholars to lie with their wives[3]. A body of law that legislated nearly everything put its scholars’ lovemaking on the calendar, at the opening of the holiest day of the week.

Kept in that order, the working hours are rent paid on an evening that belongs to the body, to the table and whoever shares the bed, or to your own hands. Left undecided, the evening is eaten by the day before it, by the email answered on the sofa and the takeout eaten standing at the counter, and the body goes to bed with only its tiredness to show for the hours. Promised at dawn, it turns the whole day into an approach, the dish already simmering in the mind by mid-morning and the skin expecting hands by the afternoon, and the last hour of work is done by someone already halfway out the door.

Declaration: My day starts at dusk, at the table and in the bed, and whoever pays me gets the leftovers.

The Rite

Before work begins, change the sheets, buy the dish you crave, and tell your lover, or yourself, the hour. At that hour wash the day off, put the phone in another room, and begin.

Testament · Which pleasure would you build a whole working day toward, and who shares it?

Sources

[1] Gen 1:5

[2] Ps 104:21–23

[3] b. Ketubot 62b


CVI Of Millstones

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 106 of 365

Put your own name to the deed you hid.

The Death of AbimelechGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

An upper millstone, the kind a household turned by hand, killed the man Shechem had made its king[1]. Abimelech had taken Thebez and was storming the strong tower, where its people had shut themselves in and climbed onto the roof[2], and he went close to the door to burn it. A woman on the roof, whom the book never names, dropped the stone on his head and broke his skull[3]. With what strength he had left he called his armor-bearer and told him to draw his sword and finish him, so that nobody could say a woman had killed him. The young man ran him through[4], and the book gives him no name either.

Later, at the siege of Rabbah, Joab sends David word of a costly assault under the wall and coaches the messenger for the king’s anger, down to the question David will ask, who struck Abimelech, and was it not a woman with a millstone from the wall at Thebez[5]. The messenger is then to add that Uriah the Hittite is dead too, Uriah who had carried to the front, in his own hand, the letter that ordered his death[6].

Abimelech’s dying order bought nothing. The armor-bearer who ran his own king through to change the story stays nameless, and the woman’s stone became the fact about Abimelech a general expected a king to know by heart. David’s letter went the same way and sits in the Bible. One man hid the manner of his death and the other a murder, and both deeds were told in the end by other voices, in other words, and the only account either man controlled was the one he could have signed while he lived.

Declaration: I sign my own deeds, and the armor-bearers can keep the secrets of kings.

The Rite · No faith

Chalk the deed you hid and your full name on a stone you can hold in both hands, and set it on your doorstep for the day where anyone coming in will read it. Say the deed, then your name, as you set it down.

Testament · Which act have you hidden or postponed for fear of how the story would be told?
