CVII Of Debts

Reckoning

Day 107 of 365

Pay first whoever kept faith with you.

Faust and Mephistopheles GallopingEugène Delacroix, 1828

Theophilus, steward of the church at Adana in the sixth century, lost his office under a new bishop and won it back by signing his soul to the devil in a written charter[1]. Then he repented, and the legend, told in Latin and Greek and carved in stone over the doors of French churches[2], sends the Virgin down to take the charter back from its holder and lay it on the sleeping penitent’s chest. The devil had kept every term. The bishop burned the document before the congregation, and the Church preached the theft as a miracle for centuries.

The village stories of the devil’s bridge, built overnight for the price of the first soul to cross, mostly end with an animal sent over first, a goat or a dog or a cockerel, and the builder cheated. The doctor of the German chapbook, printed at Frankfurt in fifteen eighty-seven, pledged his soul for twenty-four years of service[3] and got every one of them.

The legend and the bridge tales ruled the contract by the standing of the party. The devil delivered first, the office restored and the bridge standing by morning, and the Christian side defaulted with the Virgin’s help or a villager’s goat, and the tale is told as a victory for the faithful. Only in the chapbook is the lender paid, and there the printer sets his collection before the reader as a warning. A debt is owed to whoever lent it, whatever the lender’s standing in the parish, and the tale would have you pay the outsider last.

Declaration: My debts are settled by the creditor’s conduct, and the parish’s opinion of him is no legal tender.

The Rite

Pay back today, early and in full, a debt or favor owed to someone your old community frowned on who has held to every term with you, and tell them You kept your word, so here is mine.

Testament · Whom have you left waiting for what you owe because your old community thought less of them?

Sources

[1] Paul the Deacon, Miraculum S. Mariae de Theophilo

[2] Notre-Dame de Paris, north transept portal, tympanum

[3] Historia von D. Johann Fausten (Frankfurt, 1587)


CVIII Of Leaders

Heresy

Day 108 of 365

Unfollow whoever sells you their direction.

Samuel Blesses SaulGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

When the elders of Israel came to Ramah asking for a king like all the nations, the god told the old prophet to give them what they asked[1] and to read them the price first. A king would take their sons for his chariots and their daughters for his kitchens, the best of their fields for his servants, a tenth of their grain and their flocks[2], and in the end the people themselves for slaves, crying out to a god who would not answer[3]. They heard all of it and asked anyway, because they wanted a man to go out before them and fight their battles.

The man the record supplies was out looking for his father’s lost donkeys[4]. Saul, son of Kish, stood head and shoulders above everyone in Israel[5]. Samuel poured a flask of oil on his head[6] in private, and when he was shown to the assembly the people shouted for the king[7] at the sight of him. A few chapters later the god regretted the choice[8]. The people had heard the whole bill in advance and paid it for the sight of a tall man going out in front of them.

The demand for a man to go out before us now sits under a pastor whose word settles what a person would otherwise have to settle alone, and it pays for the course that promises direction. What it purchases is relief from deciding, and it pays with the last line of Samuel’s bill, a people that has made itself a servant. A decision handed forward is a decision never learned, and a follower who hands forward enough of them finds a leader standing where his judgment used to be.

Declaration: No man goes out before me. I fight my own battles and keep my own tenth.

The Rite

Find the person whose posts, sermons or videos you check before deciding how to live. List the last three things they told you to do and whether they do them, then unfollow them everywhere or stop attending, and cancel any paid course or membership.

Testament · What has following the voice you check before deciding how to live actually cost you?

CIX Of Temptation

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 109 of 365

Yield to one temptation you were forbidden for nothing.

The Temptation of Saint AnthonyAfter Hieronymus Bosch,

Genesis, in the King James, states in so many words that God did tempt Abraham[1], ordering him to offer up his son, and the letter of James says outright that God tempts no one[2]. The Lord’s Prayer asks him not to lead us into temptation[3], which assumes he does. James and Genesis use one Greek root, peirazo[4], for testing and tempting alike, so the quarrel is over a word and the churches left the fear standing.

In the print above, the saint sits at the right edge under a lean-to of sticks and cloth, his head propped on his hand, and the rest of the sheet belongs to the other side, a giant fish with a domed house on its back, a sea full of boats and swimmers, men scrambling up ladders at the left and a gallows on the far hill. The saint got a stick shelter at the margin of his own legend.

Most of what you were trained to resist harms nobody. The laws in question mostly stand outside the ten commandments, the fast, the modest hem, the lowered gaze of sura 24[5], and each can be broken in an afternoon. The forbidden thing is usually small, a sleeve, an hour of music or a second glance, a warning recorded in Abu Dawud and Tirmidhi[6], and a church council in six ninety-two thought a mask and a dance worth forbidding. The appetite was yours before any tempter arrived, and a test you pass by refusing a sleeve proves only that you can be told.

Declaration: The saint got the lean-to, and I take the sea and everything swimming in it.

The Rite · Christian

Buy the food your church’s fasts kept from you, the meat or the sweet, and eat it on the spot, slowly, to the last crumb. Then say the Lord’s Prayer line turned round. Lead me into temptation.

Testament · Which harmless law of appetite do you still keep out of old reflex?

[1] Gen 22:1

[2] Jas 1:13

[3] Matt 6:13

CX Of Councils

Mastery

Day 110 of 365

Convene your own council, and rule for the chair.

The Fallen Summoned to CouncilGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book I, 1866

Constantine summoned the bishops to Nicaea in the year three hundred and twenty-five, three hundred and eighteen of them by the traditional count. He brought them there on the imperial post[1] to settle whether the son was of one substance with the father[2]. The emperor who paid their passage went unbaptized until his deathbed[3]. The creed was written down, and by the old account every bishop signed it but two[4], who went into exile with Arius.

The first Christians settled their worst quarrel the same way. At Jerusalem the apostles and elders heard Peter, then Barnabas and Paul[5], on whether gentile converts had to be circumcised, and James gave his judgment. The letter they sent to the gentile brethren in Antioch and Syria and Cilicia[6] announced the ruling as what seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us[7]. The bodies in question belonged to gentile men, and no gentile speaks anywhere in the chapter.

Both assemblies ruled on lives that had no voice in the room. Nicaea fixed what every Christian must believe, for churches from Spain to Persia. Jerusalem settled what every gentile convert must keep at table and in bed, spared his flesh by a vote he never cast, and put heaven’s name on the verdict ahead of its own. A decision circled for a month is usually a council with one chair and too many members, a parent or a partner claiming a vote, when the only one with standing to convene it is the person whose life it governs. The arguments deserve a hearing once, at their strongest, as Jerusalem heard Paul. After that the ruling stands under one name, in the first place on the page, where Jerusalem put the Holy Ghost.

Declaration: The emperor paid the bishops’ fares and got his creed. I pay my own way and get my life.

The Rite

Name the one person who claims a vote in a decision that is yours alone. Write your ruling on a sheet and sign it, then tell them the ruling in one sentence and do not answer a reply. Act on it today.

Testament · What ruling will you give the one who claims a vote in a decision that is yours alone?

CXI Of the Glutton

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 111 of 365

Eat long with someone your old community will not seat.

The Gluttons in the RainGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto VI, 1861

John came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, Jesus told the crowds, and they said he had a demon. The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they said, look at him, a gluttonous man and a winebibber, a friend of tax collectors and sinners[1]. Glutton and drunkard are the charge the law’s parents bring against the rebellious son[2], whose parents bring him to the elders to be stoned, and the only man the Gospels call a glutton is Jesus, in the mouths of people who disliked his dinner guests.

At Antioch Peter ate with the gentile converts until certain men came from James[3], and then he drew back and kept himself apart for fear of the circumcision party, and the other Jewish believers followed him, Barnabas among them, until one table had become two. Paul, who tells it in Galatians, called it hypocrisy to Peter’s face. Jehovah’s Witnesses apply the apostle’s instruction not even to eat with such a one[4] to anyone removed from the congregation, sparing only the household[5].

The Pharisees in Luke 15 murmured that this man receives sinners and eats with them[6], and he answered with a lost sheep, a lost coin and a son welcomed home with the fatted calf killed for a feast. The church later made gluttony a capital sin[7], so the one glutton its Gospels name is its own founder. A long meal with the shunned has the best precedent of any gluttony, and whoever commits it sits in the founder’s chair while the accusers stand in the crowd.

Declaration: The elders can shun whom they like, and I will be at that table with a second course and the person they shunned.

The Rite · Christian

Eat a long lunch with someone your church cut off or warned you against, the table Paul told the Corinthians not even to share with such a one, and order what you both want.

Testament · Who is missing from the tables you grew up at, and what would the two of you order?

CXII Of Height

Beauty

Day 112 of 365

Look down on your city from a height nobody gave you.

Satan Flies Toward EarthGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book III, 1866

Abram and Lot came up out of Egypt with more herds than the land could carry, and on the high ground between Bethel and Ai their herdsmen quarreled over pasture[1]. Abram gave his nephew the choice of direction. Lot lifted up his eyes and saw the whole plain of the Jordan well watered everywhere, like the garden of the Lord, and chose it for himself[2], and the narrator sets its wicked men down[3] two verses after the choice.

Once Lot had gone, the god told Abram to do what Lot had done. Lift up your eyes, he said, and look from the place where you stand, north and south and east and west[4], for all the land you see I will give to you and your seed for ever. It is the same raised eye over the same country. The chapter darkens the look in the man who took and blesses it in the man being handed the land, and the tempter of Matthew offers the same view from an exceedingly high mountain[5], every kingdom of the world.

The god who promised Abram every acre his eye could reach later sent him up a mountain in the land of Moriah[6] to lay the promised seed on an altar, and the promise was renewed because he did it[7]. The tempter named his price, a single bow[8], before the kingdoms had cleared from sight. Lot took his view from his uncle’s open hand and owed no god for it, whatever the plain cost him later. A rooftop above your own city lays the country out the way the Jordan plain lay before him, and whoever looks at it from there owes the view to nobody’s gift.

Declaration: Abraham paid for his view with a knife raised over his son, and I paid for mine with the stairs.

The Rite

Climb to the highest place above your town you can reach, a rooftop, a terrace or a hill. Sit with the whole town below you for an hour.

Testament · Which height near you have you never climbed because no one sent you up it?

CXIII Of the Spectacle

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 113 of 365

Speak up the next time your people shame someone.

The Traveller FaintsGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto V, 1861

A Christian of Carthage, writing around the year two hundred to warn believers away from the circus and the theater, promised them a better show. On the day of judgment, he wrote, they would watch kings groaning in the lowest dark, magistrates melting in hotter flames than they had ever lit for Christians, philosophers burning beside the pupils they had taught, tragedians louder-voiced in their own tragedy, and actors made nimbler by the fire[1]. He asked what praetor, consul or priest could ever put on such a sight.

Not everyone in the Church could manage the view. Origen of Alexandria wrote that the goodness of God would bring all creatures to one and the same end[2], and in five hundred forty-three, nearly three centuries after his death, the emperor Justinian condemned him as a heretic and his writings with him[3]. The Carthaginian ranked his promised show above the circus, both theaters and every racecourse.

A congregation with a ban or a shunning keeps a smaller gallery. The name read out from the front, the excommunicated cousin, the woman discussed over the meal after the service, each has an audience, and the Witnesses’ platform announcement that a person is no longer one of them is read to a full hall, which then goes home to its dinner. The psalm the Church sang says the righteous man rejoices when he sees the vengeance[4], and that joy was the reward on offer. A room that sits through a shaming in silence has taken a seat in that gallery the Carthaginian promised, and whoever crosses the floor to stand beside the shamed has left the gallery before heaven raises the curtain.

Declaration: Heaven promised its saints a free view of the burning, and I spit on the ticket.

The Rite · No faith

Write on a card a public shaming you once watched in silence, and burn it. Then send the person who was shamed, or anyone a church cast out, two plain sentences on their side.

Testament · What would you say now to the person whose public shaming you once watched in silence?

Sources

[1] Tertullian, Spect. 30

[2] Origen, De principiis 1.6.1–3

[3] Justinian, Letter to Menas (543)

[4] Ps 58:10


CXIV Of the Beloved

Indulgence

Day 114 of 365

Wear your dead to rags.

Beatrice Sends the GuideGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto II, 1861

And it came to pass, as Peter passed throughout all quarters, he came down also to the saints which dwelt at Lydda. And there he found a certain man named Aeneas, which had kept his bed eight years[1], and was sick of the palsy. And Peter said unto him, Aeneas, Jesus Christ maketh thee whole, arise, and make thy bed. And he arose immediately. And all that dwelt at Lydda and Saron saw him, and turned to the Lord[2].

Now there was at Joppa a certain disciple named Tabitha, which by interpretation is called Dorcas, and this woman was full of good works and almsdeeds which she did[3]. And it came to pass in those days that she was sick, and died, and when they had washed her, they laid her in an upper chamber[4]. And forasmuch as Lydda was nigh to Joppa, and the disciples had heard that Peter was there, they sent unto him two men[5], desiring him that he would not delay to come to them.

Then Peter arose and went with them. When he was come, they brought him into the upper chamber, and all the widows stood by him weeping, and shewing the coats and garments which Dorcas made[6], while she was with them. But Peter put them all forth, and kneeled down, and prayed, and turning him to the body said, Tabitha, arise[7]. And she opened her eyes, and when she saw Peter, she sat up. He gave her his hand, and lifted her up, and when he had called the saints and widows, presented her alive[8]. It was known throughout all Joppa, and many believed in the Lord[9]. And it came to pass, that he tarried many days in Joppa with one Simon a tanner[10].

Declaration: What my dead made for me goes on my back and out into the weather.

The Rite

Take one thing a dead person made or gave you, a coat, a tool, a pen, and use it for its job today and every day this week. Say their name aloud as you start.

Testament · What did someone who died give you that you keep too carefully to use?

CXV Of Hosannas

Heresy

Day 115 of 365

Withhold your thanks from the year that hurt you.

Heaven Sings HosannasGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book III, 1866

Twenty-four elders cast their crowns before the throne[1] in Revelation, four creatures covered in eyes cry holy without rest day and night[2], and a hundred and forty-four thousand sing a song that no one else is able to learn[3]. When the martyrs under the altar cry how long, they are handed white robes and told to rest a little while longer[4].

The Hebrew name of the book of Psalms is Tehillim, praises, and among its hundred and fifty the compilers kept one that never turns. The eighty-eighth opens by calling the god the God of my salvation and gets no answer in anything that follows, the singer counted with those who go down to the pit[5], his eye wasted with affliction, crying to a god who hides his face, and it ends with lover and friend put far away and darkness for company[6]. Many of the other laments in the book break off into thanks before the end[7].

The command to give thanks now comes down without its throne, to the notebook of three good things written every night and the affirmation recited to the bathroom mirror, and it presses hardest on the bad year, when the death, the layoff or the diagnosis is to be counted a blessing in disguise. The superscription gives the eighty-eighth psalm to a temple choir[8], the sons of Korah, and the book called praises has carried it for over twenty centuries without a line of it softened. A complaint with that pedigree needs no one’s permission to say what it says.

Declaration: Heaven kept its martyrs waiting in white robes, so whoever calls my loss a gift can wait as long for my gratitude.

The Rite

Buy a printed thank-you card. Inside, write your curse on the thing you were told to be thankful for, in the plainest words you have. Read it aloud alone at full voice, then mail it to yourself and leave it sealed.

Testament · Which loss did someone ask you to see as a gift, and what name does it deserve?

[2] Rev 4:8

CXVI Of Guides

Blasphemy ●○○○

Day 116 of 365

Release every shepherd you never asked for.

The Descent BeginsGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto I, 1861

A Latter-day Saint bishop is a layman chosen from the ward, with a day job and no training required, and he sits across a desk from members to judge their worthiness and hear the confession of serious sin. A Witness elder arrives for a shepherding call appointed, his own literature says, by holy spirit[1]. In the nineteen seventies an American movement of biblical counseling began[2] teaching pastors that scripture is sufficient for nearly every trouble of the mind, so that much depression was to be traced to sin and repented of.

Each of these offices is filled without training in medicine or psychology, and the word for the work comes from the shepherd. The Witnesses call the elder’s visit shepherding, and the shepherd of that psalm leads beside still waters and through the valley of the shadow of death[3], and the flock ends by dwelling in his house for ever[4]. A mountain guide’s work ends at the trailhead, and a shepherd’s work never ends. The flock is the purpose.

Ezekiel, speaking for the same god, already knew where that claim leads, and charged the shepherds of Israel with ruling the flock by force and cruelty[5], the sick never healed and the broken never bound up. The desk interview and the shepherding call both assume a sheep that stays a sheep. The inside of your head was never a pasture, and anyone who takes a shepherd’s office over it unasked is owed the notice a flock cannot give, a sentence in your own voice and the door.

Declaration: Nobody was appointed to my head, so I took it back and left the crook at the door.

The Rite · Christian

Say the first lines of the shepherd psalm aloud with yourself in the shepherd’s place. I am my own shepherd. I lead myself beside still waters.

Testament · What will you say to the person who still counsels you without ever having been asked?

Sources

[1] Acts 20:28; Watchtower, elders’ appointment

[2] Jay E. Adams, Competent to Counsel (1970)

CXVII Of Sons

Reckoning

Day 117 of 365

Mourn the relative who harmed you, and stop excusing them.

David Mourns the Death of AbsalomGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

When Amnon raped his half-sister Tamar, the Hebrew of Samuel says only that King David was very angry[1]. The Greek translation, and a scroll of Samuel found at Qumran, carry a clause the Hebrew lacks, that he would not grieve his son Amnon, because he loved him, since he was his firstborn[2]. The king’s love for the rapist was the whole of the sentence passed. Tamar stayed desolate in Absalom’s house[3].

Absalom waited two full years and had Amnon struck down at a sheep-shearing feast[4], then fled to his mother’s father in Geshur for three years. The chapter keeps the king’s grief, mourning for his son every day, and when he was comforted concerning Amnon, seeing he was dead, his soul longed for Absalom[5], who had killed him. Brought home at last, Absalom was kept from his father’s face for two more years[6] and had Joab’s barley set on fire to win an audience, and the kiss he got there did not keep him from raising an army.

David passed no sentence on the son he loved, so his other son passed it at a feast, and the story runs on to Absalom caught in an oak[7] and his father weeping over the gate[8]. Love that withholds judgment hands the judgment to whoever is angriest in the house. The counsel Absalom gave his sister, hold your peace, he is your brother[9], is the one the wronged still hear under the name of forgiveness. Absalom’s way of settling the harm and David’s way of leaving it unsettled ended in the same grief. A harm named aloud at home, with its price said to the one who did it, costs a family less than either.

Declaration: Forgiveness that asks me to hold my peace is Absalom’s hush to Tamar, and I have read the chapters that follow it.

The Rite

Say aloud, alone, the harm a family member did you and what it has cost them with you. Then withdraw one thing today, the visit, the call or the gift, and say You did this, and this is what it cost you.

Testament · Which relative do you grieve and resent at once, and what have they got coming?

CXVIII Of the Fleece

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 118 of 365

Refuse the sign and take the next step.

The Midianites Are RoutedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Gideon had his commission from an angel at the winepress and a sign already given, fire from a rock that consumed his offering[1], and he asked for another. He laid a fleece of wool on the threshing floor and asked that in the morning it be wet with dew while the ground stayed dry, and it was, and he wrung a bowlful of water out of it[2]. Then he asked again the other way round, begging the god not to be angry with him, the fleece dry and the ground wet[3]. That too was granted.

He had now asked for three signs, the last with an apology already attached, and before the battle the god volunteered a fourth, sending him down by night to overhear a Midianite tell his dream of a barley loaf[4] that tumbled into the camp and flattened a tent. Every sign came back yes. The victory went to three hundred jars smashed at once and three hundred torches flaring in the dark[5], and the man who had needed proof upon proof before he would lift a sword came home holding a record of a god who answered whenever he was asked.

He made the Midianites’ golden earrings into an ephod[6], the priestly vest used elsewhere to put questions to the god, and set it up in his own town, where, the book says, all Israel went whoring after it, and it became a snare to Gideon and to his house. The man who asked for proof three times made himself a standing way to ask, out of spoil he never needed, and the house that once wanted a sign for every step now kept an oracle in the yard.

Declaration: I will take my next step without a sign, and the door I open will be one I chose.

The Rite · Christian

Open your own Bible at random for a sign, the divination a council of Gaul condemned in the fifth century, read aloud the verse it gives you, then tear the page out and line the kitchen trash can with it.

Testament · What sign are you waiting on before you do what you already know?

CXIX Of Crossing

Mastery

Day 119 of 365

Go close enough to the barrier to see how it works.

The Israelites Cross the Jordan RiverGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Jordan stopped at a crossing in the valley north of Jericho. A Mamluk chronicler records that in the year twelve sixty-seven part of the high bank near that place slid into the river and dammed it, leaving the bed below dry for some hours[1], and in nineteen twenty-seven an earthquake brought down the clay cliffs at the same spot and the river stood still for most of a day[2]. The book of Joshua puts its miracle in the same reach. When the feet of the priests carrying the ark touched the water, in the season the river runs over its banks[3], the waters coming down stood up in a heap a long way off at the town called Adam[4], usually identified with a mound beside that same crossing, and the people crossed on dry ground[5].

The river had fords, named a chapter earlier when the king’s men chased the spies toward them[6], and a bank that gives way, and the book of Joshua puts the priests between the people and the water. The people were ordered to keep two thousand cubits behind the ark[7], to know, the book says, a way they had never gone, and so the dry bed was first seen under priestly feet and the crossing credited to the box they carried.

A recommend interview stands between a member and a temple door, a form letter between a family and a university, and both are run by someone who stands in front of a place you could walk to. Close up such a barrier comes apart into a few questions and a form, and the rest is the nerve to look foolish in front of strangers. The riverbed was dry for everyone that day, and held the whole host as well as the priests.

Declaration: No priest walks ahead of me into the river. I find the ford myself.

The Rite

Pick one door you were told was not for your kind, a school, a club, a neighborhood, a job, and go through it today. Send the application without the reference, or walk in without the introduction.

Testament · Who taught you to keep your distance from what you wanted, and what did they gain by it?

CXX Of Concupiscence

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 120 of 365

Treat your desire the way its lawgivers treated their own.

The Lovers ApproachGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto V, 1861

For about fifteen years before his conversion the future bishop of Hippo lived with a woman he never names, and she bore him a son[1]. When his mother arranged a better match, the woman was sent back to Africa, and he took another mistress[2] while he waited two years for the bride to come of age. He had been praying, he recalls, for chastity and continence, but not yet[3].

Once he was a bishop he wrote the doctrine. Before the fall, he argued, the first man would have moved his genitals as he moved his hands, at the bidding of the will[4], and lust came afterward as the penalty for disobedience. The Quran allows a man four wives and then makes an exception for one man. A verse of the sura named for the confederates lets the Prophet marry any believing woman who offers herself to him, for him alone and for no other believer[5], and the next lets him put off whichever wives he likes and take to him whichever he likes[6]. Aisha, Bukhari reports, told him that his lord hastened to satisfy his desires[7].

Two men whose words still bind the desires of millions had their own served first, one with fifteen years behind him and one with a verse that exempted him. The bishop’s doctrine charged the body shame for wanting. A body that wants is a body in working order, and the one law desire answers to is consent, the other person’s and your own. A confession still owed for a harmless pleasure is paid into the account of the bishop who took his own fill first and his chastity on the schedule of his own prayer.

Declaration: The lawgivers had their fill and then wrote the rule, so I take mine and write none.

The Rite · No faith

Undress fully in your own room, read aloud from a cheap Bible the verse where the first couple find they are bare and sew fig leaves, then strike the verse out in ink and stay unashamed for an hour.

Testament · For which pleasure that harmed nobody do you still feel you owe a confession?

CXXI Of Rizpah

Reckoning

Day 121 of 365

Stay in sight of power until it answers you.

Rizpah’s Kindness toward the DeadGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A famine had lasted three years in David’s reign. When he inquired of the god, the answer came that it was for Saul and his bloody house[1], because Saul had put Gibeonites to death in breach of an oath[2]. The Gibeonites asked for seven of Saul’s descendants, and David handed them over, among them Armoni and Mephibosheth, the two sons Rizpah had borne to Saul[3]. They were hanged on the hill before the god in the first days of the barley harvest[4] and left where they hung.

Rizpah spread sackcloth on the rock beneath them and stayed from the beginning of harvest until rain fell on the bodies, beating off the birds by day and the wild beasts by night[5]. Nobody in the chapter asks her to, and she stays.

The hangings settled nothing. The rain came with Rizpah still on the rock. Then David was told what Rizpah had done[6], and he went and fetched the bones of Saul and Jonathan from the men of Jabesh-gilead, had the bones of the hanged gathered, and laid Saul and Jonathan in the tomb of Saul’s father, and only after that, the text says, the god was entreated for the land[7].

A woman with no office and no petition kept watch over what the king had given away, and a king who had answered a god with a gallows answered her with a burial. Grief that goes home leaves the dead to the birds, and the bones of her sons came down off the hill because Rizpah stayed on the rock.

Declaration: A god who hangs seven sons for a famine and answers only after a woman has shamed a king into a burial gets no harvest offering from me.

The Rite

Lay on a cloth outdoors the photo or name of someone a church or state treated as nothing, and sit by it an hour. Write I am still here, and so are they. on the cloth, say it aloud, and tie it to a railing outside that church or office.

Testament · Whose wrong would you sit beside in public until the people responsible came out to deal with it?

Book II

Refusal

Days 122 to 243

The second book takes the sum found in the first and sets some of it down, and Day 123 is where it says so. Most days decline a demand, in a form the hands can carry out: a word said aloud, a page burned, a price named, a door shut. The old books supply the occasion and the wording. What was refused may be taken back if it proves worth the carrying, and then by choice.

I will not serve

Jeremiah 2:20, Vulgate


CXXII Of Judgment

Heresy

Day 122 of 365

Buy facts from experts and decide the rest yourself.

The Judgment of SolomonGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Solomon called for a sword to settle a case that had no witnesses. Two prostitutes shared a house, and the woman who brought the case said that nobody else was in it[1] on the night one of them lay on her own baby and smothered it[2], so that each now said the living boy was hers and no one could contradict either. The king ordered the child cut in two, half to each woman[3]. The real mother begged him to give the boy to her rival and let him live, and got him back[4].

Every fact in the case was known before the sword came out, and known to the women. Solomon supplied a threat. The mother supplied the truth, and the chapter closes by crediting the wisdom of the god, which all Israel saw in the king[5], and they feared him. In the version Bukhari preserves, where a wolf carries off one woman’s son and David first rules for the elder woman[6], Solomon calls for a knife, and the knowledge again comes out of the mother’s mouth.

Advice on fact is worth buying, a lawyer reading over a lease or a surgeon reading a scan, because the facts sit with someone else. On what you want, the case has one witness, as the case in Solomon’s house had only the two women to testify, and the witness is you. A counselor who calls for a sword is asking you to say aloud what you hold, so say it first and spare him the blade.

Declaration: The only witness to what I want is me, and I will not hand my verdict to any adviser.

The Rite

Write the decision you keep taking to a pastor, parent, imam or coach as one sentence beginning I have decided, sign it, and send it to that person today, asking nothing back. Then say aloud The case is closed.

Testament · Which answer did you already have the last time you asked someone for advice?

CXXIII Of Refusal

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 123 of 365

Refuse once today and give no reason.

LuciferFranz von Stuck · etching, c. 1890

Tradition has put two Latin words, the ones that mean I will not serve, in Lucifer’s mouth. They come from the book of Jeremiah in the Latin Bible, and the speaker there is Israel. In the Latin the god reminds his people that long ago they broke his yoke and burst his bonds and said they would not serve[1]. The King James translators followed a Hebrew reading that differs from the written text by one letter, so English readers found the mouth vowing not to transgress[2].

The name this plate carries is the Latin Bible’s word for the morning star, in a taunt the book of Isaiah aims at a king of Babylon[3]. That king is given five declarations of will, the first to ascend to heaven and the last to be like the most high[4], and none of them is a refusal to serve. Later readers joined the two passages. The sentence tradition hands to the devil was first a nation’s account of its own freedom, and moving it to the adversary put the accent of the pit on every refusal a pulpit would hear afterward.

The refusal in the verse gives no reasons, and the god answers the bare no with a full speech anyway, the noble vine planted from right seed and gone wild, and the stain no soap can wash[5]. A refuser who offers reasons hands the master clauses to dispute, and the one who demands service also judges whether the reasons are good. A claim on your service you never signed gets the bare word, and the speech that follows it is the master’s business.

Declaration: Non serviam was a free people’s vow before the preachers gave it to the devil, and I take it back from both.

The Rite · Christian

Buy a small statue of any god but the Bible’s, the graven image the second commandment forbids, set it at the head of your table and eat a meal facing it. I will not serve.

Testament · What do you still explain every time to people who were never owed an account?

[1] Jer 2:20

[2] Jer 2:20

[3] Isa 14:4, 12

[4] Isa 14:13–14

CXXIV Of Combat

Mastery

Day 124 of 365

Name the rival and the prize before you draw.

Combat between Soldiers of Ish-bosheth and DavidGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Abner proposed a game. His army, holding out for the house of Saul, and Joab’s, fighting for David, had sat down on either side of the pool at Gibeon, and Abner suggested that the young men get up and play before them[1]. Twelve went out from each side, each caught his opposite by the head and put a sword in his side, and all twenty-four fell down together[2]. The place was named for it, the field of sharp edges[3], and the game won neither house a yard of ground and opened a long war[4].

The man who proposed the game was the first to want it stopped. At sundown Abner called down to Joab, shall the sword devour forever[5], do you not know it will be bitter in the end, and Joab blew the trumpet and the pursuit stopped. Nothing had been settled. Nineteen of David’s men lay dead besides Joab’s brother Asahel, whom Abner had killed with the butt of his spear[6], and three hundred and sixty of Abner’s[7]. The account came due at Hebron, after Abner had come over to David, when Joab drew him aside in the gate as if to speak privately and stabbed him for his brother’s blood[8].

The war for Saul’s throne had a prize, and it closed when David was anointed over all Israel[9]. Joab’s quarrel with Abner, kept for a dead brother, closed only in the gate. Most rivalries in a life are fought on Joab’s terms, the office feud and the dinner-table quarrel, and they stop when somebody tires and start again when somebody remembers. A rival who wants your client is beaten by the better bid on the day the decision is made, and a feud with no prize keeps its dead on the books until somebody lies under the fifth rib[10].

Declaration: I draw only for a prize I can name, and the family feud can go on with one fewer player.

The Rite

Write your rival’s name and the prize on one card and cut it in two. Burn the name in the sink, put the prize in your wallet, and today send the bid, file the application or call the client you both want.

Testament · What exactly do you mean to take from your rival?

CXXV Of the Census

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 125 of 365

Answer for what you did, never for what arrived.

The Plague of JerusalemGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and the second book of Samuel has him move David to go and count the people[1]. Joab protested, the count took nine months and twenty days[2], and when it was finished David’s heart struck him. The prophet Gad offered famine, flight or plague[3], the king chose the god’s hand, and seventy thousand men died between Dan and Beersheba[4], none of whom had ordered the count.

The impulse in this story came from outside the man, and the book names its owner. A later historian could not let the admission stand. When Chronicles retells the census, generations later, the anger of the Lord is gone and an adversary rises to provoke the king[5], so that the figure who would grow into the devil enters the record of Israel’s kings as an editor’s correction to the god’s authorship. In both books the god halts the angel at a threshing floor, where his temple would later stand[6], and David asks him what the sheep have done[7].

A child taught from the Sermon on the Mount that a lustful look is adultery already done in the heart[8] learns to search every thought that arrives, the obscene picture in the middle of a prayer and the flash of hatred at a funeral, as though each came signed by the one who had it. A faith that has you confess the thought beside the deed is less honest than its own older telling. Your acts carry your name. The thought that walks in during the hymn was never yours to confess, and every hour spent confessing it is taken from the deeds you will answer for.

Declaration: The god signed the census in the first verse, and I have stopped confessing his handwriting.

The Rite · No faith

Tell someone you trust the ugliest thought that crossed your mind this week, then name one thing you did this week that you will answer for. The second one is mine.

Testament · Which guilt do you still carry for an impulse you never chose to have?

CXXVI Of Allies

Reckoning

Day 126 of 365

Reward the difficult friend who turned up.

Abishai Saves David’s LifeGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A Philistine of the giants’ line meant to kill David, who had gone down to fight the Philistines one more time and grown faint. The giant’s spearhead weighed three hundred shekels of bronze[1], and he wore a new sword. The book gives the rescue a single sentence. Abishai, David’s nephew, came to his help and struck the Philistine dead, and afterward David’s men swore that the king would never again go out with them to battle, lest he put out the lamp of Israel[2].

Abishai had volunteered before. When David asked in the wilderness who would go down with him by night into Saul’s camp, Abishai alone answered[3], and standing over the sleeping king he begged leave to pin him to the ground with one thrust of a spear[4]. When Shimei cursed David on the road, Abishai offered to go over and take off his head[5], and when Shimei came back over the Jordan, Abishai asked again for his death. David refused him each time he asked, and on the road he asked what he had to do with the sons of Zeruiah[6], the brothers he had called too hard for him after Abner’s burial[7]. The hardness he complained of is the same thing that took Abishai into the camp at night and down to a fainting king.

A family sorts its members by how easy they are to have at the table, and the record of one hard man runs against the sort. David rebuked Abishai three times and kept him, and when the giant came, the man who had begged to spear a sleeping king did the one thing the pleasant could not, and spent his hardness on David’s side.

Declaration: Pleasant company has never once pulled a giant off me, and my debts are paid to those who did.

The Rite

Do for the friend who stood by you while hard to like the one job they would never ask of anyone, a shelf put up, a car cleaned or a form filled in, then tell them in one sentence what they did that earned it.

Testament · What did the hardest of your friends do for you that the pleasant ones never did?

CXXVII Of Brick Kilns

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 127 of 365

Weigh your fear of sacrilege against the kiln scripture let pass.

David Attacks the AmmonitesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

When Rabbah fell, the second book of Samuel records, David took the crown from the head of the Ammonite king, a talent of gold set with precious stones, and it was put on his own head[1]. Then he brought out the people of the city and put them under saws and under harrows of iron and under axes of iron, and made them pass through the brick kiln, and he did the same to all the cities of the Ammonites before he went home to Jerusalem[2].

The same book kills a man for steadying a box. Six chapters earlier the oxen stumbled, Uzzah put out his hand to keep the ark of the god from falling, and the god struck him dead beside it for the error[3]. The chapter that ends on the kiln opens with Nathan rebuking David over Bathsheba[4], and no rebuke follows the saws. Modern translators often turn the saws into tools and the kiln into a brickworks, so that the Ammonites are put to forced labor, and on that gentler reading every city of a people was still enslaved by the man scripture calls one after the god’s own heart[5], whom the Quran honors as a prophet for whom iron was made soft[6].

A believer is raised to weigh by those two chapters, where a hand laid on a holy box is death on the spot and a nation under the iron harrow is a verse that needs no comment, written of the sweet psalmist of Israel[7], whose songs are read over the dead. Harm done to a book or a plaster cross hurts nobody. The keepers of the objects fixed the dread you were taught to feel before it, and never put the kiln on the scale beside a torn page.

Declaration: I save my horror for the saw and the harrow, and a burnt Bible gets a shrug.

The Rite · Christian

Shape a cross from bread dough and bake it hard in a hot oven for half an hour, the brick kiln David sent the Ammonites through. Let it cool, spit on it, and smash it with a hammer on your doorstep.

Testament · Whom did the act you were taught to fear most ever hurt?

[5] 1 Sam 13:14; Acts 13:22

[6] Quran 34:10

CXXVIII Of Cedars

Beauty

Day 128 of 365

Spend the temple’s money on the rooms you live in.

Cedars Are Cut Down for the Jerusalem TempleGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Hiram, king of Tyre, had the cedars cut on Lebanon and floated down the coast in rafts, and took his payment in wheat and oil, twenty thousand measures of wheat a year[1]. Solomon raised a levy of thirty thousand men from Israel and sent them up the mountain in shifts of ten thousand a month[2], and kept besides seventy thousand who carried loads and eighty thousand who hewed the great stones.

All of it was for a god who had told David, through Nathan, that he had never once asked for a house of cedar and had lived in a tent since Egypt[3]. At the dedication Solomon himself conceded that heaven and the heaven of heavens could not contain the god, and how much less this house[4]. In the oracle to David the god promised that David’s son would build him a house[5], and when the son had built it in cedar the god hallowed it[6], and let the Babylonians burn it nearly four centuries later.

He took seven years over the temple and thirteen over his own palace[7], and one hall of the palace, the House of the Forest of Lebanon, ran a hundred cubits on its rows of cedar pillars against the temple’s sixty[8]. The king who said heaven could not hold the god kept the longer job and the longer hall for himself. Congregations still raise cedar for a god who told David he had never asked for it, through building funds and roof appeals and the tithe that pays for marble, and some of the givers go home to rooms they have not finished.

Declaration: Cedar belongs where somebody sleeps, so the good wood comes home with me and the god can keep his tent.

The Rite

Spend today the sum a month’s offering once cost you, or the price of an ordinary gift if you never gave, on one thing made well in wood, wool, stone or glass for the room where you live most, and use it daily.

Testament · Which room of yours has gone without while the god’s house got cedar?

CXXIX Of Wisdom

Heresy

Day 129 of 365

Read each inherited rule as its maker’s life.

King Solomon in Old AgeGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A rabbinic tradition holds that Solomon wrote three books at three ages, the Song of Songs in youth, Proverbs in his middle years and Ecclesiastes when he was old[1]. The young man compared a lover’s breasts to two fawns[2]. The man of middle years called wisdom a tree of life to all who lay hold on her[3] and promised that the rod would drive folly out of a child[4]. The old man said that in much wisdom is much grief and advised eating bread with joy, since the grave has no work in it[5]. Each book was wisdom in its decade, and the last takes back the tree of life.

The first book of Kings supplies the old man’s circumstances. Seven hundred wives and three hundred concubines turned his heart after Ashtoreth of the Sidonians[6], and he built high places on the hill facing Jerusalem for Chemosh of Moab and for Molech of the Ammonites, so that the wisest king the god ever made spent his last years raising shrines for his wives[7]. His counsel moved with his life, and the canon that kept all three books kept the drift.

A man who married at twenty and never left his county will tell you that roots are everything, and a woman who never had to earn her living will tell you that money does not matter, and each is giving an honest report of a life that is not yours. The cult of the elder assumes the old have walked your road. They walked one road to its far end, and a map of another country is worth reading and owed no obedience. Parents still take the rod to children on the word of Proverbs, whose author, by the same tradition, ended his life calling all of it vanity.

Declaration: I honor my elders by letting their rules die with the lives that made them.

The Rite

Choose the rule you inherited from an elder who never stood where you stand, never spend on yourself, work before pleasure, dessert last, and break it today with a pleasure you can finish before the day is out. This decade is mine, and so is its rule.

Testament · Whose rule are you still keeping about a life they never had to live?

[1] Song of Songs Rabbah 1:1:10

[2] Song 4:5

[3] Prov 3:18

[4] Prov 22:15

[6] 1 Kgs 11:3–5

[7] 1 Kgs 11:7–8; 3:12


CXXX Of Lions

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 130 of 365

Ask any messenger to show the angel before you obey.

The Disobedient Prophet Is Slain by a LionGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A man of God came out of Judah to Bethel to cry against King Jeroboam’s altar, and the god gave him three conditions beside the errand. He was to eat no bread there, drink no water, and go home by another road[1]. The altar split. The king’s hand, stretched out to have him seized, withered until the man prayed it whole[2]. He refused the king’s dinner and reward on the god’s orders.

An old prophet of Bethel overtook the man resting under an oak. He said an angel had told him, by the word of the Lord, to bring the man home to eat. The text says outright that he lied.[3] The man went back and ate. At the table the word of the Lord came to the liar, who pronounced sentence on his guest for disobeying[4], and on the road a lion met the man of God and killed him[5]. The lion stood by the body beside his donkey, eating neither, and was still standing there when passers-by reported it. The old prophet fetched the body and buried it in his own grave[6].

The man had his orders at first hand and gave them up because a man with a title claimed a later message. The god sent the correction through the mouth that had deceived him, and the liar told his sons to lay his bones in the dead man’s grave[7]. Of the two prophets only the deceived one is punished, and when Josiah burned the bones of Bethel three centuries later, the liar’s were left alone because they lay beside his guest’s[8].

A revision of your orders that reaches you through a third mouth, with a title on it and a dinner waiting, is the signal to get up from under the oak and take the other road home.

Declaration: Every later word from heaven comes from a man who wants me at his table, and I eat at mine.

The Rite · Christian

Write yourself an order, signed in your own name, to swear aloud by heaven that you keep your own orders, the oath the Sermon on the Mount forbids, and carry it out now. By heaven, I keep my own orders.

Testament · Whose claim of a newer message from above has turned you off your own road?

CXXXI Of Absalom

Reckoning

Day 131 of 365

Count who stood by you before you give again.

The Death of AbsalomGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Absalom died in the wood of Ephraim, caught by the head in an oak[1], run through by Joab and finished by ten of his armor-bearers, against the king’s own order[2]. When the news came, David went up to the chamber over the gate and wept, crying that he wished he had died in his son’s place[3].

The army that had saved his throne crept back into the city like men ashamed. Joab went in and told the king that he had shamed every man who had saved his life that day, that he loved those who hated him and hated those who loved him, and that unless he went out and spoke kindly to his men there would not be one of them left with him by morning. The king got up and sat in the gate.

Absalom had stolen the hearts of the men of Israel[4], gone in to his father’s concubines in a tent on the roof in the sight of all Israel[5], and crossed the Jordan with an army after his father to finish him. David spent his tears on that son while the men who had fought for him came home to a city in mourning for the man they had beaten.

Then the king sent word to Amasa, who had led Absalom’s army, that he would be captain of the host in Joab’s place[6], and the offer bowed the heart of Judah[7] to call the king home. The men who saved the throne got the king’s face in the gate, and the man who had marched against it got their general’s command. Amasa’s first errand was to call up the men of Judah against a new revolt within three days, and he was late[8], and before the revolt was put down Joab had the army back[9].

Declaration: My keys and my name go to the ones who stood in the field with me, and whoever marched against me can ask his own general.

The Rite

Take back today something you still give a person who turned on you, a key, a reference, a standing invitation or a loan of your time, and tell them it is withdrawn. That was for the ones who stayed.

Testament · What have you given to someone who marched against you that belongs to the one who stood by you?

CXXXII Of the Prophets of Baal

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 132 of 365

Hold the god you were raised on to Elijah’s test.

The Prophets of Baal Are SlaughteredGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

At noon on Carmel, after the prophets of Baal had called on their god since morning and leaped about the altar they had built[1], Elijah mocked them. Shout louder, he said, for he is a god, so either he is musing, or he has gone aside, or he is away traveling, or he has fallen asleep and must be woken[2]. Rashi took the third as a trip to the privy[3]. The prophets cut themselves with knives and lances until the blood ran, and nothing answered.

Elijah had named the test himself, that the god who answers by fire is the god[4], and every joke he made at noon rests on it. Fire fell for him, ate the bull and the wood and the stones and licked up the water in the trench[5], and he had the prophets taken down to the brook and killed there[6].

Isaiah and Jeremiah aimed the same joke at other people’s gods. Isaiah’s carpenter burns half a tree to bake his bread, carves the rest into a god and kneels to it, begging to be delivered[7], and Jeremiah’s idols are a scarecrow in a cucumber field, carried about because they cannot walk[8]. Each joke is an argument from silence, and Elijah trusted that argument far enough to kill by it at the brook Kishon. A believer who laughs at the scarecrow has granted that a god who never answers is no god, and by Elijah’s own rule the god your family called on for years, at bedsides and in waiting rooms, has left the bull raw on the wood.

Declaration: I mock the god of my childhood with the jokes his own prophets wrote, and I need not change a word.

The Rite · Christian

Boil an egg, and for the whole time it boils call aloud on the god as Baal’s priests called on theirs. Lord, answer me. Then eat the egg and say He must be asleep.

Testament · What did your family keep asking heaven for, and what did the asking cost them?

CXXXIII Of Fruit

Indulgence

Day 133 of 365

Eat something today for the first reason Genesis gives.

Adam and Eve at Their MealGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IV, 1866

Genesis supplies a menu before it issues a single prohibition. The god gives the first pair every plant that yields seed and every tree with fruit in it[1], sets the man in a garden of trees that were a pleasure to see and to eat from[2], and tells him he may eat freely of every one save one, which alone comes with a threat of death[3].

She saw that the tree was good to eat and lovely to look at and desirable for the wisdom it would give[4], and she took of the fruit and ate. Appetite comes first in that list. The narrator reports what she saw and never says she saw wrongly, and the word sin has not yet appeared anywhere in Genesis, where it waits for Cain[5].

The sentence fell on the table. The god cursed the ground for the man’s sake and made it bring up thorns, so that he would sweat for his bread until he returned to the dust[6]. One meal taken freely was punished by turning every later meal into a wage, and the garden’s menu gave way to a field that had to be worked.

The believer’s table still serves that sentence. Gluttony stands among the seven deadly sins[7], and the holiest day of the Jewish year is spent without food[8]. Both keep the meal out in the field of thorns, where food is earned and owed for. The first reason scripture records for eating anything is that the thing was good to eat, and a mouth that eats for that reason alone is back at the garden’s table, with every tree on the menu.

Declaration: I say no grace over food I bought and cooked, and the god who cursed the ground for my sake gets no share of the plate.

The Rite

Buy one fruit, the dearest ripe one the best grocer near you sells, a kind you have never eaten, and eat all of it with your bare hands, with cream or honey beside it, until the juice runs to your wrists.

Testament · Which food did you learn to eat with an apology, and what does it taste like without one?

CXXXIV Of the Lying Spirit

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 134 of 365

Count no prophecy as proof because it came true.

The Death of AhabGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Ahab went into his last battle in disguise. Four hundred prophets had promised him Ramoth-gilead, and one, Micaiah, had told him that the god had put a lying spirit in all their mouths[1], so he sent Micaiah to prison on bread and water[2] and rode out unmarked[3], with Jehoshaphat of Judah in his robes beside him. An archer drew his bow at a venture[4], aiming at nobody, and the arrow found the joint of Ahab’s armor. He was propped up in his chariot facing the Syrians until evening, his blood running into the floor of it, and died at sunset[5].

The god of that chapter confesses, through the one prophet who would not flatter the king, that he planned the deception and sent the liar himself. Ezekiel has him say it again in his own voice, that if a prophet is deceived, it is the god who deceived him[6], and he will then destroy that prophet, and Deuteronomy warns that a prophet who calls you after other gods may give a sign that comes true[7], because the god is testing you.

The text calls Ahab’s death the word of the Lord fulfilled. They washed his chariot at the pool of Samaria, the dogs licked up his blood, and the Hebrew adds that the prostitutes bathed there[8], a line the King James translators turned into the washing of his armor. So Ahab’s story ends on a prophecy come true, from a god who sent a spirit to lie to the king. Four hundred prophets spoke with one mouth, and their agreement was the instrument the god chose for his lie. A congregation that speaks of your future with one voice proves no more than they did.

Declaration: Satan never had to testify against the god, who confessed the lying spirit himself, and on that one point I take him at his word.

The Rite · No faith

Open a Bible you own, or a cheap one you buy for the purpose, at the lying spirit in the first book of Kings, and write in red across the page the words Unreliable Witness.

Testament · Which promise of scripture did you stake something real on, and what did it cost you?

CXXXV Of Raising

Mastery

Day 135 of 365

Ask no more what fault killed the work you dropped.

Elijah Raises the Son of the Widow of ZarephathGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The widow of Zarephath’s son had stopped breathing[1], and she turned on the prophet who lodged with her and asked whether he had come to bring her sin to remembrance and to kill her son[2]. Elijah took the body from her arms, carried it up to his own bed in the loft and turned the accusation on the god, asking whether he had brought this evil even on the widow who sheltered him[3]. Then he stretched himself on the child three times, and the breath came back[4].

Elisha’s raising at Shunem goes further into the body. The boy died on his mother’s knees at noon[5], and Elisha went in, shut the door on himself and the boy[6], and lay on him, mouth to mouth and eyes to eyes and hands to hands, until the flesh grew warm and the child sneezed seven times[7]. Neither prophet asked what sin had killed a child. Both prayed, and the text gives the prayers a sentence or two and spends the rest of its detail on the bodies, a man’s weight and heat pressed on the dead.

A dropped ambition goes cold the same way in its own house, the manuscript in the drawer and the instrument in its case, each once meant to win the seat a rival has since taken. Anyone taught that sin brings death learns the widow’s reflex, a search through the past for the fault that killed it. The prophets’ method is a body laid on the thing until it warms, the pages sent out again and the case opened in front of the one stranger who can say yes.

Declaration: The prophets gave the god a sentence and the dead boy their bodies, and I can do without the sentence.

The Rite

Carry the work you abandoned into your bedroom and lay it on your bed, as Elijah laid the boy on his. Then send it, enter it or show it to the one person who can say yes to it today.

Testament · What would it take to lay your whole weight on the work you let go cold?

CXXXVI Of Despair

Heresy

Day 136 of 365

Feed the body before it votes on your life.

Elijah Is Nourished by an AngelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Catholic catechism ranks despair under the first commandment[1] as a sin against hope, the state of a man who has ceased to hope for help from his god. One of the Bible’s own wishes to die belongs to a prophet at the height of his power. Elijah sat down under a broom tree a day’s walk past Beersheba and asked to die.

He had called fire down on Carmel and killed the prophets of Baal, and Jezebel had sent word that she would do the same to him within a day[2], so the man who had stood alone against a nation ran for his life. It was enough, he told the god[3]. An angel touched him and told him to get up and eat, and by his head lay a cake baked on hot stones[4] and a jar of water. He ate and drank and lay down again.

The angel came a second time and told him to eat because the road was too much for him. He slept between the meals, and then walked forty days on the strength of that food[5]. The angel’s whole speech under the tree comes to two sentences, and both are about food[6].

The first question anyone puts to him comes forty days later, in a cave at Horeb, when the god asks what he is doing there[7]. Until then no one in the chapter argues with his wish to die or files it among the sins. At Horeb the god hears his complaint twice and answers it with three errands[8], and lays no charge. A verdict on a life reached under a broom tree on an empty stomach belongs to the hunger, and the chapter overrules it with bread.

Declaration: I hold no court on my own life before I have eaten, and no priest sits on that bench.

The Rite

Cook or buy a hot meal built on the fat and salt you like best, tear bread to go with it, pour a cup of thick hot chocolate, and eat all of it at a table with the phone in another room.

Testament · Which verdict on your life have you been reaching on an empty stomach?

CXXXVII Of Fire from Heaven

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 137 of 365

Decline any summons that claims the sky as backup.

Elijah Destroys the Messengers of AhaziahGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Two captains of fifty climbed toward Elijah’s hill with the same message from King Ahaziah, man of God, the king says come down, and each burned with his fifty[1]. The king had fallen through the lattice of an upper room[2] in Samaria and sent to ask the god of Ekron whether he would recover, and Elijah had turned the messengers back with word that the king would die in his bed[3]. The second captain added the word quickly[4]. The third fell on his knees and begged for his life, and was spared[5].

A hundred and two soldiers burned for delivering a summons. Elijah answered with a pun, if I am a man of God let fire come down, and the Hebrew words for man and for fire are ish and esh, a vowel apart[6]. The sky made the pun good twice, so that the only safe approach to him was on the knees. He went down with the third captain only when an angel told him to, repeated his answer to the king’s face, and the king died as the word had said[7].

Summonses still come with heaven named behind the messenger, from an elder who wants a word or a bishop who wants an interview. Elijah’s title was tested by fire twice, and theirs has never been tested once. The captains who climbed Elijah’s hill had a throne behind them, and they burned anyway. The one at the foot of yours holds a letter under a letterhead calling you before a council, and it carries exactly the force of your willingness to go down to it.

Declaration: Elijah needed fire from heaven to refuse a king, and I refuse a bishop with one sentence.

The Rite · Christian

Climb to the highest open ground within reach and boast aloud for a full minute of the best you have done, the pride the Church lists first among the deadly sins. I come down for nobody. Let the phone ring.

Testament · By what authority do you still answer the body that believes it can summon you?

CXXXVIII Of the Chariot

Indulgence

Day 138 of 365

Give your exits the money you would spend on an entrance.

Elijah Ascends to Heaven in a Chariot of FireGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Elijah tried three times to leave his disciple behind, at Gilgal and at Bethel and at Jericho, and three times Elisha refused. The sons of the prophets kept reminding him that his master would be taken that day, and he told them to hold their peace. At the Jordan Elijah rolled up his mantle and struck the water, and it parted, and they crossed on dry ground. A chariot of fire with horses of fire came between them, and Elijah went up by a whirlwind[1]. The mantle fell. Elisha, who had asked for a double portion of his master’s spirit[2], picked it up.

Fifty men of the prophets’ guild searched the hills for three days for the body and found nothing[3]. Elijah had lived on ravens’ bread at a brook[4] and a widow’s last handful of meal[5], slept under a broom tree and in a cave, and the one luxury the text allows him is the manner of his leaving. Jewish custom still keeps a chair for him at every circumcision[6], set for a guest who left no grave.

Many exits in a life are made apologizing, out of parties through a string of excuses and out of jobs through months of resentment, and what the room keeps of the person is the trailing end. Elijah went in a single stroke, with the sons of the prophets watching from across the river[7], and the mantle he dropped went to the one disciple who had refused to be left behind. Leaving is the part of a life that other people carry away, and the man of the ravens’ bread is remembered for his horses.

Declaration: I owe a room my company while I stay in it and nothing on the way out.

The Rite

Leave one shop, cafe or room today by the grandest ride you can pay for, a hired car or a taxi called to the door, and say aloud on the step, as you go, the line you wrote for today’s question.

Testament · What line would you say at the door if horses of fire were waiting outside?

CXXXIX Of Bears

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 139 of 365

Drop the hushed voice you keep for jokes about a god.

Some Children Are Destroyed by BearsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Bethel was the town where Jeroboam had set up a golden calf[1], and Elisha was on his way up to it, fresh from his master’s ascension. A crowd of small boys came out of the town and jeered at him, go up, baldhead, go up, baldhead[2]. He turned and looked at them and cursed them in the name of the god, and two she-bears came out of the wood and tore forty-two of them[3].

Apologists have spent great ingenuity making the boys older, a gang of youths menacing a holy man on a lonely road, though the Hebrew calls them little lads. The text records no fault in the curse and none in the bears. Some nine centuries later soldiers crowned the god’s own son with thorns, knelt to him in mockery and spat on him[4], and the wood stayed empty.

In Medina, Islam’s prophet answered one mocker with men. Ka’b ibn al-Ashraf had made verses against him[5] and stirred up his enemies, and Bukhari records the Prophet asking who would kill the man who had hurt the god and his messenger, and granting the volunteer leave to lie his way close[6]. Ka’b was called down from his fortress at night and killed. No bears came out of the wood for Ka’b, and the answer to his verses came from volunteers with knives.

Many a child hushed for a giggle at prayer grows into an adult who lowers his voice to joke about a god. Heaven has let every one of those jokes pass, as it let the soldiers’ spit pass, and the hush a child learns at prayer has only ever guarded the temper of the adults in the room.

Declaration: I have laughed at a god inside his own house, and the only thing that ever answered me was an usher.

The Rite · No faith

At the story of the bears in a Bible you own, or a printout of it, write the boys’ joke in the margin, draw two bears eating it, and read it aloud alone.

Testament · Which joke about the sacred cost you something at home or in worship?

Sources

[1] 1 Kgs 12:28–29

[2] 2 Kgs 2:23

[3] 2 Kgs 2:24

[4] Matt 27:27–30

CXL Of Famine

Reckoning

Day 140 of 365

Count what stands at your gate before you search your soul.

A Famine in SamariaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A donkey’s head sold for eighty pieces of silver during the siege of Samaria, and a small measure of what the text calls dove’s dung for five[1]. The king was walking on the city wall when a woman cried out to him for help, and he answered that if the Lord did not help her he had nothing to give from the threshing floor or the winepress. Another woman, she said, had told her to give up her son to be eaten that day and promised her own for the next, and they had boiled her son and eaten him, and now the other mother had hidden hers[2].

The king tore his clothes, and the people on the wall saw that he wore sackcloth underneath, against his skin[3]. He swore that Elisha’s head would not stay on his shoulders that day, and declared that this evil came from the Lord and he would wait for the Lord no longer[4]. Ben-hadad’s army stood outside the gate[5], the one fact in the chapter that needed no interpreting, and the king walked past it on his own wall to swear vengeance on a prophet.

The city was fed by four lepers at the gate. They reckoned that if they sat there they would die and if they went over to the Syrians they could do no worse than die[6], and at dusk they walked out to the camp, found it empty and carried off the silver and gold[7]. The chapter credits the god with a noise of chariots in the night[8], and the bread reached Samaria because four outcasts did a sum the king in sackcloth had not tried. Many a shortage in a house has its army at the gate, a deposit withheld or a wage cut, and the lepers worked their sum sitting there.

Declaration: I wore the sackcloth once, and the only one who ever profited from it was the man at my gate.

The Rite

Write down the person or firm behind your shortage and file the claim against them today, in small claims court, with the labor board or the state consumer office, signed in your own name.

Testament · Which hardship did you take as a judgment on yourself, and who profited from it?

CXLI Of Jezebel

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 141 of 365

Meet the unthinkable in your best clothes.

The Death of JezebelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jezebel asked whether Zimri had had peace[1], and that was the last sentence the book allows her. She put it from a window in Jezreel to the man riding in at the gate, and Zimri was the officer who murdered his king and lasted seven days on the throne. The man was Jehu, who had killed her son and thrown him into the field of Naboth. She had painted her eyes and dressed her hair[2] before she went to the window to say it.

Jehu shouted up to know who was on his side. Two or three eunuchs looked out, and he told them to throw her down, and they did[3]. Her blood spattered the wall and the horses, he trod her underfoot, and then he went indoors and ate and drank.

She was a Phoenician princess, the daughter of the king of the Sidonians. She worshiped Baal in her husband’s capital and fed four hundred prophets of the goddess at her table, and she arranged the judicial murder of Naboth for a vineyard[4]. That was a real crime, and the book punishes it. The pulpit kept the paint. A painted Jezebel became the preacher’s name for a woman who dresses to be looked at, and some American charismatic preachers still cast out a Jezebel spirit as a demon[5].

The paint in the chapter was put on for an executioner, by a woman who knew who was riding in at the gate. A woman who arranges her own face for the man come to kill her has taken the one thing the hour left her to own, and Jehu, who could take the rest from her, had to lift his face to the window[6] to see it.

Declaration: Jehu trod on her and went in to his dinner, and the pulpit has kept his place at that table ever since.

The Rite · No faith

Put on your best clothes and paint your eyes, then paint the same lines onto the eyes of a picture of Jesus you own or print, and hang him where a crucifix would hang in a believing house.

Testament · What would you call down from the window to whatever you fear most, if you stood there painted and dressed?

CXLII Of Remains

Beauty

Day 142 of 365

Settle what your death means before your funeral planners do.

Jehu’s Companions Find Jezebel’s RemainsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The men Jehu sent to bury Jezebel found only the skull, the feet and the palms of her hands[1]. The dogs had left nothing else in the field of Jezreel. Jehu heard the report and recalled a sentence of Elijah’s, that the dogs would eat her flesh and her carcass would lie like dung on the face of the field, so that nobody could say this was Jezebel[2].

The prophet’s sentence, as Jehu recalled it, wanted a heap with no name, and the heap kept its name anyway, and later readers set about deciding what the leftover bones meant. A rabbinic tradition found the reason the dogs had spared the hands and the feet in her own habits. Her house stood by the market, it says, and whenever a wedding or a funeral passed she came out of her palace, clapped her palms, raised her voice and followed the procession ten steps[3], and over the limbs that had done it the dogs had no power. One reading made her remains a curse fulfilled and the other made them a reward for courtesy to the bridegroom and the dead, and both were settled over bones that could not object.

The eulogy, the hymn, the verse on the card and the photograph on the easel are chosen by whoever plans the funeral, and they choose from what they wanted you to be. A family that prayed for your return can bury a believer who strayed and was surely coming home. The only correction the dead can make is one they wrote beforehand, in their own hand, where the planners must read it before they speak. Without it, the funeral you get will be theirs, with your name printed on the program.

Declaration: The prophet’s sentence made a heap of her and one rabbi made a saint of the heap, and I would sooner be eaten by the dogs than explained by either.

The Rite

Write the paragraph you want read at your funeral before anyone else speaks, saying in your own words what your life meant, and sign it. Hand it today to whoever will plan your funeral, and tell them Read this first.

Testament · What would the people who bury you decide your life had meant?

CXLIII Of the Boy King

Heresy

Day 143 of 365

Learn whose voice your conscience speaks in.

The Death of AthaliahGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

For six years a boy named Joash was hidden in the temple by his aunt[1], while his grandmother Athaliah ruled Judah. She had seized the throne when Jehu killed her son, and slaughtered the royal line, missing one infant. In the seventh year the priest Jehoiada armed the captains and the guards with King David’s spears and shields from the temple stores[2], brought out the child and crowned him. Athaliah heard the shouting, came in, tore her clothes and cried treason[3], and they killed her at the horses’ entrance to the palace[4]. The new king was seven.

The chronicler says he did right all the days of Jehoiada the priest[5]. When Jehoiada died, the princes of Judah came and bowed to the king, and the king listened to them[6], and the court left the temple for sacred poles and idols. When the priest’s son Zechariah stood up to rebuke it, the king had him stoned in the court of the same house[7] that had hidden him, and the same book says he forgot the father’s kindness.

When the priest died, only the voice in the room with Joash changed. The same ear that heard the priest heard the princes, and nothing the king had been taught told him which voice to trust. A piety that rests on one teacher is borrowed, and the lender can be replaced the day he dies. Any rule of yours with no reason behind it but the teacher is still the priest’s, and it will serve the next man who speaks to you as faithfully as it served him.

Declaration: Joash obeyed the priest and then the princes with the same ear, and I have stopped lending mine.

The Rite

Write on a card one rule that harms no one and that you keep only because you were taught it. Under it write a reason in your own words and sign it, or if no reason comes, break the rule before you sleep.

Testament · Which of your convictions would change hands if the person who taught it died tonight?
