CXLIV Of the God of the Land

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 144 of 365

Retire one charm and fix the cause it stood in for.

Foreign Nations Are Slain by Lions in SamariaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Assyrians deported much of the northern kingdom and resettled its towns with people from Babylon and four other cities. Because the newcomers did not fear the god of the place, the second book of Kings reports, he sent lions among them[1], which killed some of them. The Assyrian king, told that the nations he had planted did not know the manner of the god of the land[2], sent back one of the deported priests, who settled at Bethel and taught them how they ought to fear the Lord[3].

The chapter never says the lions stopped. It records the complaint, the diagnosis and the priest, then turns to the gods each nation went on making for the high places, the Sepharvites burning their children to theirs[4], all of them fearing the god of the land and serving their own, the text says, to this day[5]. The remedy went into the record and the result did not.

The god’s own law had already explained the lions. In Exodus he promises to drive out the Canaanites little by little, lest the emptied land fill with wild beasts[6], and Sargon’s annals boast of twenty-seven thousand carried off from Samaria in one campaign. Hill country stripped of its farmers breeds predators, and the same country plowed and herded again pushes them back to the thickets, with a priest at Bethel or without one.

A former believer keeps the same books. The bedtime prayer said just in case, the cross signed as the plane drops and the medal on the mirror are each a remedy with no result on file. Behind each stands a real danger with a real cause, and while the gesture makes the cause feel handled, the cause stays where it was, the bald tire on the car and the dead battery in the smoke alarm.

Declaration: A god who teaches manners with lions gets my deadbolt and none of my prayers.

The Rite · No faith

Tape the luck-piece you keep, or any coin, to your fire alarm, then press the test button until it sounds. Say This one works. If it stays silent, fit a new battery before you sleep.

Testament · What danger do you still answer with a gesture instead of a repair?

CXLV Of the Herdsman

Mastery

Day 145 of 365

Correct the credentialed from what you know firsthand.

The Prophet AmosGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Amaziah, priest of the royal shrine at Bethel, sent word to King Jeroboam that Amos had said the king would die by the sword. He told Amos to go home to Judah, eat his bread there and prophesy there, since Bethel was the king’s sanctuary and a royal house[1]. Amos answered that he was no prophet and no prophet’s son. He was a herdsman and a dresser of sycamore figs, and the god had taken him from following the flock[2].

Amaziah’s advice assumes that prophecy is a living, to be practiced where the customers are one’s own. Amos refused the title along with the trade. Amaziah drew his bread from the king’s chapel, and the one voice in it that drew none was the voice that foretold a sword against the king’s house. What he brought in place of a lineage was his work. The sycamore fig had to be gashed with a blade while it grew, an art the Egyptians used to bring on ripening[3], so a dresser walked the rows wounding each fruit at its moment. His book is built from that ground, a basket of summer fruit whose Hebrew name sounds like the word for the end[4], and a remnant of Samaria likened to what a shepherd pulls from a lion’s mouth, two legs or a piece of an ear[5].

The nurse who watched a protocol fail and the member who counted the offering both know what the credentialed are paid to overlook, and a title would only have proved they belonged to the house. Amaziah’s weapons were the king’s house and a charge of conspiracy[6], and a man who wants nothing from the shrine can answer them with his trade and pronounce sentence on the priest in the king’s own sanctuary.

Declaration: A priest who eats the king’s bread calls the truth a conspiracy, and I believe the man with sap on his hands.

The Rite

Write to someone who holds a title over your field, a manager, a pastor, an official or an author, the correction you learned on the job, in three sentences. Sign it with your trade and your years, such as a mechanic of twelve years, and send it today.

Testament · What does your own work know that the titled in your field are paid to overlook?

CXLVI Of Burning Lips

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 146 of 365

Say aloud the word your upbringing burned out of you.

The Prophet IsaiahGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Isaiah dates his call to the year King Uzziah died. He saw the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up. His train filled the temple. Above it stood seraphim with six wings apiece, two to cover the face and two to cover the feet and two to fly[1], and one cried to another, Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts, the whole earth is full of his glory. The posts of the door moved at the voice of him that cried, and the house was filled with smoke[2]. Isaiah said he was undone, a man of unclean lips among a people of unclean lips[3], and one of the seraphim took a live coal from the altar with tongs, laid it on his mouth and said his iniquity was taken away[4].

He heard the question whom the Lord should send, and said, Here am I, send me. The commission that followed was to tell the people to hear and not understand, to see and not perceive, to make their hearts fat and their ears heavy and their eyes shut, lest they understand and turn and be healed[5]. When Isaiah asked how long, the answer was until the cities lay waste without inhabitant[6], the houses without man, and the land utterly desolate, with men removed far away and a great forsaking in the midst of the land.

If a tenth part were left in it[7], that too would be consumed, like a terebinth or an oak whose stock remains when it is felled, so the holy seed is its stock.

Declaration: Whatever my tongue says tomorrow, it says on its own authority, and nobody holds a coal over it.

The Rite · No faith

Say aloud, at the volume you would use to order dinner, the oath a Christian house winced at most, God damn it, then turn it on its author. God damn you.

CXLVII Of the Vine

Reckoning

Day 147 of 365

Plant something that will outlive the forecast.

Micah Exhorts the Israelites to RepentGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Micah of Moresheth[1] gave Jerusalem the harshest sentence in his book, that Zion would be plowed like a field and the city become a heap of ruins[2]. A century later, when the priests and prophets wanted Jeremiah dead for saying much the same, elders of the land stood up and quoted Micah, and they remembered it as a sentence that had been put off. Hezekiah had feared, they said, and the god had repented of the evil he pronounced[3], and the city was still standing for them to argue in.

The same book, a chapter on, holds the other picture. In the latter days the nations will beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks[4], and every man will sit under his vine and under his fig tree, and none shall make him afraid[5]. A grapevine gives its first real crop in about its third year, so the man in the shade is a man who planted long before and stayed to see it.

A child raised on the sentence of ruin can carry it out of the faith for life, an end so near that every long plan looks foolish and every pleasure looks borrowed. Micah’s ruin did come, when Babylon burned Jerusalem over a century after he spoke, and a vine set in the ground the day he said it would have fed four generations before the fire. Whatever year you were first told the end was near, the plans you shelved that year are the only part of the prophecy that has come true.

Declaration: Jerusalem stood a century under its sentence, and I plant my vines under every sentence passed on me.

The Rite

Buy a vine or a fig tree and plant it in your own ground or a large pot, with a tag tied on bearing the year you were told the world would end, or failing one, the year you left.

Testament · What would you start today if you trusted you had decades to finish it?

[1] Mic 1:1

[2] Mic 3:12

[3] Jer 26:17–19

CXLVIII Of Ransom

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 148 of 365

Put the sacred thing in your house to work.

Sennacherib’s Army Is DestroyedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Hezekiah paid first. When Sennacherib of Assyria took the fortified cities of Judah, the king sent to him at Lachish to say that he had offended and would bear whatever was laid on him, and he was charged three hundred talents of silver and thirty of gold[1]. He emptied the treasuries of the god’s house, and then he cut the gold from the temple doors and pillars, gold he had overlaid himself[2], and sent it to the king of Assyria.

The same chapter calls him the king who trusted the god as no king of Judah before or after him[3]. The next has the angel go out in the night and strike down a hundred and eighty-five thousand[4] in the Assyrian camp, and the old English rendering has men rising early in the morning to find that they were all dead corpses[5]. Sennacherib’s own annals record the tribute reaching Nineveh and boast that he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage[6], and they mention no angel. Both records agree that the tribute was paid, and the book says where the gold came from, stripped off the god’s doors by that same trusting king on the day he needed it.

Asa had sent the temple’s silver and gold to one Syrian king and Joash its hallowed things to another before Hezekiah touched the doors. The Bible on the shelf, the siddur, the prayer mat and the crucifix are what that gold was, material held in reserve and sacred until the day it is useful. The book of Kings records each payment without a word of blame, and the Bible kept unopened on a high shelf is guarded more carefully than any of those kings guarded the temple.

Declaration: I handle holy things the way their keepers do when the money runs short.

The Rite

Take one object you own that is gilt or silver and held back as too good to use, and spend it today, sell it or pawn it or melt it, and put the money toward a bill. Gold is for the day it is needed.

Testament · Which object of your old faith are you still afraid to handle carelessly?

CXLIX Of Spoil

Indulgence

Day 149 of 365

Carry the spoil home before the next battle.

The Ammonite and Moabite Armies Are DestroyedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The army of Judah spent three days stripping the dead, and the chronicler gives the reason, that there was so much. Among the bodies they had found riches and precious jewels, more than they could carry[1]. It was the end of a war in which they had struck no blow. Moab and Ammon had come with the men of Mount Seir, Jehoshaphat had proclaimed a fast throughout Judah[2], and on the day of battle he sent singers out at the head of his army to praise the god[3]. The enemy turned on itself. Ammon and Moab first destroyed the men of Seir and then each other[4], and when Judah reached the watchtower over the wilderness there were only bodies, and not one had escaped[5].

The chronicler records the gathering with a quartermaster’s satisfaction. A fast came before the battle and a song opened it, and the spoil after it is set down in the same approving hand. On the fourth day the people assembled in a valley to bless their god and named the place Blessing[6], with the jewels already gathered. A people that had begged for rescue took the reward as part of the rescue.

The promotion is answered by a fuller inbox and the finished manuscript by the next proposal, as if pleasure taken at the moment of winning were a vanity. A reward put off until the next goal is met is paid to a stranger, since the winner has already been replaced by the one chasing the next. The one who earned it walks off his own field with empty hands, and the jewels stay where they fell among the dead.

Declaration: Judah took three days over the spoil of a battle it never fought, and I take at least an afternoon over the one I won.

The Rite

Spend a tenth of your last raise, bonus or fee today on one thing you can carry home from the shop in your own hands, and take an unhurried hour with it, doing nothing anyone could pay you for.

Testament · Which recent win did you hurry past without taking anything home from it?

CL Of the Hundred Thousand

Heresy

Day 150 of 365

Measure your days by what they gave you.

The Israelites Slaughter the SyriansGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The servants of the king of Syria told him the god of Israel was a god of the hills, so the next battle should be fought on the plain[1]. A man of God promised Ahab that because the Syrians had called his god a god of the hills and not of the valleys, he would hand the whole multitude over[2]. The armies faced each other for seven days, and on the seventh the Israelites killed a hundred thousand Syrian foot soldiers in a single day[3]. The survivors fled into Aphek, where a wall fell on twenty-seven thousand of them[4].

The book keeps the Syrian dead to the last thousand and gives no figure for Israel’s dead. The god who wanted to prove his reach over the valleys had the proof entered in thousands. No Israelite death in either battle is entered. The book of Numbers opens with a count of its own, the god ordering a census of every Israelite man of twenty and over fit for war[5], Levites aside, and the women and children of the camp stand in no column.

Until late 2023 every rank-and-file Jehovah’s Witness was expected to report the hours spent preaching each month[6], a figure that took in the doorsteps and never the evenings they cost. A streak of four hundred days on a language app counts the days you opened it and nothing you can now say in the language. The blank beside each figure is where your life went, and no keeper has ever printed a number for it.

Declaration: The clerk who keeps my streak and the elder who once collected my hours are one trade, and neither has ever paid a cent for the time he logged.

The Rite

Break the longest streak you keep for an app that profits from your return and watch it fall to zero, sparing any count kept for health or recovery. Then spend the freed half hour in a hot bath or in bed with a novel, and say Count that.

Testament · Who decided that the number you check every day should matter to you?

CLI Of Zedekiah

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 151 of 365

Contradict the next sermon that calls a child’s death a plan.

Zedekiah’s Sons Are Slaughtered before His EyesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Zedekiah was twenty-one[1] when Nebuchadnezzar set him on the throne of Judah, a vassal under oath to Babylon[2]. He rebelled, and in the ninth year of his reign the Babylonian army came and laid siege to Jerusalem, and the siege lasted until the bread in the city ran out. He fled by night through the gate between the two walls, was overtaken in the plains of Jericho, and was brought to the king of Babylon at Riblah. There they slaughtered his sons before his eyes, then put out his eyes, bound him in bronze fetters and took him to Babylon[3]. The last thing he saw was his children dying.

Ezekiel, writing among the exiles, has the god swear by his own life that because Zedekiah despised the oath sworn in the god’s name to the king of Babylon, he would bring it down on his head and spread his net for him[4]. The historian says it was through the anger of the god that all this came upon Jerusalem and Judah[5]. The sons appear in neither verdict. Their deaths were the sentence, and the sentence was addressed to their father.

A theology that can read the murder of boys in front of their father as the settlement of a broken treaty has told you what it will make of any child’s suffering, and the same reasoning still turns up at hospital beds and after earthquakes, as a plan or a punishment. Whatever happens to a child is an event with causes, and where the cause is a man, the charge belongs to him, in court and in the record. At Riblah it was the king of Babylon who killed the sons of Zedekiah[6], and he had a name.

Declaration: When heaven claims a massacre as its anger, I hear a killer being handed his alibi.

The Rite · No faith

Cut from a cheap Bible the verse that blames the fall of Jerusalem on the anger of the Lord, and nail it to a board under the word Accused written in your own hand.

Testament · Where have you heard a child’s suffering explained as the will of a god?

CLII Of the Stocks

Reckoning

Day 152 of 365

Carry your complaint from the altar to the face that earned it.

The Prophet JeremiahGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Pashhur son of Immer, a priest and chief officer of the temple, heard Jeremiah prophesy that the city would fall, had him beaten, and fastened him overnight in the stocks[1] at the upper gate of Benjamin. In the morning he let him out, and Jeremiah met him with a new name. The god no longer called him Pashhur, the prophet said, but Terror on Every Side[2], and he would watch his friends fall by the sword, go captive to Babylon and be buried there with every friend to whom he had prophesied lies[3].

Then the chapter turns to prayer. The god deceived him, Jeremiah complains, and he was deceived[4]. Partway through he repeats the phrase he had thrown at the priest, fear on every side[5], now as the talk of friends watching for him to stumble, and he lays his cause before the god and asks to be shown the god’s vengeance on them[6].

At the gate the words were a sentence, aimed at a man who could see who was speaking. In the prayer the same words went upward as a complaint. The prayer supplies its own answer, a verse of praise for a deliverance it never names[7], and the next verse curses the day he was born[8]. The book never records the vengeance he asked for, and Pashhur drops out of it with no fulfillment recorded.

A wrong taken to heaven is a wrong kept from the one who did it. The man who put you in the stocks is owed his sentence in your own voice, on the morning he lets you out, at the gate where he can see who is speaking.

Declaration: I said the worst of my enemy to his face, and I sleep better for it.

The Rite

Write the complaint you have carried to prayer or to your pillow as five sentences addressed to the person by name. Hand or send it to them if that is safe. If it is not, read it aloud standing in your doorway and burn the page.

Testament · Whom have you been complaining about to heaven, and what would you say to their face?

CLIII Of the Burned Scroll

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 153 of 365

Hear the threat to the end without tearing your clothes.

Baruch Writes Jeremiah’s PropheciesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jehudi read Jeremiah’s scroll aloud to Jehoiakim king of Judah in the winter house, where a fire burned in the brazier before the king. Whenever three or four columns had been read the king cut them off with a scribe’s knife and threw them into the fire[1], until the whole scroll was gone. Three of his officials begged him to stop. The chapter records that neither the king nor any servant who heard all these words was afraid or tore his clothes[2].

His father Josiah had heard a scroll read once and torn his clothes on the spot[3], and the book of Kings says no king before or after turned[4] to the god as he did. The son kept his clothes whole and judged the text a column at a time. The god answered with a second scroll, everything the king had burned taken down again by Baruch with many similar words added to them[5], and with a sentence on the king. Jehoiakim would have no one to sit on the throne of David, and his corpse would lie out in the sun by day and the frost of the night[6].

The book of Kings closes his reign in one line. Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, it says, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place[7], so the god’s own chronicle seats an heir on the throne the sentence had emptied, if only for three months. A reader who hears every threat out to the last column dry-eyed, warming his hands, is doing what the king did, and Kings reports no trembling from the heir either.

Declaration: Let them write the second scroll longer. I have a knife, and the winter is long.

The Rite · No faith

Print the first ten chapters of Jeremiah, read them aloud, and feed each finished column into a paper shredder, or tear it by hand into strips, until nothing is left.

Testament · Which verse still frightens you when it is read aloud, and what exactly does it threaten?

CLIV Of Ruined Walls

Mastery

Day 154 of 365

Answer every summons from the plain with the same refusal.

Nehemiah Views the Ruins of Jerusalem’s WallsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Nehemiah had been cupbearer to the king of Persia[1], and he came to Jerusalem with the king’s letters and for three days said nothing. Then he rode out in the night, by the Valley Gate past the Dragon Well to the Dung Gate[2], looking at the broken walls and the burned gates, and where the King’s Pool left his horse no room to pass he went up the gully and came back in by the gate he had left from. The officials of the city never knew where he had been[3].

Sanballat and Tobiah were displeased that anyone had come to seek the good of Israel[4], and when the building began, so did the mockery. Tobiah said a fox climbing on it would knock their stone wall down[5]. The builders worked with swords belted on[6].

When the wall was almost up, his enemies sent four times asking him down to a village on the plain of Ono, meaning him harm, and four times he sent the same answer, that he was doing a great work and could not come down[7]. The fifth message came as an open letter charging him with building the wall to make himself king. He replied that they had made it up out of their own hearts[8].

They meant to frighten the builders, Nehemiah writes, so that their hands would drop from the work[9], and when the open letter failed they hired a prophet to scare him[10] into hiding in the temple. Whoever waits on your collapse, the relative who predicted the bankruptcy or the partner who left before it, will send the same invitation down to the plain, and every hour given to that meeting is an hour taken off the wall. It stood in fifty-two days[11], and his enemies were cast down in their own eyes[12].

Declaration: The man who laid no stone gets no vote on my wall, and no look at it until the gates hang.

The Rite

Walk the ruin you keep describing instead of mending, the debt or the half-built thing, and measure it alone, on paper. Make the one repair you can finish today, and answer whoever asks after it. I am doing a great work and cannot come down.

Testament · Who would most enjoy watching your ruin stay a ruin, and what will they see when the wall stands?

CLV Of Dung

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 155 of 365

Give the pulpit back its own dung.

The Prophet EzekielGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Deuteronomy issues the army of Israel a paddle among its weapons[1]. A soldier who needs to relieve himself is to go outside the camp and bury what comes from him, because the god walks in the middle of the camp and must see nothing indecent there and turn away[2]. The same god dictates Ezekiel’s bread down to its weight, six grains and pulses baked in the people’s sight over human dung[3], as a sign of the defiled bread Israel would eat in exile. The prophet protests that he has never eaten anything unclean, and heaven relents so far as to allow him cow dung[4].

Through Malachi the god promises the priests who displease him that he will spread the dung of their feasts across their faces[5]. Paul, ranking everything he once valued beside the knowledge of Christ, chose a word for it that politer translations still soften to rubbish[6]. The King James and the Douay both kept dung.

Those raised on these books were told that foul speech defiles the mouth. Ephesians bans filthiness and coarse jesting among the saints[7], and Colossians orders filthy talk put out of the mouth[8] altogether. The same canon hands the word to its god and his apostle to shame with, in a prophet’s bread, on the faces of priests, in a verdict on a former life. The believer was trained to flinch at a word his own Bible throws. Said aloud over the open page, the word goes back to naming what every body makes each morning, the bodies of the priests in Malachi included.

Declaration: Heaven’s favorite insult is mine now, and I say it at dinner.

The Rite · No faith

Print the verses of Deuteronomy in which the god walks through the camp and must see nothing indecent, cut them into squares, and hang them by your toilet. Take one in with you, read it aloud, and bin it. The god has seen enough.

Testament · Who taught you the disgust you still carry for the plain facts of your own body?

CLVI Of the Feast of Belshazzar

Indulgence

Day 156 of 365

Let nothing in your house be too good to use.

Daniel Interprets the Writing on the WallGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A thousand lords sat down to drink with Belshazzar. Partway through the wine the king sent for the gold and silver vessels carried off from the temple in Jerusalem, so that he and his lords, his wives and his concubines could drink from them[1]. They drank and praised gods made of everything from gold down to stone. In the same hour the fingers of a man’s hand came out and wrote on the plaster of the wall by the lampstand, and the king’s knees knocked together[2]. Daniel read the words as numbered and weighed and divided[3], and that night Belshazzar was killed[4].

The vessels had been put in a Babylonian treasury, and the night the book records anyone lifting them to a mouth is the night it condemns. When Daniel reads the king his charge, it names the cups before the idols[5]. The book of Ezra finishes the story of the cups. Cyrus had them counted out to the returning exiles, five thousand four hundred vessels of gold and silver[6], and they went home to Jerusalem to be put back in the temple, every one in its place.

Many households keep temple vessels of their own, the good glasses and the bottle saved for a day that keeps failing to arrive. Those vessels waited decades in a treasury and came out on the one night that cost the king his life, and Daniel’s charge counts the drinking from them beside the praise of idols. Yours were bought to be used. The set on the top shelf will be counted and carried out of the house by someone else, as Cyrus’s treasurer carried out Babylon’s, and the only question is whether anyone drank from it first.

Declaration: I drink from the good cup on a weekday, and any hand that likes may write on my wall.

The Rite

Lay the table with the glasses and plates kept for occasions, for yourself and whoever is in the house, fill them with the best you can buy, wine or whatever you drink, and toast the hand on the wall. I have been weighed, and I am still at the table.

Testament · What are you saving for an occasion, and whom would you pour it for?

CLVII Of Ruins

Heresy

Day 157 of 365

Plaster over the patch you keep bare.

People Mourn over the Destruction of JerusalemGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A householder who plasters his walls, the Talmud rules, should leave a patch about a cubit square bare opposite the door, in memory of Jerusalem[1]. Some observant homes still keep it[2], a square of raw brick seen by everyone who comes in, a small ruin maintained so that a far one is never allowed to heal.

A whole fast day each year mourns the fall of both temples[3], and a glass is broken under the groom’s heel at many Jewish weddings for the same Jerusalem. The passage of the Talmud that sets out the bare patch tells of mourners who refused meat and wine, since the altar that received them was gone, until a sage persuaded them that a people cannot be asked to grieve beyond what it can bear[4].

The present age has given private mourning a creed. The shrine on the dresser and the anniversary spent in bed rest on the doctrine that grief is the form love takes once its object is gone, and that the mourner who stops has stopped loving. The guilt that maintains it is the suspicion that pleasure taken after a loss is stolen from the dead, and it asks more than the Talmud’s mourners did, who gave up only what the altar had once received.

The dead collect nothing from the brick or the shrine. Even the sage who talked the mourners out of their fast left every house its cubit of raw wall. What the living owe the dead is the use of what they left. The dead man’s coat belongs in the weather he bought it for, on the back of whoever loved him, wet through by the first winter.

Declaration: Every pleasure I take after a death is mine outright, and the grave gets no tithe of it.

The Rite

Take down the memorial you keep in order to stay sad, the framed card, the shrine or the standing photograph, put it in a drawer, and fill the space with something you bought this week for no one but yourself.

Testament · What pleasure have you forbidden yourself out of loyalty to a loss you keep open?

[1] b. Bava Batra 60b

[2] Shulchan Aruch, OC 560:1

[3] m. Taanit 4:6

CLVIII Of Dry Bones

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 158 of 365

Cancel the appointment at the graveside.

Ezekiel’s Vision of the Valley of Dry BonesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Ezekiel was set down in a valley full of bones, very many and very dry. He prophesied, and the bones came together with a rattling, bone to its bone, and took on sinew, flesh and skin, and when he called breath from the four winds they stood up on their feet, an exceedingly great army[1]. The god then explains his figure. The bones are the whole house of Israel, who say that their hope is lost[2], and the graves he will open are the exile, out of which he will bring them home to their own land.

Later readers argued whether the figure promised anything to a corpse. In the tractate Sanhedrin one sage called the vision a parable[3], and another rose to say he was descended from the risen and owned the phylacteries his grandfather had received from them[4]. The rabbis made the rising of the dead an article of faith[5], and the Church read the valley as the resurrection of the body.

The Church that read the promise into the valley kept the right to withhold it. The 1662 Prayer Book commits the body in sure and certain hope[6] of the resurrection, and its opening rubric forbids that office for anyone who dies unbaptized, excommunicate, or by his own hand[7]. The priest was told whose grave to leave without it.

The god of the vision explained his bones as a nation coming home[8], and the reunion read into them afterward came with an admission list drawn up by the readers. A widow who keeps her pew to meet her husband again pays dues on a promise the prophet never carried, to a church that refused the same words to the suicide in the next plot. Her husband lies where the bones lay before anyone prophesied over them, and the dues buy him nothing.

Declaration: My dead are finished, and I would rather keep them finished than share them with a priest.

The Rite · Christian

Say the Creed aloud, standing, and stop before its clauses on the resurrection of the dead and the life of the world to come. Say in their place the name of someone you loved who has died, or your own.

Testament · What do you still give a church for the sake of meeting your dead again?

CLIX Of Vashti

Reckoning

Day 159 of 365

Keep your own banquet.

Queen Vashti Refuses to Obey Ahasuerus’ CommandGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

For a hundred and eighty days[1] the king of Persia displayed the riches of his kingdom to his nobles. Then he gave a feast of seven days for everyone in the citadel of Susa, in a court hung with white and blue hangings on silver rings, with couches of gold and silver on a pavement of marble[2]. On the seventh day, merry with wine, he sent seven eunuchs to fetch Queen Vashti in her royal crown, to show the peoples and the princes her beauty[3]. She refused to come[4]. The book gives no reason, and records only that she was holding a banquet of her own for the women[5] of the palace.

A counselor named Memucan told the king that the queen had wronged every prince and every people in his provinces, because when the women heard of it they would look on their own husbands with contempt[6]. Letters went out to all hundred and twenty-seven provinces, each in its own script and language, decreeing that every man should be master in his own house[7].

By Memucan’s own reckoning the queen’s appearance had never been a private favor to one husband, since every household in the empire stood on her coming when called. The family that produces its children at dinner as proof of its righteousness runs on the same terms, and so does the parent who still brings the grown child out to perform piety for the relatives. Refuse once and someone will answer with an argument about the whole order of things, and the size of the argument measures what your compliance was holding up. The court’s sentence was that she come before the king no more[8] and that her crown go to a better woman, and the book never has her ask for it back.

Declaration: Send seven eunuchs if you like. Any house that needs my face at its feast to stay standing can fall.

The Rite

Decline, without giving a reason, one appearance someone expects of you for their own standing, the dinner, the service or the photograph, and spend that hour at a table of your own with someone who has never asked you to perform.

Testament · Who has been drawing credit on your appearances without ever paying for them?

CLX Of the Furnace

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 160 of 365

Hold your head up where you were taught to bow it.

Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego in the FurnaceGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Nebuchadnezzar set up an image of gold, sixty cubits high, on the plain of Dura. Whenever his horns and pipes and harps struck up, every people and nation was to fall down and worship it, on pain of the furnace[1]. Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego would not. Their god was able to save them, they told the king, and if he did not, they would still not serve his gods or bow to his image[2].

The furnace was heated seven times hotter than usual, the men who threw them in died of the heat[3], and the king, looking in, saw four men walking loose in the fire, the fourth like a son of the gods[4]. Then the king made a law of his own. Any people or language that said a word against the god of the three would be cut in pieces and their houses turned into dunghills[5]. A chapter that praised three men for defying the king’s god closes on a king who makes a word against their own god a capital crime, a blasphemy law enforced by dismemberment, and on the three promoted under his law[6].

The clause that matters in their answer is the second, if he does not, because it refuses with no rescue in view, and a refusal that waits on a rescuer is a bargain. The bowing you were trained in outlives the belief behind it, in the head that dips at a name and the knee that bends at a hymn, and a reflex of that kind yields only to a body held upright on purpose, with nobody coming to pull you out of the fire.

Declaration: A Babylonian decree once guarded the god of the furnace with a butcher’s knife, and I say every word against him anyway.

The Rite · Christian

Say the Lord’s Prayer aloud standing upright, with your head up and your eyes open, and say your own name in place of the word Father.

Testament · Where in your body does your old worship still live, and what sets it off?

CLXI Of Beauty Treatments

Beauty

Day 161 of 365

Make yourself splendid on your own instructions.

Esther Before the KingGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Twelve months of oil lay behind Esther when her turn came to go in to the king, six with myrrh and six with perfumes and ointments[1], and she had chosen none of it. A decree had gathered her into the keeping of Hegai[2], the eunuch in charge of the women, and when she was allowed to take with her from the women’s house whatever she asked for, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai advised[3]. The king loved her above all the others and set the crown on her head.

The Greek version of the book, printed in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles, stretches one moment of the Hebrew into a scene. When she has to go in to the king unsummoned, which the law punished with death[4], Esther first puts on mourning and ashes and prays, then takes them off and dresses in her full splendor, one maid to lean on and another to carry her train, her heart stiff with fear[5]. The king looks at her in fierce anger and she faints, and the god, the Greek says, turns his anger to gentleness[6].

Scripture elsewhere warns women off braided hair and gold[7]. Esther, the Hebrew book records, won favor in the sight of all who looked at her[8]. It was the power the harem left in her hands, and the first time she spent it as Hegai advised. The second time Mordecai had told her to go in, and she dressed in the royal robes herself, went in unsummoned with a fast behind her, and put a banquet where a plea would have been. The king held out the scepter[9]. The gown worked because she chose it.

Declaration: I dress for my own eyes first, and the room is welcome to the rest.

The Rite

Spend an evening on your body as Esther spent her year, the oils, the scent, the best clothes you own, every choice your own, and go out where you will be seen.

Testament · How would you present yourself if you did it entirely for your own ends?

CLXII Of Haman

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 162 of 365

Leave every warning sent after you unanswered.

Esther Accuses HamanGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Haman’s gallows stood fifty cubits high at his own house[1]. His wife Zeresh and his friends proposed it the day Mordecai again refused to rise for him[2] at the king’s gate, though every other servant there bowed, and the thing pleased Haman, and he had it built to hang the one man in the king’s service who would not bow. Esther named him her enemy[3] at the second banquet, the king came back from the garden to find him fallen across the queen’s couch[4], and a chamberlain named Harbonah[5] mentioned the gallows standing ready at Haman’s house.

Haman built it for one man and hanged on it himself, by the king’s word. A hell preached at those who leave is preached in the same rooms to those who stay, and Paul’s words there, to work out their own salvation with fear and trembling[6], are read to the whole congregation. The hell a congregation keeps for its leavers is built to the same plan. The one who walked out goes to work and to bed under an empty sky.

Whatever was promised you on the way out, the burning or the outer dark, was cut from their timber. The warnings are old and written down. The Amidah has its blessing against the heretics, Trent ends each of its canons on justification with anathema sit, and the Quran says of those who leave the faith that they are companions of the fire. Haman meant his beam for the man at the gate and hung from it himself.

Declaration: Their hell was the last gift they made me, and I left it unopened on the step.

The Rite · No faith

Draw a gallows on a sheet of paper and write on its rope the worst thing a believer ever promised would happen to you. Pin the sheet at the foot of your bed and sleep the night beside it.

Testament · What threat were you handed on the way out, and who does it still frighten?

CLXIII Of the Chronicle

Indulgence

Day 163 of 365

Stop waiting for the chronicle to be read.

The Triumph of MordecaiGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Mordecai, sitting in the king’s gate, learned that Bigthan and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs, were plotting to lay hands on King Ahasuerus[1]. He told Queen Esther, she told the king in Mordecai’s name, the two were hanged, and the matter was written in the book of the chronicles in the king’s presence. Nothing else was done. Years passed before the night[2] the king could not sleep and had the chronicles read to him, and when he heard the entry and asked what honor had been given this man, his servants told him nothing had been done[3].

When the reward came, its designer was Haman, standing in the outer court[4] with a hanging to ask for, who supposed the king meant to honor him[5]. He asked for the royal robe the king had worn, the horse the king had ridden with a royal crown, and one of the noblest princes to lead the rider through the city square proclaiming him[6]. The king sent him to do every bit of it for Mordecai[7] the Jew, who sat at the king’s gate.

Haman knew to the stitch what he wanted because he had pictured himself wearing it. Whoever does good work and waits for the manager or the family to remember it has staked the reward on someone else’s sleepless night, and gets the honor someone else thinks fitting, if any. Mordecai rode through the square in another man’s fantasy, and when the parade was over he went straight back to sit at the gate[8], and Haman hurried home with his head covered[9].

Declaration: Praise that arrives years late is a receipt for patience I should never have spent.

The Rite

Write the deed nobody rewarded as one line of chronicle, and beneath it the honor you would design if you knew it was yours. Buy the best piece of that honor today with money already yours, and wear or use it where people will see.

Testament · What did you do well that went into someone’s records and no further?

CLXIV Of Diets

Heresy

Day 164 of 365

Retire the food rule you keep like a commandment.

Daniel among the ExilesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The proof the steward accepted was fat. Daniel and his three friends, taken to Babylon to be trained for the king’s service, were assigned a daily portion of the king’s food and of the wine he drank[1], and Daniel resolved not to defile himself with it[2]. He asked the steward for ten days on vegetables and water[3], and at the end of them the four looked fairer and fatter in flesh[4], the old translation says, than all the young men who ate from the king’s table. The steward then took the meat and wine away from all four and left them the vegetables.

Churches now keep a fast in his name, twenty-one days of plants and water, and take its length from the tenth chapter, where Daniel, an old man in the reign of Cyrus[5], mourns for three full weeks. In those weeks, the book says, he ate no pleasant bread and let no meat or wine into his mouth[6]. The same verse sets aside the oil for his skin along with the bread, the flesh and the wine, and ends the list at three weeks. The book files all of it under mourning, not under merit.

Whoever counts each bite as a sin and each lost pound as grace is eating supper as penance. The steward of the first chapter judged by the faces in front of him[7] after ten days, and asked for no tally. Daniel’s three bare weeks had a grief behind them, and the Daniel Fast keeps the plate and drops the reason.

Declaration: I am hungry, and no regime gets to weigh my plate.

The Rite

Delete the calorie counter or fasting app you track your food with, or tear the diet log out of its notebook, and eat your next meal without a count. Say No one is counting.

Testament · What would you eat this week if nobody, yourself included, were keeping count?

CLXV Of the Lions’ Den

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 165 of 365

Take your escape off heaven’s account.

Daniel in the Lions’ DenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Darius the Mede had been talked into a decree that for thirty days nobody might pray to any god or man except the king[1]. Daniel went on praying three times a day at his window, facing Jerusalem[2]. He was thrown to the lions, a stone was laid over the mouth of the den and sealed with the king’s ring, and the king spent the night fasting and awake. At dawn Daniel called up that his god had sent an angel to shut the lions’ mouths[3], and there the children’s version stops.

At the king’s command the men who had accused Daniel were thrown into the den, and their children and their wives with them, and the lions overpowered them and broke all their bones before they reached the floor[4]. Deuteronomy forbids Israel’s courts to put children to death for their fathers’ crimes[5], and the book that holds Daniel up as a model of piety records the killing without a word of regret. Darius then wrote to every people on earth commanding them to tremble before Daniel’s god[6].

Lions that broke the bones of children that same morning had been made gentle for one man overnight. A god who can shut a lion’s mouth and shuts it once has chosen the rest, and every rescue credited to him carries the same choice. A driver walks out of the crash that killed the family in the other car and thanks the god who spared him, and a congregation praises the answered prayer for one sick child in a ward full of them. Gladness at being alive needs no god to aim it at. The rescue that praises a hand that chose has to praise the same choice at the foot of the den, where the accusers’ children lay.

Declaration: I owe the god of the den nothing for the one supper his lions skipped.

The Rite · No faith

Print a children’s-Bible picture of Daniel at ease among the lions, write across the floor of the den in red the verse where the accusers’ wives and children go into the den, read that verse aloud, and put the picture in the bin.

Testament · Who paid for the rescue or answered prayer you once told as a story of grace?

CLXVI Of Beasts

Mastery

Day 166 of 365

Stop waiting for the court to sit.

Daniel’s Vision of the Four BeastsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Babylon lined its processional street with lions in glazed brick, some sixty on each side[1], so that whoever walked to the Ishtar Gate walked between them. In Daniel’s dream the lion came back plucked. Four beasts climbed out of the great sea[2], the first a lion with eagle’s wings whose wings were torn away until it stood on two feet like a man[3], then a bear told to devour much flesh[4], a leopard with four wings and four heads[5], and a fourth beast with iron teeth and ten horns that stamped on whatever it had not finished chewing. The angel explained that they were kings[6].

A horn on the fourth beast made war with the saints and prevailed against them[7], and went on prevailing until the Ancient of Days came and the court sat. Only then was the kingdom given to the saints of the Most High[8]. In the whole vision they lift no hand. The beast falls to a verdict delivered from above, at a date the angel gives as a riddle, a time and times and half a time[9], and the saints are told to wait until it is read.

A landlord or a lender has reason to like a dream like that. Tenants who expect a court in the clouds are not reading the lease, and the landlord loses something each time one of them reads the lease, finds the notice the other side owes or the repair it promised, and holds the beast to its own paper. Daniel’s last chapter counts the riddle out in days[10], and no count made since has produced a court a tenant could cite. The notice period in a lease can be cited this week, to the landlord, in a dated letter.

Declaration: Heaven’s court has kept the saints waiting for two thousand years, and I have stopped taking a number.

The Rite

Find the one term in your lease, loan or work contract that binds the other side, a notice it owes you, a repair, a refund or a raise it promised, and send a dated letter today holding it to that term.

Testament · Which power over your life has made a promise it hopes you never read?

[2] Dan 7:2–3

CLXVII Of Babylon

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 167 of 365

Keep your grudge off anyone smaller than its cause.

Isaiah’s Vision of the Destruction of BabylonGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Isaiah’s burden of Babylon promises that everyone who is found will be run through. Their infants will be dashed to pieces before their eyes[1], their houses plundered and their wives raped. The god will stir up the Medes, whose bows will cut down the young men and who will have no pity on the fruit of the womb[2]. Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, will never be lived in again, and its palaces will be left to jackals and owls and to the goat-demons who will dance there. The faithful are told that vengeance belongs to the god and he will repay[3].

The Babylonian chronicle records that the army of Cyrus entered the city without a battle[4], and Babylon went on being lived in for centuries. Neither that chronicle nor Cyrus’s own cylinder records a massacre in the city. The exiles kept the promise alive in their own song. The psalm by the rivers of Babylon first asks the god to remember against the Edomites the day Jerusalem fell, when they shouted to raze it to its foundations[5], and two verses later blesses whoever takes Babylon’s little ones and dashes them against the rock[6].

Across those verses the hatred slides from Edom, who shouted for the razing, to Babylon, whose army did it, to Babylon’s infants, who did nothing. A grudge handed upward to wait on a god’s timing widens from the hands that did the harm to everyone standing near them, and everyone near them includes infants. A grudge kept to the hands that earned it has nowhere to slide.

Declaration: I curse with my own mouth, and no god carries my grudges to the cradle.

The Rite · No faith

Print Isaiah’s burden of Babylon, write across it the name of the adult who most wronged you and what they did, read it aloud as the curse, then tear it to strips and put them in the bin.

Testament · What exactly did the person who earned your hatred do to earn it?

Sources

[1] Isa 13:16

[2] Isa 13:17–18

[3] Deut 32:35; Rom 12:19

[4] Nabonidus Chronicle (ABC 7) iii.15–16

[5] Ps 137:7

[6] Ps 137:9


CLXVIII Of Judith

Reckoning

Day 168 of 365

Let them grow used to you.

Judith and HolofernesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Judith took off her widow’s sackcloth, bathed, anointed herself, braided her hair and put on the clothes she had worn while her husband was alive, with anklets and every jewel she owned[1]. She walked with her maid into the camp of the army besieging her town. She told the outposts she had fled a people about to be destroyed and could show their general how to take the hill country without losing a man.

Then she spent three days teaching the camp a custom. She ate only the food she had brought, had Holofernes order his guards to let her out to pray, and every night toward dawn she went out to a spring to bathe and pray[2]. On the fourth day Holofernes gave a banquet meaning to seduce her, and drank more wine than he had drunk on any day since he was born[3]. When he lay senseless across his bed she took his own sword down from the bedpost, took him by the hair, and struck his neck twice[4]. Then she and her maid walked out as they did every night, with his head in their food bag[5].

Three nights of walks on the general’s own pass bought one night when nobody stopped two women carrying a bag. The guards had their general’s word and three nights of custom, and custom is the thing a watchman has stopped watching. Whoever means you harm, a manager building a file or a former partner counting on your silence, has made a custom of you too, and each week you keep to it the picture grows more certain in their mind. An answer prepared inside that picture passes their outposts with the guards’ blessing and reaches them while they still think you have gone out to pray.

Declaration: An enemy who has learned my comings and goings knows exactly as much as I chose to show him.

The Rite

Gather the record of your own that undoes your enemy, the email or file they think you lost. Go about your days as usual for three days, and on the fourth carry it by hand to the court, the regulator or the person they wronged.

Testament · Which of your comings and goings has your enemy stopped watching?

Sources

[1] Jdt 10:3–4

[2] Jdt 12:7–8

[3] Jdt 12:20

[4] Jdt 13:6–8

[5] Jdt 13:10


CLXIX Of the Dragon

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 169 of 365

Outlast the story that casts you as the beast.

The Destruction of LeviathanGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A psalm reminds the god of Israel that he broke Rahab in pieces like one of the slain[1]. Isaiah calls on his arm to wake as in the days of old, when it cut Rahab and pierced the dragon[2]. This Rahab, spelled differently in Hebrew from the harlot of Jericho, is a monster of the deep. The psalm founds heaven and earth in the very next verse[3], and Isaiah a few verses on.

Babylon recited its own version at the new year festival. The gods make Marduk their king when he agrees to fight Tiamat, the salt sea, and once he has killed her he splits her body in two like a sea creature[4], raising one half as the sky. Genesis opens over the deep[5], the Hebrew word for which is kin to her name, and on its fifth day the god creates the great sea monsters[6] as ordinary creatures among the fish, the fight edited out. The engraving above puts it back, a robed figure in the clouds with his sword drawn and the coils of the beast churning the sea.

A throne that stands on a slain monster needs the monster forever, since every call for the god to act again retells the kill. The small sovereigns of a household or an office keep the same part open, and whoever will not be tamed is cast as the thing from the deep. The part has two exits written for it, the rage on cue that proves you a monster and the vanishing that proves you slain. Take neither and the arm Isaiah begs to wake finds no monster in your house to cut, and the song about the kill has nothing to be sung over.

Declaration: Every victory hymn sung over me is proof that I am still alive.

The Rite · Christian

Draw the god above and a sea dragon beneath him, draw yourself standing dry on the water between them, and sign your own name.

Testament · In whose story do you play the monster someone needs to defeat?

Sources

[1] Ps 89:10

[2] Isa 51:9

[3] Ps 89:11; Isa 51:13

[4] Enuma Elish IV 137–138 (translations differ on the creature)

[5] Gen 1:2

[6] Gen 1:21–23


CLXX Of the Companion

Indulgence

Day 170 of 365

Pay your helpers in things a body can use.

Tobias and the AngelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A dog goes all the way to Media and back in the book of Tobit. Tobias needed a guide for the road, and the man outside called himself a kinsman and agreed to go for a day’s silver and his keep[1]. The two set out with the dog. On the first evening, by the Tigris, a fish leaped out of the river[2] at Tobias as he washed his feet, and the stranger told him to catch hold of it. On his advice they saved the heart, the liver and the gall, and roasted the rest.

The guide was the archangel Raphael, who had given his name as Azarias[3], a kinsman, and he steered the boy to a wife[4] and showed him that the smoke of the heart and liver drives a demon from a bridal chamber and the gall cures a blind father. When they came home the father and son offered him half of everything they had brought[5]. He answered the offer by telling them to bless the god of heaven, and said that all those weeks he had neither eaten nor drunk, and that what they saw was a vision[6]. Then he went up out of their sight[7].

Scripture’s most courteous companion gave a false name, answered the offer of his wages with an order to praise heaven, and said he never ate or drank at all. His answer teaches that help is owed upward and costs the helper nothing. Yours had a body. The friend who drove through the night or sat beside you in the waiting room lost the sleep and missed the meals. Thanks sent past that friend to heaven pays the one party at the bedside who, as Psalm 121 says of him[8], neither slumbers nor sleeps.

Declaration: An angel who turns his wages into a hymn has sent me a bill, and I do not pay it.

The Rite

Cook a fish for the friend who stood by you at your worst, as Tobias roasted his by the Tigris, with whatever they love beside it, and eat it with them to the last bite. Tell them You were there, and this is your half.

Testament · Who stood by you through a hard stretch, and what did they get for it?

CLXXI Of Permission

Heresy

Day 171 of 365

Stop asking who commanded you.

Artaxerxes Grants Freedom to the JewsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A clay cylinder dug out of Babylon in eighteen seventy-nine carries Cyrus’s boast that he returned the gods of many cities to their sanctuaries and gathered their peoples back to their homes[1], and Judah is nowhere on it. Ezra gives the same policy a divine author. The Lord stirred up the king’s spirit[2], he writes, and Cyrus proclaimed that the god of heaven had charged him to build a house in Jerusalem, and that any of that god’s people who wished might go up and build it[3].

In the second year of Darius the house still stood at its foundations[4], and no new decree was on its way. Then two prophets spoke[5], and the builders began again with no new letter in hand. When the governor beyond the river came asking who had commanded them to build[6], they named a decree of Cyrus eighteen years old[7], kept laying great stones[8] while his report went to the king, and the archive at Ecbatana[9] turned up the decree to confirm what they were already doing. Artaxerxes, the king the engraving shows granting freedom, sent Ezra off with silver and gold for its offerings nearly sixty years after the house was finished[10]. The offerings went to an altar the exiles had built in their first autumn home[11].

Some of the permission a person waits for is of that kind, the confirmation of a right already held, and here it arrived to agree with those who had already begun. Where a law or another’s property bars you, it bars you, and Judah’s neighbors barred it for years[12]. But Haggai’s charge against the people was that they themselves said the time had not come[13], and the stone went up the month they stopped saying it[14].

Declaration: Some gatekeepers hold a lock, and many hold a stamp, and I know which are which before I wait.

The Rite

Write down a right you already hold and keep waiting to have confirmed, act on it today, and ask for the confirmation only after you have begun, as the builders did.

Testament · What are you waiting to be allowed to do, and whose sign-off have you mistaken for a law?

CLXXII Of the Priests of Bel

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 172 of 365

Feed your own household before any god’s.

Daniel Confounds the Priests of BelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Twelve great measures of fine flour, forty sheep and six vessels of wine[1] went before Bel each day, and each morning the table was bare. When the king asked Daniel why he would not worship a god who ate and drank so much, Daniel laughed and said the idol was clay inside and bronze outside[2] and had never eaten anything. So the food was laid out again, and before the door was shut and sealed with the king’s signet, Daniel had his servants sift ashes over the whole floor[3] of the temple, with only the king watching.

In the morning the seals were whole, the table was bare, and the king cried out in praise of Bel. Daniel laughed again and showed him the floor. Footprints of every size[4] ran across the ashes to a secret door under the table[5], by which the seventy priests had come[6] in the night with their wives and children, as they always did, and eaten and drunk everything.

Israel’s law needed no ashes, because it wrote the eaters into the statute. Leviticus gives what is left of the grain offering to Aaron and his sons to eat in the holy place[7], and Numbers gives the waved portions to the priest and to his sons and daughters with him[8], by a statute for ever. Bel’s priests came in under the table with their children, and the priests of Israel came in through the law with theirs. A god’s table has fed the family that keeps his door, in Bel’s temple and in Israel’s statutes alike.

Declaration: The god never ate a crumb of what I gave him, and his priests have had their last.

The Rite · No faith

Set the food you like best on a plate before a Bible, or a cross drawn on paper, as an offering to the god of Abraham, a coin beside it. Then eat it, pocket the coin and laugh at the empty altar.

Testament · What did you once lay before a god who cannot eat, and who was eating it?

CLXXIII Of the Scribe

Mastery

Day 173 of 365

Seek great things for yourself.

BaruchGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Baruch son of Neriah took Jeremiah’s prophecies down from the prophet’s mouth[1] and read them aloud in the temple when the prophet was barred from it[2]. When the king cut the scroll apart and fed it to the fire a few columns at a time, Baruch wrote the whole of it again[3]. In five verses addressed to him alone he complains that the god has added sorrow to his pain and that he is worn out with groaning and finds no rest[4]. The god’s reply asks whether he seeks great things for himself and forbids him to, since the god is pulling down what he built, and promises him nothing but his life, his only spoil wherever he goes[5].

Both scrolls went out as the words of Jeremiah. His story in Jeremiah ends in Egypt[6], where officers fleeing the Babylonians took him with the prophet. Later centuries found his name worth more than the god had let him think it. The book of Baruch opens under his name in Babylon[7], a city the book of Jeremiah never sends him to, and the introduction in the American Catholic Bible allows for its final editing in the last two centuries before the common era[8].

The god took a scribe’s labor twice over and gave catastrophe as his reason for wanting nothing back. The name he was told not to seek was the one a later writer chose to put on a book, in Babylon, where Jeremiah never sent him. Nothing in the chapter says he ever got to answer.

Declaration: My masters called the wish for great things a sin and kept the great things for themselves.

The Rite

Find one piece of work you made that went out under someone else’s name and is yours to show. Write your full name across your own copy and hang it where visitors will see it.

Testament · What would you seek for yourself if no one had ever called the wish a sin?

CLXXIV Of the Apostate

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 174 of 365

Leave again, this time on purpose.

Mattathias and the ApostateGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

At Modein the king’s officers asked Mattathias, the town’s priest and leading man, to sacrifice first, for the king’s friendship and silver and gold[1], and he refused aloud. Then one of the Jews came forward in the sight of everyone to sacrifice as the king commanded. Mattathias saw him and burned with zeal, and ran and killed him on the altar, and killed the king’s officer with him, and tore the altar down[2]. The book compares the deed to Phinehas spearing Zimri[3] and calls it zeal for the law. It never records the dead man’s name. Josephus, retelling the scene for Greek readers, arms the priest’s sons with swords and names Apelles, the king’s general they killed[4], and leaves the Jew as nameless as the book did.

The man at the altar, whose fear or belief the book never reports, survives only as the first body of the revolt. He went to the altar at the king’s summons and died at the priest’s hand, and neither the hour of the summons nor the hour of the blade was his. The zeal passed to a dynasty that held the high priesthood and the throne for about a century.

A departure made under that pressure is timed by others. If you went over the first time in a hurry, half hidden, with an eye on whoever might come running, the watchers set your schedule as surely as the officers and the priest set his. The leaving stays theirs until it is done again, slowly, at an hour nobody summoned you to, with no one to please on either side of the altar.

Declaration: No summons sent me out, and no blade will call me back.

The Rite · Christian

Go to a church service, or play a recorded one, and leave before the final blessing. Stand up slowly, and walk out or switch it off at a pace you choose.

Testament · What would it look like to leave deliberately the thing you first left in fear?

Sources

[1] 1 Macc 2:17–18

[2] 1 Macc 2:23–25

[3] 1 Macc 2:26; Num 25:7–8

[4] Josephus, Ant. 12.270


CLXXV Of Susanna

Reckoning

Day 175 of 365

Lend no one your belief on the strength of their seat.

Susanna in the BathGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The law of Moses would put a person to death on the word of two witnesses[1]. In Babylon two elders of the exiles, appointed judges that year[2], used to watch Susanna walking in her husband’s garden, and each lusted after her in secret until each caught the other at it. One day she sent her maids for oil and soap and had the garden doors shut so she could bathe, and the two men, who had hidden among the trees, ran out at her. Lie with us, they said, or we will testify that a young man was with you and that this was why you sent your maids away[3].

She cried out and refused them, and they shouted too. The next day she was tried before the assembly, with her parents and her children watching, and the elders had her veil taken off, the book says, so that they could feed their eyes on her beauty[4]. They laid their hands on her head[5], the two witnesses the law required, and told their story, and the assembly believed them because they were elders and judges of the people, and condemned her to death[6].

The threat failed on her and worked in the assembly, which put no question to either man. They brought a story and two seats on the bench, and the crowd supplied the rest, its own belief lent to an appointment and spent against the one person in court with no seat at all. Two men could only accuse. The assembly that believed them for their chairs was the one that led her out to die[7].

Declaration: Two chairs on a bench nearly killed Susanna, and no chair borrows my belief again.

The Rite

Strike one person who used their position against someone weaker from every list you control, your references, your introductions and your guest list, and refuse to vouch for them to the next person who asks.

Testament · Which judgment of someone weaker did you accept because of who delivered it?

[1] Deut 17:6

[2] Sus 5

CLXXVI Of the Mother

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 176 of 365

Refuse to trade a person for a promise.

The Courage of a MotherGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Seven brothers and their mother were arrested and ordered, under the whip, to eat swine’s flesh, and the second book of Maccabees records each death in turn. The eldest said they would die sooner than break the laws of their fathers. The king had pans and cauldrons heated, had the boy’s tongue cut out and his scalp torn off and his hands and feet cut away while his family watched, and then fried him in a pan, still breathing[1]. The others followed one by one, several of them promising as they died that the king of the world would raise them up[2].

The book’s highest admiration goes to the mother, who watched seven sons die in one day and bore it, the book says, because of her hope[3]. When the king urged her to counsel the youngest to save his life[4], she leaned over the boy, reminded him that she had carried him nine months and nursed him three years[5], and told him to accept death so that she might receive him back with his brothers in the mercy to come. She died after him. The rabbis later made the same choice the rule for a decree against the faith, that a Jew must then accept death before breaking even a minor commandment[6].

The king offered her the last boy’s life, and she told the boy to refuse it on the strength of a promise. The reunion she offered the child was payable only after both of them were dead, on terms neither could ever check, and that promise turned a mother into the voice that talked her child to his death. What would have sent the youngest home that day, rich on the king’s sworn word[7], was one mouthful of pork.

Declaration: The holiest mother in that book is the one I would never let near my children.

The Rite · Christian

Phone the relative you were taught to give up for the faith, say I will not trade you for a promise, and set a date to eat dinner with them.

Testament · What were you taught was worth dying for, and who would have collected on it?

[1] 2 Macc 7:3–5

[2] 2 Macc 7:9, 14

[4] 2 Macc 7:24–26

CLXXVII Of Vindication

Beauty

Day 177 of 365

Question your accusers one at a time.

The Justification of SusannaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A young man named Daniel stopped the procession taking Susanna to her death and shouted that he was clear of her blood. Fools, he called the people, to condemn a daughter of Israel without examination and without knowing the truth[1], and he sent the court back to its seat. He had the two elders separated. To the first, after a rebuke, he said, if you saw her, under which tree. Under a mastic tree, the elder said. Daniel had the second brought in and asked the same thing, and he said under an evergreen oak[2]. The whole case came apart in two answers, and the people turned on the pair and gave them the death they had meant for her[3].

Two men who had watched the same garden day after day[4] could not agree on its trees. They had agreed on the lover, the shut doors and the maids sent off[5], the parts that carry a sentence, and neither had fixed the scenery, which nobody in the assembly thought to ask about.

A story a family or a congregation keeps about a member who left can be built the same way, in company, each teller nodding along with the rest, and nobody has asked it for a tree. Ask each teller alone where it happened, and write down the answers before any of them can compare notes. The first two that disagree are the first crack in the verdict, and a story that holds only while its tellers stand together has nothing under it but their word.

Declaration: My accusers agree on the story and part ways on the tree.

The Rite

Write on a card what your old family or congregation says about you. Ask each person who repeats it, alone, where they saw it happen, and write each name and answer under it. Bury the card under the nearest tree, blanks and all.

Testament · Which story about you has only ever been told in company?

Sources

[1] Sus 48

[2] Sus 58

[3] Sus 61–62

[4] Sus 8–12

[5] Sus 36–37


CLXXVIII Of Causes

Heresy

Day 178 of 365

Keep no rule its leaders would break to survive.

Mattathias Appeals to the Jewish RefugeesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

After the killing at the altar Mattathias went through the town shouting that everyone zealous for the law and faithful to the covenant should follow him. He and his sons fled to the hills and left everything they owned in the town[1]. Many others went down into the wilderness with their wives and children and cattle[2]. The king’s troops found one band of them in hiding and attacked on the Sabbath. The people would not fight back or throw a stone or even block the openings of their hiding places[3], because of the day, and they died, about a thousand of them[4], saying that heaven and earth would witness they were killed unjustly[5].

When Mattathias and his friends heard of it they mourned bitterly, and then decreed at once that they would fight anyone who attacked them on the Sabbath[6]. If they all did as their brethren had done, they said, the heathen would soon root them out of the earth[7]. The rabbis later went further and ruled from Leviticus that the Sabbath and most commandments were given to live by and not to die by[8], with idolatry, murder and adultery excepted.

The thousand died keeping the principle, and the men who led the cause amended it the moment they saw that they were next. The wilderness had no ruling yet that the Sabbath could bend, and the ruling, when it came, was bought with a thousand bodies that were not the leaders’. The amendment was narrow, fighting only when attacked, and the men who wrote it were the men now under the spear.

Declaration: The rule I was told to die for bent under the first leader it threatened, and I will bend it too.

The Rite

Pick the strictest food, dress or Sabbath rule your old faith still asks of you. Break it once today, and say I bend it as they bent it.

Testament · Which law are you keeping to the letter that its leaders have already bent?

[1] 1 Macc 2:27–28

[2] 1 Macc 2:29–30

[3] 1 Macc 2:36

CLXXIX Of Elephants

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 179 of 365

Look under the royal armor before you charge it.

The Death of EleazarGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Elephants were shown the juice of grapes and mulberries[1] before the battle at Beth-zechariah, the first book of Maccabees says, to rouse them against the army of Judas Maccabeus. Each carried a wooden tower full of fighting men[2]. Eleazar, called Avaran, one of Judas’s brothers[3], saw that one elephant stood higher than the rest and wore royal armor, and supposed that the king was on it. He gave his life, it says, to save his people and win himself an everlasting name. He ran at it through the ranks, killing to the right and the left, got underneath and stabbed it from below, and it fell on him, and he died there[4].

The book never puts the king on the animal. The boy king Antiochus came through the battle alive, Judas’s army fell back[5] from the field, and after a siege the king made peace with the defenders of Jerusalem[6]. Eleazar died under a beast in the king’s armor, and the book grants him the everlasting name he wanted in the space of four verses.

Royal armor draws the bravest man on the other side to the wrong place, and it drew Eleazar. The king’s army was filled out with hired soldiers from other kingdoms and the islands of the sea[7]. Whoever goes for the sign of a power spends himself where the power is not. Eleazar’s name cost him his life, and it cost the king one elephant and the men who stood in his path, out of a host of a hundred thousand foot[8], twenty thousand horse and thirty-two elephants.

Declaration: I stab nothing that wears a king’s armor until I have seen the king inside it.

The Rite

Pick the figurehead you have raged at, a pastor, a founder, a president. Find in the organization’s own records who signs its budgets and decisions, write that name and title on a card, and mail the person one line, I know where the decision was made.

Testament · Which power have you been fighting that was only its armor?

Sources

[1] 1 Macc 6:34

[2] 1 Macc 6:37

[3] 1 Macc 2:5

[4] 1 Macc 6:43–46

[5] 1 Macc 6:47

[6] 1 Macc 6:57–61

CLXXX Of Pursuit

Mastery

Day 180 of 365

Cross the water before you feel ready.

Judas Maccabeus Pursues TimotheusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Timotheus camped beyond a stream with his army and told his captains what would decide the battle. If Judas crossed the water first, they would not be able to stand against him[1]. If he was afraid and camped on the far side, they would cross over themselves and beat him[2]. Judas posted officers along the bank with orders to let no man stay behind in the camp[3], and went over first, and the whole army after him, and the enemy threw away their weapons and ran[4].

Timotheus told his captains what he feared, and the book gives Judas’s scouts a report of a very great host and no word of that plan, yet Judas did what the enemy feared. The order he gave left the army no vote on whether it was ready to wade. Staying had been made impossible, and the only ground left to stand on was the far side.

Judas set his officers at the stream with orders that no one camp, because the danger to his crossing lay behind him. The near bank holds the tents and the reasonable voice that counsels one more night, and a man who waits for his nerve to carry him past them waits for a thing that comfort exists to dissolve. Clear the camp and the nerve is unnecessary. The men who waded that day were no braver than the men who would have stayed behind, and they were the same men. Timotheus had staked his battle on Judas being afraid to cross, and he lost it to a few officers standing at the stream.

Declaration: My enemies are counting on my fear of the far bank, and I am already across.

The Rite

Name the contest you have been camped beside. Cancel the one thing that lets you put it off another week, the extension or the second opinion, and make your offer, application or demand today, before the other side moves.

Testament · What keeps the near bank comfortable for you?

CLXXXI Of Dagon

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 181 of 365

Break the reflex your god left behind.

Jonathan Destroys the Temple of DagonGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The first book of Samuel says, And the Philistines took the ark of God, and brought it from Eben-ezer unto Ashdod. When the Philistines took the ark of God, they brought it into the house of Dagon, and set it by Dagon. On the morrow Dagon was fallen upon his face to the earth before the ark of the LORD. They took Dagon and set him in his place again. On the next morning the head of Dagon and both the palms of his hands were cut off[1] upon the threshold, and only the stump of Dagon was left to him.

Therefore neither the priests of Dagon, nor any that come into Dagon’s house, tread on the threshold of Dagon in Ashdod unto this day[2]. But the hand of the LORD was heavy upon them of Ashdod, and he destroyed them, and smote them with emerods, even Ashdod and the coasts thereof. And when the men of Ashdod saw that it was so, they said, The ark of the God of Israel shall not abide with us[3], for his hand is sore upon us, and upon Dagon our god.

The first book of Maccabees names the same city Azotus. It says, Then brought Simon forth his host[4], and set them against the footmen, who were discomfited by him, and fled. The horsemen also, being scattered in the field, fled to Azotus, and went into Bethdagon, their idol’s temple, for safety. But Jonathan set fire on Azotus, and the cities round about it, and took their spoils, and the temple of Dagon, with them that were fled into it, he burned with fire. Thus there were burned and slain with the sword well nigh eight thousand men[5].

Declaration: I walk across the threshold the priests of Dagon kept clear, and I owe no god a detour.

The Rite · No faith

Play any hymn or church chant that makes the room go quiet, sit sprawled in your chair, and eat something and talk over it at full voice until it ends. Then say I am not in your house.

Testament · Which reflex of your old faith still moves your body before you can stop it?
