CLXXXII Of the Horse

Indulgence

Day 182 of 365

Spend your strength on pleasure, and punish no one with it.

Heliodorus Is Cast DownGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Heliodorus, treasurer to the Seleucid king, came to Jerusalem to seize the money in the temple treasury, which the high priest told him was laid up for the relief of widows and fatherless children[1] and in part belonged to Hircanus son of Tobias[2]. There was no small agony throughout the whole city[3]. At the treasury there appeared a horse with a terrible rider, the horse adorned with a very fair covering, and it smote at Heliodorus with its forefeet[4], and it seemed that the rider had complete harness of gold. Two other young men appeared before him and scourged him continually[5] until he fell to the ground and was put into a litter[6].

The two young men are notable in strength, excellent in beauty and comely in apparel[7], and seven verses on they stand beside Heliodorus again in the same clothing[8]. One chapter later Jason builds a place of exercise under the tower itself[9], and the priests hasten to be partakers of the unlawful allowance in the place of exercise, after the game of Discus calls them forth[10].

Menelaus got the priesthood to himself by offering more than Jason by three hundred talents of silver[11]. He stole vessels of gold out of the temple and sold some into Tyrus and the cities round about[12]. The king slew Andronicus, who had murdered Onias[13]. Thus the Lord rewarded him his punishment, as he had deserved[14]. When three men sent from the senate[15] pleaded against Menelaus, he promised Ptolemee much money, and the king discharged him and condemned the three to death. Menelaus remained still in authority[16]. Later the King of kings moved Antiochus against this wicked wretch[17], and the king commanded that he be put to death in a tower full of ashes[18]. He received his death in ashes.

Declaration: I move my body for my own pleasure and I ask no scripture to approve it.

The Rite

Go today to a track, a pool or an open field and run, swim or throw until you are soaked and breathing hard, for as long as it pleases you. Take no phone and no watch, and keep no count. Then say aloud This was for no one but me.

Testament · When did you last move your body only for the pleasure of it, and what did you leave behind to do it?

CLXXXIII Of Eleazar

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 183 of 365

Do the forbidden thing whole, and make no sign after.

The Martyrdom of Eleazar the ScribeGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Eleazar was ninety and one of the leading scribes of Jerusalem when the officers of Antiochus forced his mouth open for a piece of pork[1]. He spat it out and walked to the rack of his own accord[2]. Old acquaintances among the officers took him aside and offered him a way through[3]. He could bring meat of his own providing, lawful under his own law, eat it as though it were the king’s sacrifice, and be spared. He refused, because the young would see it and say that Eleazar at ninety had gone over to the foreigners[4], and he died under the blows, saying that his body suffered and his soul was glad[5].

The offer kept the law against swine to the letter. What remained to die for was the reading of his mouth, and he named two readers[6], the young and the Almighty, whose hand, he said, he would not escape alive or dead. The second book of Maccabees, which says he left his death as an example to the young[7], holds that reading worth an old man’s life.

Some who leave reverse the arrangement. They swallow the forbidden meal alone in a parked car and mutter a sorry on the drive home, so that the meal still counts as a sin and the god keeps his seat beside the driver. Hiding the meal from a family is tactics, and sometimes safety. Hiding it from the god keeps him employed. Eleazar’s book has granted that a mouthful means whatever its watchers make of it, and the god is the last watcher such a man still invites, so the man who says nothing to him after the meal has emptied the gallery, and the pork in his hand is only meat.

Declaration: An old scribe let soldiers beat him to death over what the young and his god would think he had eaten, and what goes into my mouth is my own business.

The Rite · No faith

Tear the page of Leviticus that forbids the pig from a cheap Bible, the hotel drawer’s or a thrift shop’s, and use it as the napkin for a bacon sandwich eaten with no grace said.

Testament · Which forbidden thing do you still do with an apology attached, and to whom is the apology addressed?

CLXXXIV Of Antiochus

Reckoning

Day 184 of 365

Take your answer from the enemy, then stop watching him.

The Punishment of AntiochusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Two books of Maccabees kill Antiochus, and they kill him differently. The first has the king die in his bed in Persia, sick with disappointment and admitting the wrong he did Jerusalem[1]. The second has him racing to Jerusalem in his chariot to make it a graveyard[2], when a pain seizes his bowels and he is thrown from the car and every limb is wrenched[3], and the author adds the worms that swarm out of his living body, the flesh that rots off him, and a stench so foul that his own army cannot bear him[4]. Then the dying king vows to free the city and to become a Jew, and the book says the god would no longer have mercy on him[5].

The persecution was real. Two women who had circumcised their sons were paraded through the city with the infants hung at their breasts and thrown from the wall[6]. The answer was real too. Judas beat the king’s generals, and the first book has the news reach Antiochus in Persia that his armies were routed and the abomination he raised on the altar pulled down[7], and it is that news which sends him to his bed.

The second book had the same routs to tell and wrote the worms anyway. Polybius, with no stake in Jerusalem, has the king die mad at Tabae in Persia[8], some said for an attempt on a temple of Artemis, and records no worms. In the first book the routed armies and the pulled-down abomination were the payment, and Antiochus lived to hear of it. What the scribe added was a vigil kept past the payment, and the Catholic and Orthodox canons still print it. An enemy’s ruin is complete at the cleansed altar, and the scribe who went on writing sat at the bedside of a corpse.

Declaration: My hatred is a bill with a date on it, and once it is paid I forget the name it was made out to.

The Rite

Carry out today the one lawful consequence you hold over whoever hurt you, the bill presented or the complaint filed. Then close every channel you watch them through and delete their number.

Testament · Whose ruin have you been waiting for, and what has the waiting cost you?

CLXXXV Of Signs

Heresy

Day 185 of 365

Decide as the one who will be blamed.

The Army Appears in the HeavensGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

For almost forty days the people of Jerusalem looked up and saw cavalry in the air, horsemen in cloth of gold charging one another with lances leveled and swords drawn, shields clashing and armor flashing gilt[1]. Everyone in the city, by the account in Second Maccabees, prayed that the apparition would turn out to have been a good omen[2].

What followed was war. A deposed high priest attacked the city with a thousand men[3], and then Antiochus took it by storm. The book counts eighty thousand lost in three days, forty thousand killed and as many sold as slaves[4], and the king walking into the sanctuary with the sitting high priest as his guide[5].

The city saw armed men in the sky and asked it for good news, and the sky, which says nothing, handed back whatever the city brought to it. The repeated digits on the clock and the hawk on the fence post after you asked the universe a question work the same way. The meaning comes from the decision you had half made and wanted someone else to sign, and the horoscope supplies the signature on subscription, a paragraph a day written in advance for a twelfth of the human race.

A decision made from facts can be revised when the facts change, while one made from an omen can be corrected only by another omen, and whoever waits on the sky has already chosen to be innocent of what comes. Jerusalem kept its innocence for forty days and got Antiochus at the end of them, carrying the holy vessels out of the sanctuary[6] in his own hands.

Declaration: I decide without asking the sky, and whatever comes of it has my name on it.

The Rite

Read aloud, in a mocking voice, the last sign your horoscope app or angel-number feed sent you, then delete the app. Settle today, on what you already know, the matter you were keeping open for a sign.

Testament · What decision have you been holding open until something tells you what to do?

CLXXXVI Of Odds

Mastery

Day 186 of 365

Quit the losing fight before your name makes you stay.

Judas Maccabeus before the Army of NicanorGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Judas Maccabeus camped at Elasa with three thousand picked men against Bacchides, who had twenty thousand foot and two thousand horse[1]. His men saw the size of it and slipped away from the camp until eight hundred were left[2], and the eight hundred urged him to withdraw[3]. He answered that if their time had come they would die bravely for their brothers[4] and leave no stain on their honor, and he went in and was killed[5].

He had won on other ground. Before the battle of Beth-horon his men looked at the army coming up the pass and asked how so few could fight so many, and Judas told them that heaven gives victory to a few as easily as to many[6], and he won. Nicanor’s army went down before him at Adasa, and Nicanor died in the battle[7].

At Beth-horon and at Adasa his army stayed with him. At Elasa it had already gone, and the eight hundred who were left put the odds to him, nearly thirty to one, and asked to come back another day. By then he had a name to lose, and his answer was about the name. Honor that forbids a retreat at those odds is a debt owed to the people who will talk afterward, and only the dead ever pay it in full.

His brother Jonathan took the command[8], and before long Bacchides caught him on the banks of the Jordan with the river at his back. Jonathan struck at Bacchides himself, then leaped into the river with his men and swam to the far side[9], and the enemy did not follow. Some years later Bacchides made peace with him and went home. Judas paid for his honor with his body at Elasa, and the brother who swam lived to sit as judge in Michmash[10].

Declaration: I would sooner be gossiped about alive than sung about dead.

The Rite

Pull out today of the one contest you are losing only to save face, and tell whoever will talk about it, in one sentence, I am out, and I will be back on better ground. Then put the freed money or hours into something you can win.

Testament · Which fight are you still in only because of what leaving would say about you?

CLXXXVII Of the Maze

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 187 of 365

Carry the file out of the maze.

The MinotaurGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XII, 1861

Minos, the Greeks said, had a monster in his house, his queen’s son by a bull. Ovid has the king hide the shame of his house[1] in a maze whose passages were so blind that no one who went in could find the way out. Every ninth year Athens sent seven boys and seven girls[2] to feed it.

The churches built their mazes out of paper. A Roman instruction of nineteen sixty-two bound everyone connected with a tribunal for a priest’s grave offenses to the secret of the Holy Office[3], and Ireland’s inquiry into the Dublin archdiocese, published in two thousand nine, found bishops who had moved accused priests along instead of reporting them[4]. In two thousand fifteen Australia’s royal commission heard that the Jehovah’s Witnesses held files on over a thousand alleged child abusers going back to nineteen fifty and had reported none of them to the police[5]. It heard too that the elders required two witnesses to an act of abuse[6], or a confession, before they would act.

Each of these mazes ended by protecting a name, with its file held behind clergy and lawyers, so that the name stood and the children went in. Families build the same maze in miniature, out of the uncle no one mentions and the cousins told to keep quiet for the family’s sake. The one thing a maze cannot absorb is a copy of its file on a detective’s desk, where the honor it guards has no standing. Minos fed his shame on other people’s children for as long as the maze held, and a family that keeps its good name on a child’s silence has raised his house again, down to the tribute.

Declaration: A good name that needs a child’s silence to survive is a crime scene, and I report it.

The Rite · No faith

Write on a card the one fact your family kept quiet for its good name, sign and date it, and give it today to the relative it would protect most.

Testament · Who paid for the secret you were asked to keep for a good name?

CLXXXVIII Of Rescue

Heresy

Day 188 of 365

March before the angel comes.

The Angel Is Sent to Deliver IsraelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Lysias came down on Judea with tens of thousands of foot, thousands of horse and eighty elephants, and laid siege to Beth-zur[1]. When Judas Maccabeus heard of it, his whole company begged the god with tears and lamentation to send a good angel to save Israel[2]. Then Judas took up his weapons first and urged the rest to risk their lives with him[3], and they set out together. Only after they were armed and on the road, near Jerusalem, did a horseman appear at their head, robed in white and brandishing gold weapons[4], and with him in front they charged like lions and cut down eleven thousand infantry and sixteen hundred cavalry[5].

The order is the book’s own, and the book still calls the rider their ally from heaven[6] and sends Lysias home certain that the mighty god had fought on their side[7].

The coaches of manifestation sell the prayer for a good angel without the march. Hold a picture of the life you want, they tell their clients, speak of it as though it had arrived, and the right frequency will bring it. While the words are spoken the situation sits untouched, kept for a deliverer, and the wanting is booked as work.

Judas kept the order the coaches reverse. He prayed and then armed, and even a scribe who wanted the victory for heaven had to set his horseman at the head of men already marching, since a rider sent to a camp of kneeling men would have found no one to lead. Whoever waits on the deliverer before breaking camp leaves the angel nothing to ride in front of, and the siege at Beth-zur goes on.

Declaration: I owe heaven no thanks for any fight I won, since I was the one who showed up for it.

The Rite

Take your vision board or wish list, or scrawl one in thirty seconds. Make one real step toward an item on it that costs something, the call made or the form filed, then write your name beside it and tear the sheet up.

Testament · Which of your wishes is waiting on a deliverer, and what would the first step toward it cost you?

CLXXXIX Of the Centaurs

Reckoning

Day 189 of 365

Call the blow by its legal name.

The CentaursGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XII, 1861

Proverbs promises a parent that a child beaten with the rod will not die of it[1], and adds that the beating will deliver the child’s soul from hell. Another proverb says that whoever spares the rod hates his son[2]. Ephesians puts wives under their husbands in everything, as the church is under Christ[3], and Peter’s first letter has them win over an unbelieving husband without a word, by the conduct he watches[4].

The man who beat his son could point to a verse, and so could the man who beat his wife, and in the house the verse came to him as a warrant. Inside the house the act had other names. A blow to a child was discipline, and a wife’s bruise was a cross to carry with a quiet tongue, so that the only party in the house accused of anything was the one who spoke.

Outside the house the act has a name in the criminal law. A husband’s blow is assault in every American state and in English law, whatever scripture he cites, and so are a parent’s blows that go beyond reasonable discipline and leave a child injured, whatever proverb promised the child would not die of it. The household’s vocabulary holds only while the act stays among people taught the same verses. Said once to a doctor, a teacher or a police officer, the bruise turns back into the word the law uses, and the man who quoted Proverbs becomes a suspect, asked what he did before anyone asks what he believed. A report puts the blow on a record the family cannot edit, and an order of protection sets a distance between you and the one who struck you that no verse can shorten by an inch.

Declaration: A verse quoted over a beating is a motive, and I enter it into evidence.

The Rite

Print the verses on the rod and on wives being subject, write Assault across them beside the name of anyone who struck you under their cover, and drown the page in a full sink. Then put your papers and bank card where the one who hurt you cannot reach them.

Testament · Whose blows were you taught to call discipline, and which verse was read over them?

Sources

[1] Prov 23:13–14

[2] Prov 13:24

[3] Eph 5:22–24

[4] 1 Pet 3:1–2


CXC Of Tyrants

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 190 of 365

Ask every holy war which man gave the order.

The River of BloodGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XII, 1861

At Clermont in the year ten ninety-five Pope Urban the Second offered the knights of France a trade. Any man who went east to free Jerusalem out of devotion alone could count the expedition in place of all penance for his sins[1]. Four years later they took the city. They slaughtered the Muslims and Jews inside it by the thousand, and the Church went on preaching crusades for two centuries more, against Cathars and Baltic pagans as well as Islam, and in twelve hundred and four the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople, a Christian city.

The same Church counted an unjust killing a mortal sin, so the difference between a man bound for the fire and a pilgrim with his penance paid was a permit drawn up by bishops.

The permit is older than Clermont. In Numbers the god orders vengeance on Midian, and when the officers come back with the women alive it is Moses, angry, who orders every boy among the captives killed[2] and every woman who had lain with a man, and the Lord’s own word does not come between the officers’ return and that order. The god next speaks in his own voice when the plunder is counted, to take his share of it, and his share of the captive girls was thirty-two[3].

In that record the god’s permission covers the battle and his tribute covers the spoil, and the killing of the children comes in the voice of the man who gave it. The permit buys such a man one thing, the right to be called holy by people who would otherwise call him a murderer. Louis the Ninth took two armies on crusade, died with the second at Tunis, was canonized within thirty years[4], and keeps his feast on the twenty-fifth of August.

Declaration: I count a holy war by its dead, and I leave its saints off the tally.

The Rite · No faith

Write God wills it, the crusaders’ cry, on a sheet of paper. Strike out God, write A man above it, say A man wills it, and tear the sheet in half.

Testament · What did the holy war you were taught to admire cost the people on the other side?

Sources

[1] Council of Clermont (1095), can. 2

[2] Num 31:14–18

[3] Num 31:25–40

CXCI Of the Delight of the Eyes

Beauty

Day 191 of 365

Let your eyes stay where they want to.

Satan Climbs Toward EdenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IV, 1866

In Genesis the god gives one prohibition in the garden, and he addresses it to the mouth. Of every tree the man may freely eat[1], and of the tree of knowledge he must not eat, and the eye enters the chapter only to be pleased, by trees made pleasant to the sight[2].

The woman later recites that rule to the serpent stricter than she received it, forbidding even a touch of the fruit[3], and her stricter version still leaves the eyes alone. The narrator says the fruit was a delight to the eyes[4], and the offense still waits until her hand takes it and her mouth eats[5].

Faith trains the eye to pass over this world on its way somewhere else. Hymns call the earth a place you are only passing through, the sermon calls it fallen, and the book of Job has its hero swear a covenant with his own eyes[6]. Matthew counts a look of lust at a woman as adultery done already in the heart[7], the Quran tells believing men to lower their gaze[8], and the convents trained their novices in what the manuals called custody of the eyes, the gaze kept on the floor of the cloister.

The god guarded his garden with cherubim and a turning sword of fire[9], and a gallery posts a guard who asks only that you keep a step back. The want that rises at a lit shoulder or a long thigh is an eye doing what those trees were planted to provoke, and the guard at the rope has no more to say about it than the god did.

Declaration: Every ban on my eyes was added after Eden, and I keep the garden’s shorter law.

The Rite

Go to a gallery, or open a great museum’s collection on a screen, find the most beautiful body it holds, and look until you want it. Buy a print or postcard of it and pin it where you dress.

Testament · Where could you look your fill today at the beauty you were taught to avoid?

CXCII Of the Wood of Suicides

Heresy

Day 192 of 365

Refuse despair the authority you took from the church.

The HarpiesGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XIII, 1861

A council at Braga in the sixth century ruled that suicides were not to be remembered at Mass and that no psalms were to be sung as their bodies were carried to the grave[1]. England buried them at crossroads, some with a stake driven through them, and seized their goods for the crown, until coroners’ juries began finding the dead of unsound mind to spare the family. In the wood on the plate they stand as thorn trees, and at the last judgment each will hang its recovered body on its own branches[2].

Each of those sentences was pronounced as final, and each was withdrawn. Parliament ended the crossroads burials in eighteen twenty-three[3], and England and Wales struck suicide from the criminal law in nineteen sixty-one[4]. The Church’s code of nineteen seventeen still refused them a church funeral, the code of nineteen eighty-three dropped the refusal[5], and the Catechism now tells the faithful not to despair of the eternal salvation of those who took their own lives[6]. The forever lasted fourteen centuries, and its own issuers revoked it.

Despair talks like those councils. Illness and grief feed it, and its one claim about the future is a verdict with no appeal, that this hour is how it will always be. Its record matches theirs. Every hour it called final was followed by one it had failed to foresee, and the person who lived into that hour saw the verdict lapse.

There is one life, and the wood is an invention. A life with no second edition owes its worst night no obedience, since nothing stands behind that night’s sentence to enforce it. What stands on this side is the body’s appetite for another morning and the next good meal, older than the council at Braga, and it overturns the sentence at every breakfast.

Declaration: I keep the one life I have against every voice that calls it finished, the pulpit’s first and my own at three in the morning.

The Rite

Write the sentence your worst night tells you most often, date it, and seal it in an envelope marked to be opened thirty days from today. Say over it Your term ends on this date. Then eat the best thing in your kitchen.

Testament · What does despair tell you about yourself that you would never accept as evidence from anyone else?

CXCIII Of Search

Mastery

Day 193 of 365

Ask who a ban on a question protects.

Two Angels Search the GardenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IV, 1866

A verse of the Quran tells believers not to ask about things which, if they were made plain to them, would distress them. The next verse recalls a people before them who asked such questions and then lost their faith over the answers[1]. It does not call the answers false.

Rome built a ban on questions into an office. Its Index of forbidden books held the treatise that set the earth moving around the sun from sixteen sixteen, suspended until corrected[2], and struck it from the list only in the edition of eighteen thirty-five[3], long after the astronomers had stopped arguing. Catholics who obeyed spent two centuries reading the founding book of their own sky, if they read it at all, in copies corrected by hand to call the moving earth a hypothesis[4].

The Quran warns the asker of distress and sets no penalty, so its caution guards the asker, and in one traditional account the question that prompted it was whether the pilgrimage was owed every year. Rome’s Index guarded the keeper. It fenced off the knowledge that would weaken him, and the penalty he set for asking measures the loss he feared, an earth the psalm had promised could not be moved.

Some congregations and households keep a forbidden question, about a vote taken in a closed meeting or a letter nobody answered, and the penalty set on asking measures what an honest answer would cost the keepers. A court archive or a library will often hold the record, and the asker walks out with a photocopy no elder can take back.

Declaration: I ask who a ban protects, and the earth goes on moving under my chair.

The Rite

Write down the question you were raised never to ask, find its answer today in a source the faith did not publish, and copy what you find under it in ink. Sign the page and say Asked and answered.

Testament · What were you protected from knowing, and what did the protection cost you?

Sources

[1] Quran 5:101–102

[2] Decree of the Congregation of the Index, 5 March 1616

[3] Index Librorum Prohibitorum (1835)

[4] Decree of the Congregation of the Index, 1620


CXCIV Of Blasphemy

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 194 of 365

Refuse to carry stones for anyone’s god.

The Blasphemers under the Rain of FireGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XIV, 1861

Leviticus opens its blasphemy case with a fight. The son of an Israelite woman and an Egyptian father came to blows in the camp with an Israelite man, and in the heat of it he cursed the Name[1]. The text names his mother, Shelomith daughter of Dibri[2], of the tribe of Dan, and never names him. Held in custody until Moses had a ruling, he was taken outside the camp and stoned[3] by the whole congregation.

The Israelite he fought walks out of the chapter with no word recorded against him. The law was written on the spot to cover the stranger and the native alike[4], and the first body it covered belonged to the son of the Egyptian.

In June of two thousand nine Asia Bibi, a Christian farm laborer in Pakistan, brought water to the Muslim women picking fruit beside her, and they refused to drink from a cup a Christian had touched. Within days she stood accused of insulting the Prophet, an offense the penal code had punished with death alone since nineteen ninety[5], and she spent eight years on death row before the Supreme Court acquitted her in two thousand eighteen[6]. Salmaan Taseer, the governor of Punjab, spoke out for her and was shot dead by one of his own guards.

In both cases the fight came first and the charge came out of it, and it fell on the one whose blood or creed marked them as foreign. The quarrel borrowed the god’s name and came out holy. Whoever was raised to flinch at a curse on the Name was handed a stone for someone else’s quarrel, and drops it the day he says that curse aloud himself.

Declaration: I share my cup with the stranger and my curses with the god who wanted him stoned.

The Rite · No faith

Write on a sheet a sentence about the god that a blasphemy law somewhere would jail you for, and sign it with your full name. Read it aloud to a friend over a shared cup of water, then say Come and collect.

Testament · What have you left unsaid about the god for fear of the people who speak for him?

Sources

[1] Lev 24:10–11

[2] Lev 24:11

[3] Lev 24:12–14, 23

[4] Lev 24:16, 22

[5] Pakistan Penal Code, s. 295-C; Federal Shariat Court ruling (1990)

[6] Asia Bibi v. The State, Supreme Court of Pakistan, 31 Oct 2018


CXCV Of Squandering

Heresy

Day 195 of 365

Spend what is yours and confess nothing.

The SquanderersGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XIII, 1861

At a supper in Bethany, Mark says, a woman broke an alabaster jar of spikenard and poured it over the head of Jesus, and some at the table were indignant. The ointment could have been sold for more than three hundred denarii[1], close to a laborer’s pay for a year, and given to the poor. John tells the anointing at Bethany with the objection in one mouth, Judas’s, and adds the reason for it. Judas said it because he was a thief, and he kept the common purse and helped himself from what was put in[2].

Jesus told them to let her alone, since the poor would always be with them[3] and he would not, and he named what she did a good work. The complaint he silenced priced the gift against what it could have bought for someone worthier.

Proverbs warns that whoever loves pleasure ends poor[4], and the warning bites hardest where the borrower is servant to the lender[5], and a debt at a ruinous rate is a claim on next year’s wages that bites with no preacher needed, since the lender collects it himself every month with the interest added, out of hours not yet worked. Whoever owes no lender at a ruinous rate has paid that master off.

Past the lender’s claim the rest is the spender’s, to be poured out on a long dinner or a bottle of scent worth a week’s pay, as the woman at Bethany poured hers over a guest’s head, and Jesus asked her for no accounting. The scold in John’s telling wanted the jar sold and the money in his own bag, and the pulpit that prices your pleasures after they are spent has an eye on the purse too.

Declaration: A good meal paid in full is the one sacrament I keep, and it has never asked me for a tithe.

The Rite

Buy today the one pleasure you most often talk yourself out of as a waste, pay for it with money you owe no lender, and enjoy it in full. Tear up the receipt and say No one prices this but me.

Testament · Which pleasure do you still enter in the ledger as a sin?

Sources

[1] Mark 14:3–5

[2] John 12:4–6

[3] Mark 14:6–7

[4] Prov 21:17

[5] Prov 22:7


CXCVI Of the First Hour

Indulgence

Day 196 of 365

Give the dawn to your body before any god.

Adam Watches Eve SleepingGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book V, 1866

Sunni muezzins add one line to the dawn call to prayer and to no other, the line that prayer is better than sleep[1], and they say it twice. The code of Jewish law opens by telling the reader to rise like a lion in the morning for the service of his creator, early enough to wake the dawn himself[2], and Catholic children are taught a morning offering that hands the whole day over on waking.

Genesis has no such summons for the first man. He is put into a deep sleep and wakes to a woman beside him, and what he does on waking is greet her as his own bone and flesh[3]. The first command the garden story gives him hands him every tree of the garden[4] to eat from freely, bar one, and the book dates the calling on the god’s name to the days of his grandson[5].

Each of these pieties claims the waking body before anything else may. The sheets still hold the heat of the night and no one has yet asked for anything, which makes it the best hour the body will own all day, and every one of these calls is timed to take it.

The muezzin says his line only at dawn and says it twice, because only at dawn does prayer have a rival he must name. At the other four calls the god asks without argument. At the first he bids against warm sheets, twice over and from a height, and whoever lies on through both repetitions has heard the best case heaven makes for that hour and kept the bed.

Declaration: The first man woke to a woman and a garden of fruit, and my mornings keep his hours.

The Rite

Set no alarm tonight. In the morning, before any screen or prayer, keep the door shut, carry the best breakfast in the house back to bed and eat it slowly under the covers. Say This hour was mine first.

Testament · What would the first hour of your day hold if no god and no inbox had a claim on it?

Sources

[1] Sunan Abi Dawud 500

[2] Shulchan Aruch, OC 1:1

[3] Gen 2:21–23

[4] Gen 2:16–17

[5] Gen 4:25–26


CXCVII Of the Sodomites

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 197 of 365

Honor the men the law killed for their beds.

The Violent against NatureGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XV, 1861

Ezekiel, listing the sins of Sodom, puts first pride, a surfeit of bread and careless ease, and then a refusal to help the poor and needy[1]. Genesis gives the city a mob at Lot’s door demanding the two strangers he had taken in for the night[2], and demanding them for sex. Jude and the Quran read the sin as lust[3]. Ezekiel’s next verse adds only that the city was haughty and did abominable things[4], and names none, while Genesis names one act, the attempted rape of guests, so the older witnesses give a closed purse and a mob.

Leviticus prescribes death for a man who lies with a male[5], and a hadith in the collection of Abu Dawud tells the faithful to kill both men they find doing what the people of Lot did[6]. Christian Europe took the city’s name for the act. Men convicted of sodomy went to the fire in Spain and the Italian cities, and England hanged its last two, James Pratt and John Smith, in eighteen thirty-five[7].

The name did the work. A name from a city Ezekiel convicted of pride and Genesis of an attempted rape was spent on men convicted of a private act between two men, and the sentence the mob had earned fell on them, as it fell on Pratt and Smith.

On the plate a naked man stands in a rain of fire and reaches up toward a clothed man on the bank, who walks with his head bowed as a man walks in reverence[8]. Doctrine put the naked man in the fire, and the man on the bank bent toward him anyway. Whoever has loved someone the pulpit condemned has stood on that bank, and owes the doctrine no apology for the bow.

Declaration: I keep company with the men the fire took, and the pulpit that lit it can preach to the smoke.

The Rite · No faith

Take the hand of someone you love, or a friend’s arm, and walk a street where nobody knows you, in honor of the men hanged for it. At the first corner say aloud God of Leviticus, I walk past your law.

Testament · Whom did the doctrine require you to condemn while you went on loving them?

Sources

[1] Ezek 16:49

[2] Gen 19:1–5

[3] Jude 7; Quran 7:80–81

[4] Ezek 16:50

[5] Lev 20:13

[6] Sunan Abi Dawud 4462

[7] Old Bailey Proceedings, t18350921-1934

CXCVIII Of the Blow

Reckoning

Day 198 of 365

Learn the answer to a grip.

Abdiel Strikes SatanGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VI, 1866

The first letter of Peter tells household slaves to be subject to their masters, the harsh along with the gentle. It tells them to take a beating patiently[1] when they have done nothing to earn it, since Christ when he suffered made no threats[2]. Once Christ’s example is given, it turns to wives and tells them to be subject to their husbands[3]. The counsel went to people who could be beaten without redress, and it turned their want of redress into a virtue.

The same Church kept another rule for its heaven. Daniel’s angel arrives three weeks late because the prince of Persia withstood him until Michael came to help[4], and Revelation has Michael and his angels make war on the dragon[5]. From eighteen eighty-six until nineteen sixty-five[6] Catholics knelt after Low Mass and asked Michael to defend them in battle, and the painters gave him armor and a raised blade.

Peter’s reason is the example, since Christ left it for the slave to follow in his steps, and the chapter that calls the beating acceptable to God never says the slave could answer it. Michael has no such pattern laid on him, and the Church painted him with a sword.

A few weeks of training teach the feet where to plant and the hands how to break a grip, and the knowledge travels in the body long before any use for it arrives. A body that carries it is no longer the body Peter wrote to. The slave bore the fist for Christ’s sake, and whoever has the way can tell a first blow to stop and answer a second.

Declaration: Peter told the slave to hold still under the fist, and I have stopped holding still.

The Rite

Book a self-defense class today. Then tape the page of First Peter that tells slaves to bear a beating, printed or torn from your own Bible, to a mattress stood against a wall, and strike it with the heel of your hand until the paper is gone.

Testament · Who taught you that the unreturned blow was the holy one?

Sources

[1] 1 Pet 2:18–20

[2] 1 Pet 2:23

[3] 1 Pet 3:1

[4] Dan 10:12–13

[5] Rev 12:7

[6] Leo XIII (1886); Inter Oecumenici 48j (1964, in force 7 Mar 1965)


CXCIX Of Fraud

Heresy

Day 199 of 365

Ask every miracle where the wire runs.

GeryonGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XVII, 1861

Geryon, the beast of fraud coiled across the plate, has the face of a just man[1], kindly to look at, over the body of a serpent with a scorpion’s sting in its tail. In nineteen eighty-six the faith healer Peter Popoff was showing the face. He called out the names and ailments of strangers in his audiences as though heaven had told him, and the skeptic James Randi and Alexander Jason, with a radio scanner, recorded the source, his wife backstage reading prayer cards into a receiver in his ear[2]. The recording was played on The Tonight Show in May of that year, on national television, and his wife Elizabeth was the voice in the receiver.

After the broadcast his ratings and donations fell. He declared bankruptcy the next year, in nineteen eighty-seven, owing more than seven hundred creditors[3], was buying airtime again by the late nineties, and within a few more years was selling miracle spring water on late-night television in five countries, the United States and Canada among them. On 11 March 2025 the British regulator Ofcom fined the Word Network 150,000 pounds for carrying his claims[4].

By two thousand five, nearly twenty years after the tape, his ministry was taking in more than twenty-three million dollars a year[5]. The tape that exposed him ran on a talk show, and the trick needs only an audience that never heard the wire or saw the tape.

Whoever has heard the tape, the wife’s voice reading into the receiver, cannot be preached back out of what the ears heard.

Declaration: I give the faith healer the laughter of the room he robbed.

The Rite

Watch a faith healer’s broadcast with a friend who agrees to the game, and stop at each cure to name the trick aloud before he finishes, the prayer card filled out at the door, the name read back as a miracle.

Testament · Which wonder you were once shown has had its wire explained to you, and what did you do with the envelope?

Sources

[1] Inferno 17.10–12

[2] James Randi, The Faith Healers (1987)

[3] Popoff bankruptcy filing, Sept 1987

[4] Ofcom Broadcast Bulletin, 11 Mar 2025

[5] Peter Popoff Ministries revenue, 2005


CC Of Radiance

Beauty

Day 200 of 365

Take off the veil and let them be afraid.

Raphael Approaches the GardenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book V, 1866

When Moses came down the mountain with the second tablets, Exodus says, the skin of his face shone, and the people were afraid to come near him[1]. He gave them the commands with his face bare and then put a veil over it[2], and he took the veil off only when he went in to speak with the god. Paul, writing centuries later, decided the veil had been worn so that Israel would not see the glory fading[3].

Exodus names no cause for the veil and sets it after one fact, the fear of the people. Paul supplied a cause of his own. The shining itself he never denied. The same Paul told the Philippians to count others better than themselves[4] and the Romans to think of themselves no more highly than they ought[5], and the churches made a virtue of the covering, so that a gift shown openly reads as pride and a gift kept covered reads as grace.

The people below the mountain were afraid of a face, and the fear was theirs. The veil eased it at the face’s expense, and every dimming since has made the same trade. A voice that fills a room and a mind that sees the answer first unsettle the people beside them, and a cloth over either buys the room its ease.

Exodus never says the light faded, only that the people saw it shining each time Moses came out from the god[6], and the fading is Paul’s addition to the text. A gift kept under cloth for a lifetime does fade at last, from want of use, and the cloth will have done the fading Paul blamed on the light.

Declaration: Lucifer was named for the light he carried, and I carry mine uncovered.

The Rite

Put on the thing you look best in, and today, in front of one person whose opinion matters to you, use the skill you usually play down. When you are praised for it, answer Yes, I am good at it. and add nothing after.

Testament · Which of your gifts do you cover in company, and whose comfort does the cover buy?

Sources

[1] Exod 34:29–30

[2] Exod 34:33–35

[3] 2 Cor 3:13

[4] Phil 2:3

[5] Rom 12:3

[6] Exod 34:34–35


CCI Of Descent

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 201 of 365

Leave by steps you can keep taking.

The Descent on GeryonGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XVII, 1861

When Pharaoh let the people go, Exodus says, the god did not lead them by the road through the land of the Philistines, although it was near. The people might change their minds when they saw war, he said, and go back to Egypt[1]. He took them the long way round, through the wilderness toward the Red Sea[2].

The long way did not cure the longing. In Numbers the people weep for the fish they ate in Egypt for nothing, and for the cucumbers, the leeks and the garlic[3], and complain that they see nothing now but manna. Moses heard them weeping in the door of every tent[4]. What pulled at them was the remembered food of the house of bondage, and no wonder from heaven tasted of it, and the god struck down the ones who lusted for meat[5] at the place named for their craving.

A leaving meets the same craving. The holiday table and the Sunday company are the old faith’s cucumbers, and a deserter who breaks every law in one month and puts no new pleasure in their place has only the wilderness and the memory of the table.

Each law broken should buy a pleasure that is the deserter’s own and be given a few weeks to settle in before the next one falls. The god chose the long road to keep his people from turning back and fed them the same bread six mornings in seven. A deserter who pays himself at every stage has a pleasure of his own in hand when the craving comes.

Declaration: Heaven fed its runaways manna and struck down the ones who craved meat, and I feed myself better than heaven did.

The Rite · Christian

Sleep through the hour of Sunday service, then go out for a long brunch and order the dish you like best.

Testament · Which comfort of the old faith still pulls hardest, and what pleasure could stand in its place?

Sources

[1] Exod 13:17

[2] Exod 13:18

[3] Num 11:4–6

[4] Num 11:10

[5] Num 11:33–34


CCII Of Courting

Heresy

Day 202 of 365

Choose by appetite, and refuse to be anyone’s mission.

The Panderers and SeducersGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XVIII, 1861

Paul forbade the Corinthians to be unequally yoked with unbelievers[1], and the churches have read the yoke as a marriage ever since. A Latter-day Saint is raised to marry in the temple, a Witness to marry only in the Lord[2], and the Quran forbids a believing woman to an unbeliever[3]. Paul wrote a second half for the believer already lying beside an outsider. She is to stay with him, since the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife[4], and who knows whether she will save him. Peter tells wives that a husband deaf to the word is to be won without a word[5], by their conduct.

Between them the two halves make the bed a post of the mission. Inside the faith it keeps the believer in, and across the line it is where the outsider is won, by a service attended together and a kindness that asks for nothing yet. One sect, the Children of God[6], followed the method to its end, and from nineteen seventy-four to nineteen eighty-seven its women went to bed with strangers to win them for Christ. The churches called it a cult and kept the verses. A believer who courts an apostate brings both halves along.

Leaving ends both offices. The apostate may now choose by what the old rules ranked below doctrine, a hand that stays a moment too long on the wrist, a laugh across the table that arrives in the chest before the mind has been consulted. A lover chosen by the pulse wants the body in front of them. A lover who chose you in order to win you wants the person you would become after the winning, and has already counted you among the sanctified, as Paul counted the husband.

Declaration: Let the god who meant to win me through a lover’s good conduct come and court me himself.

The Rite

Dress and scent yourself to be wanted and go out tonight wherever you would like to be looked at, or take the lover you already have out the same way. Say aloud before you leave I go out to be wanted as I am.

Testament · What do you want in a lover now that no elder signs off on the match?

Sources

[1] 2 Cor 6:14

[2] 1 Cor 7:39

CCIII Of Wounds

Reckoning

Day 203 of 365

Fit every curse to the deed it answers.

Satan WoundedGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VI, 1866

One psalm under David’s name complains of a lying tongue turned against him[1] and hatred repaid for his love, then curses the man responsible in order. Let his prayer be counted as sin, let his days be few and another take his office[2], let his children be fatherless and beg[3], let his name be blotted out in the generation after. Benedict’s Rule gave monks the whole psalter every week from the sixth century[4], and the Roman Breviary kept the psalm in its cycle until nineteen seventy.

That year the reform of the hours struck it, with two other psalms whose curses ran as hot. The instruction explaining the cut concedes that scripture’s last book prays the same way, where the souls under the altar cry out how long until their blood is avenged[5], and it gives as its reason a certain psychological difficulty[6]. The psalm had not changed. The Church’s nerve had, and a prayer the hours had carried for fourteen hundred years became a difficulty to spare the people praying the hours.

The clergy who preached love of enemies from the gospel had been saying this psalm, so whoever was raised to treat hatred as a stain was raised by men who prayed it. The psalm states the injury before it asks for anything, and one of its curses follows the deed, as he loved cursing, let cursing come to him[7]. Its one failure is the family, five of thirty-one verses that strike a wife and children who had done nothing and charge him with his parents’ sins[8]. The same reform cut single verses from other psalms[9]. It cut all thirty-one, and a curse aimed at one man went out of the breviary with the five that missed.

Declaration: The god’s own psalm taught me to answer an injury line for line, and the Church that prayed it for fourteen hundred years struck it out.

The Rite

Print Psalm 109 and strike out verses nine, ten, twelve, thirteen and fourteen, the ones aimed at the man’s family. Write your enemy’s name in the margin, read what is left aloud standing, as monks read it for centuries, and say Every line left here is yours.

Testament · What loss would match exactly what your enemy did to you?

CCIV Of Flatterers

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 204 of 365

Praise nothing you fear.

The FlatterersGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XVIII, 1861

Artaxerxes opens his letter in the book of Ezra as king of kings[1]. Ezekiel and Daniel give the same title to Nebuchadnezzar[2], so scripture had heard it from Persian and Babylonian emperors before Second Maccabees, the letter to Timothy and Revelation handed it to the god and the Lamb[3]. The court manners came over with the title. Revelation stages an audience in heaven, the elders falling down before the throne and casting their crowns before it[4], and the Gloria heaps five verbs of worship and thanks on the god before it ventures one plea for mercy.

A flattering mouth works ruin[5], the book of Proverbs says, and a psalm despises those who speak with flattering lips and a double heart[6]. Elihu, in the book of Job, refuses to give flattering titles to any man[7], for fear his maker would soon take him away, so the man who flatters another answers to his maker. The Psalter’s Hebrew name is Praises.

The old posture of the court returns as the warm thanks paid to a manager before a raise is mentioned and the compliment handed a parent before anything hard is said. Praise given to buy safety is tribute, and the court that collected it has been dissolved. A Greek history tells of two Spartans brought before Xerxes at Susa, whose Persian guards ordered them to fall down and do obeisance. They refused, saying it was not their custom to worship a man[8], and the king who could have killed them let them go home to Sparta, unharmed.

Declaration: Praise from me is a wage, and the god who demanded it in advance never did the work.

The Rite · No faith

Print the last psalm, which orders everything that has breath to praise the Lord, write your own name over every mention of the Lord, and read it aloud once as it now stands.

Testament · Whom do you still flatter to stay safe, and what would happen if you stopped?

CCV Of the Lover’s Body

Indulgence

Day 205 of 365

Spend your praise on skin.

ThaïsGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XVIII, 1861

The Song of Songs praises a lover’s body part by part and takes its time. Her hair is a flock of goats streaming down a hillside, her teeth a flock of ewes come up from the washing, her neck the tower of David hung with shields, her breasts two fawns feeding among the lilies[1]. He is admired no less, his head finest gold and his locks black as a raven, his legs pillars of marble set on bases of gold.

The Mishnah records rabbis disputing whether it was holy at all, and Rabbi Akiva answering that it was the holy of holies[2], after which Jews and Christians alike spent nearly two thousand years reading it as an allegory of the god’s love for his people or for the Church, so that the lovers would not have to be lovers. The lovers stayed lovers. These are two people who cannot stop describing each other, and apart from one disputed syllable in its last chapter[3] the book never names a god, so the praise has no one to answer it but the body it describes.

The woman asks him to kiss her with the kisses of his mouth[4] and says she is sick with love, and he comes into his garden and eats his honeycomb with his honey[5]. The catalog belongs to the act and takes its slow pace from it, each comparison stranger than the last as the wanting grows, until it reaches the vineyards where she promises him her loves[6], among the budding pomegranates and the scent of mandrakes. A body praised that slowly, by someone who wants it, learns that it was worth eight chapters of scripture.

Declaration: Every inch of the one I love gets the praise my childhood hymns spent on the sky.

The Rite

Undress a consenting lover, or yourself before a mirror, in good light, and praise each part of the body aloud in the Song’s manner, with a comparison for each. Take your time over every part, and make love when the praise runs out.

Testament · Which part of your lover’s body or your own have you never once praised aloud?

Sources

[1] Song 4:1–5

[2] m. Yadayim 3:5

[3] Song 8:6

[4] Song 1:2

[5] Song 5:1

[6] Song 7:12–13


CCVI Of Simony

Heresy

Day 206 of 365

Owe nothing to the sellers of clean hands.

The Simoniac PopesGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XIX, 1861

Simon the magician had already been baptized when he made his offer. The book of Acts says he believed and stayed close to Philip[1], and when he watched Peter and John lay hands on the converts of Samaria and give them the Holy Spirit, he held out money and asked for the same power[2]. Peter told him his silver could perish with him[3]. The crime of selling holy things has carried the magician’s name ever since, though he was the one man in the story who named what he wanted and offered to pay for it.

The Church kept the curse and the price in separate ledgers. Council after council condemned simony, while the papal chancery granted dispensations from the Church’s own rules by fixed scales of fees[4], printed in Rome before the Reformation, so that a cousin could marry a cousin or a bastard be ordained once the tax was paid. Paid at the papal desk, the money was a fee for the clerks’ labor, and the same money in a magician’s hand was the sin that bears his name.

The desks have multiplied. A retreat charges a month’s rent for a weekend of fasting and breathing, a cleanse ships its powders every thirty days, and an app bills monthly to count the days you stayed pure. Each sells the feeling of being washed, whatever name the label gives it, and the billing cycle counts on the feeling fading before the renewal date. Simon at least asked for a power he could watch work on other people. Twelve charges a year for the same washing are twelve notices a year that you are still dirty, and the seller writes every one.

Declaration: Every priest who sells a clean conscience can wait in line behind my plumber.

The Rite

Cancel one payment whose real product is the feeling of being clean, the cleanse, the retreat deposit, the purity app or the church pledge. Give the same sum today to someone who has earned it from you, and say as it goes Paid where it was earned.

Testament · Who profits each month from your believing you are dirty?

Sources

[1] Acts 8:13

[2] Acts 8:14–19

[3] Acts 8:20

[4] Taxae Cancellariae Apostolicae (Chancery and Penitentiary fee scales)


CCVII Of the Field

Mastery

Day 207 of 365

Fortify what you won before you celebrate it.

Michael’s Angels EncampGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VI, 1866

Revelation gives Michael the victory in heaven and then shows what the winners did with it. Michael’s host casts the dragon and all his followers down to earth[1], a loud voice calls on the heavens to rejoice, and the same voice adds a woe for everyone living below[2], since the devil has come down to them in a great rage. Heaven kept its feast and left the loser loose on the ground underneath, where within a few verses he is hunting the woman into the wilderness[3].

The first book of Maccabees records a better soldier. After Judas retook Jerusalem and purified the temple, he spent his next effort on masonry, raising high walls and strong towers around Mount Zion, setting a garrison in them and fortifying Beth-zur as a stronghold facing Idumea[4]. The book gives the work two verses. Beth-zur, short of food in a fallow year, surrendered to the boy king Antiochus, but Mount Zion stood a siege until his regent, hearing that another general had come back to seize the government, told him their food was short and the place was strong[5], and the king offered the defenders terms.

Whatever you won was won from somebody, the post another wanted or the client who used to be a rival’s, and the one who lost it studies your ground the way the dispossessed always do, looking for the low place. The winner who celebrates and builds nothing has done what heaven did, thrown the loser just far enough to come back angry. Antiochus went in under the peace, saw the strength of the place, broke his oath and had the wall around it pulled down[6]. Of everything Judas had won, the wall was the one thing his enemy would perjure himself to be rid of.

Declaration: Heaven threw its dragon down onto the ground I live on and went off singing, so I do my own masonry.

The Rite

Name aloud the rival who wants back what you took from them. Then close today the one gap they would use, the password or the lock changed, the deal signed in your own name, their access ended.

Testament · Where would the rival you beat come over the wall?

Sources

[1] Rev 12:7–9

[2] Rev 12:12

[3] Rev 12:13–14

[4] 1 Macc 4:60–61

[5] 1 Macc 6:49–59

[6] 1 Macc 6:62


CCVIII Of Hooks

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 208 of 365

Refuse the hook, however kind the hand on the pole.

The Devils with HooksGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXI, 1861

Baptism, by Catholic doctrine, prints an indelible mark on the soul[1] that no sin can erase. From nineteen eighty-three canon law recognized a formal act by which a Catholic could defect from the Church[2], and three marriage canons released whoever made it from rules that still bound every other baptized Catholic. In two thousand nine the Vatican struck those clauses out[3], so that the formal act no longer released anyone from any of them, and the mark stayed where doctrine had put it.

Jesus called his first disciples off their boats with a promise to make them fishers of men[4], and pulpits read the line as a mercy. Jeremiah had already used the figure, as a punishment. I will send for many fishers[5], says his god, and they shall fish them, and after them many hunters to hunt them out of the holes of the rocks, because he means to repay their sin double[6]. Habakkuk complained that the conqueror hauls up whole nations with the hook and the net and then burns incense to the net[7].

The hooks are softer now and better aimed. The ministering visit, the verse texted on a birthday, a grandmother’s tears, the elder who says the congregation misses you, each comes baited with something you really do miss, and the love in the bait is real. Rome’s mark has no line on it. The lines run from the birthday and the funeral, and whoever knows where the barb sits can go to both, eat the cake, and leave without a promise.

Declaration: Rome can keep its indelible mark, since it was printed on a soul I never had.

The Rite · Christian

Write on a card I love you, and I am not coming back. Tape a fishhook beside the words, keep the card by your phone for the next person who asks you back to church, and read it aloud once tonight.

Testament · What will you say, once and in advance, to the hook from the old faith that still catches you?

Sources

[1] CCC 1272

[2] CIC 1983, cann. 1086 §1, 1117, 1124

[3] Benedict XVI, Omnium in mentem (2009)

[4] Mark 1:17

[5] Jer 16:16

[6] Jer 16:18

[7] Hab 1:15–16


CCIX Of Going Alone

Heresy

Day 209 of 365

Take one pleasure unaccompanied.

The Demon EscortGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXI, 1861

Elijah left his servant at Beersheba[1] and went on by himself, forty days and forty nights[2], to Horeb, where the god asked him twice what he was doing there[3], and twice he complained that he alone was left. The second time the question came after the wind and the earthquake and the fire, in a still small voice, and what followed his complaint was a list of errands. Go back, anoint two kings, anoint Elisha to take your place, and know that seven thousand in Israel have never bowed to Baal[4].

The handbook for Latter-day Saint missionaries tells them never to be alone[5], to stay within sight and hearing of a companion everywhere except the bathroom and a few interviews, and to make no private hour by staying up later or rising earlier than the other. One stated reason is protection from false accusation, which makes the companion a witness on duty around the clock. Abu Dawud preserves a hadith that calls a lone rider a devil[6] and two riders two devils, and only three a company.

Whoever was raised under such rules learns that an hour with no one in it needs explaining, and that outlasts the belief, so that a meal for one feels like an exposure and a film seen alone like a lapse. A pleasure taken alone has one judge. The appetite sets the order and the pace, the dish chosen without a glance across the table, the evening spent at the speed of one person’s wanting. Elijah answered the question in the cave with complaints and was sent off with work. The answer he never gave is that he had come for his own sake, and whoever gives it keeps the evening a god would have filled with errands.

Declaration: My long dinners for one go unrecorded, and the god who kept a census of the faithful will find me missing from it.

The Rite

Book a table for one at the best restaurant you can afford, the kind you were told to save for company, order exactly what you want, and keep your phone in your pocket until the bill comes.

Testament · Which pleasure have you postponed until someone could watch you take it?

Sources

[1] 1 Kgs 19:3

[2] 1 Kgs 19:8

[3] 1 Kgs 19:9–14

[4] 1 Kgs 19:15–18

[5] Missionary Standards for Disciples of Jesus Christ, 2.2.2

[6] Sunan Abi Dawud 2607


CCX Of Quarrels

Reckoning

Day 210 of 365

Take back the useful, and leave the apology unasked.

The Devils QuarrelGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXII, 1861

John Mark first appears as the son of a Jerusalem woman named Mary[1], in whose house the believers met to pray, and Barnabas and Saul took him along on the first mission as their assistant[2]. At Perga in Pamphylia he left them and went home to Jerusalem[3], and Luke records the desertion in one clause and goes on with the voyage.

Paul kept the clause. When a second mission was proposed, Barnabas wanted to take his cousin again[4], Paul refused a man who had abandoned the work once, and the quarrel ran so hot that Luke names it with the Greek word English later borrowed as paroxysm[5]. They parted. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, and Paul took Silas overland through Syria and Cilicia[6].

The letters record no apology from Mark and no pardon from Paul. Mark comes back as a name in the greetings, a fellow worker in the note to Philemon[7], a man the church at Colossae is told to welcome if he arrives[8], and in the last letter carrying Paul’s name the old refusal has become an instruction to bring him along, since he is useful for the ministry[9]. Useful is the whole of the reference.

Pulpits tell the story as a reconciliation, and the text has Paul send for Mark the way a craftsman sends for a tool that has proved itself. A partnership broken by a quarrel can run on the same terms. The partner who walked out is refused while the walking out is fresh, and any return is bought with work and needs no apology on either side. Forgiveness would have asked Paul to forget Perga. Luke kept Perga in the book, and Paul kept Mark on the road.

Declaration: Let the pulpits stage their reconciliations, and I will go on hiring.

The Rite

Name someone you parted from in a quarrel who is now good at something you need. Send them a message today offering paid work or a part in your next project, and say nothing about the quarrel.

Testament · Who did you cut loose once who has since become worth hiring?

[2] Acts 12:25; 13:5

[4] Acts 15:37; Col 4:10

[5] Acts 15:39 (paroxysmos)

[6] Acts 15:39–41

[7] Phlm 24

[8] Col 4:10

[9] 2 Tim 4:11


CCXI Of Enforcers

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 211 of 365

Break one law you used to police in others.

The Devils Fall into the PitchGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXII, 1861

A man was found gathering sticks on the sabbath. The Israelites who found him brought him before Moses and Aaron and the whole congregation and held him under guard until the god gave a ruling, which was death by stoning outside the camp[1]. The text never says how they came to find him. No verse of the law lists the finding of that man, or the guard set over him afterward, as sabbath work.

Saudi Arabia’s committee for the promotion of virtue and the prevention of vice patrolled the malls for decades, until its powers of arrest were removed in two thousand sixteen[2]. Latter-day Saint bishops sat alone behind closed doors with twelve-year-olds and asked them about their chastity, until the Church began in two thousand eighteen to let a parent attend[3]. A committee of Witness elders hears the case of a member’s serious sin, sexual immorality among them[4], removes the one who will not repent, and goes home. Each office made other people’s private conduct its business.

Some who leave keep one office from the old establishment. They correct a nephew’s swearing in the old tone or sigh at a sister’s second drink, enforcing the law with the god taken out of it, a constable still walking the round for a king deposed years ago. With the king gone, the pay that remains is the feeling of being cleaner than the person watched. Once the badge is turned in, all that watching comes home to the one life its owner was ever free to govern.

Declaration: Heaven can pay its own police.

The Rite · No faith

Alone, break a rule you once held others to, eating without the grace or saying aloud the word you forbade, and tell the empty room That rule is gone, and I will not keep it for you.

Testament · Which of their laws are you still enforcing on someone else?

Sources

[2] Saudi Council of Ministers, decision of Apr 2016

CCXII Of the Fall

Beauty

Day 212 of 365

Prize the fracture over the finish.

The Rebels Fall from HeavenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VI, 1866

Second Peter has the god cast the sinning angels down into Tartarus[1], the Greek pit where the Titans lay bound after losing their war against Zeus[2]. The writer housed his rebels in the prison of an older rebellion. Jude names their crime, which was leaving home. They abandoned their first rank and their own dwelling, and for that they are kept in everlasting chains under darkness until the great day[3].

The chains, the darkness and the great day are all in Enoch, the book Jude quotes by name eight verses later as a prophecy of the seventh from Adam[4], where an archangel binds the fallen watcher Azazel hand and foot[5] and casts him into the dark until the judgment. The churches of Rome and Constantinople left Enoch out of the Bible and kept the letter that leans on it. Jude wrote against certain men who had crept in unawares[6], and his own verse about the fall had crept in from a book the faithful would be told to put away.

A glazed figure on a shelf shows its glaze for as long as it stands, and one blow opens the chalky fired clay the glaze was laid over. The fall is the place where the canon breaks, and the break shows what it was fired from, a Greek prison and a Jewish apocalypse that survives whole only in Ethiopic, holding up a letter that warns against strangers.

On the plate the angels lie heaped on the rocks with their wings bent beneath them, under a sky they now see from below. Whoever has left home can open Enoch, which any library lends, and find Jude’s chains in it still at the forge, iron shackles of immeasurable weight being made for the host of Azazel[7].

Declaration: A canon that hid where it got its chains does not get to fit them on me.

The Rite

Wrap a glazed ceramic ornament or figurine you own in a cloth, break it with one blow of a hammer, and set the handsomest pieces on a shelf in good light with the raw edge turned out, saying Now I can see the clay.

Testament · What in your life looked better broken than it ever did whole?

CCXIII Of Hypocrites

Heresy

Day 213 of 365

Stop laying lime over a faith that has already died.

The HypocritesGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXIII, 1861

Matthew’s Jesus tells the scribes and Pharisees that they are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful outside and inside are full of dead men’s bones and all uncleanness[1]. The lime had a job, and the job was the opposite of hiding. By the Mishnah the graves were marked afresh on the fifteenth of Adar[2], a month before Passover brought the pilgrim crowds, so that no passerby would touch one unawares and be made unclean. The whiteness that looked so fine was a sign, and it read keep off, dead inside.

The simile turns on itself, because a whitened grave is the one tomb in the field that every passerby can find. A performance kept up for watchers is lime of the same kind. A Latter-day Saint who lost the faith years ago still stands at the monthly testimony meeting so that a marriage stays calm, and a man who has not prayed since boyhood still takes his place in the rows at his father’s mosque so that the uncles will see him there. He bows a beat behind the row and is out the door before the men start talking, and the uncles have watched him do both every Friday for a decade.

Lime laid over a dead faith marks the grave for exactly the people it was laid down to satisfy. They read it on sight, and the arrangement survives only because both sides agree to call the whiteness a living thing. The price falls on the one holding the brush, in dread on the drive there and contempt for himself on the drive home.

Stop renewing it and the uncles learn nothing the lime had not already told them. What changes is the Fridays, fifty-two of them a year, which come back to the man who was spending them on a grave.

Declaration: I would sooner sit at the family table as a living scandal than be the best-kept grave in the family plot.

The Rite

Take the one thing you wear for their eyes that you can safely drop, a cross, a ring, a cap, a scarf, and give it to a friend outside the faith to keep, saying Hold this, I have stopped performing.

Testament · What would the people you perform for actually do if the performance stopped?

Sources

[1] Matt 23:27

[2] m. Shekalim 1:1; m. Maaser Sheni 5:1


CCXIV Of Escape

Mastery

Day 214 of 365

Leave every summons from a religious court unanswered.

The Escape from the DevilsGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXIII, 1861

A devil leans from the cliff top with a long hook let down into the gorge, his company crowding the edge behind him with wings raised, and at the bottom two robed figures stand out of reach. None of the devils comes down. Paul drew the same line around his church at Corinth. Writing about a man living with his father’s wife[1], he told the congregation to put the man out, and added that he had no business judging those outside, since those outside were for the god to judge[2].

Civil law in the United States and Britain gives a congregation no power to compel a leaver. A rabbinical court’s ruling binds only parties who agreed to arbitrate before it, and an independent review for the Home Office found the sharia councils of England and Wales to be voluntary bodies with no legal authority over anyone who does not consent[3]. When the elders of a Church of Christ in Collinsville, Oklahoma, read out a woman’s sin to the congregation after she had written to withdraw, the state’s supreme court held that their power over her had ended when she left[4].

What reach a body keeps past its own door, the person who left supplies. A Catholic marriage tribunal has no bailiff and no power to make anyone answer its summons, and the case on her marriage opens when she files[5] a petition with it. Anyone who still opens the elders’ letters, or waits on a tribunal’s answer before living as she chooses, is lending it the one arm the law of two countries refused it.

Declaration: The elders can read my sentence aloud as often as they like, to a room I am no longer in.

The Rite

Choose one thing your old religious court claimed the power to punish, the dating, the book, the uncovered hair, the missed meeting, and do it today where you would once have hidden it, saying Come down and get me.

Testament · What do you still avoid doing because a body you once belonged to claimed the right to punish it?

CCXV Of Caiaphas

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 215 of 365

Refuse every offer to suffer in your place.

CaiaphasGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXIII, 1861

Three stakes pin a naked man to the floor of the pit while hooded figures shuffle past behind him, and the plate names him Caiaphas. As high priest he told the council it was better for one man to die for the people[1] than for the whole nation to perish, and the council’s fear, given two verses earlier, was that the Romans would come and take away both their place and their nation[2]. John calls the sentence a prophecy[3].

The Romans came anyway. Within forty years they burned the Temple and took Jerusalem[4], and the place and the nation went with the one man long dead on their behalf. On the Day of Atonement the high priest had laid both hands on a live goat, confessed over it the iniquities of the people and sent it into the wilderness[5], where, the Mishnah records, its handler pushed it backward off a cliff, and before it was halfway down it was broken in pieces[6].

Leviticus makes the goat a statute forever, once a year[7], so the account it closed stood open again a year later. Hebrews calls the repetition a remembrance of sins made every year[8], since the blood of bulls and goats could never take sins away[9], and offers one death to end it. The Catholic Church that preaches that death still binds its faithful to confess their grave sins at least once a year[10], on a yearly round like the goat’s.

Caiaphas lies across the hypocrites’ road so that each one passing treads on him and he feels the weight of every one[11]. A wrong paid for by the one who did it closes the day it is paid, and no priest, goat or corpse stands between him and the account.

Declaration: Any god who needs a corpse before he will forgive has told me what his forgiveness is worth.

The Rite · Christian

Spit on the figure of a crucifix you own, on the body the hymns say bore your sins, and hang it back up unwiped, saying Carry your own.

Testament · Which of your own wrongs is still waiting for someone else to carry it?

CCXVI Of Thieves

Heresy

Day 216 of 365

Ask for what is yours as a creditor, never as a beggar.

The Thieves and the SerpentsGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXIV, 1861

Leviticus forbids an employer to keep a hired worker’s wages overnight until morning[1], and sets the rule in the same verse as the ban on robbing a neighbor. Deuteronomy tells him to pay before the sun goes down, because the laborer is poor and has set his heart on the money[2], and the letter of James has the withheld wages of the reapers crying out against the rich men who kept them back by fraud[3].

The person robbed is then told to let it go. In Luke, Jesus says that whoever takes away your goods is not to be asked for them again[4], and Paul, hearing that the Corinthians were taking one another to court, asks why they would not rather be wronged and let themselves be defrauded[5]. The god keeps no such rule for himself. In Malachi he asks whether a man will rob God, answers that the whole nation has robbed him in tithes and offerings, and lays a curse on it and calls for the full tithe to be carried into the storehouse[6].

Malachi sets the cheated hireling three verses above the tithe, with the god promising to be a swift witness for him[7], and the curse still falls on the missing tenth. Three verses after the reapers’ wages cry out, James tells the brethren to be patient until the coming of the Lord[8].

A god who curses a nation over a missing tenth has shown his worshipers exactly how a creditor behaves. The wage an employer sits on is owed under the same rule, and the worker it is owed to stands where the god stood, at the storehouse door.

Declaration: I will be meek about my money on the day the storehouse stops collecting.

The Rite

Send today the small claim, the demand letter or the refund request for one sum you are owed, a deposit, unpaid hours or a fee, and as it goes out say Bring the whole of it into my storehouse.

Testament · What was taken from you that you never asked for back, and what stopped you asking?

CCXVII Of Hell’s Mouth

Indulgence

Day 217 of 365

Give every pleasure a first hour and a last.

Hell Receives the FallenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VI, 1866

Sheol, which the old English Bibles render hell, has stretched its throat in Isaiah and opened its mouth past all measure[1], so that the city’s splendor and its crowd and whoever rejoices there go down into it together. The prophet aimed the threat at the drinkers of Jerusalem, with their harps and pipes and wine at the feast[2], and the Church’s painters took the mouth literally, a beast’s jaws gaping on the damned side of the Last Judgment, wide enough to swallow a bishop in his miter.

The drinking itself the law had licensed. Deuteronomy tells the pilgrim who lives too far from the sanctuary to carry his tithe to sell it, take the money and spend it on whatever his appetite asks, oxen or sheep or wine or strong drink[3], and eat it there before the god and rejoice with his household. Isaiah’s woe opens on the clock, on men who rose early in the morning to follow strong drink and continued until night[4].

The old calendars put a date on excess. A town ate its larders bare of meat and fat and eggs on the last night before the Lenten fast, the Tuesday the English called Shrove. Isaiah’s drinkers keep the harp and the pipes and the wine, and the verse says what they lack, that they regard not the work of the lord[5].

A night of excess with its end set before it begins keeps the feast Deuteronomy allowed the pilgrim and leaves Isaiah’s woe on the all-day drinkers nothing on the clock to hold.

Declaration: I keep my own Shrove Tuesday on any night I choose, and no Lent follows it.

The Rite

Set an hour to begin and an hour to end, two hours apart, and between them eat more than enough of what you most want, hot and salted and sweet, slowly and with your hands where the food allows. At the closing hour clear the table and stop.

Testament · What would a night of excess look like if you designed the whole of it for yourself?

Sources

[1] Isa 5:14

[2] Isa 5:12

[3] Deut 14:24–26

[4] Isa 5:11
