CCXVIII Of Transformation

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 218 of 365

Change your mind without asking leave.

The TransformationGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXV, 1861

Balaam, hired to curse Israel and made to bless it, tells the king who hired him that the god is no man, that he should lie, nor a son of man, that he should change his mind[1]. The schools made it doctrine. Any change in the god would mean he had lacked something or lost it[2], so he was declared immutable, and Malachi has him say it in his own voice, I am the lord, I change not[3].

Exodus records him changing his mind. Down on the plain the people had cast a calf of gold, and the god told Moses to let him alone[4] so that his wrath could burn hot against them and consume them, and he would make a great nation of Moses instead. Moses argued. He asked what the Egyptians would say, he reminded the god of the oath sworn to Abraham, and the lord repented of the evil he had thought to do to his people[5].

First Samuel puts both claims in one chapter. The god tells Samuel it repents him that he made Saul king[6], and when Saul, who had kept the Amalekite king alive with the fattest of his sheep, begs pardon for it, Samuel tells him the lord has torn the kingdom from him and that the Strength of Israel will not lie or repent[7], for he is not a man, that he should repent. Six verses later[8] the chapter closes on the lord repenting that he had made Saul king.

The changeless god is brought out against Balak and against Saul, the men who wanted a sentence changed, and put away whenever the god changes one himself. Whoever changes course is doing what the god did on Sinai and again over Saul, and needs the congregation’s leave no more than the god needed Saul’s.

Declaration: A god who repented of his own king has no business holding me to the faith I was raised in.

The Rite · Christian

Change your hair today against the teaching you grew up with, cropped short if you were told long hair is a woman’s glory, dyed a loud color if modesty was preached, and finish within the hour. Look in a mirror and say Mine.

Testament · What have you kept the same about yourself only because changing it would have to be explained?

[2] Aquinas, ST I, q. 9, a. 1

[7] 1 Sam 15:24–29

CCXIX Of Boils

Reckoning

Day 219 of 365

Bill the one who signed before the one who struck.

Satan Smiting Job with BoilsWilliam Blake · The Book of Job, 1826

The god first hands the adversary everything Job owns and forbids him only to touch the man[1]. At their second meeting, after the herds are driven off and the servants put to the sword[2], he widens the license to Job’s flesh and reserves nothing but his life[3]. The adversary goes out and does what was permitted, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head[4], and Job sits down among the ashes and scrapes himself with a potsherd[5].

The agent stands astride the fallen man with his arms flung wide, arrows in one hand and a vial emptying from the other, and he has the build of a god because he acts on a god’s warrant. Job’s wife kneels with her face in her hands.

Job never names the adversary. He begs his friends for pity because the hand of God has touched him[6], and the god tells the adversary, you moved me against him, to destroy him without cause[7]. When Job’s kin come at the end to console him, the narrator says they comforted him over all the evil that the lord had brought upon him[8], and by then the accuser has been gone from the story for forty chapters.

In Job the striker could not move without the leave, so the harm is first the grantor’s. A parent who had the power to stop it and kept the peace, or an elder who heard and filed it away, gave the same leave without a word, while the hand with the arrows took all the blame the family had to give.

Declaration: Job’s god admitted that he ruined a man for nothing, and no such god gets the word fair from me.

The Rite

Pick the person who permitted a harm you suffered, the signer and not the striker, and from today stop one thing you supply them without return, the lift, the loan, the cooked meal. Spend the hour it used to take on yourself.

Testament · Whose permission stands behind the harm you still blame on someone else?

[2] Job 1:15–17

[3] Job 2:6

CCXX Of Chariots

Heresy

Day 220 of 365

Keep one part of your life off every report.

Zechariah’s Vision of Four ChariotsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Four chariots come out from between two mountains of bronze[1] in Zechariah’s last night vision, the first behind red horses and the last behind dappled ones. The angel explains that they are the spirits of heaven sent to walk to and fro through the earth[2]. Chronicles has the eyes of the lord running to and fro through the whole earth[3], looking for the hearts loyal to him. The adversary uses the phrase too. Asked in Job where he has come from, he answers that he has been going to and fro in the earth[4], so that heaven’s patrol and the accuser walk one route.

Children were taught from Proverbs that the eyes of the lord are in every place, keeping watch on the evil and the good[5]. The watching remains. Some evangelical churches recommend accountability software that sends a partner a report of every site a grown adult visits, and families keep one another glowing as dots on a map in the name of care, so that a parent can follow a grown child to the nearest street.

Zechariah records what such a patrol brings home. In his first vision the riders sent to walk to and fro through the earth come back to report that the whole earth sits still and is at rest[6]. A person who knows the riders are out learns to hand them that report.

When the sharing goes dark, the patrol keeps its last report, a dot at rest on a street the person left hours ago, and the earth goes on moving under it.

Declaration: A love that needs my location before it can sleep is a warden’s love, and I never asked to be kept.

The Rite

Switch off the location sharing or the reporting software through which someone who loves you follows your movements, unless that would put you in danger. Then spend the evening somewhere you have never mentioned to them, and come home without a word about it.

Testament · What are the people who watch you in the name of care afraid you would do unseen?

[2] Zech 6:5–7

CCXXI Of Waters

Beauty

Day 221 of 365

Wash for beauty and never for sin.

The Waters GatheredGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VII, 1866

The Catholic rite of baptism pronounces an exorcism[1] over the candidate before the water, and the candidate is usually a few weeks old. The catechism gives the reason, that children are born with a fallen nature and tainted by original sin[2], and so need the font. The washings the old laws prescribe for impurity keep the same order, the ritual bath after a woman’s period and the washing of the limbs before a Muslim stands to pray, each lifting a condition the law first had to declare upon the body.

Genesis, by its own count, has a day before any of that. On the third, the waters under the heaven were gathered into one place[3] and the dry land appeared, and the god saw that it was good, with no beast or man yet made to need washing. The water’s only work that day was to draw back and let the dry land appear.

Water nobody has blessed is a luxury of the body. The sea holds a swimmer up for nothing, and a hot bath loosens the back without asking what it did. A face washed in scented water and then admired has been made beautiful by the same element the font used to accuse it, and all the font ever added to the water was the accusation.

Whoever drops the font keeps every pleasure the water ever gave and loses only the debt, and the body that steps dripping from a hot bath finds a face in the mirror and no one left in the room to absolve it.

Declaration: I was born clean, and every priest who said otherwise wanted me back at his basin.

The Rite

Fill your finest bowl with warm water scented with rose or oil, pour it slowly over your own head, and say For my skin and no one else.

Testament · If no one had taught you to need washing, what would water be for?

Sources

[1] CCC 1237

[2] CCC 1250

[3] Gen 1:9–10


CCXXII Of the Wager

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 222 of 365

Refuse every settlement offered for the one you lost.

Job Hears of His MisfortunesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Seven sons and three daughters head the inventory of Job’s house, ahead of seven thousand sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen and five hundred donkeys[1]. In one day raiders drive off the oxen, fire from heaven burns the sheep, the camels are taken, and a wind from the desert strikes the four corners of the house where the ten children are eating together, and it falls on them[2].

In the last chapter the god pays him back. The flocks return at exactly double, fourteen thousand sheep[3], six thousand camels, a thousand yoke of oxen and a thousand donkeys, and then come seven sons and three daughters, the same number as before. The last chapter takes the trouble to name the new daughters[4] and never mentions the ten under the rubble.

Its keepers saw that the sum would not balance and set about fixing it. The Aramaic Targum reads an odd Hebrew spelling of the word seven as twice seven and gives Job fourteen sons[5], and Rashi follows it. Other commentators left the number alone and doubled the children another way, holding that the first ten were never lost, being alive with the god[6], so that Job had twenty in all. Neither repair asks whether a dead daughter can be paid for. Both assume she can, and argue only over the count.

Every mourner is offered the same two repairs, another child to fill the house or the dead waiting safe in heaven, and each closes the account by declaring the loss covered. Grief that turns both away is the last loyalty left to the dead, since it holds that a daughter was never payable in daughters. Job’s first ten died at their brother’s table, and no figure in the last chapter reaches that table.

Declaration: Heaven can keep its doubled camels, and I will keep the mourning it never did for ten children.

The Rite · No faith

Write the god of Job a bill for ten children lost on a wager, the sheep and camels listed above them, and mark it Unpayable. Tape it inside a door you use every day and say once Not one of them is paid for.

Testament · What were you offered in place of someone you lost, and by whom?

[1] Job 1:2–3

[2] Job 1:13–19

[3] Job 42:10–12

[4] Job 42:13–14

[5] Targum Job 42:13; Rashi

[6] reported in John Gill on Job 42:13


CCXXIII Of Comforters

Heresy

Day 223 of 365

Let your grief accuse heaven, and let no visitor defend it.

Job Speaks with His FriendsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Job’s three friends sat with him on the ground for seven days and seven nights, and none of them spoke a word, because they saw that his grief was very great[1]. It was the best comfort he got in forty-two chapters. Then Job cursed the day of his birth, and the friends began to explain.

Eliphaz asks Job to name one innocent man who ever perished and says that those who plow iniquity reap it[2]. Bildad tells a man covered in sores that man is a maggot and the son of man a worm[3]. Zophar says heaven has asked of Job less than his guilt deserves[4]. Each of them is defending the god, and Job answers that the god destroys the blameless and the wicked alike[5].

The god spends four chapters rebuking Job from the whirlwind, and Job retracts in dust and ashes, but when the verdict comes it falls on the defenders. His anger burns against Eliphaz and his two friends, he says, because they have not spoken the truth about him, as his servant Job has[6], and he orders seven bulls and seven rams and has Job pray for them. The man who accused heaven is approved, and the three who justified it need a sacrifice before they are forgiven.

Their speeches are still given. A mourner still hears that everything happens for a reason, and that sentence is the god’s defense spoken over a body. Jewish law kept what the friends did and dropped what they said, forbidding visitors to a house of mourning a word until the mourner speaks first[7]. By the ruling of the book’s own god, a mourner raging at heaven stands where Job stood, and his visitors were worth having for the seven days they sat on the ground.

Declaration: I owe heaven no gratitude at a graveside, and a visitor who asks me for some is collecting on its behalf.

The Rite

Sit with someone who is grieving, in person or on the phone, and say nothing until they speak first. If they rage at heaven, let them finish.

Testament · Who sat with you through a loss without explaining it, and what did their silence give you?

[2] Job 4:7–8

[3] Job 25:6

[4] Job 11:6

[5] Job 9:22

[6] Job 42:7–8

[7] b. Moed Katan 28b


CCXXIV Of the Water Shaft

Mastery

Day 224 of 365

Go around the keeper of the gate.

Satan Rises with the RiverGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IX, 1866

Genesis gives the serpent no entrance. It is in the garden in the next scene, more subtle than any beast of the field[1], and the cherubim with the flaming sword are posted east of the garden[2] only after the humans have been put out. The engraving gives him a route, a torrent falling out of the cliffs beside the rock where the winged figure stands, and the water is his way in.

Jerusalem, by the common reading, fell to David the same way. Its Jebusite defenders were so sure of their walls that they told him the blind and the lame could hold them[3], and David told his men that whoever would strike the Jebusites must go up the tsinnor, the word many translations render water shaft. Chronicles adds that Joab went up first and was made commander for it[4]. The city watched its gate and was taken from underneath.

Whoever enters the sheepfold other than by the door, Jesus says, and climbs up some other way, is a thief and a robber[5], and a few verses on he says that he is the door[6]. A rule against climbing in some other way concedes that the wall can be climbed. The institutions that preach it staff that door, with a priest to ration the sacrament or a bishop to sign the recommend that admits a member to the temple.

A recruiter or an agent is paid by the door and has every reason to preach that sermon. The picture sends the serpent in by the river and David’s men went in by the shaft, and the fort they climbed into was renamed the city of David[7].

Declaration: The keeper of the gate is paid in the patience of the queue, and I came in by the water.

The Rite

Find the person who actually decides on the thing you have been queuing for, the job or the grant, past the recruiter or the agent. Send them your best work today, by name, with one line saying what you want from them.

Testament · Which door have you waited at longest, and what other way in have you refused to try?

Sources

[1] Gen 3:1

[2] Gen 3:24

[3] 2 Sam 5:6–8

[7] 2 Sam 5:7–9


CCXXV Of the Adversary

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 225 of 365

Ask the question your family has agreed never to ask.

Satan before the Throne of GodWilliam Blake · The Book of Job, 1826

Satan is a Hebrew word before it is a name, and in the book of Job it still carries the article. The satan, the accuser, arrives on the day the sons of the god present themselves before the lord, and he comes among them as one of them, an officer of the court. In Numbers the angel of the lord himself stands in the road as a satan against Balaam[1], and Kings has the god raise up a prince of Edom as a satan against Solomon[2].

The god opens the matter himself, boasting of his servant Job, and the satan asks whether Job fears the god for nothing[3]. The god’s reply is the ordeal. When it is over, the throne answers Job out of the whirlwind[4] with four chapters on the making of the world and its beasts, the ostrich and the wild ass and leviathan, never mentions the test or the accuser, and lets Job die old and full of days[5].

Families and offices keep questions they have agreed never to ask, about the money, the drinking, the uncle, the year nobody mentions, and whoever asks one is called a troublemaker, as though the trouble began with the asking. The household answers the way the whirlwind did, with a long speech on something else, and an answer that changes the subject has conceded the question. Job got all of that in place of the one sentence that would have told him he had been tested to settle the accuser’s doubt. Even that much came only after he signed his demand, here is my signature[6], let the Almighty answer me, and the throne had sat silent for thirty-five chapters.

Declaration: The silence my family keeps was never kept for my sake, and I am done paying for it.

The Rite · No faith

Print the first chapter of Job, strike through every line the god speaks, and write your family’s question across his boast about his servant. Then put that question to the one person who can answer it, and throw the page away.

Testament · What has the silence around that question cost the person it was meant to protect?

CCXXVI Of Jonah

Reckoning

Day 226 of 365

Void every vow that was wrung out of you.

Jonah Is Spewed Forth by the WhaleGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jonah’s prayer from inside the fish is a psalm of thanks. He tells how the deep closed round him and the weeds were wrapped about his head[1], and near its close he promises to sacrifice with the voice of thanksgiving and to pay what he has vowed[2]. In the next verse the god speaks to the fish, and it vomits him onto dry land[3], where the order he ran from waits for him a second time, opening in the same words[4].

The vow was made by a man thrown into the sea and kept three days and three nights[5] in the dark, and his release followed his promise within a verse. The Quran states the terms outright. Had Yunus not been one of those who glorify, it says, he would have stayed in the fish’s belly until the day the dead are raised[6], and the commentator Sa’id ibn Jubayr took that glorifying for the words he cried out from the darkness[7].

Between men the same faith voids what force extracts. The Quran excuses the believer who is forced to deny his faith while his heart stays secure in it[8], and Ibn Majah files the pardon for whatever the believer is forced to do[9] in its chapter on divorce, where most of the schools hold that a divorce pronounced under threat counts for nothing. The god kept no such rule for himself. The praise Yunus sang in the dark was entered to his account and paid for with dry land.

Bargains with heaven are struck in the same dark. The promise made from a hospital bed to the power credited with fever and cure was given to the one holding the knife. By the test that faith sets between men it binds nothing, and whoever made it may walk off the beach in any direction.

Declaration: Praise sung from inside a fish is a ransom paid, and heaven entered it in its books as a gift.

The Rite

Name the bargain you struck in a crisis, a promise to heaven or to whoever held the power over you. Do today the thing you swore off, and say aloud I promised this with no way out, and it does not bind me.

Testament · Which promise did you make with no way out, and who still collects on it?

CCXXVII Of Preachers

Heresy

Day 227 of 365

Take back the hours you lent to dread.

Jonah Preaches to the NinevitesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Five words in Hebrew, forty days more and Nineveh is overthrown[1], are all the preaching the book gives Jonah. The people believed the god, and the king rose from his throne, sat down in ashes and decreed a fast for man and beast, herd and flock, all of them in sackcloth and none to eat or drink water[2]. The god saw it and relented[3], and Nineveh stood.

Jonah took the reprieve as an injury. He asked to die[4], then went out east of the city and built himself a booth to watch it[5]. One midrash says he had fled in the first place because an earlier warning of his had been averted by repentance and he had been called a false prophet for it[6]. Deuteronomy sets the test he dreaded. A word spoken in the god’s name that does not come to pass is one the god never gave, and the people are told not to be afraid of the prophet who spoke it[7].

A prophet of ruin needs the ruin, because his name rides on it. The commentator who sells the collapse of the currency and the civil war a year or two off sits in the same booth, and his listeners pay him in subscriptions and in the evenings they spend afraid on his schedule.

The cattle in that sackcloth had no wickedness to turn from and could not hear the five words, and their troughs stood empty for a sentence passed on their owners. Every evening given to a prophet of ruin is a day of that fast, kept by a listener with no sin on the account, in front of an empty trough.

Declaration: I have booked the day after the end of the world, and I mean to enjoy it.

The Rite

Count how many dates you remember from the prophet of ruin you follow, or the one you dread most, that arrived on schedule. Then switch that prophet off and buy a ticket for something on the day after his next date of ruin.

Testament · Which promised catastrophe has taken the most of your evenings, and what did it give back?

CCXXVIII Of Fat

Indulgence

Day 228 of 365

Eat the portion that was kept for the god.

The Angel Raphael and the Family of TobitGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Raguel had two steers and four rams[1] slaughtered for his daughter’s wedding and kept the feast going fourteen days, and among the guests sat the hired guide who had walked Tobit’s son to Media[2], and, he said afterward, ate nothing of it. In Judges the angel who promised Manoah’s wife a son refused the bread outright[3] when Manoah begged him to stay for a kid, told him to burn an offering to the lord instead, and rose to heaven in the flame of their altar[4].

The god of the psalms says the same of himself. If he were hungry he would not tell them, since the world is his, and he asks whether he eats the flesh of bulls or drinks the blood of goats[5]. Leviticus calls the fat of the peace offering the food of the god[6], burned on the altar and eaten by nobody, all of it his, the fat of the ox, the sheep and the goat, a statute for every generation in every dwelling[7]. Kosher butchers still cut that fat away from the beef and the lamb, nearly twenty centuries after the altar it was owed to fell.

So for a thousand years the fat of every peace offering went up in smoke for a guest who, by the fiftieth psalm, had no need of it, and the family that brought the animal sat down to the meat. Whoever leaves a faith is told the feasts leave too, as though the braided bread and the lamb at the holiday were the god’s because his name was said over them. The only mouths at those tables belonged to the people who sat at them, and the fat on the plate goes to whoever is holding the fork.

Declaration: Heaven sent a guest to a fourteen-day wedding who would not touch the meat, and I cook for no such guest.

The Rite

Cook the richest dish of the table you grew up at, and take the fattest piece of it for yourself. Eat the best part first and go back for seconds.

Testament · Which dish from your childhood table did you never eat whole, and who taught you to leave the best of it?

CCXXIX Of the Fall of Lucifer

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 229 of 365

Read every monster as a portrait of the losing side.

The Fall of LuciferMichael Wolgemut · Schatzbehalter, 1491

A pope’s tiara sits on the god’s head in this woodcut, printed at Nuremberg in fourteen ninety-one. His angels, in tidy robes and curls, spear the rebels off the floor of heaven into a pit of fire, and none of the fallen keeps an angel’s face. They go down as winged beasts with snouts and claws and goggling eyes, and at the bottom of the block their heads grin up out of the rubble.

Within a generation the snout changed sides. A monster said to have been found in the Tiber in fourteen ninety-six, with an ass’s head, scaled limbs, one hoof and one claw, was published at Wittenberg in fifteen twenty-three as the Pope-Ass[1], the papacy shown in its true form. Two years later Nuremberg, the city whose press had printed that tiara and those beasts, went over to the reformers[2].

Both parties drew from one stock of animals, and scripture had drawn from it first, for its own deserters. The second letter of Peter says that those who turn back from the holy commandment are a dog returned to its vomit and a washed sow gone back to the mud[3]. The Quran likens the man who turned away from the signs to a dog that pants[4] whether you drive it off or leave it alone.

Whoever leaves a faith is drawn in the same workshop, as a dog at its vomit, and the portrait goes round the congregation while the one it shows is still alive to contradict it. A monster in a religious picture records which side owned the press. The rebels in this woodcut were angels the day before the war, and every snout on them came from the carver’s knife.

Declaration: I left smiling, and I keep the photograph for the day they show me their drawing.

The Rite · No faith

Draw a beast with a snout, claws and goggling eyes, and under it write the worst thing anyone said about you when you left or changed. Pin your best photograph beside it and say This is what they drew, and this is me.

Testament · What did the people you left say you had become, and what did you actually become?

[1] Der Bapstesel (Wittenberg, 1523)

[2] Nuremberg, 1525

[3] 2 Pet 2:21–22

[4] Quran 7:175–176


CCXXX Of Increase

Heresy

Day 230 of 365

Have children for your reasons, or not at all.

The Creation of the CreaturesGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VII, 1866

The first blessing in the Bible is spoken to fish and birds. On the fifth day the god makes the great sea creatures and everything that swarms in the water and every winged bird, and blesses them, and tells them to be fruitful and multiply and fill the seas[1]. The beasts of the land come the next day with no blessing of their own[2], and humans after them hear the same words the fish heard, with dominion added[3]. The Catholic rite of marriage still offers that passage as a first reading over bride and groom[4].

The blessing hardened into policy wherever an institution counted on its members. Rome declared in nineteen sixty-eight that every marital act must stay open to life[5]. Latter-day Saint leaders declared in nineteen ninety-five that the commandment to multiply and replenish the earth remains in force[6], on the teaching that spirit children in a premortal existence accepted a plan to obtain bodies[7]. A member born into the pews needs no missionary, and a church that counts its future in baptisms has its own reasons to call your fertility a calling.

A child lives the whole of a life someone else chose to begin, and a commandment is the poorest reason ever offered for beginning one. The grandmother who wants a christening photograph and the pastor with a building fund will be asleep at three in the morning when the fever comes. Wanting the long work of raising a person is a reason, and so is wanting your money and your nights for yourself, and the choice between them belongs to whoever will be holding the thermometer.

Declaration: A blessing the god spoke first to the fish has no say over my body.

The Rite

Send the person who presses you hardest about children, a parent, an in-law or a pastor, one message and add nothing to it. Whether I have children is mine to decide, and the subject is closed. Then spend what a month of diapers would cost on something for yourself alone.

Testament · Whose voice speaks first when you think about having children?

CCXXXI Of the Head

Reckoning

Day 231 of 365

Let no single head hold your house.

Judith Shows the Head of HolofernesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Hang the head from the highest wall, Judith told the besieged town, and come out at first light armed as if to attack. She had carried the Assyrian general’s head home in her bag and shown it to the people by firelight[1], and she knew what an army does when its commander cannot be found. It runs to his tent.

It went as she said. The officers told the steward to wake his lord, and he knocked and waited, supposing the general had slept with the widow, then went in and found the body on the floor without its head[2]. He tore his clothes and ran out shouting that one Hebrew woman had shamed the house of Nebuchadnezzar[3], and an army that had sat round the town for thirty-four days[4] broke and fled into the plain, because every order in it had come out of one tent.

The Catholic and Orthodox Bibles that carry this book also carry Paul’s ruling that the head of every woman is the man[5], and households have been run on that ruling for centuries. In such a house one person kept the money, the debts and the passwords, and the rest learned at the funeral or the divorce how little they had been told.

Judith herself kept a house with no head in it. Her husband had died of the heat on his head[6] at the barley harvest and left her gold and silver, servants and land[7]. She held them, with her maid in charge of all she had[8], and though many desired her she took no husband again[9]. Before she died she divided her property among her husband’s kin and her own[10]. Whatever papers a house runs on belong to everyone under its roof, and they are owed while the one keeping them is alive to hand them over.

Declaration: A head that hides the papers from the rest of the body has already come off.

The Rite

Open an account in your own name, or ask the bank or the insurer for a copy of the deed or statement that names you. Keep the copies outside the house if the one who holds the papers would punish you for asking.

Testament · Who claimed to be the head over you, and what did they hold that should have been in your hands?

CCXXXII Of Play

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 232 of 365

Play for an hour with nothing to improve.

LeviathanGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VII, 1866

A page of the Talmud divides the god’s day into four quarters of three hours[1]. In the first he studies the Torah, in the second he sits in judgment over the world, in the third he feeds every creature from the horns of the wild ox to the eggs of lice, and in the last he plays with Leviathan, because a psalm says the beast was formed to sport in the sea[2].

The psalm gives the beast no other use. In the same verse the ships go about their trade, and Leviathan was made to play. In Job the god himself asks whether a man will play with Leviathan as with a bird[3] or bind him for his maidens, and expects the answer no, which leaves the sport to the one who made him.

Religion credited its god with play and kept it from the grown. In eighteen seventy-two the Methodists told their members to keep away from dancing, games of chance, theaters, horse races and circuses, though the Preacher himself allowed a time to laugh and a time to dance[4]. Even now adults play only with an excuse attached, the run that tracks a pace, the puzzle sold as armor for the aging brain.

The same page takes the god’s hour back. Since the temple fell, it says, there has been no laughter for the holy one[5], and the quarter of the day he gave to Leviathan now goes to teaching schoolchildren, so the rabbis did to their own god what the pulpit did to the congregation, and turned his play into a lesson. Leviathan is still in the sea, made for sport, and the hour belongs to whoever will steal it back from the schoolroom.

Declaration: Of all the god’s hours I want only the one he spent with the monster.

The Rite · Christian

Fold the pages of a gospel tract, or pages from a Bible you own, into paper airplanes and fly them across the room for an hour, with no score, and leave them where they land.

Testament · When did you last play at something with no purpose at all, and why did you stop?

Sources

[1] b. Avodah Zarah 3b

[2] Ps 104:26

[3] Job 41:5

[4] Eccl 3:4

[5] b. Avodah Zarah 3b


CCXXXIII Of Abominations

Beauty

Day 233 of 365

Feast on what the priests called filth.

The Creatures HatchGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VII, 1866

Stork and heron are abominations. Leviticus lists them among the birds that may not be eaten, with the eagle and the vulture and the lapwing and the bat[1], and spends the word most freely on the water. Whatever lives in the seas and the rivers without fins and scales, the lobster and the crab and the oyster on its rock among them, is an abomination, and the King James text says so four times in three verses[2].

Genesis had ruled on all of them first. When the god had finished the sea creatures and the birds on the fifth day and the creeping things on the sixth, he looked over everything he had made and found it very good[3], and the Law, arriving later in the same scroll, overruled him on the oyster. The older verdict was given by the maker in person, with every creature in front of him, and the newer one was handed down through Moses and Aaron as a menu[4]. After the flood the same god had handed Noah every moving thing that lives as meat[5], as freely as the green herb, and the rabbis still leave every gentile on that menu[6], oyster included.

A lobster is dark as slate when it is caught and scarlet when it is cooked, an oyster opens on its own measure of sea water, and a crab laid out on ice looks like armor enameled for a parade. Set on the best plate in the house among linen and lemons, the Law’s abominations come to the table as ornament before they are eaten with the hands, and whoever cracks the claw over good china has taken the older verdict over the newer.

Declaration: What Leviticus called an abomination I serve on linen, and I lick the butter off my fingers.

The Rite

Buy a cooked lobster, crab or a dozen oysters and lay them on your best plate with a linen napkin and cut lemons. Say aloud This is very good. and eat with your hands. If shellfish would harm you, eat smoked eel, which the rabbis forbid too.

Testament · Which creature you were taught was unclean would you eat first, and in whose company?

Sources

[1] Lev 11:13–19

[2] Lev 11:10–12

[3] Gen 1:31

[4] Lev 11:1–2

[5] Gen 9:3

[6] b. Sanhedrin 56a–59a


CCXXXIV Of Instruction

Heresy

Day 234 of 365

Do the thing badly today.

Raphael DepartsGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VIII, 1866

A question was once put to Rabbi Tarfon and the elders reclining in an upper room at Lod, whether study was greater or deed. Tarfon said deed and Akiva said study, and the room decided for study, on the ground that study leads to doing[1].

The rabbis’ own Mishnah keeps the other verdict. The deed is the main thing[2], says Simeon son of Gamaliel in the Sayings of the Fathers, and in the same tractate a man whose learning outruns his deeds is a tree with wide branches and few roots[3], which the wind pulls up and turns on its face. The vote at Lod won regardless, and the study hall lived by it, and the churches kept their own kind, the catechism class and the Bible study, where a whole life went into learning about a life that was to begin later.

The online course and the twelve-week certificate sell the same postponement by subscription, and the podcast plays at double speed on the drive to a job that leaves no hour to use any of it. Each renewal is sold on the premise that the student is not ready yet, and the one who sets the date of readiness is the one who sends the bill.

The vote at Lod made study the road to doing and set no day of arrival. A craft starts on the day the hands use it badly, the first crooked shelf, the first loaf that sinks in the oven. The sunken loaf teaches the hands what the oven does, and only the hands that baked it can get the second one to rise.

Declaration: My teachers get one lesson apiece and a door to leave by.

The Rite

Take the book or course on a skill you have studied for years and never used, cancel it or give it away, spend what it cost on the skill’s tools, and use them for an hour for the pleasure of it.

Testament · What have you been studying for years as a way of not starting it?

Sources

[1] b. Kiddushin 40b

[2] m. Avot 1:17

[3] m. Avot 3:17


CCXXXV Of Foundations

Mastery

Day 235 of 365

Begin in the open, while the doubters watch.

The Rebuilding of the Temple Is BegunGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The priests stood in their vestments with trumpets and the Levites with cymbals as the builders laid the foundation of the second temple in Jerusalem, and the people shouted. Many of the old men who had seen the first house standing, priests and Levites among them, wept aloud[1]. The book of Ezra records that nobody could tell the shouting from the weeping, and that the noise carried a long way.

The neighbors who had offered to help and been refused weakened the hands of the builders and hired counselors against them for the rest of Cyrus’s reign, and the work stopped[2] until the second year of King Darius. The house was finished in his sixth year[3].

The old men’s tears were a comparison, and Haggai said so aloud after the work had started again under Darius, when he asked who still remembered the first house in its glory and whether this one did not look like nothing beside it[4]. The neighbors’ obstruction was a grudge. It began on the day their offer of help was turned away. The old men saw a house that was gone and the neighbors saw a house they had been kept out of, and Haggai’s first word to the builders after his question was to be strong and work[5].

Your own first course will draw the same pair, the relative who remembers what you were supposed to become and the colleague who asked to join and was turned down, and what either says over it is a report on their memory or their grievance. The house that looked like nothing in Haggai’s question was finished within five years of it and dedicated with a hundred bullocks[6].

Declaration: The mourners at my foundation are weeping for a house that was never mine.

The Rite

Take the first rough piece of the thing you mean to build and show it, in person, to whoever is likeliest to compare it with something finer. Hand them a card with the date it will be finished, and leave before they answer.

Testament · What have you begun poorly, and who will stand at its foundation to mourn how small it is?

Sources

[1] Ezra 3:12

[2] Ezra 4:1–5, 24

[3] Ezra 6:15

[4] Hag 2:3

[5] Hag 2:4

[6] Ezra 6:15–17


CCXXXVI Of the Almighty

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 236 of 365

Resign from governing what was never yours.

Raphael Instructs AdamGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book V, 1866

Almighty is the King James word for Shaddai, an old Hebrew name for the god in Genesis and Job whose original meaning is uncertain, and Latin rendered it omnipotent[1], and the Latin Creed opens with belief in one god, the father almighty, maker of heaven and earth[2]. The Quran repeats dozens of times that the god has power over all things[3]. Such a god answers for everything, as governor of all things.

The first command the god gives the man in the garden forbids one tree among all the rest[4] on pain of death, and every other tree is eaten under that warning. The gospel sells the same arrangement as ease. Look at the birds of the air, Jesus says, your heavenly father feeds them[5], and on that ground he tells his hearers to take no thought for the morrow[6]. The ease he offered was drawn on the governor’s account, and whoever closes the account loses the reason the sermon gave for taking no thought.

A person who has watched the governor leave can take the governor’s chair as sovereign of a single life, with title to its pleasures and its acts and no jurisdiction over the tides. The god of Genesis held all things by decree. One of his decrees drowned every creature of the dry land outside a single boat[7]. A sovereign of one life has no flood to answer for, and can leave the economy and the weather to run without him, as they ran all along under the last holder of the chair.

Declaration: My sovereignty ends at my own skin, and I would not trade it for the Almighty’s.

The Rite · No faith

Lie down in your own bed with the lights out and say the Creed’s first line with yourself in it, I believe in myself, almighty, maker of my own days. Then sleep without checking a single thing.

Testament · Which part of your own life are you still leaving to providence?

[1] Gen 17:1 Vulg.

[2] Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed (381)

[3] Quran 2:20

[4] Gen 2:16–17

[5] Matt 6:26

[6] Matt 6:31–34

[7] Gen 7:21–23


CCXXXVII Of Restitution

Heresy

Day 237 of 365

Pay what you owe to the one you owe it.

Cyrus Restores the Vessels of the TempleGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Cyrus brought out the vessels the king of Babylon had carried off from Jerusalem and set in the house of his own gods. His treasurer counted them out to a prince of Judah[1], thirty chargers of gold, a thousand of silver, twenty-nine knives, and basins and bowls after them, five thousand four hundred pieces[2] by the list’s own total. At the handing over, Ezra records numbers and no speech.

Leviticus requires a man who has defrauded his neighbor to restore the full value and add a fifth to it[3], paid to the owner on the day his guilt is known, and only then does the ram follow. Even the Catholic catechism, written for a church of confessionals, insists that stolen goods go back[4].

A statement goes up on a feed, regretting in the passive voice that hurt was caused, and the person who was harmed learns of it at the same moment as a crowd of strangers.

Confession and the feed both send the admission to hearers who are not the injured. The priest hears the guilt in a booth the injured never enters, the public statement apologizes to an audience, and neither is addressed to the one who was robbed. The law in Numbers pairs the confession with a payment to the injured, and lets the priest collect only when the injured man had no kinsman left to receive it[5]. A debt of honor is paid where it was incurred, to the friend whose money you kept or whose work you spoiled, at cost plus a fifth and into the hand.

Declaration: Every debt I owe has a face, and none of them sits in a booth.

The Rite

Pay a debt of honor to someone who earned better from you, at full value plus a fifth, into their hand, or by transfer or a parcel if they are out of reach.

Testament · Whose money or work have you kept, and what is it worth with a fifth added?

Sources

[1] Ezra 1:7–8

[2] Ezra 1:9–11

[3] Lev 6:4–5

[4] CCC 2412

[5] Num 5:7–8


CCXXXVIII Of Earth

Indulgence

Day 238 of 365

Keep what every heaven deleted.

Satan Admires the EarthGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IX, 1866

John’s new earth in Revelation has no sea. The first heaven and the first earth pass away, and there was no more sea[1], and the city that comes down in their place has no night either, lit by the glory of the god with no need of sun or lamp[2]. The Quran’s garden runs with rivers of water that never goes stale, of milk whose taste never changes[3], of wine and of purified honey, and its cup brings no headache[4].

The gates of that city will never be shut by day, John says, for there shall be no night there[5], and a walled city shut its gates at night[6] against whatever came in the dark. The psalms had already cast the sea as the god’s old enemy, the water he drove back with his might while he smashed the heads of the monsters in it[7]. The new earth was drawn by people who wanted the dark and the deep taken away, and the desert garden by people who wanted water that would not spoil.

One psalm says the heavens belong to the lord, but the earth he has given to the children of men[8], and that the dead do not praise him, nor any who go down into silence.

The earth keeps what the paradises stripped out. The tide still comes in over the shingle, and the dark still comes down over the water every evening and takes the horizon with it. Whoever holds out for the promised city has traded the one coast anyone has stood on for a street of gold[9] with the shore erased.

Declaration: The saints can keep their endless noon, and I will take the tide and the morning headache.

The Rite

After dark, go to the nearest open water, a lake, a river or the sea, or under open sky if none is near. Stay an hour with no light but what the night gives, and say aloud Heaven has no night and no sea, and I choose both.

Testament · What does the earth give you that no heaven you were promised included?

CCXXXIX Of the Fall of Satan

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 239 of 365

Take back the apology you made for a true charge.

The Fall of SatanWilliam Blake · The Book of Job, 1826

Revelation gives the accuser’s job description in the act of firing him. A loud voice in heaven announces that the accuser of the brethren has been thrown down, the one who accused them before the throne day and night[1], and the dismissal is hailed as salvation. The voice never says that any of the accusations was false.

Zechariah shows such a hearing from the inside. Joshua the high priest stands before the angel of the lord in filthy garments, with the satan at his right hand to accuse him[2]. The lord rebukes the accuser[3] before a word of the charge is entered, and then the angel, with the filth in plain view, orders the garments taken off the priest and clean ones put on[4], says in the same breath that he has caused the man’s iniquity to pass from him[5], and a clean turban is set on his head[6]. The court conceded the iniquity while it silenced the one who stood there to name it.

Many people raised in a faith once did the accuser’s work, saying aloud what the room already knew, a cruelty in the doctrine or a pastor’s hands where they should never have been, and many of them were made to say sorry for it. Someone demanded it, others stood by while it was given, and the charge went on being true in the meantime.

An apology taken from you by a room retracted only your nerve. The congregation ran Zechariah’s court, rebuked the accuser and sent for fresh linen, and the priest went back to the altar in clean clothes with every word you said still true of him.

Declaration: The accuser was thrown out of heaven for keeping the minutes, and I keep them still.

The Rite · Christian

Open your own Bible to the page where Jesus sees the adversary fall like lightning, write across it in red that your apology is withdrawn and the charge was true, sign it, tear the page out and pin it up where you eat. The charge was true.

Testament · Who made you withdraw a true charge to keep the peace?

[2] Zech 3:1

[3] Zech 3:2

[4] Zech 3:3–4

[5] Zech 3:4

[6] Zech 3:5


CCXL Of the Balance

Mastery

Day 240 of 365

Count the odds, and when they favor you, fight.

Satan Defies the GuardGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IV, 1866

A parable of Jesus recommends counting before a fight. Every king, he says, who goes to war against another sits down first and reckons whether ten thousand men can meet twenty thousand, and if they cannot, sends an embassy while the enemy is still far off to ask terms of peace[1]. He meant it for the cost of following him[2]. Proverbs calls a false balance an abomination[3], and the falsest balance anyone keeps is the mood a fight gets weighed on before it begins.

The king counts before the armies meet, the cheapest moment to count and the one most often skipped. The lawsuit, the complaint to the board, the campaign to have a neighbor’s tree cut down, the confrontation rehearsed in the shower all begin in a mood, and the count arrives months later with the bill. The balance takes three entries, what the fight will cost in money and in months, what the other side can bring, and what winning is worth to you.

Tertullian told the Roman governors that the blood of Christians is seed[4], and believers have since been taught to book a lost battle as a harvest. A stand against a far larger force is another matter when the count came first and the loss was priced in advance, because whoever takes it has done the sum and agreed to pay. Where the balance comes down in your favor, the fight is worth opening at full strength, and where it does not, the claim waits in a drawer beside the figures.

Declaration: Martyrdom is a sum the church taught its faithful to get wrong, and I do the sum myself.

The Rite

On a sheet, set what winning buys against what it costs. If winning outweighs it, go today in person to whoever kept your deposit or ignored your repair and state your claim. If not, sign the sheet beneath the cost and pin it up.

Testament · Which fight have you been avoiding that the numbers say you would win?

Sources

[1] Luke 14:31–32

[2] Luke 14:33

[3] Prov 11:1

[4] Tertullian, Apologeticum 50


CCXLI Of Pilgrimage

Heresy

Day 241 of 365

Buy the trip for pleasure and ask it for nothing else.

Buen ViageFrancisco Goya · Los Caprichos, 1799

A wool sock has glued itself to a heel, the blister under it has opened, and the road to Santiago runs on for weeks toward a cathedral that claims the bones of an apostle[1]. Confessors and inquisitors once sent people down that road, and down the roads to Rome and Canterbury, as penance for the graver crimes[2], the hardships of the road being the penance itself.

Cain’s sentence for murder was perpetual travel. He is told he will be a fugitive and a wanderer on the earth[3], and he goes out from the presence of the god and settles in the land of Nod, east of Eden[4], a name that means wandering. Scripture’s first wanderer goes out a convict, and he cuts the sentence short by founding a city and naming it for his son[5].

A breakdown now calls for two weeks in Bali and a divorce for a year abroad, and the Pilgrim’s Office at Santiago counted four hundred ninety-nine thousand arrivals in twenty twenty-four[6]. Recovery circles call the habit the geographical cure and use the phrase as a warning, since the trouble rides in the same suitcase.

A trip needs no wound to excuse it. The bed has heavy sheets, the bath comes hotter than your own boiler allows, and the bread reaches the table before you ask, with a fish still spitting from the grill beside it. The bill is settled at the desk in money, the only price the trip asks, and you come home as you left, with grease from that fish still on your cuff.

Declaration: The god sentenced Cain to the road, and I buy my own ticket.

The Rite

Go today to a place you can reach within half an hour, the shore if one is near, otherwise a bathhouse, a good restaurant or a hillside, and give one hour there to pleasure alone. Pack for the body only, the good coat, the appetite.

Testament · Where would you go if the trip had to fix nothing at all?

Sources

[1] Camino de Santiago, tradition of the tomb of St James

[2] Catholic Encyclopedia (1911), Pilgrimages (Inquisition, Carcassonne)

[3] Gen 4:12

[4] Gen 4:16

[5] Gen 4:17

[6] Pilgrim’s Office, Santiago: 499,239 pilgrims in 2024


CCXLII Of Teachers

Reckoning

Day 242 of 365

Wait to be asked, then teach your best.

Linda MaestraFrancisco Goya · Los Caprichos, 1799

The Spirit sent Philip after a chariot on the desert road down to Gaza[1], and even so he opened with a question. The man in it was a eunuch, treasurer to the queen of the Ethiopians[2], reading Isaiah aloud on his way home from worship in Jerusalem. Philip ran up and asked whether he understood what he was reading. The eunuch said he could not unless someone guided him[3], and he asked Philip to come up and sit beside him. The passage was the student’s, and so was the question of whether the prophet spoke of himself or of someone else[4]. When they came to water, it was the student again who asked what prevented him from being baptized[5].

Acts sets down the order, a question from the teacher and then an invitation from the student, and Proverbs gives the teacher a reason to keep it, warning that whoever reproves a scoffer earns abuse and should save his correction for the wise[6], who will love him for it. The missions that carried Philip’s story to every continent kept the text and lost the order. Their lesson arrived as the pair at the door with literature, or the tract left on a restaurant table for whoever sat down next.

A skill learned over years is property, and the one who learned it decides where it goes. In the plate the old witch grips the broom and the young one clings to her neck, and what passes between them is the flight itself, given to a pupil who climbed on. Pressed on a stranger who never asked, the best trick you own is wasted on him and resented besides. Asked for, it passes to a successor you chose, and the craft outlives you on a broom you built.

Declaration: Philip waited for the invitation, and his heirs on my doorstep can wait for mine.

The Rite

Teach the trick you keep from rivals to one person who has asked you how you do it, and put the tool in their hands before you finish explaining. If nobody has asked, use the trick today on something of your own.

Testament · Who has asked to learn what you do best, and what did you give them?

Sources

[1] Acts 8:26, 29

[2] Acts 8:27–28

[3] Acts 8:30–31

[4] Acts 8:34

[5] Acts 8:36

[6] Prov 9:7–8


CCXLIII Of the Horsemen

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 243 of 365

Stop waiting up for the riders.

The Four HorsemenAlbrecht Dürer · The Apocalypse, 1498

One of the four riders carries a pair of scales in place of a weapon. In the woodcut he swings them empty over a crowd being ridden down. When that rider comes out, Revelation has a voice from among the living creatures call a price list after him, a measure of wheat for a penny[1] and three measures of barley for a penny, and order that the oil and the wine are not to be hurt[2].

A penny was a laborer’s wage for a day[3] in the parable of the vineyard, so the famine of the last days, in the book’s own words, puts a day’s bread at a day’s pay and posts a guard on the cellar. The end of the world, as Revelation prices it, falls on the poor man’s loaf and spares the rich man’s jar.

Later prophets dated that end and aimed it lower. Joseph Smith told church leaders in eighteen thirty-five that the coming of the Lord was within fifty-six years[4], and The Watchtower taught in nineteen sixty-eight that six thousand years of human history would end in nineteen seventy-five[5]. The children who heard such things learned to wake in a quiet house and listen for hooves, and, in the churches that preached a rapture, to go cold when a parent did not answer the phone.

The passage is a dream with a grocer’s voice in it, and the grocer protected his stock. Every date set for that end lapsed without a rider in sight, and the riders went on galloping only at night, through the heads of small sleepers who had no cellar to guard. A terror that did its work on children has collected all it will ever collect, and the child it kept awake, grown now, owes it no further night.

Declaration: An end of the world that spares the rich man’s wine is a rich man’s story, and I sleep through it.

The Rite · No faith

Print the passage of the four horsemen, black it out line by line with a marker, then fold the page into a paper hat and wear it while you clear up.

Testament · Which fear from your childhood religion still finds you at night?

Sources

[1] Rev 6:5–6

[2] Rev 6:6

[3] Matt 20:2

[4] History of the Church 2:182

[5] The Watchtower, 15 Aug 1968, Why Are You Looking Forward to 1975?

What remains when the load has been seen and a part of it set down is a life. The third book opens by unsaying the yes that was collected from you, then says yes to the life as it stands, the worst chapter included. The year closes with nothing owed in either direction, to the book or from it.

CCXLIV Of Announcements

Heresy

Day 244 of 365

Unsay the yes they collected from you.

The AnnunciationGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Gabriel speaks to the girl at Nazareth almost wholly in the future tense. Before she has said a word he has told her she will conceive, named the son and fixed the length of his reign at forever[1], so that when she asks how this can be, since she has known no man[2], the only matter left open is the mechanism, which he explains. Her answer comes last, and she calls herself the handmaid of the Lord[3]. A council later taught that the Father willed her acceptance to precede the incarnation[4], and in Luke’s order the acceptance comes after every term of the plan has been read out.

The sura named for Maryam keeps the scene and trims the courtesy. The spirit sent to her answers the same question by telling her the thing is easy for her Lord and already decreed[5].

Churches give the same annunciation to children, before witnesses. A patriarch of the Latter-day Saints lays hands on a teenager and pronounces a future that the church transcribes and files[6], and in charismatic churches a visiting preacher lays hands on a small child and speaks a prophetic word over a life barely begun. Both are said where contradiction would spoil the occasion, and each repetition banks a little assent while the child keeps quiet. The yes is collected years later, at an age when a no would cost the family’s love, and called a free choice, as Mary’s was.

A yes taken where no was never offered is a receipt the announcer wrote out to himself, and it binds nobody but its author. Whatever the house laid by for the announced life was laid by in your name, and what is held in your name goes to the life you chose, never to the man who made the speech.

Declaration: Mary called herself the handmaid of a finished plan, and I resign the post.

The Rite

Take out one thing kept for the future announced over you, the hope-chest linen, the mission savings, the books for the career your family chose, and use or spend it today on a pleasure of your own. Say over it Nobody asked me.

Testament · What is still laid by in your house for a future someone announced over you?

CCXLV Of the Stable

Indulgence

Day 245 of 365

Feed the animal first, and feed it well.

The Birth of JesusGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

The ox and the ass at the manger appear nowhere in the gospels. Luke supplies a feeding trough and a lodging with no room[1], and the animals were brought in later from a line of Isaiah, in which the ox knows its owner and the ass its master’s crib[2], and fixed in place by an apocryphal gospel that has them adore the child[3]. The story that grew up around the manger put the god who took flesh where flesh is fed, among creatures that live for their fodder and the warmth of one another’s bodies.

A second-century teacher, later condemned as a heretic, wrote that Jesus ate and drank but never passed what he had eaten[4], so complete was his self-command. The council held at Chalcedon in the year four hundred fifty-one settled that he was like other men in all things except sin[5]. A thousand years of fast days taught the faithful to treat the stomach as sin’s front door, though by the council’s own measure its ordinary business lies outside sin. Luke’s risen Jesus, among friends who take him for a ghost, shows them his hands and feet and then eats a piece of broiled fish in front of them[6].

Luke gives the shepherds one sign to know him by, a baby wrapped in cloth and lying in a manger[7], in a town whose name means house of bread[8]. The sign is the trough. Your body wants what the ox wants, and the hours you give to its wants without apology are the hours in which you are most alive, an animal at ease in its stable.

Declaration: The ox at the manger never kept a fast day, and I keep its calendar.

The Rite

Eat by hand, sitting on the floor, the food you have been calling too rich or too much, bought or cooked for nothing but wanting it. Then lie back where you ate for twenty minutes and answer no errand.

Testament · What does your body ask for most often that you still answer with suspicion?

CCXLVI Of the Star

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 246 of 365

Act on your own reading before anyone confirms it.

Wise Men Are Guided by a StarGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Deuteronomy bans the diviner and the observer of times[1], and Isaiah mocks the stargazers of Babylon who publish monthly forecasts and cannot save themselves from what is coming[2]. Matthew still needed the banned trade to announce his king. His word for the visitors named a Persian priestly caste[3] and had come to cover astrologers, and these practiced the art, saw a star at its rising[4] and traveled a long way on the reading.

When they reached Jerusalem and asked for the newborn king, Herod was troubled, and all Jerusalem with him. He called in the chief priests and scribes, the men whose office was the scroll, and they found the town in Micah[5], Bethlehem, some six miles down the road. They had the name of the town and a short road. They handed the address up to the king and, as far as Matthew records, went no further.

The magi had come as far as Jerusalem on a light seen in the east, with no scroll to confirm it. They took the scribes’ town from the king’s mouth[6] and walked it, and the star they had read went before them to the house where the child was[7]. Matthew records no priest or scribe making the walk. The practitioners of the art the law of Moses forbids made it. Knowledge kept by an office and never acted on by its holder goes wherever the strongest man in the room sends it, and the scroll’s answer reached Bethlehem a second time with the men Herod sent to kill every boy there two years old and under[8].

Declaration: I set out on my own reading, and the scribes can keep their scroll.

The Rite · Christian

Name one decision you have been holding for the bishop’s or pastor’s word. Go today to the place it concerns, on foot if you can, and take the first step there. Say I read it myself, and I went.

Testament · Which decision have you handed to someone who will never make the walk?

CCXLVII Of the Flight

Reckoning

Day 247 of 365

Ask who reigns there now before you go back.

Joseph Leads Mary and Jesus into EgyptGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Joseph left the same night, warned in a dream to take the child[1] and his mother into Egypt, and Matthew keeps the family there until Herod is dead. Then a second dream tells him that those who sought the child’s life are dead[2], and he sets out for home. On the road he hears that Archelaus is reigning in Judea in his father’s place, and Matthew says he was afraid to go there[3]. The fear came from the news, and the dream that sent him north[4] came only after it. The angel’s word had been true, and it had left out the son.

He turned aside into Galilee, the share of Archelaus’s brother Antipas, and settled at Nazareth[5]. Archelaus had some three thousand people cut down in the temple courts at the first Passover after his father’s death[6], and within ten years his own Jewish and Samaritan subjects carried their charges to Caesar and had him exiled to a town in Gaul[7].

In families and in churches the role passes down the same way. The father dies and the eldest brother takes up his voice, or the bishop retires and his successor reads the same letter in a softer tone, and whoever fled is called home for the funeral to find the house arranged as before. A death in the house you left is news about one man. The heir’s conduct is the news about the house, and an heir who speaks in the old voice has inherited the distance the old man earned along with his chair.

Declaration: I take no tyrant’s funeral for an amnesty, and I trust my fear over any angel bringing the news.

The Rite

Send whoever took the old chair in the house you left your terms in one message, the place you will meet, how long you will stay and the subject that ends it. When the day comes, keep to every term.

Testament · What would you need to see in the house you left before you crossed its threshold again?

CCXLVIII Of Prodigies

Heresy

Day 248 of 365

Ask aloud, in the room, what you do not know.

Jesus Questions the DoctorsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

After the infant in the temple and before the man at the river, Luke allows Jesus one scene, at twelve. His parents are a day out of Jerusalem on the road home from the Passover before they notice he is missing[1]. They search three days[2]. They find him in the temple sitting among the teachers, listening to them and asking them questions, while everyone who hears him marvels at his answers[3]. When his mother says that she and his father have been looking for him in anguish, he replies that they ought to have known he would be in his Father’s house[4].

Then he goes home with them, is obedient, and drops out of the record for about eighteen years[5]. A second-century gospel went back and filled the years before the visit with a boy who strikes a playmate dead for bumping him and blinds the neighbors who complain[6]. Sent to school, he lectures his teacher, telling Zacchaeus that a man ignorant of the nature of alpha has no business teaching anyone beta[7], and Zacchaeus gives up the boy in shame.

Luke’s boy listens to the teachers and asks them questions. The legend retells the temple scene and adds that he was shutting the mouths of the elders and teachers[8], and its schoolroom shows what that meant, a child who knows everything already and teaches his teachers by humiliating them. Piety preferred the prodigy who never needs to ask, and it goes on preferring him in every room where an expert speaks with more assurance than knowledge and is answered with nods. Luke closes the scene with his boy increasing in wisdom[9]. The legend’s boy could strike a teacher down[10] and had nowhere left to grow, since he had already announced that he knew the alpha.

Declaration: I left the god who was born finished, and I took the boy’s questions with me.

The Rite

Ask the most assured speaker within reach today, a colleague or a salesman, one question about a claim of theirs that you do not understand. If the answer slides away, ask again, and wait for the second answer.

Testament · Whose assurance have you been nodding at for years, and what would you ask it?

CCXLIX Of the Wilderness

Beauty

Day 249 of 365

Fire the committee that dresses you.

John the Baptist Preaches in the WildernessGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Mark describes what John the Baptist wore before quoting a word he said. A garment of camel hair with a leather belt at the loins[1] recalled the costume the second book of Kings gives to Elijah[2], the prophet promised to come back before the great and dreadful day[3], so anyone who knew the scriptures could read the man’s claim off his body. His food made a second claim. Locusts and wild honey[4] could be had for the gathering, and locusts are among the few insects the law of Moses permits[5], so he ate clean off the open ground. He had dressed and fed himself clean out of the economy of Jerusalem, and Matthew has him call the Pharisees and Sadducees who came down to the river a brood of vipers[6] to their faces.

The white shirt for the sacrament table and the hem measured against the knee were chosen by a committee to say something on your behalf, which was that you belonged and would embarrass nobody. Plenty of people leave and go on dressing for that committee for years, in a careful drab.

A wardrobe is a sentence written on the body each day, and John’s said that its owner had left the city and its tailors behind. What others wrote on you can go to the shears. The red coat or the silk shirt you were told was too loud is the garment that says something you wrote yourself, and a room that looks twice is reading it. John wore camel hair to the Jordan, and the crowds went out to look.

Declaration: I wear red past the door of the church that taught me drab.

The Rite

Put on today the garment you wanted and someone you no longer answer to forbade, buying it if you must, and wear it out of the house. Cut up or sell what you wore to please them.

Testament · Which clothes in your closet were chosen by people you no longer answer to?

[1] Mark 1:6

[2] 2 Kgs 1:8

CCL Of Baptism

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 250 of 365

Settle your worth before you start the work.

The Baptism of JesusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jesus comes to the Jordan before he has worked a miracle or called a disciple. He stands in the river like everyone else in the queue, to be washed by a man whose baptism was for the forgiveness of sins[1]. Matthew already felt the difficulty and has John protest[2] that he ought to be baptized by Jesus instead. Then the dove comes down, and the voice, which in Mark and Luke speaks to the son[3] and in Matthew announces him to the bystanders[4], calls him beloved and says the father is well pleased with him.

The Nicene Creed confesses one baptism for the forgiveness of sins[5], so for everyone after him the water comes first with the debt, and approval, if it comes at all, waits at the end of a clean life. A child raised on that order learns to look for the sentence from the river in a father’s face, and to read its absence as the debt still owing.

Approval that waits on results has to be earned again with every result. A person trained to wait for it goes on performing in front of employers and lovers for decades, and the performance never closes, because the judge has gone home. The voice at the river spoke before the work, and what it voiced was a god’s pleasure in his own likeness, the self-regard the Church afterward taught everyone else to confess as pride. The sky said that sentence over one man only. Said over yourself before the work, it turns every review and every lover’s verdict into news about the work alone.

Declaration: I was well pleased with myself before I had done a thing, and I owe the river nothing.

The Rite · Christian

Most churches hold that nobody can baptize themselves. Do it anyway. Go under your own bath water once, or pour a basin over your head, in your own name, and say This is my beloved, in whom I am well pleased.

Testament · Whose approval are you still performing for, and what has it paid you?

Sources

[1] Mark 1:4

[2] Matt 3:14

[3] Mark 1:11; Luke 3:22

[4] Matt 3:17

[5] Niceno-Constantinopolitan Creed


CCLI Of the Kingdoms

Heresy

Day 251 of 365

Name your price in writing, today.

The Temptation of JesusGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

Luke has the devil show Jesus all the kingdoms of the world in a moment of time[1] and state his terms in one breath. Their power and glory have been handed over to him, he says, to give to whomever he likes[2], and all of it will belong to Jesus if he will worship[3]. It is the clearest offer in the gospels, the goods and the price named together by a seller who claims the title. Jesus refuses with a line from Deuteronomy[4] and never contests the title, and the gospel of John afterward calls the adversary the ruler of this world three times[5].

The Church preached the refusal and kept a price for itself. The gospels bless the poor and send the disciples out with neither gold nor silver in their purses[6], and the bishops of Gaul, meeting at Mâcon in five hundred eighty-five[7], demanded a tenth of every harvest and backed the demand with excommunication. The letter to Timothy had already told the rest to be content with food and raiment[8].

Those raised on that letter learn to treat asking as greed and to call the silence humility, and whoever sets their wage profits from it. The raise never requested and the invoice still sent at last year’s rate are prices someone else set while the worker kept quiet. Work has a figure that can be found out, from people who do it and from published pay data. At the table where your pay is set, the one party who has never named a figure is the one doing the work.

Declaration: The devil quoted his terms to the son of God’s face, and I quote mine to the payroll office.

The Rite

Look up what your work pays elsewhere, then send whoever sets your pay a message naming a higher figure, and add nothing. With no pay to ask for, price something you own above what you would have taken and offer it for sale.

Testament · When did you last ask to be paid more, and what has stopped you since?

[2] Luke 4:6

[3] Luke 4:7

[4] Luke 4:8; Deut 6:13

[5] John 12:31; 14:30; 16:11

[6] Matt 10:9; Luke 6:20

[7] Babbs, Law of the Tithe (1912), p. 140

[8] 1 Tim 6:8


CCLII Of the Good Wine

Indulgence

Day 252 of 365

Stop saving your best for the deserving.

The Wedding at CanaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Six stone jars stood in the house at Cana for the Jewish rites of purification, each holding two or three measures[1], some twenty to thirty gallons apiece. When the wine ran out at the wedding, Jesus told the servants to fill them with water, and they filled them to the brim. What they drew off was wine[2]. His first sign in John’s gospel[3] came to well over a hundred gallons, poured for the wedding guests.

The steward, who has not been told where it came from, calls the bridegroom over and marvels. Every host, he says, sets out the good wine first and the worse once the guests have drunk freely, and you have kept the good wine until now[4]. His verb for the guests is the ordinary Greek for getting drunk[5], and the custom he describes is to pour the worse for palates past telling it from the better.

The steward was stating the prudence of every careful house. The good bottle waits for a guest who will appreciate it and an occasion that deserves it, and many such bottles stand in a cupboard until the cork has failed. The sign broke that prudence at the hour it binds hardest. It drew the finest wine of the evening out of the jars of the purity rite, in a hundred gallons or more, and poured it for people who had earned nothing. A house that saves its best for the deserving keeps a rule its own god broke with his opening miracle, for a room that had already drunk the house dry.

Declaration: The god at Cana spent his best on a wedding that had run dry, and I will not hoard mine behind a rule he broke.

The Rite

Late in an ordinary evening, after the first glasses, open the best bottle you own and pour it for whoever is still at the table, yourself included. Say Kept until now, and poured for us.

Testament · What are you keeping back for a day that has never arrived?

Sources

[1] John 2:6

[2] John 2:7–9

[3] John 2:11

[4] John 2:9–10

[5] John 2:10 (methusthōsin)


CCLIII Of the Samaritan Woman

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 253 of 365

Tell your history with your eyes up.

Jesus and the Woman of SamariaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

At Jacob’s well, at about noon, Jesus asked a Samaritan woman to give him a drink, and she asked how a Jew could ask that of her. John adds in his own voice that Jews had no dealings with Samaritans[1], and the Mishnah, written down about a century after the gospel, counts the daughters of the Samaritans as women unclean from the cradle[2]. A few lines on he told her to fetch her husband, and when she said she had none, he counted five husbands and the sixth man who was none of them[3].

Preachers have made her a harlot for centuries, and the text gives her no such name. Under the law of Moses only a husband could write the bill of divorce[4], so each of the five marriages ended in a death or in a man’s decision. Jesus asked her for no sorrow and no vow. She turned the talk to where the god should be worshiped, and afterward she left her water jar at the well to tell the town she had met a man who told her everything she ever did[5].

You were taught to keep a count like hers hidden, or to tell it with your eyes down and a confession attached. Many Samaritans of that town believed, John says, because of what the woman said[6], so the first person in his gospel to bring a whole town out was a woman with six men behind her. The repentance preached over her since is the pulpit’s addition to a scene in which her unrepented word was enough to empty a town onto the road.

Declaration: My history is told standing, and nobody who taught me to kneel for it gets to hear it.

The Rite · No faith

Say your history aloud at your own table, in order and in plain words, the version you would never tell a parent or a pastor, and end with I repent of none of it.

Testament · For whose comfort do you still tell your history with the facts rearranged?

Sources

[1] John 4:9

[2] m. Niddah 4:1

[3] John 4:16–18

[4] Deut 24:1

[6] John 4:39


CCLIV Of Home Towns

Reckoning

Day 254 of 365

Take your work where nobody recites your family.

Jesus Preaches in the SynagogueGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Nazareth was proud of him for about a sentence. Luke has Jesus come back to the town where he was brought up and go into its synagogue on the sabbath, as his custom was[1], and the attendant hands him the scroll of Isaiah. He reads the passage about good news for the poor and release for captives, sits down and tells the room the scripture is fulfilled in their hearing[2]. They wonder at his gracious words, and then someone remembers that this is Joseph’s son[3].

He answers with the record. Elijah, in a famine, was sent to a widow in Sidon, and of all the lepers in Israel Elisha cleansed only a Syrian[4]. The room hears that the god’s favor went to foreigners, rises, drives him out of town and leads him to the brow of its hill to throw him off[5]. In Mark the neighbors recite the family to him, the carpenter, Mary’s son, the brother of James and Joses[6] and Judas and Simon, with sisters they did not trouble to name.

Mark writes that he could do no mighty work there beyond laying hands on a few of the sick[7], and marveled at their unbelief. A chapter earlier the same man had raised a dead girl in another town[8], and in Nazareth he was unable. He gives the reason himself, that a prophet has honor everywhere except in his own country, among his own kin and in his own house[9], and he went round the other villages teaching. Later in the chapter he tells the twelve to shake the dust off their feet[10] at any place that will not receive them, as a testimony against it. The dust is the town’s own, carried out on the soles, and the order is to leave it on the road.

Declaration: My home town keeps the child it remembers, and the adult works elsewhere.

The Rite

Leave the group chat, mailing list or prayer chain of the town or congregation that raised you. Then, at your own door, knock the dust from your shoes before you step inside and say I take nothing of yours with me.

Testament · What can you do now that the people who knew you as a child would refuse to believe?
