CCLV Of Exorcism

Heresy

Day 255 of 365

Weigh your friends by what they give back.

Jesus Heals a DemoniacGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A man had lived among the tombs of the Gerasenes, and no chain had held him[1]. Jesus let the spirits go out of him into a herd of about two thousand pigs[2], and the herd ran down the slope into the lake and drowned. The townspeople came out, found the man sitting clothed and sane, and were afraid, and the witnesses told them what had happened to him and to the swine[3]. Then they begged Jesus to leave their district[4].

Mark sets the two reports side by side, the man and the swine, and the town chose the swine. A madman in chains had cost the place nothing it could count, and his cure cost it a herd. The healed man asked to go with Jesus and was refused[5], and sent home to tell his own people what had been done for him, so the town kept the cure walking its streets and sent away the one who worked it.

Protect your peace, the slogan runs now, and cut out whoever brings bad energy, which files the friend who told you something unwelcome and true alongside the bores and the takers. The slogan counts what a person costs you in comfort and leaves out what they hand back, and the Gerasenes kept that ledger against a man who had just handed them back a neighbor in his right mind.

Weighed by what comes back instead, the friend who once spoiled an evening with the truth and spared you a bad marriage holds a claim on you above a year of easy company.

Declaration: My peace was never worth the friend it would have cost me.

The Rite

Write to the friend who told you the hardest true thing you ever heard, name exactly what it spared you, and send it today. If they are dead, read it aloud to a photograph of them and keep it with the photograph.

Testament · Who have you kept at a distance for telling you something true?

Sources

[1] Mark 5:3–4

[2] Mark 5:11–13

[3] Mark 5:14–16

[4] Mark 5:17

[5] Mark 5:18–19


CCLVI Of the Boat

Mastery

Day 256 of 365

Keep a boat between you and the crowd.

Jesus Preaches at the Sea of GalileeGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

Keep a small boat ready, Jesus told the disciples, so that the crowd would not crush him[1]. Mark gives the reason in the same breath, that people had come from as far off as Tyre and Sidon and the sick were pressing forward to touch him[2]. A chapter on, he gets into the boat and teaches the multitude on the shore from the water[3], sitting, with a strip of the lake between his body and their need. The same gospel has him rise long before daylight to get away to a deserted place[4], and when Simon and the others hunt him down to tell him everyone is looking for him, he answers by leaving for the next towns[5].

The pulpit preaches a savior who was always available. Mark records a procedure. If you were raised on the sermon, you learned that access is owed and that every claim on your time carries the force of the sick pressing to touch him.

A chapter before the boat sermon, Mark has him go up a mountain, call to him the ones he wanted and appoint twelve to be with him[6]. Then he went into a house, and the multitude gathered again so thickly that he and the twelve could not so much as eat, and his own family came out to seize him, saying he was out of his mind[7]. Access left open to whoever pressed cost him his supper and his family’s belief in his sanity, and the twelve he had chosen to be with him went without bread.

Declaration: I was preached a savior with no door, and I have since read about his boat.

The Rite

Set your phone so that after nine at night only the people you choose can ring through. Add them one at a time, saying each name aloud, then say The rest can wait until morning.

Testament · Who has the run of your time without having earned it, and who has earned more of it than they get?

CCLVII Of the Mount

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 257 of 365

When struck, ask for the charge.

The Sermon on the MountGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The sermon on the mountain tells whoever is struck on the right cheek to turn the other also[1]. Its preacher was struck more than once in the gospels, and only John gives his reply. Questioned by the high priest about his disciples and his teaching, Jesus said that he had spoken openly to the world and that the high priest should ask those who had heard him[2]. An officer standing by struck him with the palm of his hand[3] for answering so. Jesus told the man that if he had spoken wrongly he should bear witness to the wrong, and if well, why strike him[4]. He offered no second cheek. He asked for the charge.

Paul, brought before the council in Acts, had barely begun when the high priest Ananias ordered the men beside him to strike him on the mouth[5]. Paul answered that the god would strike him, the whitewashed wall[6], for sitting to judge by the law and ordering a blow against it. Told whom he had insulted, he apologized to the office, quoting the law against cursing a ruler of the people[7], and withdrew nothing about the blow.

The congregations that recited the sermon kept the meekness for the pews and left the protest to the men in the stained glass. Most blows now arrive as words, a sigh at the family table or a message calling you selfish, and the trained reflex is to absorb them or to apologize for something nobody named. Asked calmly what exactly was wrong in what you said or did, the speaker has to produce a charge, and the high priest’s officer produced none[8].

Declaration: My meekness was the striker’s best protection, and I have stopped providing it.

The Rite · Christian

Open your own Bible, or a cheap one, to the sermon’s command to turn the other cheek, lay it on the floor, and strike the page with a belt, then tear it out, saying Name the charge.

Testament · What accusation did you last swallow that would have collapsed if you had asked for its grounds?

CCLVIII Of the Sabbath

Heresy

Day 258 of 365

Take back one idle hour, on rules you wrote.

The Disciples Pluck Grain on the SabbathGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Two offenses against the sabbath fit into a handful of grain. Reaping and threshing both stand on the list of thirty-nine kinds of work the rabbis later wrote down[1], so when the disciples walked through a field, pulled off the ears and, in Luke’s telling, rubbed them in their hands[2], the Pharisees who saw it could name both. Jesus answered that the sabbath was made for people and people were never made for it[3]. A rabbi in the early commentary on Exodus says nearly the same, that the sabbath was handed over to Israel and Israel was never handed over to the sabbath[4].

Deuteronomy gives the commandment a reason Exodus lacks. You rest, and your servants and your ox and your ass rest, because you were once a slave in Egypt[5]. Pharaoh’s complaint against Moses in Exodus was that he made the people rest from their burdens[6], and the Hebrew verb is the one the sabbath is named for. The day off was a freedman’s possession. In Exodus the day is guarded by a death sentence[7], and Numbers has the whole congregation stone a man found gathering sticks[8] on it.

The stoning law moved the day from the freedman to whoever could punish its breach. The employer holds that power now, and the weekend he grants goes one day to the errands the week displaced and the next to dread of Monday. A rest granted on another’s terms is recalled on them, and the free afternoon ends with the first message from the office asking for a quick answer.

Declaration: My idle hour keeps one law, and its lawgiver is lying in bed.

The Rite

Make the next two hours a sabbath with one law, that nothing useful gets done, and fill them with a long meal, a book or a walk with nowhere to go. When the law stops pleasing you, break it and say I wrote it, and I repeal it.

Testament · What would your week look like with one day nobody else could claim?

[1] m. Shabbat 7:2

[2] Luke 6:1

[3] Mark 2:27

[4] Mekhilta, Shabbata 1 (Exod 31:14)

[5] Deut 5:14–15

[6] Exod 5:5

[7] Exod 31:14–15

[8] Num 15:32–36


CCLIX Of Ointment

Indulgence

Day 259 of 365

Wear a scent for nobody but yourself.

A Sinful Woman RepentsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

She let her hair down in a Pharisee’s dining room. Luke calls her a woman of the city who was a sinner and gives her no name, and his account of what she did is physical. She came in with an alabaster jar of ointment while the guests reclined at table, stood behind the guest of honor at his feet, wet them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them over and over and rubbed the ointment into them. The host said to himself that a real prophet would know what manner of woman was touching him[1]. Jesus told Simon that his house had offered no water for the feet, no kiss and no oil, and that she had supplied all of it[2].

The Church could not leave her there. Preaching in Rome in five hundred ninety-one, Pope Gregory made her one woman with Mary Magdalene and Mary of Bethany, and explained that the ointment she had once spent on sin she now offered to God[3]. The Golden Legend later sent her thirty years into a desert[4], and the engraving above kneels her among bare rocks beside a skull, the scent long gone. Rome dropped the identification from its calendar[5] in nineteen sixty-nine.

The law of Exodus reserved one blend of myrrh and sweet spices for the tent, its furnishings and its priests, and forbade it on the flesh of anyone else[6] on pain of being cut off from the people. Gregory’s own sermon says the woman had used her ointment to perfume her flesh[7] in forbidden deeds, so the scent changed owners twice.

Declaration: The Church gave her ointment to God, and I keep mine for my own throat.

The Rite

Try scents on your own skin until one stops you, from the bottles you own or one you buy today because you want it. Put it on your wrists and neck, wear it wherever you go next, and say Mine, and unrepented.

Testament · Which pleasure of the senses do you still deny yourself because someone once called it vanity?

[1] Luke 7:39

[2] Luke 7:44–46

[3] Gregory the Great, Hom. in Evang. 33

[4] Jacobus de Voragine, Golden Legend, life of Mary Magdalene

[5] Calendarium Romanum (1969), 22 July

[6] Exod 30:26–33

[7] Gregory the Great, Hom. in Evang. 33


CCLX Of Healing

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 260 of 365

Take the treatment your old faith taught you to delay.

Jesus Heals a CrippleGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

On the sabbath a man with a withered hand stood in the synagogue, and the devout watched to see whether Jesus would cure him, so that they could accuse him[1]. Jesus called the man into the middle of the room and asked them whether the law allowed one to do good on the sabbath or to do harm, to save a life or to kill, and they kept silent. Mark says he looked round at them with anger[2]. Then he told the man to stretch out his hand, and it was restored, and the Pharisees went out to plot with Herod’s partisans how to destroy him.

Their law, as the rabbis later wrote it down, lets a threat to life override the sabbath[3] and asks a sufferer in no danger to wait a day[4]. Mark records a spoken command and no touch, so the objection fell on the cure itself, from the wrong healer on the wrong day.

You were taught which hands could mend you and on which days, and some churches still set elders or a prayer where the medicine goes. The Watch Tower Society forbade blood transfusion in nineteen forty-five[5], and Witnesses have died refusing one. Christian Science teaches its members to treat illness by prayer, and children have died of diabetes and of a bowel obstruction[6] in households that trusted it. The pain carried while the elders were sent for bought nothing, and the clinic’s hands answer to results, the test the healer himself chose when he worked the cure in front of the men waiting to accuse him.

Declaration: A faith that would rather bury me than see me mended irregularly has chosen its corpses, and I decline to be one.

The Rite · No faith

Take the medicine or dress the sore you have put off out of fear or thrift. Hold out your hand to do it, as the man in the synagogue was told to, and say I stretch it out myself, with no god to command it.

Testament · What did the waiting cost you, counted in pain or in years?

Sources

[1] Mark 3:2

[2] Mark 3:5

[3] m. Yoma 8:6

[4] m. Shabbat 14:3–4

[5] Watchtower, 1 Jul 1945, pp. 198–201

[6] Com. v. Twitchell (Mass. 1993); Lundman v. McKown (Minn. App. 1995)


CCLXI Of the Storm

Reckoning

Day 261 of 365

Sleep through the storms that are not yours.

The Storm at SeaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Mark sets it at evening on the lake, in a great gale, with the waves breaking into the boat until it was filling[1]. Several of the disciples were men who had fished that water for a living[2]. The carpenter was in the stern, asleep on a cushion[3]. They woke him with an accusation, that he did not care whether they drowned. He calmed the water and asked why they were so afraid[4], and Mark says that afterward they feared exceedingly[5]. The fear had moved from the storm to the man who slept through it.

The Hebrew Bible has an older sleeper, and that storm was his. Jonah lay asleep in the hold[6] while the sailors threw the cargo overboard and cried each to his own god, and when they cast lots to learn whose fault the weather was, the lot fell on him[7]. The sea went quiet only once he was over the side[8]. A panicking household casts no lots. Somebody’s crisis arrives, the overdraft or the divorce, everyone is expected to bail and shout, and whoever goes on resting is treated as a traitor to the emergency, though an honest lot would fall on the one whose weather it is.

Some storms are yours, a child’s or a failing body’s above all, and you should be awake for those. The rest belong to people who could bail or let the thing sink, and the cost of their weather is theirs to carry. The brother whose money is always an emergency and the friend whose every romance ends in a late-night call learn from one flat refusal that this boat has a sleeper in it, and they go looking for a more frightened passenger.

Declaration: I sleep in the stern, and whoever wants company in the fear can wake someone else.

The Rite

Hand one crisis back, flatly and once, to a capable adult who keeps bringing you the same debt or romance, with no offer to help later. Then spend the hour it would have eaten on a pleasure of your own.

Testament · Whose emergencies have you been losing sleep over, and which of them were ever yours to solve?

Sources

[1] Mark 4:35–37

[2] Mark 1:16–20

[3] Mark 4:38

[4] Mark 4:39–40

[5] Mark 4:41

[6] Jonah 1:5

[7] Jonah 1:7

[8] Jonah 1:12–15


CCLXII Of Miracles

Heresy

Day 262 of 365

Pay for no cure whose only evidence is a story.

Jesus Raises the Daughter of JairusGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

A woman had bled for twelve years, and Mark says she had suffered many things of many physicians, spent all she had and grown worse[1]. Luke, whom tradition makes a doctor[2], retells the story and drops the part about her growing worse[3]. She touched a passing robe and was healed. The same chapter goes on to a house where a girl of twelve has died, and to the mourners Jesus says she is only asleep. They laughed at him[4]. He put them out, took her hand and raised her, and ordered her parents to tell nobody[5].

Mark’s woman came to the robe because she had heard of him[6], and her cure reached the page as a story no physician examined. Lourdes keeps a medical bureau to examine its own wonders, and since 1883 the bureau has recorded more than seven thousand dossiers[7] of reported cures. The Church has so far recognized seventy-two of them as miracles[8]. The rest remain reported cures, and the Church has certified none of them.

The supplement seller keeps no bureau. His juice fast for cancer and his tea that flushes out poisons nobody can name arrive with a testimonial from a woman who was given months and is still dancing, a story with no chart, no doctor and no date behind it. A remedy whose whole case is a stranger’s story has no dossier to show, and its buyer repeats the first half of the woman’s story in Mark, the spending of everything she had, for a second half nobody has examined.

Declaration: I take my illnesses to people who keep records, and the people who keep testimonials get my laughter and nothing else.

The Rite

Take one remedy from your cupboard that came to you with a testimonial, a tincture, a cleansing powder, a crystal, and drop it in the trash. Say Show me the record or keep it. and laugh as it falls.

Testament · Which remedy in your house came to you on a stranger’s word alone?

Sources

[1] Mark 5:25–26

[2] Col 4:14

[3] Luke 8:43

[4] Mark 5:38–40

[5] Mark 5:41–43

[6] Mark 5:27

[7] Sanctuary of Lourdes, The miracles of Lourdes

[8] Sanctuary of Lourdes, 72nd recognized cure, Apr 2025


CCLXIII Of Mary and Martha

Beauty

Day 263 of 365

Sit down before the work is finished.

Jesus at the House of Martha and MaryGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Martha has taken Jesus into her house and is pulled about with all the serving, while her sister Mary sits at his feet and listens[1], a disciple’s posture before a rabbi[2] and an unusual place for a woman. Martha asks him to tell Mary to help. He answers that Martha is anxious and troubled about many things, that one thing is needful, and that Mary has chosen the good part, which will not be taken from her[3].

The commentators read that last clause as a promise about death. The active life ends with this world, Gregory the Great preached[4], and the contemplative begins here to be perfected in heaven, and Aquinas set the sentence in his Summa as settled doctrine. Martha’s part, on that reading, is buried with her, and Mary’s goes on. The same Church made Martha the patron of cooks and housekeepers and reserved the sitting for the cloister[5], where it was spent on God.

By the Church’s own reckoning, then, every hour of serving is an hour that dies when you do, and the only part that keeps is the hour taken sitting down with the work undone. The gospel’s ruling on that house sides with the sister who left the dishes. Strike out the guest she sat for and the hour is yours, the record played through, the book read in the good chair while the sink stays full. Washed at midnight, the pans come out of the sink as clean as they would have at seven, and the evening between went to the music and the chair.

Declaration: The god let Martha cook his dinner while he praised her sister, and I wait on no guest who eats like that.

The Rite

Put on the best thing you own, sit down in the room with the unwashed pans, and play one record you love at full volume, from beginning to end. Leave every pan where it is until the last note.

Testament · Who taught you that rest is earned by finishing, and what did they ever finish?

Sources

[1] Luke 10:39

[2] Acts 22:3

[3] Luke 10:40–42

[4] Gregory, Hom. in Ezech.; Aquinas, ST II-II, q. 181, a. 4

[5] Aquinas, ST II-II, q. 182, a. 1


CCLXIV Of Salome

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 264 of 365

Break the promise that only the onlookers still enforce.

Herod’s Daughter Receives the Head of John the BaptistGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Herod had John the Baptist in prison for denouncing his marriage to his brother’s wife[1], and Mark says the king feared him, knew him for a just and holy man and liked to listen to him[2]. At the birthday feast[3] the daughter of Herodias danced for the guests, and Herod, delighted, swore to give her whatever she asked, up to half his kingdom[4]. She went out to ask her mother what to ask for and came back wanting the Baptist’s head on a platter, at once[5].

The head was her mother’s idea. Herodias had wanted John dead since he condemned her marriage and could not reach him[6], and she collected through her daughter on an oath made to someone else, at a feast, where refusing would cost the king his face. The girl, whom tradition calls Salome[7], carried the platter to her mother.

Mark gives Herod’s reasons in one verse. The king was exceedingly sorry, and for the oath’s sake and for the sake of those who sat at table with him[8] he sent the executioner. An oath sworn in a good mood to a dancing girl had no court to collect it but the king’s own, and the only others Mark puts in the room are the guests, who would think less of a king who took back his word. A promise kept against its maker’s will is kept for an audience, and the audience risks nothing by it. Herod kept his word before the men at his table, and their good opinion cost him the one man he liked to hear, carried in on a platter.

Declaration: My word belongs to me, and I take it back from anyone who holds me to it.

The Rite · No faith

Write on a card the promise you keep only because your family or your friends would see you break it. Lay it on a platter at your table, carve it into strips as a roast is carved, eat your meal beside it and say I owe this nothing.

Testament · Which promise do you keep now only because someone would see you break it?

[2] Mark 6:20

[7] Josephus, Ant. 18.136

[8] Mark 6:26


CCLXV Of Multitudes

Heresy

Day 265 of 365

Sound your own trumpet, and choose who hears it.

Jesus Preaches to the MultitudeGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Sound no trumpet when you give alms[1], Jesus tells the crowds and his disciples on the hillside. Give so secretly that your left hand does not know what your right is doing[2], since those who give for show have already had their reward[3]. The father who sees in secret will repay the hidden giver, and in the Greek text the King James translators worked from, he repays openly[4].

The temple where he taught had thirteen offering chests shaped like rams’ horns[5], and Mark has Jesus sit opposite the treasury, watch the crowd drop its money in[6], and call his disciples over to rank the gifts by what each giver had left[7]. The preacher of secret giving sat and graded the gifts of strangers before his disciples.

On the King James text the sermon concedes that the givers with trumpets collected their applause in full, and it promises the secret giver a better audience later, in the open. The trumpet was forbidden so that one spectator could hold the whole gallery, a father who sees in secret and settles in public.

Being looked at is a pleasure. The wish to be admired for a thing done well is an appetite with every right to be fed. A carpenter who builds a good table wants one particular person to run a hand along it, and the hand he chose is the whole reward he was after. A giver who hides the gift for the father’s sake is still giving for an audience, one he has never seen, and he dies without once watching a face change at what he gave.

Declaration: I want to be admired, and I take my applause from people who were in the room.

The Rite

Ring a bell, or tap a spoon against a glass, and tell one person whose admiration you want the best thing you have done lately, in person and in full. Take the applause.

Testament · Whose admiration have you gone without because you never let them see the work?

Sources

[1] Matt 6:2

[2] Matt 6:3

[3] Matt 6:2

[4] Matt 6:4 (KJV)

[5] m. Shekalim 6:1, 6:5

[6] Mark 12:41

[7] Mark 12:43–44


CCLXVI Of Loaves

Indulgence

Day 266 of 365

Feed people without doing the sums.

Jesus Feeds the MultitudesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Five loaves and two fish fed five thousand men, Matthew adding that the women and children went uncounted[1], and when everyone had eaten as much as they wanted the disciples took up twelve baskets of fragments[2]. All four gospels tell it, the only miracle of the ministry they share[3]. John says the loaves were barley, the cheap bread, and came from a boy in the crowd[4], and Mark has the people sit down on the green grass in companies of hundreds and fifties[5].

The disciples had done the sums first. Send them away to buy bread in the villages, they said, and Philip reckons in John that two hundred denarii of bread[6], most of a year’s wages for a laborer, would not give each of them a little. The answer was a meal nobody priced, eaten until the eaters stopped. John has the fragments gathered so that nothing be lost[7], and the gathering came after the eating, from a surplus nobody had been told to finish.

The next day the crowd crossed the lake to find him, and John has him tell them they had sought him because they ate of the loaves and were filled[8], and bid them stop laboring for food that perishes. The rebuke fell on their reason for following, and the meal itself had been his doing, eaten as much as they would[9] at his invitation, on grass he told them to sit on. A host who cooks to the penny is doing the disciples’ sums in front of the loaves, and his guests leave with exactly the little Philip’s sum allowed.

Declaration: I feed people without counting, because the surplus is the only part of the miracle I can verify.

The Rite

Cook a pot of your favorite food without measuring it and lay a table for people you like. Eat until you stop, and send what is left home with the guests, or keep it for tomorrow if you eat alone.

Testament · What has stopped you from inviting the person you would most like to feed?

CCLXVII Of Doubt

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 267 of 365

Put one article of your old faith to the test today.

Jesus Walks on the SeaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Only Matthew lets Peter out of the boat[1]. The disciples are rowing against a head wind in the fourth watch of the night when they see a figure walking on the sea, and Peter says that if it is the Lord he should bid Peter come to him on the water. The figure says come. Peter climbs over the side and walks, then sees the wind, is afraid, begins to sink and shouts to be saved. A hand catches him, and with it comes a question, why he doubted[2].

Peter’s request was an experiment, a condition stated with the one way to check it, and the experiment returned a result. The promise held while the walker saw nothing to fear and failed when he saw the wind, and the failure was entered against Peter. Little faith, the verdict says, and the water and the promise are acquitted. Deuteronomy had already forbidden putting the god to the test[3], and the Catholic Catechism still counts voluntary doubt among the sins against the first commandment[4].

Scripture wrote the verdict into a rule. Let a man ask in faith, nothing wavering, says the letter of James[5], and let the waverer not think he will receive anything, and Matthew says that in his own country he did not many mighty works because of their unbelief[6]. A promise built that way is safe from its own failures, since each one is booked to the believer who tested it. The men who stayed in the boat worshiped him and drew no rebuke that night[7], having risked nothing that could be checked. Of the men in that boat, Peter alone learned what the promise would bear, and he learned it sinking.

Declaration: Doubt is the one prayer that ever got an answer in my house.

The Rite · Christian

Read aloud the promise that faith can move a mountain, tell your heaviest piece of furniture to move with all the belief you can raise, wait one full minute, and write the result in ink across that page of your Bible.

Testament · Which failure of a promise were you taught to blame on yourself?

Sources

[1] Matt 14:28–29

[2] Matt 14:30–31

[3] Deut 6:16; Matt 4:5–7

[4] CCC 2088

[5] Jas 1:6–7

[6] Matt 13:58

[7] Matt 14:32–33


CCLXVIII Of the Sick

Reckoning

Day 268 of 365

Name the ones who carried you.

Jesus Heals the SickGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Peter’s mother-in-law lies in Simon’s house in Capernaum with a fever until Jesus takes her hand and raises her up, the fever leaves her, and then she gets up at once and waits on them[1]. By evening of the same day, when the sun has set, the whole town is at the door with its sick[2]. Mark says they were brought, and never says by whom. In the next chapter, back in Capernaum, four such bearers carry a paralyzed man lying on a mat, cannot get near him for the press, uncover the roof above the healer[3], break it up and let the mat down in front of him.

The four are never named, and neither is the man they carry. Mark says only that the healer saw their faith[4], which credits the hole in the roof to a virtue and the cure to himself. Jesus tells the man, Son, thy sins be forgiven thee, and orders him to arise and take up his bed, and he goes out in front of them all with the bed under his arm[5]. The record holds no line in which he thanks the men who dug, and none in which anyone else does.

Mark ends the scene with the crowd amazed and glorifying God[6], saying We never saw it on this fashion, and nothing in that glory reaches the four on the roof. Whoever lifted you in your own illness did work that a god gets credit for, and the credit belongs on the name of the one whose arms shook.

Declaration: I thank the hands that carried me, and I send the god nothing for the roof they dug.

The Rite

Write on a card the names of everyone who carried you through an illness and pin it where a holy picture hung or would hang. Read the names aloud and say These did the lifting.

Testament · Who got you through an illness, and where have you written their name?

[2] Mark 1:32–33

CCLXIX Of Transfiguration

Heresy

Day 269 of 365

Measure a year against nothing but itself.

The TransfigurationGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

No launderer on earth could bleach cloth so white[1], Mark says of the clothes Jesus wore on the mountain. Moses and Elijah appear and talk with him, and Peter, who Mark admits did not know what to say because the three disciples were terrified[2], offers to build three tents, one for each shining figure. A cloud covers them, a voice speaks out of it, and when they look round there is nobody with them but Jesus[3]. Then they come down the mountain, under orders to tell no one[4].

Peter’s tents were the one proposal in the scene, and the cloud answered it by taking away two of the three tenants. The Church built them anyway. Mark never names the mountain, tradition put it on Tabor, and the basilica finished on the summit in 1924[5] keeps a chapel for Moses in one tower and a chapel for Elijah in the other, over the ruins of a Crusader church whose three grottoes pilgrims took for the three huts. A vision the text dissolved in a sentence has stood in stone since the Byzantine centuries.

A wedding night or a winning year comes with Peter’s temptation in it, to build a shelter on the spot and live there. The man who frames his best year on the wall and retells it at every dinner has pitched the tents and moved in, and everything he does afterward is measured against a summit he can no longer stand on. The disciples did the other thing. They looked round and saw only a man. Whoever enshrines a summit spends the rest of his years as its pilgrim, and the three who built nothing walked down into the crowd[6].

Declaration: I build no shrine to my own past, and I kneel at none built to anyone else’s.

The Rite

Take down the keepsake you have kept on display longest from the time you call your best, a photograph, a trophy, a certificate, and put it in a drawer. Set something from this week in its place and say I came down the mountain.

Testament · Which year of your life have you framed so that every later one loses to it?

Sources

[1] Mark 9:3

[2] Mark 9:5–6

[3] Mark 9:7–8

[4] Mark 9:9

[5] Church of the Transfiguration, Mount Tabor (Barluzzi, 1924)

[6] Mark 9:14


CCLXX Of Seizures

Mastery

Day 270 of 365

Know what the exorcists did not, and command the room.

Jesus Heals the Epileptic DemoniacGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jesus’s disciples failed to cure a boy whose father had brought him to them. Moonstruck is Matthew’s word for him[1], and Mark describes the fits well enough for any neurologist to name them, the boy thrown down, foaming, grinding his teeth and going rigid. The father is told that everything is possible for one who believes, and cries that he believes and begs for help with his unbelief[2]. Afterward the disciples ask privately why they could not do it, and are told this kind goes out only by prayer, to which later manuscripts add fasting, a word the oldest copies lack[3].

Nearly five centuries before the gospels, a Greek medical treatise argued that the sacred disease was no more sacred than any other and had a natural cause like the rest[4]. Many churches kept the demon for centuries after. In nineteen seventy-five a young German woman with a diagnosis of epilepsy was given the full rite of exorcism on a bishop’s word, and she went on kneeling and fasting through it, the fasting a later scribe had written into Mark. She died the next year, at twenty-three, of starvation and dehydration, and in nineteen seventy-eight her parents and the two priests were convicted of negligent homicide[5].

A seizure is a body doing what bodies do, and the answer to it is a clock and a pair of trained hands, a skill learned in ten minutes. The trained bystander times it[6], clears the space, cushions the head, holds nobody down, puts nothing in the mouth, turns the person onto one side once the jerking stops and stays beside them, and calls for emergency help past five minutes or if they do not wake. The two priests knew their rite to the word, and they read it over her some sixty times while she starved.

Declaration: When someone seizes on my floor, I reach for the clock, and every prayer book in the house stays shut.

The Rite

Read the Epilepsy Foundation’s guide to seizure first aid, then give every order aloud, from the clock to the cushion to the turn onto the side, to an adult who agrees to lie on the floor, or to a cushion if you are alone.

Testament · Whom would you most want beside you on a floor, with trained hands?

Sources

[1] Matt 17:15

[2] Mark 9:24

[3] Mark 9:29 (absent in Sinaiticus and Vaticanus)

[4] Hippocrates, On the Sacred Disease 1

[5] LG Aschaffenburg, Apr 1978

[6] CDC, First Aid for Seizures


CCLXXI Of the Adulteress

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 271 of 365

Carry no blame alone for what two people did.

Jesus and the Woman Taken in AdulteryGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The scribes and Pharisees bring a woman they say was caught in the very act of adultery, stand her in the middle, and remind Jesus that Moses commanded such women to be stoned[1]. He bends down and writes on the ground with his finger, and the standard text never says what he wrote. The story is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts of John[2], turns up in later copies at different places in that gospel and, in one family of manuscripts, in Luke[3], and many modern Bibles print it in brackets with a note.

The law of Moses, in Leviticus and again in Deuteronomy, sentences both parties to death[4]. A woman caught in the act was caught with somebody, and the man is nowhere in the scene, released or never fetched, and nobody in the crowd remarks on it. The Torah’s ordeal for a wife only suspected, bitter water mixed with dust from the tabernacle floor, had no counterpart for a suspected husband[5]. Then the preacher tells the crowd that whoever is without sin should throw the first stone[6], and they drift away one by one, beginning with the eldest.

He tells the woman that he does not condemn her either. Go, he says, and sin no more[7]. A law enforced only on the woman is a law about women, and a schoolyard has a word for the girl in such a story and a medal for the boy. The pardon she carried home was the accusation in a gentler hand, spoken to her alone, for an act that took two.

Declaration: What I do in bed with a willing adult is nobody’s to forgive.

The Rite · Christian

Cut the story of the woman taken in adultery out of a Bible, your own or a cheap one, a passage its oldest manuscripts lack. Pin it to your wall with the last line, about sinning no more, struck through in red.

Testament · Who walked away clean from something you were made to answer for?

[1] John 8:3–5

[2] John 7:53–8:11 (absent in P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus)

[3] f13, after Luke 21:38

[5] Num 5:11–31

CCLXXII Of the Samaritan

Heresy

Day 272 of 365

Withdraw your kindness from everyone who walked past you.

The Parable of the Good SamaritanGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A lawyer who could recite the command to love your neighbor as yourself[1] asked Jesus who his neighbor was, and got a story about the road down to Jericho. A man going down it is stripped by robbers and left half dead[2]. A priest sees him and passes on the other side, and a Levite does the same[3]. A Samaritan, from a despised people, binds his wounds with oil and wine, carries him on his own animal to an inn, and leaves two silver coins and an open account[4] with the innkeeper.

Jesus asks which of the three proved a neighbor to the man the robbers left, and the lawyer answers, the one who showed mercy[5]. The neighbor is defined from the ditch, by what was done for the man lying there, and the lawyer’s own answer names the man who acted. The priest and the Levite leave the story owed nothing, and the wounded man is never asked to love them. The lawyer is sent to do likewise[6], to be the one who stops.

Four chapters earlier Jesus scorns kindness paid back to the kind, since sinners do as much[7], and orders it lent to enemies, on the pattern of a god kind to the unthankful and the evil[8]. Piety keeps that chapter and applies it to the priest and the Levite. So the cards keep going out each birthday to the church friends who went quiet the year you left, and the phone is answered every time for the relative who never came to the hospital. Kindness is paid in hours and money. Both run out, and each hour spent on the passers-by is taken from the ones who stopped, the landlord and the neighbor who watched your children.

Declaration: The priest can keep the far side of the road, and my hours go to the man who bound my wounds.

The Rite

Take the next card, call or favor you would send by reflex to someone who saw you down and kept going, and leave it unsent. Say I have no hours for this.

Testament · Who stopped for you when you were down, and what have they had from you since?

Sources

[1] Luke 10:25–27; Lev 19:18

[2] Luke 10:30

[3] Luke 10:31–32

[4] Luke 10:33–35

CCLXXIII Of the Inn

Indulgence

Day 273 of 365

Refuse yourself nothing you would gladly buy for a guest.

The Good Samaritan Arrives at the InnGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jesus sends Peter and John to prepare the Passover. He tells them to follow a man carrying a water jar, enter the house he enters and ask the goodman of the house where the guest room is[1], and they are shown a large upper room, furnished[2], where he eats his last Passover reclining with the apostles[3]. Luke’s word for that guest room[4], kataluma, is the word he uses at the birth, on a reading some scholars hold, for the place with no room, though the sense of the word there is disputed between a guest room and a lodging. The inn where the Samaritan, who has bound the stranger’s wounds and set him on his own beast, on the morrow, gives two denarii to the host[5] and promises to repay whatever more is spent has another word, pandocheion, for a house that takes in anyone who pays.

The gospel that opens with no room for him nears its end with a room furnished for him, and the man who said he had nowhere to lay his head[6] sent Peter and John ahead to claim it. He had told his followers to sell what they had and give alms[7]. When the hour came he sat down in the furnished room and Luke records no word about alms.

Those raised on holy poverty keep the manger and never reach the upper room. They pay a guest’s bill without blinking and haggle over their own, and keep the narrow bed for years. None of the four gospels records a complaint about the furniture.

Declaration: I take the furnished upper room and leave the stable to the hymns.

The Rite

Check the price once, then book the best room, table or spa hour within your means, and use everything on offer, the bath, the robe, the meal, without looking at a price again.

Testament · Which discomfort have you kept so long that you take it for character?

Sources

[1] Luke 22:10–11

[2] Luke 22:12

[3] Luke 22:14

[4] Luke 2:7; Luke 22:11

[5] Luke 10:35

[6] Luke 9:58

[7] Luke 12:33


CCLXXIV Of Little Children

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 274 of 365

Take back one pleasure your childhood faith kept from you.

Jesus Blesses the Little ChildrenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A bedtime prayer is taught before a child can read. Deuteronomy orders the commandments taught diligently to your children and talked of when you lie down and when you rise[1], and Proverbs promises that a child trained up in the way it should go will not depart from it when old[2]. The promise depends on the age of the pupil. What reaches a child before it can weigh anything stays in the old man.

In Mark, when people bring their small children for Jesus to touch and the disciples rebuke those who bring them, he is indignant[3], announces that whoever does not receive the kingdom as a little child will never enter it[4], and takes the children in his arms and blesses them[5]. He names the quality only as receiving, the way a child takes what it is handed.

What these households kept from their children was small. Witness children sit out birthday parties and Christmas, and evangelical parents in the years of the wizard novels fought to pull the books from school libraries as sorcery, the series among the most challenged in American school libraries in the late 1990s and 2000s. A child hands back the slice of cake at seven, for the god.

Whoever was raised inside a faith was that child first, and the wanting it was trained to distrust was the soundest instrument it had. The rules that reached it at four were handed down, and the child who once handed back the cake can order dessert first without asking anyone’s leave.

Declaration: I give a hearing to every rule I was handed as a child, and the ones that cannot speak for themselves I break at the next meal.

The Rite · Christian

Take up one pleasure your church kept from you as a child, a wizard novel, a pack of cards, a dance, and enjoy it in full over a long, rich lunch. If it was wizards, read the first chapter aloud, every spell included.

Testament · Which of the things you were taught as a child still has a say in your day?

Sources

[1] Deut 6:7

[2] Prov 22:6

[3] Mark 10:13–14

[4] Mark 10:15

[5] Mark 10:16


CCLXXV Of the Prodigal

Reckoning

Day 275 of 365

Walk back in without the speech.

The Prodigal Son Returns HomeGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Among the pigs, the younger son does his sums. He had taken his share of the estate while his father lived and spent it all in a far country[1], and when famine came he hired himself out to feed swine[2], work no son of Israel could take without disgrace, and would gladly have eaten the pods the pigs ate[3]. Then he came to himself. His father’s hired men had bread to spare, and he was starving[4].

Preachers have read this for centuries as repentance, and the text gives them a hungry man composing a speech. He will say he has sinned against heaven and is no longer worthy to be called a son, and ask to be taken on as a hired hand[5], the terms of a man negotiating his board. His father sees him a long way off and runs to kiss him before a word is out[6]. The son gets through the confession and the father says not a word to it. He turns to the servants and calls for the best robe, a ring and shoes[7], and in the King James text the son never reaches the hired-hand clause.

The unworthiness was the son’s own invention, drafted in the pigsty, and no one in the parable asks for it. Those who leave rehearse the same speech, the letter to the parents and the admission owed to the old congregation, and walk up the road ready to come back as hired help to their own families. A confession of unworthiness is a rank you assign yourself. A family less eager to run down the road will take the rank as offered and seat you with the hired men.

Declaration: I go home as a son or I stay gone, and no family of mine gets a hired hand out of me.

The Rite

Write out in full the apology you have rehearsed for the family or congregation you left, every line of it, then tear it up without sending it. Call or visit one of them and open with I came for dinner.

Testament · What apology have you rehearsed for a homecoming no one has asked you to earn?

Sources

[1] Luke 15:12–13

[2] Luke 15:15

[3] Luke 15:16

[4] Luke 15:17

[5] Luke 15:18–19

[6] Luke 15:20

[7] Luke 15:21–22


CCLXXVI Of the Father’s Arms

Heresy

Day 276 of 365

Reconcile only where amends were made.

The Prodigal Son in His Father’s ArmsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The elder son comes in from the field and hears music from the house[1]. A servant tells him the fatted calf has been killed for his brother. He will not go in. His father comes out to plead, and he answers that he has served for years without breaking a command and was never given so much as a young goat to eat with his friends[2], and now this son of his, who spent the estate on prostitutes[3], comes home to a calf.

The father had divided his living between his sons[4] before the younger left, so the younger had already taken his part, and when the father tells the elder that everything left is his already[5], he concedes whose calf was killed. The feast came out of the elder’s share. He was never consulted, and was then told it was fitting to make merry[6], by the man who had spent his property on the party. The parable ends with him outside and never says whether he went in.

Families stage the scene again at their long dinners, where a reconciliation is arranged by someone who did not pay for it. The peacemaker spends what belongs to the injured, their silence and their seat at the table, calls the bill joy, and tells whoever stays out in the field that life is short and blood is blood.

A welcome bought with your share was bought without your consent, and you can refuse to eat it. Amends name the harm to the one who suffered it and repair what can be repaired, and a hug at the door does neither. The elder stood in the field with a just complaint, and the parable’s keepers have spent nineteen centuries scolding the one man in it who knew what a calf cost.

Declaration: The fatted calf came out of my share, and I stay in the field until the man who spent it counts it back.

The Rite

Decline one family gathering arranged to smooth over a wrong that was never repaired, and spend that evening cooking the best meal you can afford for a friend who stood by you. Tell them it is for staying.

Testament · Whose peace in your family was paid for out of your share?

Sources

[1] Luke 15:25

[2] Luke 15:29

[3] Luke 15:30

[4] Luke 15:12

[5] Luke 15:31

[6] Luke 15:32


CCLXXVII Of the Great Gulf

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 277 of 365

Take your good things in your lifetime.

Lazarus outside the Rich Man’s HouseGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Luke gives the rich man no name, and gives the beggar at his gate the only name any invented character has[1] in the parables of Jesus. The rich man dressed in purple and fine linen[2] and feasted every day. Lazarus lay at his gate full of sores, wanting the crumbs from that table, and the dogs came and licked his sores.

When both men die and angels carry Lazarus to Abraham’s side, the rich man, in torment, begs that Lazarus dip the tip of a finger in water to cool his tongue[3]. One drop is the whole request. Abraham refuses with a ledger. You received your good things in your lifetime[4], he says, and Lazarus his evil things, and now he is comforted and you are in anguish. In the reason Abraham gives, the gate and the sores go unmentioned. The debt he names is the comfort itself.

The heaven that keeps this ledger also keeps a view of the flame, across a great gulf fixed so that nobody can cross in either direction[5]. The Quran stages the same exchange, the people of the fire begging water from the people of the garden and told that the god has forbidden it to unbelievers[6]. Thomas Aquinas, the Catholic Church’s chief theologian, taught that the blessed see the punishment of the damned so that their own happiness will be more delightful[7] to them.

A creditor who bills a man for his dinners and seats his saints where they can watch him burn has no standing to collect a coin. The parable sends its bill ahead to every comfortable reader, and each of them can eat the rich man’s dinner and leave the paper in the gulf.

Declaration: The one drop of water heaven refused a burning man is the full measure of its mercy, and I owe that mercy nothing for my bread.

The Rite · No faith

Print the parable of the rich man and Lazarus, hold the sheet under a running tap until it soaks through, and leave it on your doorstep. Then buy yourself one thing you have always thought too dear.

Testament · Which pleasure do you still take as though you will be billed for it later?

Sources

[1] Luke 16:20

[2] Luke 16:19

[3] Luke 16:24

[4] Luke 16:25

[5] Luke 16:26

[6] Quran 7:50

[7] Aquinas, ST Suppl. q.94 a.1


CCLXXVIII Of Breast-Beating

Beauty

Day 278 of 365

Walk into every room with your head up.

The Pharisee and the PublicanGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Rule of Benedict, written for monks in the sixth century, puts the highest step of humility in the body[1]. Wherever the monk is, at the Work of God, in the oratory, the garden, the field or on the road, sitting or standing, his head is to be bowed and his eyes fixed on the ground, and the Rule gives him the tax collector’s words as Benedict remembers them, that he is a sinner not worthy to lift his eyes to heaven. In Luke the man stood far off in the temple with his eyes down, beat his breast and asked for mercy[2].

Jesus said that man went home justified[3], and that the Pharisee, who stood apart and thanked his god for his fasts and his tithes[4], did not. The parable was aimed at the Pharisee’s contempt for the man beside him. The churches kept the tax collector’s posture and made it a drill. Catholics at Mass strike their breasts at the confession of fault[5], and the Orthodox repeat his plea on a knotted rope. Benedict adds that the monk should feel the guilt of his sins at every moment and think of himself as already standing at the Judgment[6], so the bow carries a verdict with it.

Benedict wanted the humility to show to everyone who saw the monk, and anyone who sees a straightened back reads it just as fast. The Pharisee’s fault, in Luke’s own framing, was trusting in himself and despising others, and he needed the tax collector beside him to measure himself by. A straight back needs nobody down there, and the room you walk into reads it before you speak.

Declaration: I meet every eye at its own level and leave the ground to the tax collector.

The Rite

Dress in the garment you stand tallest in and walk into the grandest room open to anyone today, a great library, a museum hall, a station concourse. Stand in its middle, shoulders back, and walk one slow circuit.

Testament · In front of whom did your body learn to make itself small?

Sources

[1] Rule of Benedict 7.62–66

[2] Luke 18:13

[3] Luke 18:14

[4] Luke 18:11–12

[5] Roman Missal, Order of Mass 4

[6] Rule of Benedict 7.62–66


CCLXXIX Of Lazarus

Heresy

Day 279 of 365

Set the date yourself and look for no sign.

The Raising of LazarusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

When word comes that Lazarus of Bethany is sick, Jesus stays where he is for two more days[1]. John says he loved the man and his sisters[2], and has him tell the disciples that the sickness is for the glory of God and that he is glad, for their sakes, to have been away, so that they may believe[3]. By the time he arrives Lazarus has lain four days in the tomb[4].

Martha meets him on the road and opens with one sentence, that if he had been there her brother would not have died[5]. Mary comes out of the house, falls at his feet and says the same words[6]. Two sisters, separately, bring the identical charge, and John records it twice and answers it with a miracle. At the open grave Jesus thanks his father aloud and explains that he says it for the crowd standing by[7], so that they may believe. Lazarus walks out and never speaks a word in the gospel, and the chief priests then plan to kill him as well[8], because on his account many were going over to Jesus.

Piety calls the two days God’s timing and teaches the person at the bedside to wait without complaint on a schedule kept elsewhere. The delay was for the disciples’ belief and the prayer at the grave for the crowd’s, and Lazarus and his sisters paid for both with four days. Martha and Mary kept no such patience, and Jesus, answering them with a resurrection, never once denies that his presence would have saved the man. To wait on the proper time is to wait on someone else’s display, and its cost falls on whoever lies in the rock.

Declaration: A god who let his friend lie four days in a tomb to impress a crowd keeps no calendar of mine.

The Rite

Take the thing you have put off until heaven or circumstance gives the word, and make it irreversible today, the deposit paid, the ticket bought, the letter sent. Before you do it, say aloud You were not here, so I went ahead.

Testament · What have you been told to wait for, and who gains from the wait?

Sources

[1] John 11:6

[2] John 11:5

[3] John 11:4, 15

[4] John 11:17

[5] John 11:21

[6] John 11:32

[7] John 11:41–42

[8] John 12:10–11


CCLXXX Of Palms

Indulgence

Day 280 of 365

Make a noise for your own arrival that the neighbors hear.

Jesus Enters into JerusalemGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The crowd that met Jesus outside Jerusalem had heard that he raised a dead man at Bethany[1]. They threw their garments in the road ahead of him and cut branches from the trees[2], which John says were palms[3], and the people in front and behind kept up one shout, Hosanna, blessed be the King that cometh in the name of the Lord. Hosanna comes from the psalm’s cry, save now, I beseech thee[4].

Luke adds the complaint. Some Pharisees from among the multitude asked him to rebuke his disciples, who were hailing a king with a loud voice[5] for all the mighty works they had seen, and he answered that if these kept quiet, the very stones would cry out[6]. He let the shouting stand, and it was praise for mighty works none of the shouters had done.

Whoever has arrived somewhere by their own effort has met the same Pharisees, at a finished degree or a first paycheck, and been asked to keep it down, by the pious with a warning about pride and by the envious with a nod and a story of their own. No one laid a cloak in the road for you, and the crowd at Jerusalem had less claim to the noise than you have, since the arrival they cheered was somebody else’s.

The hosanna begged for rescue. A person who got there on their own feet has nothing to beg for, so every note of the noise they make is celebration, and the neighbors who hear it are the nearest thing they will have to a crowd on the road.

Declaration: I cheer my own arrivals at full voice, and anyone who asks me to keep it down can answer to the stones.

The Rite

Strew petals, or leaves from a plant you own, from your door to your table for something you finished, began or entered. Open the best bottle you were saving, or serve the best thing you were saving, and cheer the thing aloud with the window open.

Testament · What would you strew in the road of your own uncelebrated arrival?

Sources

[1] John 12:17–18

[2] Matt 21:8

[3] John 12:13

[4] Ps 118:25

[5] Luke 19:37–38

[6] Luke 19:39–40


CCLXXXI Of the Whip

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 281 of 365

Pay no one for holiness again.

Buyers and Sellers Are Driven Out of the TempleGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A whip of cords is the only weapon the gospels ever put in the hand of Jesus, and only John mentions it[1]. He braids it himself and drives out the sellers along with their sheep and oxen, pours out the changers’ coins, overturns their tables, and tells the dove sellers to stop making his father’s house a house of trade[2]. The other gospels set the scene in his last week and give him a harsher line, about a house of prayer made into a den of thieves[3].

It is the one scene in the gospels where he takes up force on purpose, and he spends it on merchants of holiness. The institution founded in his name then went into their business. By the year twelve fifteen the trade in relics ran so freely that the Fourth Lateran Council had to forbid selling them or showing them outside their cases[4], and in fifteen sixty-two the Council of Trent abolished the traveling collectors of alms who carried indulgences from town to town, on the stated ground that no hope of their amendment remained[5]. Prosperity preachers still ask for a seed offering that will return a hundredfold[6], and a Latter-day Saint is asked whether a full tithe has been paid[7] before a temple recommend is issued.

A believer’s house fills up from the same stalls, with the scapular, the bottle of blessed oil and the vial from the shrine, each bought because a seller said it was holy. He aimed the cord at a price list. Any shelf that still holds holiness bought for money is a stall in that court, waiting for the cord.

Declaration: Every holy thing I ever paid for was a receipt from the temple court, and my house no longer keeps the merchants’ books.

The Rite · No faith

Braid a whip from cord and drive off a table every charm, crystal or lucky trinket you ever paid for because a seller promised it held a power, then bin the lot.

Testament · What is the most you ever paid for something because it was holy?

Sources

[1] John 2:15

[2] John 2:16

[4] Fourth Lateran Council (1215), c. 62

[5] Council of Trent, Sess. 21, De ref. c. 9

[6] Mark 10:30

[7] Temple recommend interview, Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints


CCLXXXII Of Caesar

Reckoning

Day 282 of 365

Give Caesar his coin and the god nothing.

Jesus Replies about the Tribute MoneyGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Pharisees and Herodians came together[1] to trap Jesus with a question about the tribute Rome had assessed on Judea since the census of the year six. It was the tax Judas the Galilean had led a revolt[2] against and died for. Either answer would cost him the crowd or deliver him to the governor[3]. He asked to see the coin[4], asked whose image and inscription were on it, and when they said Caesar’s, told them to give Caesar what was Caesar’s and God what was God’s[5].

The silver of Tiberius’s reign bore his head and an inscription naming him son of the divine Augustus, and the tribute penny is commonly identified with such a coin, so the question was argued over a small silver claim to godhead. Caesar’s half runs as far as his face and his coin. The other half runs by the same logic to the end, because Genesis says the human being was made in the divine image[6], and whatever bears an image belongs to the one it portrays. Later in the same chapter a lawyer asks for the great commandment and is told to love God with all his heart[7], all his soul and all his mind.

On this reading Caesar asked for a coin and the god asked for the whole person, and the second bill is the pattern for every claim that arrives unpriced. The employer who calls the staff a family collects by image and will not write a figure down, since a figure can be paid and a paid debt is over. Stop paying it, and the boss must say for the first time what they think they are owed, which is the first figure you can refuse.

Declaration: Let the god who wants me by my face show me what he gave for it.

The Rite

Pay one debt you agreed to, a bill, a loan or a sum owed a friend, to the exact amount, and say This is paid in full. Then tell one claimant whose demand on you has never been priced Name the sum or drop it.

Testament · Which claim on you has never had a figure written on it?

Sources

[1] Matt 22:15–16

[2] Acts 5:37; Josephus, Ant. 18.1–10

[3] Luke 20:20

[4] Matt 22:19–20

[5] Matt 22:21

[6] Gen 1:27

[7] Matt 22:35–37


CCLXXXIII Of the Widow’s Mite

Heresy

Day 283 of 365

Read the warning before you read the praise.

The Widow’s MiteGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Mark sets the widow right after a warning. Beware the scribes, Jesus tells the crowd, who love long robes and the chief seats, devour widows’ houses[1] and for a show make long prayers. Then he sits down opposite the temple treasury[2] and watches the money go in, the rich putting in much and a poor widow two small copper coins[3] worth a fraction of a penny. He calls the disciples over to tell them she has given more than all the other givers, since they gave out of their surplus and she, out of her want, gave all she had, her whole living[4].

Read in that order, she is the exhibit for the warning. A widow’s house is being devoured in front of him, coin by coin, and in the same scene he tells his disciples she put in more than all of them. The next verse opens on the great stones of the temple and his prediction that not one will be left on another[5], and within forty years[6] the building her living went into was rubble.

Stewardship campaigns kept her gift and dropped the warning. The sermon on sacrificial giving holds her up as the model of the gift that costs the giver something she will miss, and the televangelist asks the pensioner watching at home for the gift she cannot afford.

Her two coins, two lepta that make a quadrans, a quarter of an as, were a sixty-fourth of a laborer’s day[7], and a laborer’s day was one denarius, the penny a day that Matthew gives as a laborer’s wage.

Declaration: The scribes can make their long prayers over a box that gets nothing of mine.

The Rite

Write to the church, ministry or appeal you last gave to and ask for its audited accounts, the salaries and the share that reaches the poor. Say Open the box and show me. as you seal the envelope. Give nothing more until they answer.

Testament · What has ever come back to you from whoever lives on your two coins?

Sources

[1] Mark 12:38–40

[6] Josephus, J.W. 7.1–3
