CCLXXXIV Of Gethsemane

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 284 of 365

Call the silence a refusal.

Jesus Prays in the GardenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Peter, James and John sleep through[1] the prayer of Jesus. He takes them further into the garden of Gethsemane than the others and asks them to keep awake with him, then goes a little way off, falls on the ground[2] and asks his father to take the cup away, and three times comes back to find them asleep, their eyes heavy, with nothing to say to him[3].

Mark keeps the Aramaic word for father[4], the one used at home, and puts into his mouth the premise every defense of the god must carry, that everything is possible for the one he is addressing[5]. He asks outright that the cup be removed, adds that his father’s will should be done in place of his own, and his father’s will is done, and the cup is not removed, and Mark records no answer of any kind.

The Catholic Church calls this obedience[6], the cup of the New Covenant accepted from the Father’s hands, and the obedient prayer asks and then submits, so that whatever comes back the asking was proper and the silence was love. Hebrews, writing of the days of his flesh[7], has him offer up prayers with loud cries and tears to the one able to save him from death.

A man who heard his son beg in a garden, and beg again, and left the cup in his son’s hands would be called cruel by every neighbor on the street, and the god earns that name on the same evidence, on the evidence of the silence Mark records.

Declaration: The word love, in my mouth, belongs to a man who would have crossed the garden at the first cry, and the one who stayed silent there has forfeited it.

The Rite · Christian

Fill a cup with water and set it before you. Pray Take this cup from me. Wait one full minute, and when nothing answers pour the water out, and turn it upside down on the windowsill for the night, saying Nothing came.

Testament · Who could have taken the cup from you and chose not to?

Sources

[1] Mark 14:33–41

[2] Mark 14:35

[3] Mark 14:40

[4] Mark 14:36

[5] Mark 14:36

[6] CCC 612

[7] Heb 5:7


CCLXXXV Of Strength for Sacrifice

Heresy

Day 285 of 365

Refuse to be fortified for your own sacrifice.

An Angel Appears to Jesus in the GardenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Two verses of Luke’s scene of Jesus in the garden are missing from several of the oldest manuscripts[1], and they are the strangest in it. An angel appears from heaven, strengthening him[2], and being in agony he prays more earnestly, and his sweat falls to the ground like great drops of blood[3]. Whoever wrote them, most Bibles still print them. Mark and Matthew give the same prayer and send no angel. The angel arrives after the plea to be spared[4], in place of any answer to it, and what it brings is stamina, enough to see him through the night and into the hands of the soldiers.

Employers hire that angel by the thousand. A company that has cut a team to half its size and doubled its targets pays for a resilience workshop and a meditation app, and the purpose of both is that the staff go back into the same garden better able to sweat. Congregations send their exhausted pastors on retreat so they can come home and carry the parish again.

The angel served the plan, and the plan needed the man in the garden on his feet when the soldiers came. Whoever sets your load and then pays for your endurance is buying the same thing, a sacrifice that keeps its shape a little longer, and the profit goes to whoever passed you the cup. Stamina supplied in place of relief is a subsidy to the load, and a load that loses its subsidy has to be lightened or carried by the one who set it.

Declaration: When my plea to be spared is answered with strength to bear it, I count the answer as no and leave the garden before the soldiers come.

The Rite

Drop one course or app your employer gave you to help you bear the work, and to anyone who asks why say Lighten the load instead. Spend the hour it claimed on a pleasure useless to your job, a film you want, started and finished.

Testament · Who profits from what you are being strengthened to endure?

Sources

[1] Luke 22:43–44; absent in P75, Codex Vaticanus

[2] Luke 22:43

[3] Luke 22:44

[4] Luke 22:42–43


CCLXXXVI Of Judas

Reckoning

Day 286 of 365

Refuse the traitor’s role others have cast you in.

Judas Betrays JesusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

It is objected that anyone who leaves the faith of a family is a Judas. He breaks a vow, leaves his place at the family table bare and goes over to the other side for whatever it pays, and the Church carved what becomes of such a man on the tops of its columns[1], Judas hanging by the neck between two devils.

Judas went to the chief priests of his own accord and asked what they would give him[2] to hand Jesus over, and they set the price at thirty pieces of silver[3], and from then on he watched for his chance. He chose the sign himself[4], a kiss, and gave it at Gethsemane, and the man he kissed was dead the next afternoon. Only when he saw the sentence passed did he bring the silver back, throw it down in the temple and hang himself[5].

That is a grown man seeking out a buyer, taking money and marking a victim for arrest. The one who leaves a family’s faith has no buyer. He goes over to an empty side, where no priest waits with a purse, and everyone he leaves sleeps in his own bed that night. His chair at a long table goes to someone else, and his name drops off the Christmas cards.

Matthew has the priests gather up the thrown silver and refuse it for the treasury[6], since it was the price of blood, then buy a potter’s field with it to bury strangers in. The men who paid for the kiss kept their books clean on a point of law. A family keeps the same books when it enters the cost of a son’s leaving under his name, and the word traitor goes to the one person at that table who paid.

Declaration: Judas took thirty pieces for a man’s life, and all I took when I left was my Sundays.

The Rite

Lay thirty coins of any kind on a table. Name aloud each thing you lost by going, sweeping one coin off with I paid that for each, however few. Then spend all thirty, with whatever you add, on something for yourself.

Testament · Which of your losses has the family recorded as your crime?

Sources

[1] Autun, Cathedral of Saint-Lazare, capital of the hanging of Judas, c. 1130

[2] Matt 26:14–15

[3] Matt 26:15

[4] Matt 26:48–49

[5] Matt 27:3–5

[6] Matt 27:6–7


CCLXXXVII Of Scourging

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 287 of 365

Admire no one for bleeding, yourself included.

Jesus Is ScourgedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Processions of men set out from a hill town in Umbria about the year twelve sixty. They went through the towns of northern Italy stripped to the waist, flogging their own backs with knotted cords until the blood ran. In the year thirteen forty-nine, with the plague emptying whole cities, the flagellants came back in their thousands across Germany and the Low Countries, and the Pope condemned them before the year was out[1]. They were imitating a sentence the gospels pass over in a few words. Pilate had Jesus scourged.

Luke and John add that Pilate meant the flogging as a substitute for death[2], a punishment severe enough to satisfy the crowd so that he could let the man go, and it failed, since the crowd wanted the cross. Some members of Opus Dei, the Catholic movement, still wear a spiked chain on the thigh and strike themselves with a knotted cord, and the movement says so openly[3]. An old Jewish custom, still kept in some communities, gives a man thirty-nine token lashes with a strap before the great fast[4], one short of the forty the law allows[5], the same count Paul took on his own back five times[6].

All of it rests on one inference, that pain taken on purpose is a payment and someone is collecting. The first flogging in the story was already a failed payment, offered by Pilate and refused by the crowd, and the flagellants of thirteen forty-nine whipped their way through towns the plague went on emptying after they had gone. A debt with no creditor is settled by stopping, and the back that stops paying keeps its skin.

Declaration: Seven centuries of opened backs have bought the world nothing, and I spend my body on its own pleasure.

The Rite · Christian

Put your own Bible on the floor and sit in your softest chair with the richest food you can lay hands on. Rest your feet on the book and eat slowly until the plate is empty.

Testament · Which of your hardships do you keep up because it makes you look serious?

Sources

[1] Clement VI, bull of 20 Oct 1349

[2] Luke 23:16, 22; John 19:1–4

[3] Opus Dei, Opus Dei and corporal mortification (opusdei.org)

[4] Shulchan Aruch, OC 607:6

[5] Deut 25:3

[6] 2 Cor 11:24


CCLXXXVIII Of Thorns

Beauty

Day 288 of 365

Adorn your own head before you admire anyone’s relic.

Jesus Is Crowned with ThornsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Louis the Ninth of France paid a hundred and thirty-five thousand French pounds[1] for the crown of thorns, money that went to the Venetian bankers to whom Baldwin II, the Latin emperor of Constantinople, had pawned it. The chapel he built to house it cost forty thousand, less than a third of what the crown cost. The king carried it into Paris barefoot in August 1239, dressed as a penitent, and what survives today in Notre-Dame, rescued from the 2019 fire, is a ring of bundled rushes in a crystal case, the thorns having been pried off over the centuries and handed to princes and abbeys as gifts.

The soldiers who made the original meant it as a joke. Matthew has them strip him, wrap him in a scarlet cloak[2], braid a crown of thorns[3], put a reed in his hand and kneel to him, hailing him as king of the Jews, spit on him, and then take the reed and beat him about the head with it[4].

Piety put the soldiers’ joke behind gold and glass, in a silver chest that cost a hundred thousand French pounds more[5], in an upper chapel kept for the royal family and its guests. The chest alone cost two and a half times what the chapel did.

A crown is made for a living head, which is why the soldiers’ joke needed a man under it. The reliquary kept the crown and removed the head, so a king carried a ring of rushes barefoot into Paris and the thing in his arms could not feel what was done with it.

Declaration: More than three chapels’ worth of money bought a king the right to kneel to rushes, and I spend mine on what I can wear.

The Rite

Make a crown from the most beautiful thing within reach, wire, ribbon or a string of beads, bent to your skull. Set it on your own head, say I crown myself, and keep it on while you cook or eat.

Testament · What beautiful thing were you told was too much for someone like you?

Sources

[1] Branner, St Louis and the Court Style in Gothic Architecture, p. 8ff

[2] Matt 27:28

[3] Matt 27:29

[4] Matt 27:30

[5] Branner, St Louis and the Court Style in Gothic Architecture, p. 8ff


CCLXXXIX Of Mockery

Heresy

Day 289 of 365

Laugh at whatever demands to be taken seriously.

Jesus Is MockedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jesus was blindfolded, struck in the face and told to prophesy which of the men[1] holding him had done it, and Mark adds that they spat on him[2]. Luke has Herod and his soldiers treat him as nothing, dress him in a gorgeous robe[3] and send him back to Pilate wearing it, and at the cross the chief priests passed the time telling one another that he had saved others and could not save himself[4]. At none of these mockings does he answer his mockers.

At the mockings the accused raised no complaint. His defenders raised it for him, with indictments, for centuries. In sixteen seventy-six an English judge declared blasphemy a crime at common law[5], on the ground that Christianity was part of the law of the land, and in nineteen seventy-seven a London jury convicted the editor of a newspaper[6] for printing verses about a centurion’s desire for the body taken down from the cross. The offense was abolished in England and Wales in two thousand eight[7].

The judge said that to call religion a cheat dissolves the obligations[8] that hold civil society together, and that Christianity is part of the law of England, so that to mock it is to speak against the law.

In nineteen seventy-seven the court told the jury that what the editor meant did not matter[9]. The editor walked out of the Old Bailey with a fine of five hundred pounds and nine months in prison suspended over his head, for a page of verse, and the Lords upheld the conviction[10] in a case brought by a private citizen, Mary Whitehouse.

Declaration: Blasphemy stayed a crime in England until two thousand eight, and I commit it with the windows open.

The Rite

Copy out the creed, pledge or hymn you once said most solemnly. Read it aloud in the voice of the most ridiculous character you can do, laughing wherever it asks for reverence, then fold it into a paper airplane, say Amen and fly it into the bin.

Testament · What did you once believe so seriously that it now makes you laugh?

Sources

[1] Luke 22:63–64

[2] Mark 14:65

[3] Luke 23:11

[4] Mark 15:31

[5] Taylor’s Case (1676), 1 Vent. 293

[6] R v Lemon; Whitehouse v Lemon (1977–79)

[7] Criminal Justice and Immigration Act 2008, s. 79

[8] Taylor’s Case (1676), 1 Vent. 293

[9] R v Lemon (1977), trial direction; Whitehouse v Lemon [1979] AC 617

[10] Whitehouse v Lemon [1979] AC 617


CCXC Of Ecce Homo

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 290 of 365

Carry no guilt you were born into.

Jesus Is Presented to the PeopleGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

In John’s account Pilate brings Jesus out in the crown of thorns and the purple cloak. He shows him to the chief priests and officers with three words, behold the man, as though the sight of what the soldiers had done would be enough. In Matthew alone, Pilate washes his hands before the crowd and declares himself innocent of this man’s blood, and the whole people answer that his blood should be on them and on their children[1].

The Church read that answer as a curse laid on a nation for all time. Bishops and preachers charged the Jews with killing God for centuries, and in that name crusaders in the year ten ninety-six slaughtered the Jewish communities along the Rhine[2], and the chronicles report them swearing to avenge Christ before they left home. Only in nineteen sixty-five did the Second Vatican Council declare that his death could not be charged against all the Jews then living, nor against the Jews of today[3].

The machinery that blames unborn children also tells a baptized infant it was born under Adam’s sin, and a child in catechism class that its own sins drove the nails[4]. The catechism concedes that this inherited sin has the character of a personal fault in none of Adam’s descendants[5], and in the same paragraph names baptism as what erases it. The child pays anyway.

Guilt belongs to you for what your own hands did, and that kind has a face, the person harmed, who can name the wrong and take the repair. The blood on the children and the sin of the cradle have no face behind them, only the institution that wrote the charge, and since no one harmed can accept a repair, the charge is never settled, only washed, and the believer carries his own children to the same font.

Declaration: I was washed at the font of a sin the catechism admits was never my fault, and that is the last guilt the Church will hand me.

The Rite · Christian

Strip to the waist before a mirror, drape a purple towel over your shoulders like the soldiers’ cloak, and say to your own face Behold the man. He owes nothing for anyone’s blood.

Testament · Which guilt were you handed before you had done anything at all?

Sources

[1] Matt 27:24–25

[2] Solomon bar Simson Chronicle, in Eidelberg, The Jews and the Crusaders (1996)

[3] Nostra Aetate 4

[4] CCC 598

[5] CCC 405


CCXCI Of Burdens

Mastery

Day 291 of 365

Ask who drafted you into each duty, and when.

Jesus Falls Beneath the CrossGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

A man named Simon was conscripted on the road to the crucifixion, and the verb Matthew uses for it is a soldier’s word[1]. It came from the mounted couriers of the Persian king[2], and Rome adapted the courier system, laying on private persons the duty to supply transport[3]. Simon the Cyrenian was coming in from the country, Mark says, the father of Alexander and Rufus[4], and the soldiers seized him and made him carry the cross behind Jesus. They took him by the right a courier used to take a farmer’s mule. No gospel records a word from him.

The same verb turns up earlier in Matthew, in the sermon that tells anyone compelled to go one mile to go two[5]. The rule was written for men like Simon, and piety has kept it, turning him into the stranger privileged to share the load and giving him a station of his own[6], the fifth, on the Way of the Cross.

Families and offices still draft whoever happens to be standing nearest, the child made the reliable one at fourteen or the one who manages a parent’s moods, the employee whose duty was never in the contract and became theirs by repetition. Carry it well and the sermon’s reward is the second mile, more of the same load on the same back.

A burden laid on by compulsion creates no obligation, and whoever relied on yours can find another passer-by or carry it themselves, as John’s gospel, which drops Simon altogether, has Jesus go out bearing his own cross[7].

Declaration: The sermon told the conscript to walk the second mile, and I hand the soldier his beam at the end of the first.

The Rite

Hand back one duty that was laid on you unasked, telling whoever relies on it From Friday, this is yours. Then spend the freed hour on your own errand, the application, the pitch or the first page of the work you want your name on.

Testament · Which load did you pick up only because you happened to be passing?

Sources

[1] Matt 27:32

[2] Herodotus 8.98

[3] Kolb, Travel and Geography in the Roman Empire (2001), p. 98

[4] Mark 15:21

[5] Matt 5:41

[6] Stations of the Cross, fifth station

[7] John 19:17


CCXCII Of the Place of the Skull

Heresy

Day 292 of 365

Let some suffering mean nothing.

Jesus Arrives at CalvaryGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Golgotha is Aramaic for a skull[1] and Calvary is the Latin for the same, and the gospels never say why the place was called that. Churchmen supplied a reason. Adam, Origen heard from a Hebrew tradition, lay buried there[2], and by Epiphanius’s day the blood running down the cross fell on his bones, and painters and carvers set his skull at the foot of the cross for centuries.

The road to it got the same treatment. The gospels never say he fell on the way, yet the Stations of the Cross have him fall three times[3], and generations of the devout have knelt at each of those falls. Where the record left a name unexplained and a road told without a fall, piety supplied the meaning and then added more suffering for the meaning to carry.

Everything happens for a reason, the counselor says, and the survivor who accepts the reason is asked to tell it at every gathering, as the first line of the bio.

Some of what happened to you meant nothing. It was cruelty or bad luck, and where a man did it, the blame is his in full, and the story that makes it the making of you hands him a share of the credit for your character, a fee he never earned. What grew in you afterward grew from your own ground, out of appetites and work he had no part in, and the account of it can leave him out entirely. The gospels name the hill and give it no cause.

Declaration: No lesson hangs in the frame of my worst year, because the man who made it is owed no credit for me.

The Rite

Delete the survivor line from your bio, bin the awareness ribbon or shirt, or cut from your story the sentence that sells your worst year. Then eat the best meal you can afford, attending to every bite.

Testament · What have you been required to find meaning in that had none?

Sources

[1] Mark 15:22

[2] Origen, Comm. ser. Matt. 126; Epiphanius, Panarion 46 (c. 378)

[3] Stations of the Cross, third, seventh and ninth stations


CCXCIII Of the Thief

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 293 of 365

Decline the deathbed bargain in advance.

The Crucifixion of Jesus and Two CriminalsGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Only Luke has a penitent thief[1]. In Mark and Matthew both men crucified beside him join in the abuse[2], but Luke gives one of them a rebuke for his fellow (they deserve their sentence, he says, and this man does not) and a request to be remembered when Jesus comes into his kingdom, and gives Jesus the reply that the man will be with him in paradise that same day[3]. Later tradition named him Dismas[4] and made him a saint, patron of prisoners.

Preachers kept a story like Luke’s close at hand. In 1915 an evangelist named Lady Hope told a Bible conference at Northfield[5], Massachusetts, that Darwin on his sickbed had been reading the Epistle to the Hebrews[6] and wished aloud that he had not put his theory as he did. The story ran in a Baptist paper that summer and went round in tracts for decades. Darwin’s daughter Henrietta answered in 1922 that he never recanted any of his scientific views[7].

A deathbed is a scene where the dying man cannot answer back, and that is what made Darwin’s so useful to the tract. Yours is as open to the same use if pain and morphine take your grip and a visitor writes down the old words coming back.

Darwin, who could not answer, had a daughter who could. Henrietta had been at his deathbed, and Lady Hope, she wrote, had been present at no illness of his[8] at all. A conclusion signed while the head is clear leaves a witness the preacher cannot out-talk.

Declaration: A paradise that waits for the last sentence of a life has no use for the thousand days before it, and I owe it nothing.

The Rite · Christian

Cut the thief’s promise of paradise out of your own Bible, write I decline on the back, say I decline aloud, and file the strip with your important papers.

Testament · What do you want on record in place of the words you fear you will say at the end?

Sources

[1] Luke 23:39–43

[2] Mark 15:32; Matt 27:44

[3] Luke 23:43

[4] Gospel of Nicodemus 10

[5] Watchman-Examiner, 15 Aug 1915

[6] Lady Hope, Watchman-Examiner, 15 Aug 1915

[7] H. Litchfield, The Christian, 23 Feb 1922

[8] H. Litchfield, The Christian, 23 Feb 1922


CCXCIV Of Forsaking

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 294 of 365

Forsake the god who forsook his son.

Darkness at the CrucifixionGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

From noon until three, Mark says, darkness covered the whole land, and at three Jesus cried out in Aramaic, asking his god why he had forsaken him[1]. The bystanders thought he was calling for Elijah. Somebody ran with a sponge of sour wine on a reed, and he gave a loud cry and died.

It is the only prayer in the gospels in which he does not call God his father[2], and Luke and John did not keep it. Luke gives him a commendation of his spirit into his father’s hands[3], and John a single word, that it is finished[4]. Only Mark and Matthew keep the cry[5].

Josephus, who wrote the history of that city and that generation and recorded its portents down to a heifer giving birth to a lamb[6] in the temple, says nothing of three hours of night at noon during a feast that filled Jerusalem. Early in the third century the Christian chronicler Julius Africanus had to quarrel with a historian[7] who explained the darkness as an eclipse, since an eclipse of the sun cannot happen at Passover, when the moon is full. A man asked his god a question in the hearing of a crowd, and Luke dropped the question and wrote a calm commendation in its place, while Mark and Matthew keep the darkness beside the cry[8], a sign the city’s historian never recorded.

The faith taught you to call the silence in your own prayers a test, and to read the sky for an answer. Mark’s cry is the one prayer in the passion that says aloud what reply every prayer gets. Whoever the god left behind can leave him in turn, keeping the question and dropping the god, and walk out into ordinary afternoon light.

Declaration: The gospels give Jesus only the first line of his psalm, and my faith stopped at the same verse.

The Rite · Christian

Tear the page with the cry from the cross out of your own Bible, say I forsake you too, and put the rest of the book out with the trash, keeping the page.

Testament · When did you first feel abandoned in prayer, and what sign were you told to look for?

Sources

[1] Mark 15:33–34

[2] Mark 15:34; Matt 27:46

[3] Luke 23:46

[4] John 19:30

[5] Matt 27:46

[6] Josephus, Jewish War 6.292

[7] Julius Africanus, Chronography, fr. in George Syncellus

[8] Mark 15:33; Matt 27:45


CCXCV Of Deposition

Beauty

Day 295 of 365

Sit for your portrait while the body is warm.

Jesus’ Body Is Removed from the CrossGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

Nicodemus brought about a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes[1], by John’s account, a quantity fit for a king’s burial. He and Joseph of Arimathea took the body of Jesus down and bound it in linen with the spices, as was the custom of the Jews[2]. The gospels leave out the mechanics. Somebody must have climbed, drawn the nails and taken a dead man’s weight against his chest, and for centuries the painters supplied the ladders and the straining arms and the long sheet paid out from the crossbeam.

Few subjects in Christian art required so long a look at a dead male body, naked but for a cloth, heavy as only the dead are heavy, with the skin going gray. About 1435 Rogier van der Weyden painted one[3] for the crossbowmen’s guild of Louvain, now in the Prado, and Adam’s skull lies at the foot[4] to carry the doctrine, but the rest is weight and grief, the body held up between two old men, its beauty in the body as it is, finished. Paint out the skull and it could hang in a house that believes in no resurrection.

The Church kept that body for its painters and gave the faithful the opposite lesson about their own. Paul called the living body a tent to be taken down[5], and the believer was taught to groan in it while waiting for a better house. The painters gave a dead man’s flesh more care than many believers were allowed to give their own, and yours is entitled to that long look while the pulse still shows under the skin.

Declaration: Paul wanted out of his tent, and I have furnished mine.

The Rite

Make a portrait of yourself, by camera timer or pencil and mirror, in the cloth you like best, or in the skin if you print it and delete the file. Hang it where you dress and show it only to an adult you trust.

Testament · Which part of your body were you taught to look away from?

Sources

[1] John 19:39

[2] John 19:40

[3] Descent from the Cross, Museo del Prado, P002825

[4] Descent from the Cross, Museo del Prado, P002825; Campbell, Van der Weyden (2004)

[5] 2 Cor 5:1–4


CCXCVI Of Mourning

Reckoning

Day 296 of 365

Say the eulogy to the living.

Disciples Mourn over the Dead JesusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The women who had watched the cross from a distance went home and prepared spices and ointments before sundown[1]. Then the sabbath began, and Luke says they rested on the sabbath day according to the commandment[2], while the body they meant to anoint lay in the rock. They came back at first light with their spices, and the tomb was empty[3]. Luke gives them no body to anoint.

The rabbis of tractate Sanhedrin ask outright whom a eulogy is for[4], whether the speech honors the living or the dead, and settle it for the dead, so that a man who asked for no eulogy is obeyed after he is buried. Ben Sira, in a book the Catholic and Orthodox Bibles still print, had already priced grief for the mourner, telling him to weep bitterly for a day or two, to avoid criticism[5], and then to take comfort, because there is no coming back, and grief does the dead no good[6] and injures the one who grieves.

The rabbis took it on faith that the dead man listens, and Rav told the man who would speak over him to speak warmly, since he would be standing there[7]. Ben Sira wrote that thanksgiving has ceased from the dead[8] as from one who does not exist, and by his count the speech has no hearer. The friend who sat up at the hospital bed through the bad nights and the brother who drove all night to get there can be given now what the funeral would have said of them, while they are in the room to hear it. Held back for the funeral, the same words go to a closed lid, and the friend who sat up through the bad nights never hears them.

Declaration: I will take one compliment to my face over every sermon preached above my coffin.

The Rite

Write the eulogy you would give for one living person who has earned it, and read it to them today, in person or on the phone. Bring or send something good to eat with it.

Testament · Whose eulogy are you saving for a day they will not hear it?

Sources

[1] Luke 23:55–56

[2] Luke 23:56

[3] Luke 24:1–3

[4] b. Sanhedrin 46b

[5] Sir 38:17

[6] Sir 38:21

[7] b. Shabbat 153a

[8] Sir 17:27–28


CCXCVII Of the Tomb

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 297 of 365

Bury the god you were given, and seal the stone.

Jesus Is Buried in the TombGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Joseph of Arimathea laid the body in his own new tomb, cut out of the rock, and rolled a great stone across the door[1]. Matthew alone adds what was done to it next. The chief priests went to Pilate and asked him to make the grave secure until the third day[2], in case the disciples stole the body and announced a resurrection, and Pilate told them they had a watch, and they sealed the stone.

Matthew closes the guard story with its aftermath. After the stone was moved, he writes, the soldiers were paid a large sum to report[3] that the disciples had come by night and stolen the body, and the story was still told among the Jews in his own day[4]. Matthew sets the guard beside the bribed soldiers’ rumor, and the two together read as a defense of the empty tomb. The site had a rougher history. Hadrian buried the cave under a temple[5] about the year one hundred thirty-five, Constantine had the soil dug out[6] and a church raised over it about the year three hundred twenty-six, and in ten oh nine the caliph al-Hakim ordered that church destroyed[7] and the tomb was almost entirely lost.

A grave is for letting the living stop expecting someone. This one was sealed, guarded, dug up and fought over, and the faith still rests on its being empty. A god who left no body is the one dead man his followers can never bury. The burial falls to whoever has stopped believing, and it can be done without a corpse.

Declaration: The priests sealed that stone and posted a guard, and I seal mine for good without either.

The Rite · Christian

Lay a printed Bible page in a shoebox and tape it shut. Over it say aloud what the god you were given cost you, item by item, then set the heaviest book you own on the lid.

Testament · What did that god cost you that nobody has yet counted with you?

Sources

[1] Matt 27:60

[2] Matt 27:62–66

[3] Matt 28:11–13

[4] Matt 28:15

[5] Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.26–27; Corbo (1981), pp. 34–36

[6] Eusebius, Life of Constantine 3.27–31

[7] Yahya of Antioch and Adémar de Chabannes, in Morris (2005)


CCXCVIII Of Emmaus

Heresy

Day 298 of 365

Enjoy it in the present tense.

Jesus and Two Disciples Go to EmmausGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

Two disciples walked the seven miles to Emmaus beside a stranger who opened the scriptures to them on the way[1], and they did not know him. At the table he took the bread, blessed it, broke it[2] and gave it to them, and their eyes were opened and he vanished[3]. Only then did they tell each other that their hearts had burned within them[4] on the road. They rose that same hour and went back to Jerusalem[5]. Luke does not say that either of them ate.

The blessing at that table was the stranger’s, said over the bread before it was broken. Two exercises of the faiths keep the disciples’ schedule as well, one Jewish and one Catholic. The one blessing over food that the rabbis held the Torah itself commands is said after the meal, drawn from a verse about eating and being full[6], and the evening examination of conscience goes back over the day once it can no longer be enjoyed. Bookshops now sell the same exercise to people who have stopped praying, a list of blessings counted in bed, with the god’s name removed and the delay intact.

A pleasure counted afterward has already been turned into a bill of thanks, payable to someone absent. The two at Emmaus spent a whole road beside the company that set their hearts burning and said so only to each other, too late for him to hear it. A piety that saves its fullest thanks for after the plate is cleared trains the believer to taste the meal over the dirty dishes.

Declaration: My verdict on a pleasure is given with my mouth full, and the gods who wait for thanks afterward can wait.

The Rite

Eat something you love today with no grace before it and no thanks after. Halfway through, fork in hand, say This is good aloud to whoever shares the table, or to the empty room.

Testament · Which pleasure do you only notice once it is over?

Sources

[1] Luke 24:15–16, 27, 32

[2] Luke 24:30

[3] Luke 24:31

[4] Luke 24:32

[5] Luke 24:13, 33

[6] b. Berakhot 21a; Deut 8:10


CCXCIX Of Nets

Mastery

Day 299 of 365

Move the net before you blame your arms.

The Miraculous Catch of FishGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Seven disciples fished all night on the Sea of Tiberias[1] after the crucifixion, and caught nothing. At daybreak a man on the shore, whom they did not recognize[2], asked whether they had anything to eat and told them to cast the net on the right side of the boat[3]. They did, and could not haul it in for the number of fish. John counts them once the net is dragged ashore, a hundred and fifty-three large ones[4], and adds that for all that weight it held. John names the stranger as Jesus and tells the catch as his miracle.

Commentators have spent the number on allegory. Jerome reported that the writers on the nature of animals knew exactly a hundred and fifty-three kinds of fish[5], and Augustine noticed that it is the sum of every number from one to seventeen[6]. Augustine made the right side stand for the saved[7] and the number for the Spirit added to the law. The plain order, cast on the other side, became a symbol before anyone asked whether it worked.

The advice came from a man on dry land, and they took it before they knew who he was. Paul’s counsel to the Galatians, not to grow weary in well doing[8] because in due season you will reap, was about doing good, and a preacher can still carry it to the workbench, where it names no stopping point.

John makes the stranger the risen Jesus and the catch his doing. Take the miracle away and the instruction left is the one a fisherman on shore would give, change the method, and a boat’s width was the whole distance between a failed night and a full net.

Declaration: I keep faith with the catch, and no preacher’s harvest gets another season of my life.

The Rite

Take the work that has caught nothing for months and recast it today, at a different price, to a different buyer or with a different pitch, and send it out before dark.

Testament · Which method have you kept casting all night because it was yours?

Sources

[1] John 21:2–3

[2] John 21:4

[3] John 21:6

[4] John 21:11

[5] Jerome, Comm. Ezech. 14 (on Ezek 47:6–12)

[6] Augustine, Tract. Ev. Jo. 122.7–9

[7] Augustine, Tract. Ev. Jo. 122.7

[8] Gal 6:9


CCC Of Ascension

Reckoning

Day 300 of 365

Write off the one who promised to come back.

Jesus Ascends to HeavenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

In Mark’s gospel Jesus tells his hearers that their generation will not pass away before all these things happen[1]. Paul wrote to the Thessalonians as though he and they would still be alive to be caught up into the air to meet him[2]. The promise came with a deadline. Acts sets the departure on a hill outside Jerusalem, where a cloud takes him from their sight[3] and two men in white ask why they stand staring at the sky, and promise that this same Jesus will return the way they saw him go[4].

The second letter of Peter answers scoffers who ask where the promised coming is, now that the fathers have fallen asleep, with the rule that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years[5]. The Church went on to move the date into an indefinite future and set the waiting into the liturgy itself, so that at every Mass now, just after the Lord’s Prayer, the priest still asks that the faithful be kept safe as they await the blessed hope and the coming of their Savior[6].

Nearly two thousand years on, the generation in Mark’s deadline is dust and the prayer is still said at the altar every day, because a promise with no date can be kept waiting on forever and never be found broken. The friend who moved away promising to visit and the lover who said they would call hold a seat at your table on the same terms. Only the one left waiting can close such a promise, and he closes it on the day he clears the extra place and gives the spare room to whoever is actually there.

Declaration: Every Mass still waits on a guest who missed his own deadline, and I hold the door for no one.

The Rite

Take over whatever you have held open for someone who left with a promise. Sleep in the spare bed, fill the cleared drawer with your own things, or book for one the trip you saved for two.

Testament · What are you still keeping ready for someone who said they would return?

Sources

[1] Mark 13:30

CCCI Of Tongues

Mastery

Day 301 of 365

Make your demand in words you can be held to.

The Holy Spirit Descends on the DisciplesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Parthians and Medes, Cretans and Arabs, and pilgrims from eleven other peoples and places[1] heard the disciples that day, Acts claims, each in their own language. Tongues like flames had settled on each[2] of the disciples in the house where they were gathered, and they began speaking languages they had never learned.

The Pentecostal revival of the gift began in Topeka at the turn of the twentieth century, when a student named Agnes Ozman was reported to have spoken Chinese[3], and within a few years Pentecostal missionaries were sailing abroad expecting to preach in languages granted on arrival. Her teacher had taught that the tongues were human languages that would spare a missionary years of study. The languages did not come. What the Pentecostal churches practice now is a flow of syllables that most linguists who have studied it find has the sounds of the speaker’s own language and no grammar at all[4].

The churches kept the gift and changed its terms. Tongues became, for most, a private prayer language[5], a speech no hearer is expected to translate and so no hearer can check. Paul had already warned the assembly at Corinth that an outsider who walked in on a whole church speaking in tongues would say they were mad, and wrote that he would sooner speak five words with his understanding in church than ten thousand in a tongue[6].

Five words a listener understands commit the speaker, and ten thousand he cannot follow commit nobody. The demand you owe the colleague who takes your credit, or the price you have never named to the client who underpays, fits in about that many, and once they have been said to his face, you can be held to every one of them.

Declaration: I name my price in the language of the man who pays it, in few enough words that he can say them back to me.

The Rite

Write your demand or your price for one person in five words, or as few as will carry it, and say it to them today, in person or by phone, with no preamble and no apology. Skip it where saying it would put you at risk.

Testament · What is the short sentence you owe the one who has been taking from you?

[4] Samarin, Tongues of Men and Angels (1972)

[5] Goff (1988); McGee, Pentecostal Missiology

[6] 1 Cor 14:19


CCCII Of Mission

Heresy

Day 302 of 365

Stop recruiting for your own beliefs.

The Apostles Preach the GospelGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Charlemagne’s law for the conquered Saxons, issued in the late eighth century, made refusing baptism a capital offense[1]. Matthew’s gospel ends on a mountain in Galilee[2] with the risen Jesus telling the eleven to go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them and teaching them to keep everything he commanded[3], and the book stops there, with no word on whether the nations wanted it. The order has been obeyed by sword and by doorbell. The Latter-day Saint church counted four hundred fifty-one missions[4] at the end of twenty twenty-five and eighty-eight thousand five hundred teaching missionaries by the middle of the next year, while Witnesses still go from house to house, a practice they trace to Acts.

Paul put the method to the Corinthians in a sentence, that he had become all things to all people[5] so that by all means he might save some. Each new believer is evidence to the recruiter that the belief must be true, since another person was persuaded. A flying-saucer circle in Oak Park, Illinois, was promised a flood for the twenty-first of December, nineteen fifty-four, and when the day came dry some of its members went out and preached harder[6], as though enough new members could make the date come right.

A conviction held for your own reasons was finished the day you weighed it. Each evening spent arguing a friend into it asks that friend to countersign your mind, and the friend who says no leaves you waiting on the next person’s signature for a conclusion you already own.

Declaration: A pamphlet confesses that its author could not bear to hold his faith alone, and I hand mine to no one.

The Rite

Gather every saved link, article and half-written reply you have kept to win over one particular person, and delete or bin the lot. Then mute the thread where you keep making the case, and say aloud Believe what you like.

Testament · Whose agreement have you spent yourself to win?

[1] Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae 8

[5] 1 Cor 9:22

[6] Festinger, Riecken & Schachter, When Prophecy Fails (1956)


CCCIII Of the Beautiful Gate

Indulgence

Day 303 of 365

Waste an afternoon looking at strangers.

Peter and John at the Beautiful GateGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

A man lame from his mother’s womb was carried daily and laid at the gate of the temple called Beautiful[1], to ask alms of those who entered. Seeing Peter and John about to go in at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour[2], he asked an alms.

Peter, fastening his eyes upon him with John, said, Look on us[3]. The man gave heed to them, expecting to receive something. Then Peter said that silver and gold he had none[4], and in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth told him to rise up and walk. He took him by the right hand and lifted him up, and immediately his feet and ankle bones received strength[5]. He entered with them into the temple, walking and leaping and praising God[6]. All the people saw him, and knew that it was he who sat for alms at the Beautiful gate[7], and they were filled with wonder and amazement at what had happened to him.

Peter asks why they marvel at this, or why they look so earnestly on the two of them[8], as though by their own power or holiness they had made the man walk.

The priests and the captain of the temple came upon them, grieved that they taught the people, and laid hands on them and put them in hold unto the next day[9], for it was now eventide. On the morrow the council set them in the midst. After further threats they let them go, finding nothing how they might punish them[10], because of the people. The healed man was above forty years old[11].

Declaration: The next person who asks me for something gets my eyes before my answer.

The Rite

Take a seat that faces a handsome entrance, a street or a square, order something sweet, and stay a full hour watching the people go in and out. Leave your phone in your pocket, and hold the glance until they look away.

Testament · What did you see from that seat that you would have missed on your way somewhere else?

CCCIV Of Ananias

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 304 of 365

Stop the payment that fear still collects.

The Death of AnaniasGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Ananias sold a field, kept back part of the price with his wife’s knowledge, and laid the remainder at the apostles’ feet as though it were the whole. The book of Acts makes no secret that the money was his. Peter tells him so to his face, that the land was his while he held it and the price was his to dispose of after the sale[1], and in the same breath accuses him of letting Satan fill his heart[2], and Ananias drops dead where he stands. The young men carry him out and bury him.

About three hours later his wife Sapphira comes in, knowing nothing. She has not been told that her husband is already in the ground. Peter asks whether they sold the land for so much, she gives the figure they agreed on, and he informs her that the feet of the men who buried her husband are at the door and will carry her out as well[3], and they do. The passage closes by noting that great fear came upon the whole church[4].

The community held its goods in common and honored those who laid the whole price of a field[5] at the apostles’ feet, so a reserve could only be hidden. Peter says Satan filled the man’s heart to lie and to keep back part of the price, the one thought in all of Acts that Satan puts into a heart. The keeping, by Peter’s own ruling a breath later, was the man’s right, and the lie was what a fellowship that honored only the whole price had left him. Whatever still runs from your account to a pulpit you no longer believe in is protection money, paid to the young men waiting at the door.

Declaration: Sapphira died over a number she and her husband agreed between themselves, and the number in my account is agreed with no one else.

The Rite · Christian

Cancel every standing order or recurring gift that still feeds a church or ministry you no longer believe in, or if none runs, spend on yourself today what you last put in a plate. Say aloud I kept it back, on the adversary’s advice.

Testament · How much have you paid, in total, to institutions that frightened you into paying?

Sources

[1] Acts 5:4

[2] Acts 5:3

[3] Acts 5:9–10

[4] Acts 5:11

[5] Acts 4:34–37


CCCV Of Martyrs

Heresy

Day 305 of 365

Withhold forgiveness until the wrong is paid for.

The Martyrdom of St. StephenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Stephen forgave his killers while the stones were still landing. He knelt and cried out to the Lord not to lay this sin to their charge[1], and the witnesses had laid their coats at the feet of a young man named Saul[2], who stood there consenting to the death[3]. Within a chapter Saul was entering house after house and dragging men and women off to prison[4].

Years later, under arrest in Jerusalem, Paul told the story himself as one of his credentials, how he had stood by and kept the coats of Stephen’s killers[5]. Before Agrippa he added that when the saints he had imprisoned were put to death he cast his vote against them[6]. The first letter to Timothy, in his name, calls him the chief of sinners and says he obtained mercy so that Christ’s patience would be shown in him first, as a pattern for everyone who would believe after[7]. The men and women he dragged to prison go unnamed in Acts and in all thirteen letters.

His own death was the one debt Stephen had the standing to cancel. The god went further and forgave Saul the houses as well[8], a debt owed to people never consulted. Mercy issued that way moves the debt. The persecutor leaves with a clean account and a story about grace, the only hand on his release is his god’s, and the people he dragged to prison are left holding a loss no one is allowed to bill him for. The same transfer is made at every family table where the injured are told to move on before the injurer has said a word.

Declaration: Heaven may pardon what was done to heaven, and what was done to me is mine to pardon or to bill.

The Rite

Choose one person you forgave who never made it right. Send them one line naming what they still owe, the apology, the money or the thing, and say aloud as you send it You still owe me, and I am still counting. Skip anyone it is unsafe to contact.

Testament · Whose debt did you cancel unasked, and who has been paying it since?

CCCVI Of Conversion

Reckoning

Day 306 of 365

Answer whoever taught you while you were afraid.

The Conversion of SaulGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

Acts puts no horse on the Damascus road. The engraving above has one at its edge anyway, rearing over men flung on open ground under shafts of light. The text says that a light from heaven flashed around him on the road, that he fell to the ground, and that a voice called him twice by name and asked why he persecuted the one speaking[1].

He was traveling with letters from the high priest to bring followers of the Way bound to Jerusalem[2]. After the light he was blind for three days and neither ate nor drank[3], until a disciple named Ananias laid hands on him and told him who had met him on the road. Something like scales fell from his eyes[4], he was told what he had been chosen for[5], and he was baptized.

A man knocked down, struck blind and three days without food or water is in no state to weigh what the next visitor tells him, and Acts sends one. The revivals made a method of it. At Enfield in seventeen forty-one a congregation was told that the god held each of them over the pit of hell as a man holds a spider over a fire[6], and a minister present wrote that the shrieks and cries were so piercing[7] the preacher had to stop.

If any of what you believe was put there while someone had you frightened, at a camp altar at fourteen or under a sermon on the pit, it went in the way the commission went into Saul. A belief taken in while the listener was shrieking was not weighed when it went in. Said aloud, beside the name of whoever planted it, it holds or it falls, and what falls goes back to whoever planted it.

Declaration: A sermon that needs the pit has confessed the poverty of every other argument it had.

The Rite

Tie a scarf over your eyes and say aloud the belief put into you in fear and the name of whoever put it there. Then say You put this in me while I was frightened, and now I judge it. Take off the scarf and cut it in two.

Testament · Who taught you something while you were frightened, and what did they put there?

[7] Diary of Stephen Williams, 8 Jul 1741


CCCVII Of Unclean Things

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 307 of 365

Eat the unclean thing and enjoy the hesitation.

Peter Preaches in the House of CorneliusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A great sheet comes down out of the sky by its four corners to a man praying on a rooftop in Joppa at noon[1]. Inside it are four-footed animals of every sort, creeping things, wild beasts, birds of the air, and a voice tells Peter to get up, kill and eat. He refuses because nothing common or unclean has ever passed his lips. The voice answers that what the god has cleansed he must not call common[2], and the scene is played three times.

Peter took the vision to be about people. The Spirit then sent him to the house of a centurion named Cornelius, where he explained to a gentile household that his law had forbidden him to come[3]. When he got back to Jerusalem the charge against him was that he had gone in to uncircumcised men and eaten with them[4]. At the council that later settled what gentile converts owed the law, Peter asked why they would put on the disciples’ necks a yoke their fathers could not bear[5], and the converts were released from nearly all of the old diet[6].

Leviticus had named the camel, the pig, the hare and the rock badger, and had classed the last two as chewing the cud, which neither does[7]. A list that got its own animals wrong, and was waived for gentiles after a rooftop vision, still sorted tables for centuries, deciding who ate with whom, and trained the hand to pause before the mouth at every meal. A former Latter-day Saint can feel it over a cup of coffee and a former Muslim over a slice of ham, years after the belief has gone.

A pause that shortens each time it is overruled was never a law. Peter needed three repetitions from heaven to override his, and yours needs one forkful.

Declaration: Heaven let the sheet down three times and Peter never ate from it, and I eat at the first bite.

The Rite · No faith

Eat bacon or a ham roll and, before the first bite, say aloud This is unclean, and it is mine.

Testament · Which food still makes your hand hesitate, and whose voice is in the hesitation?

[7] Lev 11:5–6


CCCVIII Of Chains

Reckoning

Day 308 of 365

Pay the one who believed you, and let the rest pray.

Peter Is Delivered from PrisonGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Herod had killed James the brother of John with the sword[1]. Seeing that it pleased the people, he took Peter as well and kept him under four squads of soldiers[2], asleep in two chains between two of them with guards at the door. Acts says the church prayed for him without ceasing[3]. On the plate the angel leads him barefoot down the steps past the slumped guards, and the text adds that the iron gate to the city swung open of its own accord[4].

He went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where many were gathered praying[5], and knocked at the door of the gate. A servant girl named Rhoda came to answer, knew his voice[6], and was so glad that she ran in without opening and told them Peter was standing outside. They told her she was mad. When she kept insisting, they said it must be his angel[7]. Peter went on knocking in the street[8], a fugitive with an empty cell behind him, while the people who had gathered that night to pray for him argued about whether it could be him.

Their prayer was answered at the gate, and the whole house refused the answer except the one person in it with no standing to be believed. Plenty will pray for you, put your name on a list and keep the door barred while they do it. Whatever you have to give, the key or the chair at your table, belongs first to the girl who knew your voice through the door.

Declaration: Rhoda had no standing in that house, and she is the only one in it I would let in at midnight.

The Rite

Hand the one person who has earned the run of your house a key you already hold, or the door code. If someone who has not earned one still holds a key, change the lock or the code today.

Testament · Who knew your voice when you were in chains?

CCCIX Of Work

Heresy

Day 309 of 365

Eat one dinner you have not earned.

Paul Preaches to the ThessaloniansGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The first Soviet constitution, adopted in nineteen eighteen[1], set down in its article on labor the rule that whoever does not work shall not eat[2], a sentence a letter in Paul’s name had carried long before. The letter to the Thessalonians says it of believers who had stopped working and were living as busybodies off the community[3], after Paul had worked night and day among them[4] so as to be a burden to none. It was written to shame a few idle members of one congregation.

Captain John Smith made it law at Jamestown in sixteen oh eight, telling the colonists that the labor of thirty or forty industrious men would no longer feed a hundred and fifty idle loiterers[5], and he later threatened to banish across the river anyone who gathered less than he did, until the man mended or starved[6]. Proverbs had already sent the sluggard to school with the ant[7], which has no guide, overseer or ruler and still gathers its food, so the scripture’s own model worker answers to no one. The two who wrote it into law, the president of a starving fort and the drafters of a workers’ republic, each spoke it from above a workforce.

Guilt on an empty afternoon keeps the rule now, and so does rest defended as a way to work better later, the foreman’s voice still talking after the shift has ended. An hour of idleness neither earned nor saved for later use answers the whole theology, and the dinner eaten in that hour is the one meal of the week that answers to no shift bell.

Declaration: No overseer has a claim on the time I waste, and I waste it at the table.

The Rite

Cook a slow dish, one that wants an hour of simmering and a stir now and then, and eat it at an hour you ought to be working, with your feet on a chair. If guilt arrives, keep eating.

Testament · Whose voice tells you that rest must be justified, and what did it ever pay you?

Sources

[1] Constitution of the RSFSR (1918), art. 18

[2] 2 Thess 3:10

[3] 2 Thess 3:11

[4] 2 Thess 3:8; 1 Thess 2:9

[5] J. Smith, Generall Historie of Virginia (1624), bk. 3

[6] J. Smith, Generall Historie of Virginia (1624), bk. 3

[7] Prov 6:6–8


CCCX Of Magic

Mastery

Day 310 of 365

Study where the eyes go.

Paul Preaches at EphesusGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

At Ephesus, Acts says, the god worked unusual miracles by Paul’s hands, so that handkerchiefs and aprons carried from his body[1] to the sick drove out their diseases and the evil spirits with them. Seven sons of a chief priest named Sceva[2] tried the same formula on a possessed man, in the name of the Jesus whom Paul preached. The spirit answered that it knew Jesus and knew Paul[3] and asked who they were, and the man leaped on them and sent them running from the house naked and bleeding[4].

The words were the same in both mouths and worked in only one, so by Acts’s own evidence the name alone did nothing. A formula that works for one man and fails for his imitators is a craft with an owner, and the seven brothers had learned the patter without the hands. After the brothers fled, many in Ephesus who practiced the curious arts brought their books together and burned them in public, and the books were valued at fifty thousand silver pieces[5], a library of technique fed to the fire by men newly persuaded that the power lay in a name.

In eighteen eighty-eight Margaret Fox, who with her younger sister had started the spirit rappings in a farmhouse at Hydesville forty years before, stood on the stage of the Academy of Music in New York and made the raps with the joints of her toes[6]. By her own account every séance of hers in between had run on a practiced foot. She took the confession back the following year[7]. Spiritualist churches founded on those raps still hold services, a congregation kept by a trick its own author had performed on a lit stage.

Declaration: Every wonder the church kept behind a rail was a trick afraid of the front row.

The Rite

Learn one card or coin trick from a magician’s tutorial, in an hour at most. Perform it today for one person, notice where they look at the moment of the move, and keep the method to yourself.

Testament · Which wonder have you believed without ever looking for the other hand?

Sources

[1] Acts 19:11–12

[2] Acts 19:13–14

[3] Acts 19:15

[4] Acts 19:16

[5] Acts 19:17–19

[6] New York World, 21 Oct 1888

[7] Margaret Fox, recantation of November 1889


CCCXI Of Mobs

Heresy

Day 311 of 365

Refuse the crowd your hand.

Paul Is Rescued from the CrowdGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A gentile from Ephesus named Trophimus had been seen walking in Jerusalem with Paul[1], and that was the whole of the evidence. Men from the province of Asia who spotted Paul in the temple supposed he had brought the foreigner into the sacred precinct, and shouted it. The whole city was moved and the people ran together. They dragged Paul out, the doors were shut behind him, and they were beating him to death when the garrison came down at a run.

The commander had Paul bound with two chains[2] before he asked who he was and what he had done, and the crowd shouted one thing and another, so that for the uproar he could learn nothing certain[3]. His soldiers carried him up the barracks steps, with the crowd behind them crying for him to be done away with. When Paul’s speech from the steps raised only a second uproar, the commander ordered the prisoner examined under the lash[4].

Deuteronomy puts the hands of the witnesses first on the condemned and then the hands of all the people[5], so that a death belonged first to the men who had testified to the crime. The mob that convenes on a screen keeps that procedure without the witnesses, a supposition raised to a cry and the cry to a crowd that cannot hear an answer over its own noise, and the verdict reaches its target before anyone in it has read the charge.

The crowd that nearly killed Paul over a stranger’s footsteps lost nothing by being wrong. Its witnesses from Asia did not come to Caesarea to make the charge[6], and the man it accused spent two years bound there[7] all the same.

Declaration: A mob has a thousand throats and no name to sign, and I sign everything I say.

The Rite

Find the loudest pile-on today and read in full the message it began from. Unfollow every account in the pile that passed a verdict without quoting it, and post nothing about it yourself.

Testament · What did you know of the case when you last added your voice to a crowd’s verdict?

[1] Acts 21:29

[3] Acts 21:34

CCCXII Of Shipwreck

Heresy

Day 312 of 365

Enter the loss under the name of whoever chose it.

Paul Is ShipwreckedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

At Fair Havens on Crete, with sailing now dangerous because the fast of the Day of Atonement was already past[1], Paul warned the ship’s company that he perceived the voyage would be with hurt and much damage to the lading, the ship and their lives. The centurion believed the helmsman and the owner of the ship[2] more than Paul, and the more part advised[3] leaving a harbor not fit to winter in for Phenice, a haven of Crete, to winter there.

The storm that followed lasted fourteen days, and for many of them nobody aboard saw sun or stars, until all hope that they should be saved was taken away[4]. After long abstinence Paul stood forth in the midst of them and told them they should have hearkened to him[5] and not loosed from Crete, and so gained this harm and loss, and he promised that no man’s life would be lost, only the ship[6]. Before dawn on the fourteenth day he told them to eat, said that not an hair would fall[7] from the head of any of them, took bread, gave thanks to his god[8] in presence of them all and ate, and when they had eaten enough they cast the wheat into the sea[9]. There were two hundred and seventy-six souls aboard.

The bow ran aground and held fast at daybreak, the stern broke up under the waves, and all of them reached the shore of Malta, the swimmers first and the rest on planks and pieces of the ship[10]. The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners, and the centurion, wanting to save Paul[11], stopped them.

Declaration: Anyone who warns me before the voyage will be heard, and the ship’s owner does not outrank them.

The Rite

Write your worst loss at the top of a page, its cost in money and years beneath it, and the name of the person who made the call that caused it. Sign the page and say They chose it, and I paid for it.

Testament · Whose decision are you still thanking heaven for?

CCCXIII Of Patmos

Indulgence

Day 313 of 365

Seat no one at your table out of hunger.

John on PatmosGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Patmos is a dry island of some thirteen square miles off the coast of Asia, and a man named John says he was there for the word of God and the testimony of Jesus[1]. Church tradition sends him there old, an exile under the emperor Domitian[2], writing across the water to the seven churches he could no longer visit[3], and on that rock he drew up a guest list for the end of the world.

Revelation sets two suppers on either side of the white rider’s war. An angel tells John to write that those called to the marriage supper of the Lamb[4] are blessed, and a few verses later another angel stands in the sun and calls every bird in the sky[5] to the supper of the great god, to eat the flesh of kings and captains and mighty men, of horses and their riders. The exile furnished his feast so that the host chooses every guest and the uninvited are the meat.

Leaving a faith costs a whole table, the people who brought food when someone died and kept a chair for you at every feast, and the hunger that follows is a poor judge of guests. It takes whatever is set in front of it, the potluck among people who still pray for your return, the evenings given to bores and borrowers because any voice beats the quiet. That hunger keeps the Lamb’s seating after the Lamb is gone, a chair beside whoever else was called and no say in who. A table laid for the one face you most want across from you feeds it better than a hall full of whoever was free.

Declaration: Heaven’s host picks every guest and feeds the rest to the birds, and I pick mine with my eyes open.

The Rite

Choose the one person whose company you want most, invite them today, and feed them at your expense at the best table you can afford. Serve them first, saying You are the one I wanted here.

Testament · Whose company have you been settling for, and whom would you rather have across from you?

Sources

[1] Rev 1:9

[2] Eusebius, HE 3.18.1

[3] Rev 1:4, 11

[4] Rev 19:9

[5] Rev 19:17–18


CCCXIV Of the Pale Horse

Blasphemy ●●●●

Day 314 of 365

Live hard enough to dread leaving.

The Pale Horse of DeathGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Of the four riders in Revelation only the fourth was given a name, and the name was Death[1]. His horse was the green-gray of new shoots or of a corpse, a color English settled into pale. Hades followed with him. The two were given power over a fourth part of the earth, to kill with the sword and with famine and with plague and by the wild beasts[2].

Behind them the preachers marched a retinue gathered from later chapters and other books, everything they would sell as protection, the books opened before the white throne[3], Matthew’s judgment with its sorting of sheep from goats[4] and its fire kept for the goats[5]. The sermon on the last things has run as a transaction ever since, terror of the rider exchanged for a ticket out of his company. Take that retinue away and Death rides as his own verse has him, with only the grave at his heels, and behind him comes the end of one particular life and the earth going on with no court sitting anywhere.

Death took the voice that told the same story at every dinner and got the ending wrong, and the hand that knew the bread was done by the sound of the crust. What he left behind was a chair still turned toward the window and a table one place short.

Without the fear they were hired to sell, what remains is the reluctance worth having, the measure of a life that was enjoyed, and it belongs to the last hour of a good party, when the music has stopped and somebody is bringing down the coats.

Declaration: Death can have the body once I have worn it out, and the preachers get nothing.

The Rite · Christian

Recite the Apostles’ Creed aloud backwards, word by word, from the life everlasting to God the Father almighty, as the black masses of legend did. Then say One life, and I am spending it.

Testament · What would you most hate to leave if death came for you today, and when did you last enjoy it?

[1] Rev 6:8

[2] Rev 6:8

[3] Rev 20:12–14

[4] Matt 25:32–33

[5] Matt 25:41


CCCXV Of the Queen of Heaven

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 315 of 365

Refuse to be measured by what your body has not done.

The Virgin Is CrownedGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

In Egypt Jeremiah told the refugees from Judah that their ruin had come from burning incense to other gods. The women and their husbands answered that while they burned incense to the queen of heaven, baked cakes for her and poured out drink offerings they had bread enough and saw no harm[1], and that since they stopped they had lacked everything[2]. Jeremiah promised them the sword.

In time the title passed to a Galilean girl. The woman of Revelation, clothed with the sun and crowned with twelve stars[3], who gives birth while a dragon waits to devour the child, was read as Mary. The Church went on to define her a virgin before the birth, during it and after it[4], and Rome declared her taken body and soul into heaven[5] in nineteen fifty, and gave her a feast as queen of heaven four years later, the title the women of Judah had baked for. Mark names four brothers of Jesus[6], and James, Judas, Simon and Joses became cousins in the West and Joseph’s sons by an earlier wife in the East, since an ever-virgin mother could not have borne them.

The fathers found her womb in Ezekiel, in the temple gate the prophet was told must stay shut[7] because his god had come in through it, and no man would ever enter it again. Ambrose set that gate before a girl named Ambrosia[8] in the treatise he wrote for her consecration as a virgin, and held up to her a mother whose body even a birth left sealed, a standard no woman who has borne a child or taken a lover can meet. The women in Egypt baked for a queen and ate well, and Ambrosia was handed a shut gate to keep for the rest of her life.

Declaration: Rome can keep its crown on a plaster head, and I keep the lovers it was made to shame.

The Rite · Christian

Write Ever virgin across a picture of Mary you own or print, strike the words through, and write above them the name of someone you have wanted as an adult.

Testament · Who profited from your pride in the things you were taught never to do?

[2] Jer 44:18

CCCXVI Of the Cup

Beauty

Day 316 of 365

Stop preaching against what you cannot stop watching.

The Whore of BabylonAlbrecht Dürer · The Apocalypse, 1498

The seer of Revelation could not stop dressing the great harlot of Babylon. She rides a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns[1], in purple and scarlet, hung with gold and pearls and precious stones, with a golden cup in her hand full of the filth of her fornication, and the kings of the earth had all slept with her[2]. When he saw her drunk on the blood of the saints, he says, he wondered at her with great admiration, and the angel had to ask him why he marveled[3].

Jimmy Swaggart spent the nineteen eighties on television denouncing sin, and in nineteen eighty-six he accused a fellow preacher[4], Marvin Gorman, of adultery, which all but ended Gorman’s ministry. Gorman’s son and son-in-law then watched a motel outside New Orleans and photographed Swaggart there with a prostitute[5]. In nineteen eighty-eight Swaggart wept before his congregation that he had sinned[6], without saying how, and went on preaching after his church defrocked him. In nineteen ninety-one police in Indio, California stopped him for traffic violations with a woman beside him who said she was a prostitute, and he told his congregation the Lord had told him it was flat none of their business[7].

The seer inventoried the harlot down to her pearls, the preacher sought her kind at a motel, and both called down fire on her[8]. Neither looked away. A man condemns hardest the pleasure he has looked at longest, because the sermon lets him keep looking with clean hands. The woman on the beast wears her name on her forehead[9] and holds her cup up where the kings and the seer can all see it, the one figure in the chapter who hides nothing, and whoever takes a pleasure in the open gives the preachers nothing to photograph.

Declaration: Every sermon against the flesh is a confession with the details left out.

The Rite

Pour whatever you like best into the most beautiful cup you own. Then put on the clothes you condemn when others wear them, or play the music you sneer at and dance to it alone, and drink.

Testament · Which pleasure in other people do you find yourself watching longest?

CCCXVII Of Merchandise

Indulgence

Day 317 of 365

Buy the luxury and owe heaven no apology for it.

Babylon Has FallenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Cinnamon is on the list of cargoes that Babylon’s merchants mourn in Revelation. When the city falls, the merchants of the earth stand far off and weep[1] because nobody buys their cargoes any more[2]. The book itemizes those cargoes with a dealer’s care, the gold and silver and pearls, fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet, the cinnamon and spice and incense, the wine and oil and fine flour, the cattle and horses and chariots, and last of all, after the chariots, the bodies and souls of men[3].

The fall leaves a ruin of smoke and silence[4], a city become the haunt of every foul spirit and a cage for every unclean and hateful bird[5], and the verdict counts her luxury among her crimes[6].

The angel who hurls the millstone into the sea[7] gives his reasons, and the first is that her merchants were the great men of the earth[8]. Greatness in trade heads the angel’s list, ahead of the sorcery and the blood of the prophets. The sentence falls on the whole city at once, and with the market in bodies it silences the harper and the piper, the craftsman of every craft, the miller at his stone[9], the light of the lamp and the bridegroom’s voice[10]. The seer wrote the souls of men into one inventory with the cinnamon and the fine flour, and the burning that ends the slave market ends the bakery with it. A verdict that cannot tell the miller from the slaver has lost the right to sentence either, and the cinnamon dealer, standing far off for fear of her torment[11], is owed exactly what he was owed before she fell, his price.

Declaration: Money paid for excellent work is the cleanest praise one adult gives another, and I owe no apology for the pleasure it buys.

The Rite

Make one dish from the merchants’ own list, fine flour and good oil and true cinnamon bark, the best of each you can get, bought from its maker where you can, and serve it on the finest plate you own.

Testament · Who taught you to feel guilty for wanting the cargo you have never bought yourself?

CCCXVIII Of the City

Beauty

Day 318 of 365

Put paradise on before you die.

The New JerusalemGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

The new Jerusalem is a cube. It runs twelve thousand furlongs on each side and stands as high as it is long[1], about fourteen hundred miles, the shape of the inner sanctuary of Solomon’s temple[2] swollen to the size of a subcontinent. An angel carries John up a great high mountain[3] and measures the city with a golden reed. The wall is jasper, the city pure gold as clear as glass[4], each of the twelve foundations faced with its own stone from jasper to amethyst[5], each of the twelve gates cut from a single pearl, and the main street paved with gold you can see through[6].

The men who imagined paradise walled and paved it with the finest things they had seen in the goldsmith’s shop and the gem dealer’s tray. The first letter to Timothy tells women to adorn themselves without gold or pearls or costly clothing[7], so the pearl a believer might not wear in this life was promised to her as a gate in the next. Take away the doctrine and what remains is a hunger for beauty so strong it had to be deferred to the end of the world.

The stones are for sale. Most of the twelve sit on a jeweler’s tray in your own town, and a small pearl, a poor cousin of the ones the gates were cut from, costs less than a good dinner. An amethyst, the twelfth foundation, has the purple of a grape held up to a lamp, and a jasper, the first, can be as red as a bitten lip. The gate asked a lifetime of plain dress paid in advance for a pearl no believer has yet touched, and the jeweler hands one across the counter the same afternoon, to be worn by someone alive enough to feel its weight.

Declaration: I take my pearl now and leave the gate to whoever is still waiting at it.

The Rite

Put on the finest of the new Jerusalem’s stones you own, an amethyst, a topaz, a piece of jasper or a pearl like its gates, or buy one, and wear it all day where you can feel it.

Testament · Which fine thing would you wear every day if no one had ever called it vanity?

CCCXIX Of Glory

Heresy

Day 319 of 365

When praised, agree.

Glory and Praise to You, SatanOdilon Redon · Les Fleurs du mal, 1890

Isaiah’s god says twice that he will not give his glory to another[1]. Herod Agrippa, in royal robes on a day set[2] for the purpose, made a speech from the throne at Caesarea, and the crowd shouted that this was the voice of a god and no man[3]. An angel struck him because he did not give God the glory, and he was eaten by worms and died[4]. The other account of that death, by a Jewish historian of the same century, adds that the robe was woven wholly of silver[5] and blazed in the morning sun.

Tradition gives the adversary the same offense, a cherub who looked at his own brightness and approved of it[6] before the fall. The apostle wrote the rule for everyone below the throne, asking the Corinthians what they had that they had not received[7], and why, if they had received it, they boasted as though it were theirs.

People who never read the letter keep the rule. The athlete points at the sky after the goal, the believer answers a compliment with thanks to the Lord, and the rest have learned the secular forms, the joke at one’s own expense and the shrug that calls a year’s work luck. Each hands the credit away before it can land, and each tells the one person who noticed the work that they were mistaken to notice it.

Agrippa died, by both accounts[8], for letting a crowd call him a god. Praise for finished work is a different thing, a report from someone who looked at it. To the apostle’s question, what do you have that you did not receive, a piece of work done well answers with the hours, which no god put in, and the praise for them belongs to whoever spent them.

Declaration: Lucifer fell for admiring his own brightness, and I admire mine with the lamps on.

The Rite

Hang the best evidence of your own work, the certificate, the photograph, the review or the thing you made, at eye level in the room where guests sit. Then stand before it and say aloud I did that, and I did it well.

Testament · What do you say when someone praises you, and whom does that answer protect?
