CCCLVIII Of Defeat

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 358 of 365

Name the archers, and leave the hill out of it.

The Death of SaulGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Archers found Saul on Mount Gilboa. The last chapter of the first book of Samuel has him wounded by them, begging his armor-bearer to run him through before the uncircumcised could come and abuse him, and when the young man would not[1], falling on his own sword. The next book opens with a second account, from an Amalekite, who reaches David at Ziklag, says he finished the king off at Saul’s own request, and lays the crown and the bracelet before his new lord[2]. David has him struck down for killing the anointed[3].

Chronicles copies the archers and the sword[4] and then adds a second reason to the one Samuel’s ghost had given at Endor[5]. Saul died for his unfaithfulness and for consulting a medium, it says, and so the god killed him and turned the kingdom over to David[6]. David’s own lament over the same hill names no god at all. It mourns the mighty fallen, and curses the mountains of Gilboa, that neither dew nor rain should fall on them[7]. The first two name only human hands and disagree about who struck the last blow. The third adds the god, and the fourth curses the mountain.

A defeat attracts the same verdicts, the flattering story, the god’s displeasure and the guilty ground. People keep away from the office that let them go and the town where the marriage ended as though the hill had passed sentence, and the avoidance keeps the sentence in force. Archers and a wound are causes, and a cause can be studied and beaten. A curse on the ground can only be obeyed, and every road you take around that town obeys one.

Declaration: Let the Chronicler credit the god with my wounds. I go back up that mountain in better armor.

The Rite · No faith

Write on a card the line people gave you after your worst defeat, everything happens for a reason or God has a plan, wipe the soles of your shoes on it and throw it away. Then say aloud what actually caused the defeat.

Testament · Which place do you still avoid because you lost there?

CCCLIX Of the Hidden Way

Reckoning

Day 359 of 365

Stop asking the guards whether the gate is open.

The Hidden WayGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXXIV, 1861

Saul came to Damascus carrying the high priest’s letters, with authority to bring any man or woman of the Way back to Jerusalem in chains[1]. He stayed to preach in the synagogues the Way he had come to hunt, and the city turned on him. Luke has the gates watched day and night to kill him[2], Paul has a governor under King Aretas[3] guarding the city, and in both accounts he goes down the wall in a basket, by night in Luke[4] and through a window in Paul’s own telling.

Paul told that night as a boast. Listing his sufferings for the Corinthians, the rods, the stoning and the three shipwrecks[5], he closed with the basket, among the things he would glory in because they showed his weakness[6]. A deputy sent to bring defectors home bound went over the wall as one, and scripture tells the escape twice, both times on his side.

The letter to the Hebrews, bound into the same scripture as his basket, calls it impossible to restore to repentance anyone who has tasted the heavenly gift and fallen away[7]. The Quran voids the deeds of anyone who turns from the faith and dies in unbelief[8], and gives him the fire forever, and the Witnesses shun those removed from the congregation, their relatives outside the household included, until they return on the elders’ terms. Each prices the way out so high that the description does the work of a lock.

A lock made of description holds only while it is believed, and every leaver who lives well afterward is a hole in it. The shunning keeps the hole out of sight, since a member forbidden to speak with a leaver never hears how the leaver is doing, and so never learns that the wall had a window in it.

Declaration: I came down their wall by night, and no threat they send after me will haul the basket back up.

The Rite

Buy a meal or a coffee for someone who left a faith or a group that says no one leaves well, and say Tell me how you got out. Listen to the whole story before you pay.

Testament · Who profits from your believing that leaving would ruin you?

CCCLX Of the Father’s Bones

Heresy

Day 360 of 365

Arrange only a funeral you can stand behind.

Jacob Goes to EgyptGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jacob made Joseph swear, with a hand under his thigh[1], not to bury him in Egypt. Carry me out of this country, the old man said, and lay me with my fathers in their burying place, and when Joseph had sworn it Jacob bowed himself on the head of the bed.

Joseph kept the oath and chose everything else. He had his servants the physicians embalm his father, forty days of the Egyptian art[2], and Egypt wept for Jacob seventy days. Pharaoh’s servants and the elders of the land went up with the body, with chariots and horsemen, a very great company[3], and the Canaanites who watched the mourning at the threshing floor of Atad named the place Abel-mizraim, the mourning of Egypt[4]. The father who asked to be carried out of Egypt was carried into Canaan wrapped in it.

A dying parent can bind the ground and no more, because a promise to the dying is kept by the living, with the living’s hands and on the living’s terms. A believing mother will want her rites at the end, the priest at the bedside or the body washed and buried within the day. She will not be there to see how they are done, and the funeral will speak for whoever arranged it, as Joseph’s spoke for Joseph. Keep the letter of whatever you swore, and choose the rest yourself. Genesis sums up the burial in one line, that his sons did for Jacob exactly as he had commanded them[5], and then sends Joseph back down into Egypt[6] to live out his own life.

Declaration: I keep my word to the dying and my conscience at the graveside, and the dead have never told the two apart.

The Rite

Write down what you have promised, or would promise, a believing parent for their funeral, and beside each item the way you will do it. Sign it and give it to the sibling or executor who will stand with you.

Testament · Which of a believing parent’s last wishes would you carry out in your own manner, and how?

CCCLXI Of Resolve

Mastery

Day 361 of 365

Take your vows off the stage.

Satan on Mount NiphatesGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IV, 1866

Peter made his vow with the other disciples listening. All of them might fall away from Jesus that night, he said, but he never would, and when Jesus told him he would deny him three times before the cock crowed, Peter swore he would die with him first. The others said the same[1]. Before morning, sitting with the servants by a fire[2] in the high priest’s courtyard, he was told by a serving girl, then by another, then by the bystanders, that he had been with the Galilean. He denied it, then denied it with an oath, and the third time began to curse and swear that he did not know the man[3]. At once the cock crew, as Jesus had said.

The vow broke in front of a different audience from the one it was made to. At the fire the boast met servants and strangers, and a vow made for the twelve said nothing to them.

The Church builds resolution into penance. Absolution asks for contrition, and contrition includes a firm purpose of amendment[4], the resolution not to sin again. The same Church recommends confessing everyday faults regularly[5], which expects the faults back. Canon law says the same of the one who comes for absolution, that he must reject the sins committed and have a purpose of amendment.

A resolve made for an audience dies when the audience leaves the room. One that answers to the want alone fails on a Tuesday and starts again on Wednesday, because no one was ever owed its success, and no one is there to absolve it.

Declaration: I break my resolutions in private and keep them the same way, and no confessor takes a share of either.

The Rite

Write on a card one resolution for something you want, small enough to keep this week and exact enough to break. Tell no one. Say over it This one is for me, put it in your wallet, and do the first piece today.

Testament · Which of your resolutions was made for someone watching?

CCCLXII Of the Other Road

Blasphemy ●●●○

Day 362 of 365

Go through the wide gate and look around.

The Guide Finds the Traveller WeepingGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto I, 1861

Narrow is the way that leads to life, the sermon says, and few find it[1]. Wide is the gate and broad the way to destruction, and many go in thereat[2]. The saying gives their widths, their traffic and where each ends, and leaves the reader to supply the country.

Luke sets it as the reply when someone asks whether few are saved[3]. Strive to enter, for many will seek to enter and not be able[4]. Many take the wide road, and apart from its width, its crowd and where it ends the sermon tells you nothing about it.

The Book of Mormon fills it. The prophet Lehi dreams a tree whose fruit is sweeter than any he has tasted, a mist of darkness that takes the path from people already on their way[5], and a fountain where many drown[6]. On the far side of the river stands a great and spacious building[7] full of old and young in exceedingly fine clothes, pointing and mocking at those who eat. Those who leave the path are shown only at a distance, lost in forbidden paths and strange roads[8], and the one life off the path drawn in any detail is a crowd in fine clothes, in a building Lehi’s son later watches fall[9].

Every map of the wide road was drawn from the narrow one, and shows what can be seen from there, a crowd mocking, a mist, a fall promised at the end. Whoever goes through the wide gate finds the rest, an evening at cards or on a dance floor, a Sunday morning spent in bed, and finds destruction where the sermon placed it, at the far end, where both roads go into the ground.

Declaration: I was warned off the wide road by people who never walked it, and I walked it.

The Rite · Christian

Read aloud the verse about the wide gate, then spend two hours at what your church warned would lead you through it, a dance, a card game or an evening at a bar with a soft drink if you prefer, and enjoy it.

Testament · Which pleasure of the broad way do you know only from the warnings against it?

CCCLXIII Of the Kiss

Heresy

Day 363 of 365

Take the word of the one you wronged.

Jacob and Esau MeetGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Two decades after the stolen blessing, the brothers met in the open. Jacob bowed to the ground seven times[1] as he came near, and Esau ran to him, threw his arms round his neck and kissed him, and they wept.

In the Torah scroll the word for that kiss carries a row of dots over its letters, and two rabbis of the midrash divided over the marks. One sage held that Esau kissed him with his whole heart. Another said he had come to bite that neck and found it turned to marble[2]. The doubter could point to Malachi’s god, declaring that he loved Jacob and hated Esau[3], and would not take the wronged man’s kiss at its word.

Jacob would not either. He pressed his present on him, calling it his blessing[4], the word for what he had taken from their blind father, and Esau accepted it, so the word he had once cried over came to him from the thief’s own hand. Then Esau offered his company twice, first to travel on together, then to leave some of his own men with him[5]. Jacob turned down both. He sent him on to Seir[6] and promised to follow at the pace of the flocks and the young.

A debt kept open lets the debtor pay from a distance and spares him the road beside his creditor, where he would be looked at as an equal. Jacob had his release in the open, before both households, and spent it on a detour. The text never brings him to Seir. He went to Succoth, built himself a house there and made booths for his cattle[7].

Declaration: A wrong forgiven to my face is closed, and I walk beside the man who closed it.

The Rite

Contact someone you once wronged who has told you it is settled, and propose a meal or a walk together, bringing nothing. Say Let us go on together, and go.

Testament · By whose reckoning are you still paying for an old wrong of yours?

CCCLXIV Of the Feast in the Siege

Indulgence

Day 364 of 365

Dress for the feast while the siege is on.

Angels Descend into ParadiseGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book XI, 1866

Isaiah watched Jerusalem hold a feast in a time of siege. The god had called for weeping and mourning, for shaven heads and sackcloth[1], and instead the city was slaughtering oxen and killing sheep, eating meat and drinking wine, and saying let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die[2]. The prophet hears the god’s answer in his own ears, that this sin will not be wiped out of them until they die[3].

The feasters had named the penalty before the god did. Tomorrow we die was their reason for the meat, and the sentence handed back to them is that same tomorrow, the death the men at the spit had counted on before the prophet opened his mouth.

Paul quoted the feasters to the Corinthians as the conclusion that follows if the dead are not raised[4], and meant it to sound absurd. Take away the resurrection, as he asks his readers to suppose, and their line stops being a sin and becomes the simplest reading of a short life, and a god whose last threat is the grave has nothing left to hold over anyone who has already accepted it.

Whoever has made that peace is free to kill the ox, and owes the prophets no tears in the meantime. In the same chapter Jerusalem was counting its houses and tearing them down to shore up the defenses[5] and cutting a reservoir for water, and of all the city’s labor that day the feast alone was done for the pleasure of the people behind the wall.

Declaration: Let the prophets keep their sackcloth, and I will keep the table set.

The Rite

Answer the call to shaven heads and sackcloth with its opposite. Have your hair cut, washed and dressed today by the best hand you can afford, and leave smelling of whatever they put on it. Say Tomorrow we die to the mirror.

Testament · Which call to mourning have you obeyed lately, and what pleasure did it cost you?

[1] Isa 22:12

[2] Isa 22:13

[3] Isa 22:14

[4] 1 Cor 15:32

[5] Isa 22:10–11


CCCLXV Of the Stars

Blasphemy ●●○○

Day 365 of 365

Spend today on what you will lose first.

The Stars AgainGustave Doré · Inferno, Canto XXXIV, 1861

When the night came over him, the Quran says, Abraham saw a star and said that this was his lord, and when it set he said that he did not love things that set[1]. He tried the moon, then the sun, calling it the greater, and when it set he told his people he was free of what they set beside God, and turned from everything in the sky to the one who made it[2]. Genesis takes him out under the same sky toward heaven. The god tells him to count the stars if he can[3], promises him descendants as many, and the covenant that follows is made with his seed after him, everlasting, to be a god unto him and to his seed after him[4].

By Abraham’s test a meal that goes cold and a body that wears down by the hour would each be struck from the list of what can be loved.

Genesis calls the sign a token of the covenant betwixt me and you[5], sets it on a boy’s eighth day, he that is eight days old shall be circumcised among you[6], and sets the penalty for the man who refuses, that soul shall be cut off from his people[7]. Abraham took the sign at ninety and nine and Ishmael his son at thirteen[8]. In the selfsame day was Abraham circumcised, and Ishmael his son, and all the men of his house were circumcised with him. His sons Isaac and Ishmael bury him in the cave of Machpelah, in the field he bought from the sons of Heth[9].

Declaration: I bind no one before they can answer, and I answer for myself.

The Rite · Christian

Hold your own Bible up to the sky, or to a window, read aloud the commandment against other gods, and then name the sun or the evening star as yours for the day. Say I love what sets.

Testament · Which bond were you born into, and what would you keep of it?

The Anniversary

Anniversary · kept by you

The day after Day 365

Sit as the only judge of your own vow.

Devota ProfesiónFrancisco Goya · Los Caprichos, 1799

The plate above, Capricho 70 of 1799, shows an apprentice witch on the shoulders of a seated satyr swearing over a book that two figures in miters and capes hold out to her with pincers. The Prado manuscript glosses it as a novice swearing to obey and respect her mistresses and superiors, and the old commentary on the print lists her duties, to spin cloth and to fly every time she is commanded. Her answer to the list is I swear, and the commentary pronounces her a witch in the next sentence.

The Church binds an infant at the font on the word of parents and godparents[1], and the infant never spoke a word of the promise made in its name. Canon law, for its part, says a novice may leave the institute freely[2]. The signing screen told you the year runs 365 days from today. Today the 365 days close.

The pact you signed on your first day here opens I, the undersigned, of sound mind and my own master. After the faith you renounced it names every debt they claimed, every fear they taught me and the authority of everyone who spoke in their name, and it goes on, I answer to myself, whatever hope others hold for me. I expect no rescue, and I make the meaning I live by. I take my soul into my own keeping from this hour until my death, which ends the matter. I keep this pact for as long as it serves me and no longer. I sign freely, by my own leave.

Declaration: The devil gets from me a year signed once, judged by me, and kept to its last day.

The Rite

Read aloud your first day’s entry, or else the pact. Under it, on one line, write what the year paid you and what it cost, then sign and date the line.

Testament · What did the year give you that you did not have when you signed?

[1] Rite of Baptism for Children

[2] CIC 653 §1


By the Calendar

The Feasts

Fifty-five days that keep their own dates

The numbered days follow no calendar. These fifty-five do: fifty-four by the calendar of the faiths and the seasons, and the Anniversary by the reader’s own date. Each belongs to a date, a church, a people or a season, and on its date it takes the place of the numbered day, and that day is held. They answer the festal year of the faiths this book argues with, the older nights that came before them, and the days that belong to the reader alone. The Kalendarium at the front gives the date of each.

Omnia tempus habent

All things have their time

Ecclesiastes 3:1, Vulgate


The Feast of Your Birth

Feast · kept by you

The day you were born

Keep your birthday as a sovereign keeps his.

The WitchesHans Baldung Grien, 1510

The early Church called the day a martyr died his birthday[1], his birth into heaven, and wrote that date into its calendar while the day his mother bore him went unrecorded. Its calendar keeps the births of only three, Christ, his mother and the Baptist[2]. The Watch Tower Society keeps no birthday at all, and for evidence it points to the two birthday parties its Bible names, each of which ended in an execution.

Both parties belong to kings. On his birthday Pharaoh made a feast for all his servants and lifted up the heads of the two he had imprisoned, restoring his butler to the cup and hanging his baker[3]. Herod at his own feast swore to give a dancing girl whatever she asked and, bound by his oath, sent to the prison for a prophet’s head, which came to the table on a dish[4]. In each a sentence is passed at the head of the table with the guests looking on, and the sentence is part of the celebration.

A Church that dates nearly all its saints from the day they died and a Society that forbids the day you were born both look away from the day of an arrival, and the two birthdays in the Society’s Bible show what the day was for in the hands of kings, the table where a verdict falls, Pharaoh’s by choice and Herod’s by an oath he regretted. The rank behind the table is the point of the feast, and it passes to whoever takes the chair. Whoever earned your favor gets the cup back at your table. Whoever offended you hears your sentence there, in the modern coin of a bill presented or a door closed.

Declaration: Once a year I hold court, and the guest list is my judgment.

The Rite

Dress as for a coronation, buy yourself the thing you have wanted longest, and take the head of the table at the best meal you can command. Raise wine (or whatever you drink) first to the guest who earned it most, then to yourself. This one is to me.

Testament · What did this year teach you about who belongs at your table?

Sources

[1] Mart. Pol. 18.3

[2] General Roman Calendar, 25 Dec, 8 Sep, 24 Jun

[3] Gen 40:20–22

[4] Matt 14:6–11


Equal Night

Season · kept by everyone

20 March (22 September south of the equator)

Begin on a day no clerk chose.

EdenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IV, 1866

On the second of September seventeen fifty-two the people of Britain and its colonies went to bed and woke on the fourteenth[1]. Parliament had voted eleven days out of the calendar to bring it into line with the one a pope had introduced for Catholic Europe in fifteen eighty-two, and the same act moved the start of the year. Until then the legal year in England had begun on the twenty-fifth of March, Lady Day[2], the feast of the Annunciation, so that a deed signed in what we call February seventeen hundred was dated sixteen ninety-nine.

The book of Exodus says, And the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, This month shall be unto you the beginning of months, it shall be the first month of the year to you[3]. Later it says, This day came ye out in the month Abib[4].

The rabbis who kept the law of Moses counted four new years[5], in spring for kings and festivals, at the end of summer for the tithe of cattle, in autumn for the numbering of the years, and in winter for the trees. Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon put the new year for the tithe of cattle on the first of Tishrei, and Beit Shammai put the new year for trees on the first of Shevat while Beit Hillel put it on the fifteenth. Under the old reckoning in England a deed signed on the twenty-fourth of March bore one year and a deed signed the next day bore the next.

Declaration: I begin on a day I chose, and the calendar had no part in it.

The Rite

Buy or take out the tool that the thing you have been putting off needs. Write today’s date on a card with the name of the thing, set the card beside the tool, and give it its first hour today. Say It begins today, on nobody’s calendar.

Testament · What have you been saving for a better date to begin?

Sources

[1] Calendar (New Style) Act 1750 (24 Geo. 2 c. 23)

[2] Calendar (New Style) Act 1750

[3] Exod 12:2

[4] Exod 13:4

[5] m. Rosh Hashanah 1:1


The Longest Day

Season · kept by everyone

21 June (21 December in the south)

Increase, and leave the decrease to the saint.

Uriel Returns to the SunGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book IV, 1866

Six months before Christmas, on the twenty-fourth of June, the Church keeps the birth of John the Baptist. John had said of the one coming after him, to disciples who complained that everyone was going to him, that he must increase while John himself must decrease[1], and preachers of the fifth century set the two births against the sky, the days shortening from John’s and lengthening from Christ’s, so that the sun itself preached the saint’s diminishment. The longest days of the year went to the man who asked to grow less.

Mark dresses him in camel’s hair with a leather belt and feeds him locusts and wild honey[2] in the wilderness, and in Matthew Jesus remembers that John came neither eating nor drinking and was said to have a demon, while he himself came eating and drinking and was called a glutton and a drunkard[3] for it. The Church gave the season of longest light, when the sun at nine in the evening is still above Edinburgh, to the man of the wilderness and the locust.

The sky preached nothing. The days after the twenty-fourth shorten by the same minutes over the Baptist’s wilderness and the glutton’s table, and lengthen again after Christmas whether anyone has fasted or not, so the decrease was read into the tilt of the earth by preachers who wanted it there. The longest day is the year’s largest ration of light, and it goes to the body that takes the larger share, of the sun first and then of the table.

Declaration: I eat out of doors until dark today, and the Baptist can keep his locusts.

The Rite

Be outdoors for the sunrise and again for the sunset. Between them, take the larger share of one thing you would usually yield, the bigger portion or the better seat, and say to yourself I must increase.

Testament · Where do you still take the smaller piece when nobody requires it?

Sources

[1] John 3:30

[2] Mark 1:6

[3] Matt 11:18–19


The Falling Year

Season · kept by everyone

22 September (20 March in the south)

Name the day your debtors pay.

Evening in EdenGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VII, 1866

Michaelmas, the feast of Saint Michael on the twenty-ninth of September, came a week after the equinox and was one of the four quarter days of the English year. Rents fell due, farm servants stood at the hiring fairs to be taken on for another twelve months, and the harvest just brought in was reckoned against the debts it had to pay. A goose was eaten that day, with the proverb that whoever ate it would not want money all the year. The countryside kept its accounts as the light began to go, because that was when there was finally something to count.

Michael is the archangel who in Revelation leads the war in heaven until the dragon is thrown out[1], and the Prayer Book read that war as the epistle for his feast, so the landlords of England collected their rents under the patron of the winning side. The quarter day consulted nobody’s mood. The sum was known and the date fixed in advance, which kept a year of lending from turning into a year of charity.

Outside the rent book most debts have no quarter day. The loan to a friend or the money advanced to a brother is left unasked because asking feels mean, though the lender is the only party to the loan who has done anything generous. A debt left unasked through the falling year has become a gift by the time the next quarter comes round. The creditor who keeps quiet pays for it twice, once in the money and again in the smile he puts on whenever the borrower comes to dinner.

Declaration: Whoever calls me grasping has been living on a gift I never made, and the quarter day is when I send the bill.

The Rite

Write down what you are owed, each debt beside a name. Today ask one debtor plainly, in person or in writing, for what is yours, naming the sum and the date. Roast a bird, a goose if you can find one, and eat it as the creditor.

Testament · What have you let slide because asking for it felt mean?

Sources

[1] Rev 12:7–9


The Longest Night

Season · kept by everyone

21 December (21 June in the south)

Refuse the lamp the season hands you.

Satan at NightfallGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book VI, 1866

At the December solstice the night over London runs past sixteen hours, and many of the religions of the northern half of the world have met it by crowding it with light. Jewish households kindle the Hanukkah lamps for eight nights[1] in the same season, and at the Church’s midnight Mass of Christmas the first reading announces that the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light[2]. A city child can grow up without once seeing what the longest night of the year looks like with nothing lit.

The eye needs that dark to see in. Left without a lamp, it spends twenty or thirty minutes rebuilding the pigment that light bleaches out of the rods of the retina, and at the end of that wait a room that was black has its doorframes and its furniture back, and a clear sky over open country shows a few thousand stars that one streetlight would have hidden. A lamp switched on in the middle undoes most of it in a second.

Revelation has the dragon thrown down to the earth[3] after the war in heaven, carrying great wrath because he knew that his time was short[4], and the plate has him stretched on a ridge at nightfall, propped on one arm, with his wings spread behind him. The lamps of the season promise a light that comes to the people in darkness from outside, as a rescue. The sun returns after the solstice by the same tilt whether anyone lights a lamp, so the only thing the lamp adds is the loss of the dark. Whoever sits one evening of it out learns that the season’s lamps were never needed to see by, only to avoid sitting there.

Declaration: Nobody is coming to light my house, so I sat down and let my eyes do it.

The Rite

Put out every lamp and screen in the house, or stand outdoors away from the streetlights, and wait half an hour until the dark gives back the room. Then say I can see without it, and light nothing until you choose.

Testament · What have you lit a lamp against before your eyes could adjust to it?

Sources

[1] b. Shabbat 21b

[2] Isa 9:2; Roman Missal, Christmas Mass during the Night

[3] Rev 12:9

[4] Rev 12:12


Terms

Observance · kept by everyone

1 January

Begin in the first person.

Satan Rises from the Burning LakeGustave Doré · Paradise Lost, Book I, 1866

At a covenant service in a French church in east London on the eleventh of August, seventeen fifty-five, some eighteen hundred Methodists stood with their founder[1]. Wesley recited the covenant in the words of Richard Alleine. The Covenant Prayer in Wesley’s Directions of seventeen eighty[2] is still said at the turn of the year. Its traditional text has the speaker say I am no longer my own, but thine. Put me to what thou wilt, rank me with whom thou wilt. Put me to doing, put me to suffering. Let me be employed for thee or laid aside for thee, exalted for thee or brought low for thee. Let me be full, let me be empty. Let me have all things, let me have nothing. I freely and heartily yield all things to thy pleasure and disposal. In the British Methodist Book of Offices of nineteen thirty-six it ends with thou art mine, and I am thine. So be it. And the covenant which I have made on earth, let it be ratified in heaven. Amen.

From one hundred fifty-three before the common era the consuls of Rome took office on the first of January[3], and Romans named each year after the two men who held it.

Church tradition read Isaiah’s taunt against the king of Babylon as the fall of the devil. The king’s speech runs I will climb to the sky[4], higher than the stars of God I will set my throne. I will sit in the mount of assembly, on the summit of Zaphon. I will mount the back of a cloud. I will match the Most High. Augustine calls pride the beginning of all sin[5].

Declaration: I open the year with pride, and I mean to keep it until December.

The Rite

Head a page with the year and your own name, as Rome named each year for its consuls. Under it write one price, a rate, a raise or a refusal line, sign it, and say it to the one person it concerns.

Testament · Whom will the term you set inconvenience first?

[2] Directions for Renewing our Covenant with God, 1780

[3] Livy, Per. 47

[5] Augustine, City of God 14.13


The Lovers’ Saint

Observance · kept by everyone

14 February

Want in the open, and spend it where it is returned.

A Lady Young and Beautiful (Canto XXVII)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, Cassell edition, 1868

Three martyrs named Valentine[1] stand under the fourteenth of February in the old martyrologies, a priest of Rome, a bishop of Interamna and a third who died in Africa with companions. The Catholic Encyclopedia calls the acts of the first two late and of no historical value. The Church reduced the feast to a commemoration in nineteen fifty-five[2] and in nineteen sixty-nine took his name off the general calendar, leaving him to local devotion, so that a skull shown as his is still crowned with flowers in a church in Rome.

The lovers took the day anyway. Its link with courtship first appears in England in the fourteenth century[3], and by the time the Church dropped the saint the day belonged to cards and roses and the people who send them. Some clerics in Muslim countries still preach against it, and the roses are sold all the same.

A decree in Rome could take Valentine off the general calendar and leave the fourteenth of February untouched, since the millions who send cards had never asked his leave, and the few dozen couples who still make their promise each February at his basilica in Terni keep him by their own choice. In Chaucer’s parliament of birds every fowl comes on Valentine’s day to choose its own mate[4], and the saint lends the day his name and does none of the choosing. Desire kept the date on its own warrant. Every pulpit that claims a hand in your wanting holds the license Valentine held, a name printed over a day that went on perfectly well once the name was gone.

Declaration: The Church can keep its flowered skull, and the fourteenth of February stays with me.

The Rite

Write on a card the name of the adult you most desire and prop it where you can see it. Then, privately and slowly, take your pleasure to the finish with that name before you, or with its owner if they want you too.

Testament · What does your desire want today that you have never said aloud?

Sources

[1] Catholic Encyclopedia (1912), s.v. St. Valentine

[2] SRC, Cum nostra hac aetate, 23 Mar 1955

[3] Chaucer, Parlement of Foules

[4] Chaucer, Parlement of Foules 309–310


Walpurgis Night

Counter-rite · kept by everyone

30 April

Want in the open what the friars wanted on paper.

Witch Riding Backwards on a GoatAlbrecht Dürer, c. 1500

Walpurga, an English abbess, died in Bavaria in the eighth century, and her bones were carried to Eichstätt on the first of May, around 870. German folk belief gave the eve of that feast to the other party, when witches rode goats and brooms to the Brocken to keep their sabbath with the devil. The plate has one airborne, naked, seated backwards on her goat with her distaff raised and hail falling ahead of her.

A Dominican’s handbook for inquisitors gives a chapter to the storms witches raise against their neighbors[1]‘ fields, and an earlier one to the members they take from men and keep in a nest, where they stir like living things and eat oats and corn. A man who reached for a large one was told to leave it, because it belonged to a parish priest[2]. The same chapter explains that mostly nothing had been taken, the member only hidden from its owner by an illusion of the devil[3].

The handbook’s two showpieces need a power no one has, to raise hail or to lift a member off a man, and the second its author conceded was mostly a trick of the eye. Take the impossible powers away and what is left, beside the invented murders, is a woman’s appetite, the feast of the sabbath, the kiss given to the goat beneath its tail[4] and the coupling, which later demonologists set down with a lingering care.

No one was injured at the sabbath the handbooks describe, because no one ever flew to it. The injuries the record proves were done afterward, to the accused, women in most trials and men in many, burned in some countries and hanged in others, by courts with these books on their shelves, for a night that existed only in the books.

Declaration: A friar who kept a nest of stolen members in his head has no standing to tell me what to do with my own body.

The Rite

In your own yard, on a balcony or at your own table, eat a feast with your fingers and drink wine (or whatever you drink) in the company your appetite chose. Let appetite end it in bed with whoever wants you there, or alone.

Testament · What would your own sabbath hold, dish by dish and body by body, if nobody could burn you for it?

Sources

[1] Malleus Maleficarum 2.1.15

[2] Malleus Maleficarum 2.1.7

[3] Malleus Maleficarum 2.1.7

[4] Guazzo, Compendium Maleficarum (1608)


Mothers

Observance · kept by everyone

The second Sunday of May

Pay your mother by her record.

My Son Is Murder’d: the Widow before TrajanGustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, Cassell edition, 1868

Mark says that the mother and brothers of Jesus came to the house where he was teaching, stood outside, and sent word in to call him. He answered by asking who his mother and his brothers were, and looking round at the people sitting with him he said that these were his mother and brothers, and whoever does the god’s will[1]. Luke has him say that nobody can be his disciple without hating his own father and mother[2], and Matthew that he came to set a daughter against her mother[3].

The Watch Tower Society, whose Bible commands honor to mothers, tells Witnesses to stop keeping company with a relative[4] removed from the congregation, while a household keeps its ordinary family life. The woman in the plate above has stopped an emperor’s horse in the road and will not let him ride on until he has answered for her murdered son. She put her child above the emperor. The founder of the faith put a roomful of followers above his mother, and the Society asks its mothers to put the congregation above their children.

Mother’s Day began in nineteen hundred and eight as one daughter’s tribute to her own dead mother, a woman whose life she knew and meant to honor, and the daughter spent her last decades fighting the florists and card makers who turned it into a bill every child pays in May. Birth alone drew up no contract. A mother who stood by the child who left deserves a lavish day, with flowers and a table to match, and one who chose the faith over her child has already been paid, in the company she chose.

Declaration: The man who asked who his mother was, with her waiting at the door, left me free to ask the same.

The Rite

If your mother stood by you, pay for a meal for her or for a woman who mothered you. If she chose the faith over you, spend the card’s price on yourself.

Testament · What did your mother do when you needed her, and what is that worth today?

Sources

[1] Mark 3:31–35

[2] Luke 14:26

[3] Matt 10:35

[4] jw.org, How Do Jehovah’s Witnesses Treat Those Who Used to Belong


Fathers

Observance · kept by everyone

The third Sunday of June

Strike your father’s verdict from your own record.

Lavaine and His Father Take Leave at the Castle GateGustave Doré · Idylls of the King: Elaine, Moxon edition, 1867

Unstable as water[1] was the first verdict Jacob gave from his deathbed in Egypt, on Reuben, his firstborn, for a night in his father’s bed decades before, of which Genesis records only that Jacob heard[2]. Simeon and Levi were told that their swords were instruments of cruelty and that he would scatter them through Israel, for the slaughter at Shechem, which at the time had troubled him chiefly because it made him stink among the people of the land[3]. Dan was a serpent by the road, Benjamin a ravening wolf, and Joseph, the son of the wife he loved, had the blessings of heaven and of the deep, of the breasts and of the womb[4], heaped on his head.

Genesis is as frank about the father before him. Isaac loved Esau, it says, because he ate of his venison[5], and the blessing his younger son came for at that blind man’s bed went where an appetite and a trick could send it. The chapter of Jacob’s verdicts calls every one of them a blessing[6]. They are a record of the man who spoke them, laid on twelve tribes.

Whatever your father pronounced over you, the praise he rationed or the sentence passed at supper, is evidence of the same kind. When the Chronicler, writing after the kingdom had fallen, opened the genealogy of Reuben’s sons, he stopped to explain that the birthright had gone to Joseph’s sons because Reuben defiled his father’s bed[7], so one old man’s grievance was still being copied into the family register centuries after the night. A verdict nobody examines travels that way, from the father’s table into the son’s own mouth, and every son who repeats one keeps a dead man’s temper in force for another generation.

Declaration: Genesis calls its grudges blessings, and my father’s praise gets the same audit.

The Rite

Write down the verdict your father passed on you that you still repeat, put his name and the year beneath it, and file it with his letters or photographs. Then make today the decision it has been holding back.

Testament · Which sentence your father passed on you tells more about him than about you?

Sources

[1] Gen 49:3–4

[2] Gen 35:22

[3] Gen 34:30

[4] Gen 49:25–26

[5] Gen 25:28

[6] Gen 49:28

[7] 1 Chr 5:1–2


All Hallows’ Eve

Counter-rite · kept by everyone

31 October

Let the old fire go out.

The Mouth of HellMatthäus Küsel · after Burnacini, 1668

Hell had a mouth in the Doomsday pageant the Drapers of Coventry played at Corpus Christi, and the company paid for its upkeep. Their accounts set down eightpence in 1556 for keeping hell’s head and fourpence in 1557 for keeping the fire at it[1], and they list among the cast two devils, three white souls and three black ones, with a windlass for the machinery. The devils were hired townsmen in vizors, and their dresses included a demon’s head or vizor.

The court theaters of the next century staged hell’s mouth again on a grander scale, and the plate is engraved from a design for one of them, a stage hell with a ferryman crossing its water and a city burning in its throat. Between the Last Judgment painted over the chancel arch and the jaw on the pageant wagon, the hell a parish child saw was the work of carpenters and painters, and a guild kept the receipts.

All Hallows’ Eve puts that devil back in the street. His face hangs on the shop racks in rubber and paper for the price of a lunch, and whoever buys it does what the drapers’ townsmen did, wearing for one night the terror the Church used on them the rest of the year.

The pageant house of 1392 is Sharp’s first instance of pageants in Coventry, and the plays were still being performed in 1579. The last hell-mouth item Sharp prints for the Drapers is dated 1567[2]. A hell with a price in the account book is a hell anyone can stop paying for.

Declaration: The devil they frightened me with hangs in my closet now, between the winter coats.

The Rite

Put on a devil’s mask, bought or made, or paint a devil’s face over your own. Say Fourpence for the fire, and the rest was paint, and go out in it for an hour among the other masks.

Testament · Who has kept the fire going under your oldest fear?

Sources

[1] Coventry Drapers’ accounts (Sharp, Dissertation, 1825)

[2] Sharp, Dissertation, p. 61; Coventry plays regularly performed to 1579


Thanks

Observance · kept by everyone

The fourth Thursday of November

Send your thanks to the stove and the hands at it.

The Brothers at the Table in the Hall of AstolatGustave Doré · Idylls of the King: Elaine, Moxon edition, 1867

The Plymouth colonists feasted for three days after their first harvest in sixteen twenty-one, and the colony’s account records that Massasoit came with about ninety of his men, who killed five deer for the table[1]. The corn had been planted the local way, on instruction from Tisquantum[2], who had been taken to Europe from the village on that very site and came home to find it emptied by disease.

The first seed came from Corn Hill on the Cape, where the November before[3] an exploring party had dug into heaps of sand and found baskets of corn the people of the place had buried for themselves. Bradford’s history enters the find as a special providence of God and a great mercy[4], since it gave the colony seed for the next year’s planting. The same account says they meant to give the owners full satisfaction when they met them, and about six months later they did[5]. The colony paid the people the corn was owed to, and Bradford still put the seed down to God.

Grace before the meal keeps the same books. The turkey and the drive across three states arrive by the work of people sitting at the table, and the thanks rise past them to the ceiling. Thanks is a wage, owed for the specific thing to whoever did it and withheld from the uncle who came for the food and left the dishes. A grace sent to the heavens collects what the cook earned and hands it to a god who never lifted a hoe.

Declaration: Tonight every thanks I was raised to send upward stops at the kitchen door.

The Rite

Eat until your belt needs loosening. Raise a glass of whatever you like best to each person who earned one, by name and for the deed, present or far away, and one to the animal on the platter. Leave the other names unsaid.

Testament · Whose work is on your table today, and who at it has earned nothing from you?

Sources

[1] Winslow, Mourt’s Relation (1622)

[2] Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation, 1621

[3] Mourt’s Relation (1622)

[4] Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation, bk. 1 ch. 10

[5] Bradford, Of Plymouth Plantation, bk. 1 ch. 10


Unlucky Days

Observance · kept by everyone

Every Friday that falls on the 13th

Take back the date the passion story taught you to dread.

The Raven over the GraveyardGustave Doré · The Raven, Harper edition 1884, 1884

Thirteen sat down at the Last Supper by the gospels’ count, the twelve and their master[1], and within a day the master was dead and one of the twelve had hanged himself[2]. Folk belief tied two superstitions to that week, that thirteen at a table means a death within the year, and that Friday, the day of the crucifixion, is a bad day to begin anything, to sail or marry or move house. The earliest clear notices of Friday the thirteenth as a doubly unlucky date come from the nineteenth century, and the earliest known in English is Henry Sutherland Edwards’s 1869 life of Rossini.

The Knights Templar were arrested across France on Friday the thirteenth of October, thirteen hundred and seven, and the coincidence has since been pressed into service as an origin, though the link to the superstition is modern. Hotels and office towers still skip a thirteenth floor, and some airlines skip a thirteenth row. The Catholic Catechism counts superstition an offense against the first commandment[3], so the dread of the date has no standing even in the faith whose story supplied it.

The Church still asks its people on Fridays outside solemnities to give up meat or do a penance in its place[4], in memory of that death. The Orthodox churches also fast from meat on most Wednesdays and Fridays. The Church’s own Friday keeps the very day of the death it called good. Nobody at that table of thirteen has to die for the roof of a bad date to come down.

Declaration: I take the thirteenth seat and carve the roast at it.

The Rite

Lay thirteen places at your table, fill as many as you can with people you like, take the thirteenth yourself, and serve the best meat you can put on a plate.

Testament · Which beginning have you delayed for a luckier day, and what is the delay costing you?

Sources

[1] Matt 26:20

[2] Matt 27:5

[3] CCC 2110–2111

[4] CIC, cann. 1251, 1253


Waiting

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics and Protestants

The fourth Sunday before Christmas

Wait only for what has a date.

The Last JudgmentGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Jesus promises in the last chapter of the Christian Bible that he is coming quickly[1], and its last prayer asks him to come. The first generation expected him within its lifetime[2]. Advent begins on the fourth Sunday before Christmas, and in parts of Gaul the season was once kept as a second Lent, a fast from Saint Martin’s Day to the Nativity[3]. Its texts still look two ways at once, back to a birth and forward to the return.

In eighteen thirty-nine a Lutheran pastor in Hamburg, tired of the children at his mission school asking whether it was Christmas yet, fixed a ring of small red candles and four large white ones to an old cartwheel and lit one a day. The Advent calendar followed, a door a day with a verse or a picture behind it, and later a square of chocolate. Both answer a child’s impatience by teaching that pleasure is issued by the day on someone else’s schedule.

Waiting has its pleasures when the thing waited for is real and has a date, and a trip booked for a fixed day is half enjoyed before it starts. The return has neither a date nor, after twenty centuries, a sign that it is any nearer, and the patience the season drills into children every December is patience spent on an empty chair. The child reaches the last door on the twenty-fourth and eats what is behind it. The calendar handed to the adult has no last door, and whatever he saves against it goes into the ground with him uneaten.

Declaration: Every pleasure I was told to keep for his return I have already spent.

The Rite · Christian

Buy an Advent calendar, open every door at once, and eat the whole season’s chocolate in one sitting, slowly.

Testament · What are you still holding back for an occasion that has never come?

Sources

[1] Rev 22:20

[2] Mark 13:30

[3] Gregory of Tours, Hist. 10.31


The Innocents

Counter-rite · kept by all Christians

25 December

Keep the feast, and refuse its comfort.

The Children of Bethlehem Are MassacredGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The angel who woke Joseph in the night and sent him into Egypt with the mother and the child woke nobody else in Bethlehem[1]. Matthew alone tells the story, in a few verses after the wise men go home by another road[2], warned in a dream to keep away from Herod. Herod, finding himself tricked, sent men to kill every boy in the town and its district two years old or under[3], the age reckoned from what the magi had told him about the star, and the evangelist closes the episode with Rachel weeping for her children and refusing comfort, because they are gone[4].

Matthew files the killing as a prophecy fulfilled, so the god of the chapter knew what order Herod would give. He warned one house of what was coming, and Herod’s men did the rest. The Church keeps the dead boys three days after Christmas as the Holy Innocents and honors them as martyrs, and its prayer for the day says they proclaimed the god’s praise by dying[5]. Toddlers cut down for being born in the wrong town are enrolled after the fact as witnesses for the child who got away.

Rachel in the verse refuses comfort, and the verse lets her. The Church supplies the comfort anyway, a feast day and a prayer that files the boys’ deaths under praise, and she is the one mourner in the story who counts the dead as dead. A Christmas kept with the food and the company and with her refusal at the table owes the prayer nothing, and the crib on the sideboard holds the one boy in Bethlehem whose father was warned.

Declaration: The boys of Bethlehem were enrolled as martyrs without being asked, and I enroll none of my own dead as a blessing.

The Rite · No faith

Light two candles at your Christmas table, one for each year of the oldest boy Herod’s men were sent to kill, and say One house was warned, and the rest were not. Then eat as well as you can afford.

Testament · Which loss were you taught to call a blessing?

Sources

[1] Matt 2:13–14

[2] Matt 2:12

[3] Matt 2:16

[4] Matt 2:18; Jer 31:15

[5] Roman Missal, Collect for the Holy Innocents (28 Dec)


The Visitors

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics, Protestants and the Orthodox

6 January

Go home unconverted from every feast you attend.

Solomon Receives the Queen of ShebaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Matthew’s magi arrive as an unnumbered party of star-readers from the east, with no rank and no names. The number was inferred from the count of the gifts, which were gold and frankincense and myrrh[1], the crowns from psalms in which kings bring tribute[2], and the names came later still. In eleven sixty-four the archbishop of Cologne carried out of Milan three sets of bones[3] that had been honored there as theirs, and they lie in a golden shrine in his cathedral today.

They asked directions in Jerusalem[4], found the house, fell down before the child and opened their treasures. Then, warned in a dream not to return to Herod, they went home to their own country by another road[5]. Matthew leaves them there, worshipers sent home with no baptism recorded, still holding whatever learning had taught them to read a star. Later centuries would not leave them there. A Syriac legend, copied in the eighth century, sends the apostle Thomas east[6] to baptize them, a fourteenth-century history makes them archbishops, and the visitors Matthew let go as they came were enrolled in the Church centuries after they died.

Many who leave a faith still go home for its feasts, to a mother’s table at Christmas or a grandfather’s at the seder, and the house treats them as the Church treated the magi. A bowed head at grace is reported round the family as a return, and a carol sung for a mother’s sake is counted as the first step back. The visit and the gifts are all a guest owes, and a family that reads a convert into them has enrolled a man who only came to dinner.

Declaration: Whoever wants to enroll me after I leave will have to do as Cologne did and carry off my bones.

The Rite · Christian

Give one gift of real value, gold or scent or something good to eat, to someone in your life who never preached at you, and hand it over yourself. If no one comes to mind, give it to yourself.

Testament · Which house do you still visit at its feasts only because you always have?

Sources

[3] Floss, Dreikönigenbuch (1864)

[4] Matt 2:1–2
