Purification

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics and the Orthodox

2 February

Owe no priest for anything your body does.

The Birth of JesusGustave Doré · Pismo Święte, Warsaw edition, 1874

Forty days after Christmas the Church keeps the day Mary went up to the temple and paid for a sin offering. Luke records that when the days of purification were accomplished she and Joseph brought the child and offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, the price Leviticus allows a mother too poor for a lamb[1]. The woman the Western Church would later declare conceived without sin, and a virgin through the birth itself[2], paid the priests a sin offering for having borne a son.

The law behind the payment counts the days. After a son a mother is unclean seven days and continues thirty-three more in the blood of her purifying[3], touching nothing holy and keeping out of the sanctuary[4]. After a daughter the figures double to fourteen and sixty-six[5]. Custom kept the logic after the Church dropped the doves. For centuries Catholic mothers were churched after childbirth, met at the church door and blessed before they came back in, and the Orthodox still bring mother and child on the fortieth day with prayers that ask for her to be cleansed.

If a woman the Church holds free of every sin, who conceived without a man, paid the sin offering the law charged every mother for the birth, then the sin was never in any act. It was in the birth. The law laid it on the body for doing what bodies do, for twice as long when the body produced a girl, and collected in birds at the priests’ altar. Whatever a church has taught you to feel unclean about in your own body was priced the same way, and the price went to whoever kept the altar.

Declaration: Mary paid two doves for a sin she never committed, and the price of mine stays in my pocket.

The Rite · Catholic

Stand outside your own front door, walk in with no blessing and no one to lead you, and say I let myself in. Then spend what a lamb would have cost on a bath or a good meal.

Testament · Which ordinary function of your body were you taught to treat as a stain, and by whom?

Sources

[1] Luke 2:22–24; Lev 12:8

[2] Ineffabilis Deus (1854); CCC 499

[3] Lev 12:2–4

[4] Lev 12:4

[5] Lev 12:5


Ashes

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics and Protestants

Forty-six days before Easter

Spend the forty days on what you love.

Death Riding the Globe of Cloud, with the RavenGustave Doré · The Raven, Harper edition 1884, 1884

The ashes come after the gospel[1]. At the Roman Mass for the day the congregation hears Jesus tell those who fast to wash their faces so that nobody will know[2], and call the ones who disfigure theirs to be seen fasting hypocrites, and then it files forward to have a cross drawn on the forehead in the ash of last year’s palms, where the street will see it for the rest of the day.

The older of the two formulas said over the ash belongs to the god, who told Adam on the day of the expulsion that he was dust and to dust he would return[3], in the same speech that cursed the ground for his sake and promised him bread only by the sweat of his face[4]. The man had been shaped from the dust of the ground[5] in the chapter before, so the sentence only restated, in the god’s own voice, what he was made of. The Church draws that material on the forehead as a confession of guilt.

Ash Wednesday turns a fact about the body into a fault of the soul and opens forty days of fasting and almsgiving to atone for it. A creature made of dust has a short run in a body that can taste. Six weeks of that run spent in apology for the material are six weeks the body never gets back, and the one counsel in the whole service worth keeping is the gospel read before the ash, which sends the faster to a basin of water.

Declaration: I was dust before anyone accused me of anything, and I owe the Church no Lent for it.

The Rite · No faith

Wash your face in cold water and say Dust I am, and every grain of it is mine. Then take the best pleasure within reach today, and start on something you mean to love by Easter.

Testament · Which pleasure would you learn slowly if no one counted your fasts?

Sources

[1] Roman Missal, Ash Wednesday

[2] Matt 6:16–18

[3] Gen 3:19

[4] Gen 3:17–19

[5] Gen 2:7


The Other Annunciation

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics and the Orthodox

25 March

Refuse protection that was arranged without asking you.

Answering Not, Mine Eyes I Raised (Canto XXXI)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Paradiso, Cassell edition, 1868

The twenty-fifth of March falls nine months before Christmas, and the Church keeps on it the angel’s visit to the girl at Nazareth[1] as Luke tells it. Matthew tells the conception another way, and his version has no visit to her at all. Mary is found to be with child, and Joseph, who is betrothed to her and a just man, resolves to put her away privately so as to spare her a public example[2]. While he is weighing it an angel comes to him in a dream, tells him what has happened inside his betrothed’s body and what name to give the child[3], and Joseph wakes and takes her as his wife[4].

The facts of her pregnancy are explained to the man, in his sleep, by a messenger Matthew never shows her, and her future, divorce or marriage, disgrace or protection, is settled between the messenger and the man and carried out on waking. Matthew gives her no line. In Luke’s scene she asks a question and gives her answer[5], and the Annunciation of the painters is Luke’s, the version in which the girl speaks.

Joseph’s plan to end the marriage privately was mercy, and it was made without her. He meant to spare her a public example and Matthew shows him asking her nothing, and the angel’s correction came to him alone, in a dream. The families that shielded you from the book, the diagnosis or the friend, and the congregations that kept the news quiet for your own good, run on Joseph’s mercy. It spares the one it was made about everything except the decision.

Declaration: Whoever shelters me by deciding for me has already left me out.

The Rite · Catholic

Write to someone who once decided something for your own good without asking you, say what it cost, and send the letter or burn it.

Testament · What did someone shield you from without asking, and what did it cost you?

Sources

[1] Luke 1:26–38

[2] Matt 1:19

[3] Matt 1:20–21

[4] Matt 1:24

[5] Luke 1:34–38


The Turning Crowd

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics, Protestants and the Orthodox

The Sunday before Easter

Discount every hosanna that cost its singer nothing.

After That I Saw a Multitude in Fury Burning (Canto XV)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, Cassell edition, 1868

In Western churches palms go out at the church door at the start of the Mass on the Sunday that commemorates the entry into Jerusalem with hosannas, and the congregation that carries them in is invited to take up the hosannas of the crowd on the road to Jerusalem. Soon after comes one of the longest gospel readings of the year, the whole Passion, read in parts. In many parishes the printed order of service gives the people in the pews the crowd’s lines, and the same voices that welcomed him at the door read out together, in unison, the demand that he be crucified[1].

The gospels never make the two crowds one. Mark says the chief priests stirred up the crowd before Pilate[2] to ask for Barabbas, so the turn belongs to the priests, and when Pilate asked what evil he had done the crowd cried out all the more, Crucify him. The missalette fuses them, handing the same pews both lines within the hour, hosanna at the door and Crucify him from the pew. The turn Mark lays to the priests now comes printed on the sheet in the pews.

A hosanna sung because everyone around was singing cost its singer nothing, and it is worth exactly that on the day the crowd changes its line. The only welcome worth anything came from the few who told you to your face that you were wrong and went on inviting you, since they risked the same friends as everyone else and kept you anyway. Their table is the congregation you have.

Declaration: A crowd that sings what it is handed will read what it is handed, and I have heard both.

The Rite · Christian

Make two lists, those who praised you while you agreed and those who told you to your face you were wrong and stayed. Telephone each on the second list and say You told me I was wrong and stayed, and I noticed. The first list gets no call.

Testament · Whose praise did you trust for years, and how long did it outlast your first public doubt?

Sources

[1] Mark 15:13–14

[2] Mark 15:11


The Basin

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics, Protestants and the Orthodox

The Thursday before Easter

Refuse any kindness you are not allowed to refuse.

The Last SupperGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Only John has Jesus wash his disciples’ feet. During supper he rises, lays aside his garments, ties a towel round his waist, pours water into a basin and begins washing the disciples’ feet and drying them[1]. Peter refuses, and the answer comes at once, that unless he is washed he has no part with his master[2]. Peter gives way so completely that he asks for his hands and head as well[3]. The master took the servant’s part, and the master still decided that Peter’s feet would go into the basin.

Kings took up the basin as a ceremony. English monarchs washed the feet of poor people on this day, in a number set by the years of their own age[4], until late in the seventeenth century they stopped doing it themselves, and the sovereign now hands out purses of specially minted silver coins instead. Popes have washed a dozen pairs of feet in front of cameras. Only the very high can make a show of stooping, since a servant on his knees is at work, and the poor whose feet were washed went home with a gift in kind and their poverty.

The kneeling changes the posture of power and leaves its direction alone. A master who washes your feet still chooses the day and the witnesses, and a refusal is answered, as Peter’s was, with the terms of membership. A humility the washed cannot decline is a claim on them, and it goes into the gospel and the palace record as the washer’s virtue. A foot-washing bought and paid for ends at the door, with no membership attached and no day or witness chosen for you.

Declaration: I pay for every service I take, and a towel offered for free stays folded.

The Rite · Christian

Book and pay for a pedicure or a foot massage from someone who does it for a living, and let them wash your feet. If no one is open, run a basin and let a willing pair of hands do the drying.

Testament · Whose service would you rather pay for than be given?

Sources

[1] John 13:4–5

[2] John 13:8

[3] John 13:9

[4] Royal Maundy


The Friday Called Good

Counter-rite · kept by all Christians but Witnesses

The Friday before Easter

Thank no one for a sacrifice you never requested.

Jesus Is Nailed to the CrossGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A gospel hymn written in 1865 and still sung in Protestant churches puts the doctrine of this day into its refrain, that Jesus paid it all and all to him I owe[1]. The account is settled in full in one line and the debtor owes everything in the next. In Anselm’s version, and the Reformers’ after him, the doctrine holds that the Church’s god could cancel the bill for human sin only if it was paid, and since no man could pay a sum so large, the god became a man and had himself killed, so that the payment owed to him could be made to him by himself. Anselm called this satisfaction[2]. The Reformers sharpened it into a penalty borne in the place of the guilty[3].

The plate shows the nailing, a hammer raised over the open hand, and this edition hangs it upside down. In Matthew the man under the hammer had said at his arrest that he could ask his father for more than twelve legions of angels[4]. He did not ask. The purchase was made by the buyer’s choice, at a price the buyer set, on behalf of people not yet born.

The same arrangement turns up at home, whenever a sacrifice nobody requested is presented afterward as a claim, the career given up and the years spent, and the one it was made for is told what is owed in return. Made without that person’s consent, it buys nothing from them, neither the worship asked for on the Friday nor the thanks asked for at the kitchen table. A debt the creditor paid on your behalf and billed to you afterward is a debt he made.

Declaration: Whoever climbs a hill for me unasked has climbed it for his own reasons, and I keep this Friday for mine.

The Rite · No faith

Hang a cross of two sticks upside down, as the plate is hung, and name beneath it one sacrifice someone holds over you. Say Bought without my asking, and owed nothing. Then eat a meal you enjoy.

Testament · Who still reminds you of a sacrifice you never asked them to make?

Sources

[1] Elvina M. Hall, Jesus Paid It All (1865)

[2] Anselm, Cur Deus Homo 2.6

[3] Calvin, Inst. 2.16.5

[4] Matt 26:53


The Empty Tomb

Counter-rite · kept by all Christians but Witnesses

Easter Sunday

Spend the day on a body that dies.

The Angel and Women at the Empty TombGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The two oldest complete manuscripts of Mark[1], the earliest gospel, end with three women, Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James and Salome, running from the tomb in terror and saying nothing to anyone[2]. A young man in white had been sitting inside, on the right, and told them their crucified master had risen and would go ahead of them into Galilee. The oldest text stops there, mid-fright. The appearances, the wounds offered to the doubter, the fish eaten in front of the eleven, all arrive in later gospels or in endings added to Mark by other hands.

Paul, writing to the Corinthians before any gospel existed, staked everything on the raising, telling them that if Christ had not been raised their faith was futile and they were the most pitiable people alive[3]. His list of those who saw the risen master runs from Cephas through the twelve and five hundred brethren to himself[4], and it names no women. Paul has appearances and a burial and never mentions a tomb, and Mark has an empty grave where the risen man never shows himself.

On those two halves a church has asked twenty centuries of the living to discount the one body each of them is certain to have, and to wait on a risen body the oldest copies of Mark never produce. The plate shows the women still coming toward the angel seated in the tomb, before the fright, and the reader who stops where Mark stops finds that the only body anyone in his story has touched is the mortal one, taken down and laid in rock on a spring afternoon.

Declaration: I trust the women who ran and told nobody over every pulpit that has told everybody since.

The Rite · No faith

Take a long walk today and then a long bath, and say in the water This body is the one I have, and it is enough.

Testament · What will you do today that you postponed on the promise of a later life?

Sources

[1] Codex Sinaiticus; Codex Vaticanus

[2] Mark 16:8

[3] 1 Cor 15:17–19

[4] 1 Cor 15:4–8


The Bounds

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics, Protestants and the Orthodox

Thirty-nine days after Easter

Mark your ground, and keep it.

Down Whose Steps I Saw the Splendours (Canto XXI)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Paradiso, Cassell edition, 1868

Luke closes his gospel and opens Acts on the same departure. On a hill called Olivet, a sabbath day’s walk from Jerusalem[1], a cloud takes Jesus out of the apostles’ sight[2], and they walk back to the city without him. A small chapel on the hill still shows pilgrims a footprint in the rock that tradition names as the last mark he left on the earth, and the chapel has been in Muslim keeping since Saladin’s day.

On Ascension Day, or in the days before it, English villagers walked the boundaries of the parish with the priest, stopping at each marker stone and beating it with rods so that nobody would forget where the parish ended. The god went up. The parish went round its own fields, and on the day the Church kept for a body leaving the earth, the people spent the afternoon learning exactly how much of it was theirs.

Ground that has never been walked to its edge is ground other people feel free to cross. The relative with a spare key who lets themselves in and the old congregation still sending visitors to your door have each found an unmarked line and taken the field beyond it. A line holds where someone has walked it and struck the stone, and the parish knew it well enough to bring its boys along every year so that the line would outlive the men who had walked it. Of the two marks the day left behind, the footprint drew pilgrims and the stones turned trespassers back, and your own ground needs only the stones.

Declaration: A god who left the ground keeps no claim on it, and my share has my name at every corner.

The Rite · Christian

Go round your home, or one room, and tap each corner with a stick, as parishioners once beat the parish stones. At the last corner say aloud the name of whoever crosses your ground uninvited, and You come no further than this.

Testament · Who crosses your ground uninvited, and what will they meet the next time they do?

Sources

[1] Acts 1:12

[2] Acts 1:9–11


Ecstasy

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics, Protestants and the Orthodox

Seven weeks after Easter

Sign nothing while the music plays.

The Holy Spirit Descends on the DisciplesGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Some in the crowd at Pentecost thought the apostles were drunk[1], and Peter’s defense was the clock, since it was only the third hour of the day[2]. In January of nineteen ninety-four a visiting preacher came to a Vineyard church near the Toronto airport, and the meetings that followed ran six nights a week for a year[3]. Worshipers fell to the floor and shook and laughed, some of them roaring, and called the state being drunk in the Spirit, taking the mockers’ word from Acts as their own.

The revivalists of the eighteen thirties set an anxious bench at the front of the hall for sinners under conviction[4], where a man who felt the pull could be seen feeling it. A worship band now plays a slow song and swells it, the key goes up a step for the last chorus, the lights drop, and the preacher invites anyone who feels something to come forward now. The lift in the body is real. The call is timed to collect a decision at the top of it. Billy Graham’s crusades sang Just As I Am during the invitation, every verse ending O Lamb of God, I come[5], while the people walked down to the front.

Ecstasy is one of the best things a body can do, and the crowd that laughed at the apostles knew where it was usually found, in the third glass among friends and on a dance floor at two in the morning, where nobody waits at the front with a decision card. A choice that is sound at the top of the song is still sound after a night’s sleep and a meal, and the only decision that has to be taken before the lights come up is the kind that dies at breakfast.

Declaration: The shaking and the laughter were my own body’s work, and no pastor gets to count them as his conversions.

The Rite · Christian

Play the song that lifts you highest, loud, from the first note to the last, and let it do its work. Write down the decision it tempts you toward, leave the page unsigned, and read it again tomorrow.

Testament · What did you promise at the top of a song that you would refuse in a quiet room?

Sources

[1] Acts 2:13

[2] Acts 2:15

[3] Arnott, The Father’s Blessing (1995)

[4] Finney, Lectures on Revivals (1835), lect. 14

[5] Charlotte Elliott, Just As I Am (1835)


The Body

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics

Sixty days after Easter

Kneel to nothing you could eat.

Beneath a Sky So Beautiful (Canto XXIX)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, Cassell edition, 1868

In twelve sixty-four Pope Urban the Fourth made a feast of the whole Latin Church[1] out of a vision that a canoness in what is now Belgium had kept secret for twenty years. On it the consecrated host is carried in procession under a canopy in a gold vessel shaped like a sunburst, and the faithful kneel as it passes. The doctrine behind it was fixed in twelve fifteen, when the Fourth Lateran Council declared the bread and wine transubstantiated into the body and blood[2], so that the wafer in the sunburst is held to be the flesh of a god under the appearance of bread.

Within a generation of the feast, the charge spread that Jews stole consecrated hosts to stab them, as if bread could bleed. At Deggendorf in Bavaria in the thirteen thirties the town’s Jews were killed first and the host story arrived afterward to justify it, and the town kept a pilgrimage in its honor until nineteen ninety-two[3]. At Brussels in thirteen seventy[4] Jews were executed on the same charge and the rest of the community was banished.

The Church teaches that after the consecration only the look, taste and feel of bread remain[5], which concedes that every sense finds bread there and nothing else. A claim that no sense can check will stretch to cover anything, and at Deggendorf it stretched over a massacre and made it a shrine. In the gospels the loaves end as twelve baskets of scraps[6] gathered after a crowd sat down on the grass and ate. Nobody in that crowd knelt. Bread is honored in a mouth, and the loaf in the procession rides through the streets uneaten, in gold, held by a priest who wraps his hands in a veil before he will lift even the vessel.

Declaration: My bread goes warm into my mouth, and no loaf of mine has ever been entered as evidence against a Jew.

The Rite

Bake or buy a round loaf, carry it through every room of your home under a dish towel held up like a canopy, then sit down and eat it with butter, saying Bread, and only bread. over the first piece.

Testament · What would you feed your own body today if you honored it as the Church honors a wafer?

Sources

[1] Urban IV, Transiturus (1264)

[2] Lateran IV (1215), const. 1

[3] Eder, Die Deggendorfer Gnad (1992)

[4] Commission Nationale Catholique, Le Miracle du St Sacrement

[5] Council of Trent, Sess. 13, can. 2

[6] Matt 14:20


The Perishable

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics and the Orthodox

15 August

Use your body hard while it is ripe.

EnsayosFrancisco Goya · Los Caprichos, 1799

Pope Pius the Twelfth defined on the first of November nineteen fifty that Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory[1]. A tale attributed to Joseph of Arimathea[2] has Thomas arrive too late for her burial, see her carried up through the air, and catch the girdle she lets fall to him as proof. Prato Cathedral in Tuscany still exhibits a girdle[3] it holds to be hers.

Churches claimed nearly everything else of hers, vials of her milk, her veil, her shoes, and her girdle twice over, at Prato and on Mount Athos. No church claims her bones. The theologians reasoned that a sinless body was owed exemption from corruption[4], so every body that does decay is decaying on account of sin, as the Church had taught since Paul called death the wages of sin[5].

Pius died eight years after the definition, and his physician embalmed him by a method of his own, sealing the body with herbs and oils inside plastic. It putrefied in the October heat on the road to Rome and at the lying in state, and the guards beside it had to be relieved every fifteen minutes[6] for the stench. Rot came for the pope on schedule, as it comes this month for the peaches across much of the north. The herbs and the plastic bought his corpse not one extra hour, and a body kept clean for heaven has the season a peach has and no other, sweet for a week and then gone to the wasps.

Declaration: The worms are no judges, and I will go to them unrepentant.

The Rite · Catholic

Buy the ripest fruit you can find, the kind that will be spoiled tomorrow, and eat it today over the sink, juice and all, in honor of everything that rots.

Testament · What is your body ripe for now that it will not be ripe for in ten years?

Sources

[1] DS 3903

[2] Passing of the Blessed Virgin Mary (Ps.-Joseph of Arimathea)

[3] Prato Cathedral, Cappella del Sacro Cingolo

[4] Munificentissimus Deus (1950), 14

[5] Rom 6:23; CCC 1008

[6] press reports, October 1958


All Saints

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics and Protestants

1 November

Ask your living which day is theirs.

In Fashion, as a Snow White Rose (Canto XXXI)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Paradiso, Cassell edition, 1868

The Byzantine emperor Phocas gave Pope Boniface the Fourth the Pantheon in Rome, the temple raised to all the gods. On the thirteenth of May in the year six hundred nine, by the traditional date the pope dedicated it to Mary and all the martyrs[1], so that one crowded heaven moved into the house of another. Rome set the feast of all the saints on the first of November a century and more later, and the roll it honors has kept growing.

For four centuries the making of a saint included a lawyer for the other side. From fifteen eighty-seven under Pope Sixtus the Fifth[2] the Promoter of the Faith, the devil’s advocate of popular speech, was charged with arguing against every candidate, hunting for the faked miracle and the awkward letter. In nineteen eighty-three, by the constitution Divinus Perfectionis Magister, Pope John Paul the Second cut the office back[3]. Over the previous six centuries the popes had made, by the Pew count, about three hundred saints, and he went on to canonize about four hundred and eighty saints, more than all the popes of the previous four centuries together.

A roll that long honors the dead in bulk, one feast for all of them together. The people who earned honor from you, the teacher who corrected you without pay and the sibling who covered for you at cost to himself, are alive, and no calendar has a day for them. The roll that grows by the hundred leaves them to be honored by whoever thinks to ask.

Declaration: The Church lights candles for its dead, and my living saints get a day of their choosing.

The Rite · Catholic

Ask a living person who earned honor from you what day they would put on their own calendar, and mark it on yours.

Testament · Which living person has earned honor from you that they have never heard you say?

Sources

[1] Liber Pontificalis 69

[2] Sixtus V, Immensa Aeterni Dei (1587)

[3] John Paul II, Divinus Perfectionis Magister (1983)


The Thirty Masses

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics

2 November

Cancel the debt a priest put on your dead.

The Last JudgmentPieter Bruegel the Elder, 1558

A monk named Justus, dying in the monastery Gregory the Great had founded in Rome, confessed that he had hidden three gold coins among his medicines. Gregory, by his own account, forbade the brothers to go near him, and had him buried in a dunghill with the coins thrown in after him while they said that his money should perish with him. Some weeks later Gregory relented and had Mass said for the dead monk on thirty successive days, and afterward Justus appeared to the layman who had nursed him to say that he had been released from torment[1].

The Church still offers Gregorian Masses, thirty in a row for one soul, for a stipend. The Council of Lyon taught in twelve seventy-four that souls being cleansed after death are helped by the Masses, prayers and alms[2] of the living, and for centuries the wealthy endowed chantries where a priest sang for their dead in perpetuity, until England dissolved them in fifteen forty-seven[3] and the Crown took the money. On All Souls every priest may say three Masses for the dead, a privilege Benedict the Fifteenth extended to the whole Church in nineteen fifteen[4], with the war filling the graves.

The story behind the thirty Masses puts a debt on a corpse. Three coins went into the dung with Justus, and the Church has collected on his release ever since, from sons and widows who paid to help their dead. The dead are past every creditor. A debt that only a survivor can pay, and only to the man who announced it, is a toll on grief, and the grieving still pay it at the parish office, one stipend at a time.

Declaration: I owe my dead a good dinner, and I owe the Church nothing on their account.

The Rite

Cook the dish a dead person of yours loved best and set their place with a full plate and a glass. Invite one person who knew them, eat together, and tell one story no priest ever heard. With no such person, cook what you would want cooked for you.

Testament · What did your dead love to eat, and who should be at the table when you cook it?

Sources

[1] Gregory, Dialogues, bk. 4

[2] Council of Lyon II (1274), DS 856

[3] Chantries Act 1547 (1 Edw. 6 c. 14)

[4] Benedict XV, Incruentum Altaris (1915)


The Exception

Counter-rite · kept by Catholics

8 December

Tell your favorites to their faces.

Adam and Eve Are Driven out of EdenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Church writers had called Mary the second Eve since the second century[1], the woman who undid the first one’s disobedience. On the eighth of December eighteen fifty-four Pope Pius the Ninth defined that Mary, from the first instant of her conception, by a singular grace and privilege of almighty God and in view of the merits of her son, was preserved free from every stain of original sin[2].

Two of the Church’s own doctors had argued against it. Bernard, the abbot, objected to the new feast in the twelfth century[3], and Thomas Aquinas held that a Mary exempt from original sin would have had no need of the redemption her son brought[4]. The Franciscans answered that preserving her was a finer redemption than rescuing her, and the dispute ran for seven centuries before a pope closed it. Both sides took for granted what the dogma then made explicit. Every child of two human parents since the first pair arrives stained, and only by a singular privilege could one girl have been spared.

The friend who sat with you in the hospital is excused the lateness you would never forgive in a colleague, and the sister who covered for you is lent the money a cousin would be refused. Partiality is the evidence that love exists at all, since a love that grants nobody an exemption is only a policy. Heaven made its one exemption at the instant of a conception, for the woman who would bear the god, before she had done anything for anyone. That is favor to blood. The friend at your hospital bed has earned more from you than the girl in the womb had earned from heaven.

Declaration: Heaven calls its favoritism grace, and I have the decency to call mine favoritism.

The Rite

Write a dispensation exempting the person who has earned it most from one rule you keep for everyone else, sign it, seal it with wax or a thumbprint in ink, and hand it to them saying By singular grace and privilege.

Testament · Which of your rules will you waive for the person who has earned an exemption from it?

Sources

[1] Irenaeus, Against Heresies 3.22.4

[2] DS 2803

[3] Bernard, Ep. 174

Sustaining

Counter-rite · kept by Latter-day Saints

The first Sunday of April and of October

Sustain no one before you have sustained yourself.

Ezra Reads the Law to the PeopleGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Twice a year the officers of the Latter-day Saint church are read out by name in the Conference Center in Salt Lake City. The hall is invited to sustain them by the uplifted right hand, and any who are opposed may show it the same way. In April twenty fifteen a few voices called out opposed as the names were read. The counselor conducting turned to the prophet, said that the voting had been noted, and asked those who had opposed any of the proposals to contact their stake presidents[1].

The church calls the rule common consent, after a revelation of eighteen thirty that all things in the church be done by it[2], and the answer given in twenty fifteen shows what the rule lets a member withhold. A yes is taken as the voice of the church. A no leaves the hall. The member is told to contact the stake president, who meets the objector privately to ask whether the objection rests on conduct that disqualifies the officer. The same stake presidency signs the temple recommend, the card without which a Latter-day Saint cannot enter a temple, and asks in that interview whether the member sustains those same leaders. In Nehemiah, when Ezra opened the book of the law, the people answered amen with their hands lifted and then bowed their faces to the ground[3], and the church lifts the same hands and calls them a vote.

A vote whose yes is assumed and whose no is sent to the stake president is an acclamation, and a hand raised in it carries the weight of applause. Consent means something only where refusing it costs as little as giving it. Anywhere else the raised arm is a receipt the institution writes for itself and signs in the member’s name.

Declaration: Any officer who wants my reasons for a no can make the appointment himself.

The Rite

Write a ten-minute talk on what you want from your one life. Stand and deliver it, to anyone willing or to an empty room, then raise your own right hand and say The speaker is sustained.

Testament · Whose name did your raised hand sustain for years that you never chose?

Sources

[1] Uchtdorf, General Conference, 4 Apr 2015

[2] D&C 26:2

[3] Neh 8:4–6


A Known Date

Counter-rite · kept by Latter-day Saints

6 April

Build something of your own from what your church taught you.

Ezra Kneels in PrayerGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Six men were named as the founding members of the Latter-day Saint church on the sixth of April eighteen thirty, at the Whitmer family’s farmhouse in Fayette, New York. The revelation on church government dates the day to one thousand eight hundred and thirty years since the coming of the Lord in the flesh[1], and a tradition among Latter-day Saints holds that Jesus was born on the sixth of April, so that the church and its god keep one birthday.

It was organized as the Church of Christ. In eighteen thirty-four a conference of elders at Kirtland[2] renamed it the Church of the Latter Day Saints, and a revelation of eighteen thirty-eight[3] restored the name of Jesus Christ to the title. In twenty eighteen its president told members that to remove the Lord’s name from the Lord’s church is a major victory for Satan[4], and by that reckoning the founder’s own church spent four years of his lifetime as Satan’s victory, on the vote of a room of men.

Oliver Cowdery and David Whitmer, two of the six, were excommunicated in the same month[5] the revelation fixed the name, and Whitmer lived another fifty years in Richmond, Missouri, outside the church first gathered in his father’s house. A year before his death he published a pamphlet still affirming that he had seen the plates[6]. A member today pays for what the church teaches with a tenth of his income, a missionary with a monthly sum toward his own mission, and what he has learned there is his to carry out the door, as Whitmer carried his testimony. In 1876 he ordained his nephew first elder of a revived Church of Christ, the first name of all, which a conference of elders had voted away.

Declaration: Six men in a farmhouse made a church, and one is enough to make mine.

The Rite

Write on one page three things your church taught you that you will keep. Head it with today’s date and a name for what you will build, sign it as the only member, and pin it up. Say aloud That was the founding, and I kept it.

Testament · What did the church teach you at your own expense that you would keep?

Sources

[1] D&C 20:1

[2] History of the Church 2:62–63

[3] D&C 115:4

[4] Nelson, General Conference, Oct 2018

[5] Far West Record, 12–13 Apr 1838

[6] Whitmer, An Address to All Believers in Christ (1887)


Handcarts

Counter-rite · kept by Latter-day Saints

24 July

Believe the one who will walk the road with you.

Hagar and Ishmael in the WildernessGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Brigham Young’s company came down into the Salt Lake Valley on the twenty-fourth of July eighteen forty-seven[1], and Utah still keeps the day with parades and fireworks. Nine years later the church began bringing its poorest European converts the thirteen hundred miles on foot from Iowa City, pulling their belongings in handcarts.

The Willie and Martin companies, nine hundred eighty people between them, left the Missouri late, in the second half of August[2] eighteen fifty-six. Levi Savage, a returning missionary, warned that companies so full of the old and the very young would meet snow on the high plains and ought to winter where they were. The meeting voted to go on, and Savage went with them anyway. On the twelfth of September Franklin Richards, the apostle who ran the emigration, overtook the Willie company with a party of missionaries in carriages, rebuked Savage in open meeting for his want of faith, and promised in the name of Israel’s god that cold and every other hardship would have no power to seriously harm anyone in the camp[3] if it obeyed counsel to the letter. He reached Salt Lake on the fourth of October[4]. Snow caught the companies in Wyoming that month, and more than two hundred died of cold and hunger.

Church youth still dress as pioneers and pull handcarts on a reenactment the wards call trek, many of them over the same Wyoming ground. The warning was given by a man who would walk the trail with them, the promise by one who would reach the valley ahead of the snow, and the snow kept the warning. A promise that blames the walkers if it fails costs its maker nothing, and of everyone the trek honors, the first claim belongs to the man who lost the vote and walked into Wyoming beside the carts.

Declaration: When the man in charge rides and I pull, his orders end at the first mile.

The Rite

Eat a slice of good pie, as some of Utah’s non-members do on the twenty-fourth. Then call or write to the person whose warning you once overruled and tell them the road went as they said.

Testament · Whose warning about the road did you overrule, and what did it cost?

Sources

[1] Wilford Woodruff, Journal, 24 Jul 1847

[2] Christy, BYU Studies 37:1 (1997), 6–74

[3] Willie company journal, 12 Sep 1856; Christy (1997)

[4] Hafen and Hafen, Handcarts to Zion (1981); Bartholomew and Arrington (1993)


The Press

Counter-rite · kept by Latter-day Saints

23 December

Put every damning record beyond the reach of one marshal.

Down Whose Steps I Saw the Splendours (Canto XXI)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Paradiso, Cassell edition, 1868

Dissenters in the Illinois city that Joseph Smith governed as mayor published the first and only issue of a newspaper, the Expositor, on the seventh of June eighteen forty-four. It accused him of teaching plural marriage in secret and of drawing women into it as spiritual wives[1]. He was thirty-eight, born in Vermont two days before Christmas in eighteen oh five, and lieutenant general of the city’s militia. He had twenty days to live.

Three days later the city council, with Smith presiding, declared the paper a public nuisance[2], and on his order as mayor the marshal and a posse wrecked the press, scattered the type and burned the copies. The destruction brought a charge of riot, then martial law and a charge of treason, and the charge brought him to the jail at Carthage, where a mob with blackened faces stormed the building on the twenty-seventh of June and shot him as he fired back with a smuggled pistol.

The church’s own essay on plural marriage, published in twenty fourteen, says that Joseph Smith was sealed to some women already married, and that the youngest, Helen Mar Kimball, was sealed to him several months before her fifteenth birthday[3]. The council had consulted Blackstone’s Commentaries on what counts as a nuisance before it voted, and a city’s abatement runs only as far as the city’s officers can walk. The copies already in readers’ hands were out of the marshal’s reach, and the accusation they carried came back a hundred and seventy years later in the church’s own words.

Declaration: When a prophet burns a newspaper, I copy it twice.

The Rite

Copy out by hand a page of the Expositor, whose press the mayor ordered destroyed, or of any book a powerful body once tried to burn. Make two copies, keep one in the house and one on you, and read the page aloud once.

Testament · Which record of a powerful person’s conduct exists in only one place, and who is entitled to read it?

Sources

[1] Nauvoo Expositor, 7 Jun 1844

[2] Nauvoo City Council minutes, 10 Jun 1844; HC 6:432

[3] Gospel Topics, Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo (2014)


The Memorial

Counter-rite · kept by Witnesses

14 Nisan, after sundown

Take the seat the great crowd is refused.

The Last SupperGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

A plate of unleavened bread and a glass of red wine go along every row of the Kingdom Hall after sundown, and in almost every row they come back to the front untouched. Witnesses keep the Memorial of Christ’s death once a year, in memory of the meal at which they hold he instituted it, and it is the best-attended meeting of their year, with relatives and the curious beside the faithful. Only the anointed may eat and drink, the remnant of the hundred and forty-four thousand[1] who will rule with Christ in heaven. Everyone else passes the plate along and watches.

In Matthew Jesus hands round the cup and tells them all to drink from it[2], and in Luke, once the bread and wine have gone round, he says that the hand of the man who will betray him is with him on the table[3]. In Luke’s order the betrayer is still seated for the cup, though Matthew and Mark put the warning first and the Society, following John, has Judas gone before the bread. The Watch Tower’s division of the faithful into a little flock bound for heaven and a great crowd destined for a restored earth turns that supper into a seating plan, and the table Luke leaves the betrayer seated at is closed to the great crowd.

The Society’s report for twenty twenty-four counts twenty-one million one hundred thousand at the Memorial and twenty-three thousand two hundred who ate[4], fewer than one in nine hundred. An organization that keeps neither Christmas nor Easter gathers its largest crowd of the year for this one meal. A meal at which Luke leaves the traitor seated is now laid each spring before twenty-one million people, and the plate goes on past almost all of them.

Declaration: The plate stops at my place now, and nothing on it goes back to the front.

The Rite

Today, set out unleavened bread or any flatbread and red wine (or whatever you drink). Take the first piece and the first cup yourself before you offer any to anyone, alone or with anyone you choose, and finish both.

Testament · Which pleasures were you raised to watch others enjoy, and which will you take first?

Sources

[1] Rev 14:1–3

[2] Matt 26:27

[3] Luke 22:20–21

[4] 2024 Service Year Report of Jehovah’s Witnesses, Grand Totals (jw.org)


The Flag

Counter-rite · kept by Witnesses

4 July

Use the freedom the Witnesses won to do what they refuse.

The Testing of Abraham’s FaithGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Lillian and William Gobitas, aged twelve and ten, were expelled from school in Minersville, Pennsylvania, in nineteen thirty-five for refusing to salute the flag, which the Watch Tower Society had taught them was worship of an image. In nineteen forty the Supreme Court ruled eight to one that the school district was within its rights[1], and mob attacks on Witnesses followed that summer, with a Kingdom Hall burned in Maine and members driven out of towns. Three years later the Court reversed itself in a case brought by Witness families in West Virginia, deciding on the fourteenth of June, nineteen forty-three, which is Flag Day, that no official may compel a citizen to salute or to profess any orthodoxy[2].

The Witness families who brought the second case won freedom of conscience for every American who came after them, believer or unbeliever. The Society had already made the refusal a rule for every member before either case was decided, and kept it after the courts made the salute optional for everyone. A Witness is expected never to salute a flag, sing an anthem or join a political party, and the right the families won in court is spent at home on a uniformity of its own.

The West Virginia children won the right to keep their hands at their sides, and that same right lets you stand and cheer. Witnesses cite the three young men in Babylon who refused to bow to a gold image[3]. The story records a refusal to bow to an image. It says nothing of a cookout. What the Society asks of its members on the Fourth is no part in the holiday, and the principle its own families won covers the ex-Witness eating under the fireworks exactly as it covers the Witness who stays home.

Declaration: A conscience that waits for a governing body to rule on fireworks belongs to the governing body.

The Rite

Cook a holiday meal today, burgers or corn or whatever your country eats on its national day, and eat it outdoors where the neighbors can see you. Before the first bite say aloud I keep this feast because I choose to.

Testament · What would you celebrate today if nobody were watching to report it, and with whom?

Sources

[1] Minersville v. Gobitis, 310 U.S. 586 (1940)

[2] West Virginia v. Barnette, 319 U.S. 624, 642 (1943)

[3] Dan 3:12–18


The Book of Life

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

1 Tishri

Write a book of life you can keep.

The Last JudgmentGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The Talmud says that three books lie open in heaven at the new year. The wholly righteous are written at once for life and the wholly wicked at once for death, and everyone in between hangs for ten days until Yom Kippur seals the verdict[1]. A prayer of the day’s Mussaf service says, like a shepherd pasturing his flock, making sheep pass under his staff, so shall You cause to pass, count, calculate, and consider the soul of all the living; and You shall apportion the destinies of all Your creatures and inscribe their verdict. It goes on to say who will live and who will die, who by water and who by fire, who by sword and who by beast, who by famine and who by thirst[2].

Another page of the same Talmud tells of a father who sent his son up to the top of a building for fledglings. The boy climbed, sent the mother bird away and took the young, keeping in one errand two commandments the Torah rewards with long life, honoring a father and letting the mother bird go. On his way down he fell and died[3]. Rabbi Yaakov concluded that a reward the Torah states is paid only after the resurrection, and the page adds that, by one account, a case like it is what turned the heretic the rabbis called the Other[4] from the faith.

The passage ends with a line the whole congregation says aloud in unison, But Repentance, Prayer, and Charity mitigate the severity of the Decree[5].

Declaration: I seal my verdicts the day I write them and keep no one hanging for ten days.

The Rite

Write your own book of life, the names that earned a place at your table and those that took and gave nothing back. Send a jar of honey to the best of the first, and strike the second from every list.

Testament · Whom will you strike from your book, and whom will you feed?

Atonement

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

10 Tishri

Keep your confessions for people who can be hurt.

Ezra Kneels in PrayerGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Yom Kippur opens at evening with Kol Nidre, sung three times, which annuls a person’s vows to the god[1], and by the rabbis’ own rulings it releases no oath sworn to another person. Twenty-five hours of fasting follow in the five afflictions the Mishnah lists, without food or water, washing, anointing, leather shoes or sex[2]. At every service the congregation recites an alphabet of sins, worded in the plural and beaten out with a fist on the chest, and the list takes in sins committed under compulsion and in ignorance[3].

The Mishnah, the day’s own law in tractate Yoma, divides the account. For what a person has done against the god the day atones, and for what one person has done against another it atones for nothing until the injured one has been appeased[4]. Rabbi Eleazar ben Azariah drew the rule from the end of a verse in Leviticus, from all your sins before the Lord you shall be clean[5].

In the same chapter the Mishnah says death and Yom Kippur atone together with repentance[6], and that for the one who says, I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone, Yom Kippur does not atone. Rabbi Akiva ends the chapter of the Mishnah with the words, how fortunate are you, Israel[7]. He asks before whom you are purified and who purifies you, and answers, your Father in Heaven, as it is stated, And I will sprinkle purifying water upon you, and you shall be purified. And it says, The ritual bath of Israel is God.

Declaration: Every wrong I answer for has a name and a face, and I answer for it to that face.

The Rite

While the fast is kept, put on leather shoes and eat a full meal. Before the first bite, open the fist the confession beats on the chest, lay the hand flat on the table, and say I keep this hand for the living.

Testament · Which sin you were taught to confess has never had a victim you could name?

Booths

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

15 Tishri

Answer to your own roof, never to the sky.

Hagar and Ishmael in the WildernessGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Leviticus orders seven days in a hut of branches, so that every generation should know the god made their ancestors dwell in booths when he brought them out of Egypt[1]. Deuteronomy adds an order to rejoice at the feast, the whole household together with the stranger and the widow within your gates[2]. When Ezra read the law to the exiles back in Jerusalem, they cut olive and myrtle and palm in the hills and built the booths on their own roofs and in their courtyards[3], a hut of leaves on top of every house.

The Mishnah settles what happens when the god sends rain. Once it falls hard enough to spoil the porridge, the family is allowed indoors, and the sages give the reason in a parable. A servant comes to pour his master a cup, and the master throws the pitcher in his face[4]. Rain on the feast, in the sages’ own reading, is the god refusing the service, and the household that carries its bowls inside is staff sent from the room. The Talmud goes further and frees anyone who suffers in the booth[5] from sitting in it at all.

So the sages who enforce the booth also rank the family’s comfort above it, and grant the release in the voice of a dismissed servant. A household that reads its weather as a master’s temper has agreed to be staff before the first drop falls. The roof over you was raised by builders and is kept by wages, and it answers to whoever keeps it. Its comfort is yours to take without leave, and the thanks for a dry night go to the roofer and the heating bill.

Declaration: When the god threw the pitcher, his own sages went indoors, and I have stayed in ever since.

The Rite

Cook the best hot dinner you can and eat it indoors with the heat up and the windows shut against the weather. Before the first bite say aloud My roof, my comfort, and the rain can stay outside.

Testament · What pleasure do you still take as though someone could revoke it?

Sources

[1] Lev 23:42–43

[2] Deut 16:14–15

[3] Neh 8:16

[4] m. Sukkah 2:9

[5] b. Sukkah 26a


The Last Chapter

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

23 Tishri

Close the finished book and leave it closed.

Beneath a Sky So Beautiful (Canto XXIX)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, Cassell edition, 1868

The last eight verses of the Torah[1] report the death of the man held to have written the rest, and the Talmud could not settle who wrote them. One rabbi gives them to Joshua. Another has the god dictate them and Moses take them down in tears[2], writing out his own death on a mountain in Moab with the promised land laid out below him, the country he had walked a people forty years toward and would never enter[3]. He is buried in a valley, and nobody knows the grave[4].

On the festival of rejoicing in the law the synagogue reads those verses aloud and goes straight on, in the same hour, to the first chapter of Genesis. The scrolls are danced round the room in seven circuits, and the member called up for the last verses and the one called up for the first are both named bridegrooms. A fourteenth-century code of Jewish law gives the reason for the haste. The beginning is read at once so that Satan has no opening to accuse Israel[5] of finishing the Torah and wanting no more of it.

The one charge the code expects the accuser to bring on that day is that a reader closed the book satisfied, and the tradition answers it by never letting the book close. Moses gets his eight verses and a lost grave, and the congregation is reading about the light of the first day before his tears are dry on the page. The accusation belongs to anyone who has finished something, the degree handed in, the house paid off. A finished thing is entitled to stay finished, and the man who wept over his last page was owed a scroll rolled shut and left on the shelf.

Declaration: Satan accuses me of wanting no more, and I sign the charge sheet.

The Rite

Carry the finished thing itself, the signed papers or the keys, seven times round your table as the scrolls go round the synagogue. Set it down in the middle and say Done, and it stays done. Leave it there overnight.

Testament · What have you finished that someone keeps pressing you to begin again?

Sources

[1] b. Bava Batra 15a

[2] b. Bava Batra 15a

[3] Deut 34:1–4

[4] Deut 34:6

The Lights

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

25 Kislev

Take the credit for what you won.

After That I Saw a Multitude in Fury Burning (Canto XV)Gustave Doré · The Divine Comedy: Purgatorio, Cassell edition, 1868

Neither book of Maccabees mentions the oil. The first says that Judas and his brothers cleansed the temple they had taken back from the Greek king, rededicated it on the twenty-fifth of the month of Kislev and decreed eight days of celebration every year[1]. The second adds that they kept the eight days in the manner of Sukkot, which the war had kept them from celebrating in its season[2]. The jar of oil that was enough for one day and burned for eight is told in the Talmud[3], and it moves the reason for the eight days from a family of soldiers, who beat the general Nicanor in the field, to the god and a lamp.

Within three generations the rebels’ descendants ruled as high priests and then as kings with Greek names, and one of them, Alexander Jannaeus, struck coins in Greek. The Talmud remembers him as King Yannai, under whom the sages of Israel were killed[4], and Josephus says he crucified about eight hundred Jewish captives[5] in Jerusalem while he feasted with his concubines in sight of the city. The sages’ heirs left both books of the family’s victory out of the Hebrew Bible, and the prayer added for the eight days names Mattathias and his sons[6] and gives the battle to the god, who delivered the many into the hands of the few.

The passage recited over the lights calls them holy and forbids any use of them[7], so no one may read or count money by their glow. The law that handed the battle to the god handed him the flame as well, and left the family that lit it only the looking. The household bought the oil and struck the match, and a flame it may not use has been confiscated by the rabbis who made the rule.

Declaration: I read by my own candles, and the Talmud can bring its own oil.

The Rite

Set nine candles or lamps in a row, eight and a helper, and light them together. Count your money by their light, every note and coin, the use the law forbids, and spend some on yourself before you put them out.

Testament · What have you made with your own hands that you were taught to call a gift?

Lots

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

14 Adar

Plan your own rescue.

Solomon Receives the Queen of ShebaGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The book of Esther names no god from its first verse to its last. In the Hebrew a Jewish girl taken into a Persian king’s harem saves her people by going uninvited into the throne room at the risk of her life[1] and by two banquets, and every rescue in it is done by people. The Greek translators added prayers for Esther and Mordecai to speak[2]. The rabbis kept the Hebrew and made the feast that reads it the merriest of the year, with costumes and gifts of food.

One sage taught that a person must drink on Purim until he can no longer tell the words cursed is Haman[3] from the words blessed is Mordecai, and on the same page the tractate tells what happened when two rabbis kept the rule. Rabba and Rabbi Zeira held their Purim feast together and got drunk, and Rabba rose and slaughtered his friend. In the morning he prayed, and Zeira was restored to life. The next year Rabba invited him again, and Zeira declined, saying that a miracle does not happen every time[4].

A medieval authority, Rabbenu Ephraim, read the slaughter as the Talmud canceling its own rule. Zeira had learned his answer the hard way, and the book read at the feast agrees with him, since it has no god in it to repair what a feast breaks. Esther went in to the king having counted the cost, if I perish, I perish[5], and the night of her feast belongs to people who count it the same way, who drink as hard as they like among friends they would trust with a knife and settle the road home before the first glass.

Declaration: I seat my rescuers at the head of the table, and providence can eat in the kitchen.

The Rite

Read the book of Esther aloud today from a Jewish or Protestant Bible and mark every mention of the god. Then lift a glass (wine, or whatever you drink) to the number of marks, which is none, and one to someone who once got you home.

Testament · Who in your life has done the saving that your old prayers credited to God?

The Passover

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

15 Nisan

Keep the freedom, and leave the dead at the god’s door.

The Firstborn of the Egyptians Are SlainGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The youngest at the seder asks why this night is different from all other nights. Exodus gave the answer before the first seder was laid. Before the eighth plague the god tells Moses that he has hardened Pharaoh’s heart so that he may show his signs, and so that Moses may tell in the ears of his son and of his son’s son[1] what the god wrought in Egypt. The god gives the reason himself, that there would be something to tell. The telling is this night.

The last sign came at midnight. The god killed every firstborn in Egypt, from the son of Pharaoh on his throne to the son of the captive in the dungeon[2], who had refused no one anything, and the firstborn of the cattle with them, until there was not a house without its dead[3]. The Passover book will not let the blame drift to a servant. Glossing the verse, it says I and not an angel, I and not a seraph, I and not the messenger[4]. The one who hardened the king did the killing for the hardness.

When the plagues are named at the seder, everyone takes a drop of wine from the cup with a finger[5], one for each, and the reason usually given is that a cup of rejoicing should be less full while others suffer. Exodus gives the god a purpose for the dead and no grief over them, and when the Talmud gave him some[6], at the sea, it was the rabbis who wrote the line. The people he staged the story for supply the grief themselves, out of their own cups, and in that one gesture the table shows more mercy than the god it thanks.

Declaration: I spill my drops for the sons of Egypt and pour none for the hand that killed them.

The Rite

While leaven is forbidden, eat a cheeseburger on a leavened bun with wine (or whatever you drink). Before the first bite, tip ten drops from your cup onto the plate with one finger, one for each plague, and say These are for the sons of Egypt.

Testament · Where has your own pity outrun the scripture you were raised on?

Sources

[1] Exod 10:1–2

[2] Exod 12:29

[3] Exod 12:30

[4] Passover Haggadah, on Exod 12:12

The Mountain

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

6 Sivan

Sort what you chose from what you signed under threat.

The Giving of the Law on Mount SinaiGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Israel stood at the foot of the mountain[1], Exodus says, and one sage of the Talmud read the Hebrew as under the mountain. The god, he taught, lifted Sinai over the people like an upturned tub and told them that if they accepted the Torah it would be well, and if not, there would be their grave[2]. A second sage said that a covenant accepted under a mountain held over your head gives the people a strong protest against the whole law, since they were forced[3]. The Talmud has Rava answer him with Purim. In the days of the Persian king in Esther, it says, the Jews took the Torah on themselves again of their own free will and confirmed what they had already accepted[4].

Shavuot celebrates the giving. The custom of staying awake all night over the texts is explained by a midrash in which the people overslept on the morning of Sinai and had to be woken to receive the law[5], so that their descendants keep watch to make amends. The book of Ruth is read, the story of a woman who chose her people. The Talmud recorded the protest and the calendar kept the feast.

An obligation accepted with a mountain over your head can be protested at any time, by the law’s own reasoning, and Rava needed a second, free acceptance before he would call the bond sound. Much of what a religion lays on a child is laid there with hell or family held overhead, before the child is old enough to refuse it. Whatever you would still choose with the threat removed is yours, and what you would not choose has only the mountain to stand on.

Declaration: A mountain held over my head voided that contract, and a rabbi of the Talmud called it a great protest.

The Rite

Turn a large bowl upside down over your own printed Torah, or any book you were made to accept as a child. Lift it away, open the book, and copy out one passage you would still choose with no bowl over it, saying This much I take freely.

Testament · What would you still keep of your upbringing if nobody could punish you for dropping it?

Sources

[2] b. Shabbat 88a

[3] b. Shabbat 88a

[4] b. Shabbat 88a; Esth 9:27

[5] Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:12:2


Appointed Weeping

Counter-rite · kept by Jews

9 Av

Spend no hour of grief on a god’s schedule.

People Mourn over the Destruction of JerusalemGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

The ninth of Av begins over a boiled egg and bread dipped in ashes and runs about twenty-five hours without food. The mourners wear shoes with no leather in them, chant Lamentations sitting on the floor, and exchange no greetings. The Mishnah fixes five calamities to the date, the sentence on the wilderness generation that it would never enter the land, the fall of the first temple and of the second, the capture of Betar, the last fortress of the Bar Kokhba revolt, and the plowing of Jerusalem[1]. The same Mishnah gives five more to the seventeenth of Tammuz, the tablets broken, the daily offering nullified, the city breached, a Torah scroll burned, and an idol placed in the Sanctuary, and it adds that from when Av begins one decreases rejoicing.

The first of the five began with a reconnaissance. Twelve men were sent to look at Canaan[2], ten of them came back with a report of walled cities and giants[3] while Caleb and Joshua dissented[4], and the congregation wept that night[5]. That night, Rabba says in the Talmud citing Rabbi Yochanan, was the ninth of Av, and the god told them they had wept for nothing and that he would fix a weeping for their generations[6]. The same page supplies the rule, in the vocabulary of a court, that guilt is rolled onto a day already found guilty[7]. The Rhineland massacres of 1096 fell in other months, and the elegy for them by Kalonymus ben Yehuda says that no fast day is to be added beyond Tisha B’Av, so they are mourned on it.

Declaration: I will mourn when my own die, and I keep no fast set by anyone else’s forebears.

The Rite

Sit in a chair this morning and greet by name every person you meet, two things this day forbids. Before the first greeting say aloud This grief was decreed, and I decline it.

Testament · How will you spend the hours of a mourning that was never yours?

Sources

[1] m. Taanit 4:6

[2] Num 13:1–2

[3] Num 13:28–33

[4] Num 13:30; 14:6–9

[5] Num 14:1

[6] b. Taanit 29a

Departure

Counter-rite · kept by Muslims

1 Muharram

Honor your flight as the first emigrants honored theirs.

Adam and Eve Are Driven out of EdenGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

Umar, the second caliph, wanted dates on his letters, and the companions numbered the years from the Prophet’s arrival in Medina[1], passing over the day he was called as an apostle and the day he died. They opened the year with Muharram, the month the Arabs already counted first, so the first of Muharram of year one fell some two months before the migration itself, and the whole calendar since has been counted from the year a man left home.

The leaving was a flight. The ruling tribe of Mecca had boycotted the Prophet’s clan, his uncle and protector was dead, and his followers had already slipped away north in small groups. He left Mecca secretly, hid three nights in a cave outside the city with Abu Bakr while the searchers passed[2], and arrived in a town that had pledged to receive him. The Quran ranks the first emigrants among the foremost of the faithful[3], and its fourth sura has the angels question the souls of those who stayed where they were oppressed, asking whether the god’s earth had not been wide enough for them to emigrate[4], and assigns them Hell.

The classical jurists made that verse a law, that a believer who cannot live by his religion where he is must leave. Whoever walked out of a faith because they could not live by their own convictions inside it has kept the rule, against the faith that laid it down. When the old community calls the leaving desertion, it condemns in the apostate the very departure its own law demands of the believer. The first emigrants came back eight years later as masters of the city that had starved their clan.

Declaration: My people call my leaving desertion, and their own angels would ask why I took so long.

The Rite

Work out how long it has been since you left, and write today’s date in your own era, year first, at the top of a letter to someone who stood by you when you went. Sign it and send it.

Testament · What did the first year of your own era give you that the old calendar forbade?

Sources

[1] Sahih al-Bukhari 3934

[2] Sahih al-Bukhari 3905

[3] Quran 9:100

[4] Quran 4:97


The Tenth

Counter-rite · kept by Muslims

10 Muharram

Lay your grievance where the evidence lies.

The Children of Bethlehem Are MassacredGustave Doré · La Grande Bible de Tours, 1866

On reaching Medina the Prophet found the Jews fasting on the tenth of Muharram, and they told him it was a great day, the day the god delivered Moses and his people and drowned Pharaoh and his people[1]. He fasted it himself and ordered it fasted[2]. The day entered Islam as thanks for a rescue at the edge of the water.

In the year sixty-one of the new calendar, on the same tenth, the Prophet’s grandson Husayn was surrounded on the plain of Karbala by the caliph Yazid’s army, cut off from the Euphrates for days[3], and killed with most of the men of his household, and his head was carried to Damascus. The god who opened a sea for Moses, made the fire cool for Abraham[4] and threw Jonah up onto the bare shore[5] left the grandson’s camp thirsty within sight of a river. For Shia Muslims the tenth has been a day of mourning ever since.

The visitation prayer recited for Husayn on that day curses by name the caliph Yazid[6], the governor who sent the army, the commander who led it and Shimr, the man said to have struck the last blow. Within six years the governor, the commander and Shimr were dead, hunted down by Mukhtar’s rising in Kufa[7]. Yazid, beyond their reach, died untouched three years after Karbala, and the Umayyad house ruled until 750. Heaven settled with none of them. Yazid’s kind still hold rivers on a smaller scale, the relative who sits on an inheritance out of spite, the landlord who keeps the deposit, and each keeps the river until someone with a name goes and takes it back.

Declaration: Mukhtar’s men collected three of the names the curse left to heaven, and I collect my own debts in person.

The Rite

Write the name of the person who kept from you what you needed, and beneath it in plain words what they did. Read it aloud in full as a curse, fold it into your wallet, and carry it until the debt is paid or you write it off.

Testament · Who held your river while you watched, and what did they take from you?

Sources

[1] Sahih Muslim 1130c

[2] Sahih al-Bukhari 2004

[4] Quran 21:69

[5] Quran 37:145
